Russia stands for early entry into force of CTBT — Lavrov
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:11:22 UTC
00:11:22 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Russia supports an early entry into force of the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty (CTBT), one of the core parts of the global security, Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.
"The Russian Federation has consistently considered the CTBT as one of the key elements of the international security architecture and supports an early entry into force of the CTBT. This requires the consolidation of efforts of all states, a remarkable political will and a willingness to put common interests above market considerations. We are ready to continue actively contributing to the achievement of this goal," Lavrov said in a congratulatory telegram to Robert Floyd, executive secretary of the Preparatory Commission for the CTBT, on the occasion of the 30th anniversary of the treaty's opening for signature.
Lavrov said that the treaty became a visible expression of the collective responsibility of states to preserve global stability and security for future generations.
"Its importance cannot be overestimated: the nuclear test ban is not only an arms control measure, but also a powerful political signal about the priority of peaceful development and dialogue in international affairs. The principles laid down in the CTBT remain topical today," the telegram says.
Lavrov also praised the efforts that Floyd and his colleagues are making to universalize the treaty.
"Your work is a daily contribution to maintaining trust between states and creating conditions for preserving the international architecture in the field of arms control and non-proliferation of nuclear weapons, a clear example of how professionalism, dedication and teamwork can ensure the relevance of important agreements even in difficult political conditions," Lavrov said.
About the agreement
To date, the CTBT was signed by 188 states and ratified by 179. For its entry into force, mandatory ratification is required by the 44 states listed in the annex, which are countries with nuclear weapons or potential capabilities to create them (their list is based on IAEA data).
Currently, 35 nuclear-weapon states, including the United Kingdom and France, ratified the document. "The "nuclear club" members - the United States, China, Egypt, Israel and Iran - signed, but not ratified it, while the three "young" nuclear powers - India, North Korea and Pakistan - did not sign it.
Russia signed the treaty in 1996 and ratified it in 2000. However, in 2023, Russia withdrew its ratification, as the document was never ratified by the US Congress. The law on Russia’s withdrawal of ratification was passed by the State Duma on October 18, 2023; the Federation Council approved it on October 25; and on November 2, it was signed by the president.

Luxury firms fined £1.3m after man killed by falling window in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:10:59 UTC
00:10:59 KST

Two companies have been fined a total of £1.3m over health and safety breaches after a coach driver was killed by a falling window pane.
Mick Ferris, 53, was crushed when a window fell 26 storeys from the Corniche, a luxury development in Vauxhall, London, on 2 October 2018.
Property developer St James Group Ltd was fined £1m and specialist facade contractor Lindner Prater was fined £300,000 at a sentencing hearing at Inner London crown court on Thursday. Both firms were also ordered to pay costs of £125,000 each.
In August, the firms were found guilty of ignoring “foreseeable risks” and convicted of “failing to discharge a duty” under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.
Ferris, who was a driver for Clarkes of London, had been returning to his coach when the window pane, which weighed 130kg and was roughly 85cm wide and 190cm tall, fell from around 90 metres (300ft).
During the trial, the court heard that a window panel had previously fallen from the same development in August 2017, but that the design had not subsequently significantly changed.
The Corniche, located on Albert Embankment alongside the Thames, features panoramic views over the Houses of Parliament. Luxury flats in the building – containing a gym, pool and spa – have been listed for sale at £3m.
Ferris’s widow, Rachel, said his death “could have happened to anybody” and “could have been prevented”.
In a statement read out in court, she said: “If somebody had done something differently – anything – it would have changed our lives. One person could have asked: ‘Can’t we do this better?’ What those companies did killed my husband.
“Mick was just minding his own business. One minute there, one minute gone. The thought this could have happened to anybody is always with me. It could have been a child.”
The trial heard the design of the window in the Corniche was not safe because it opened outwards and was held in place by a single metal restrictor, so could be prised off by the wind.
Mr Justice Boyle said he was not sentencing the firms on the basis of the design itself being unsafe as they were “common within the industry” and there was no Health and Safety Executive (HSE) guidance prohibiting their use.
The judge said St James should have been more robust in “ensuring the critical safety component was present and engaged”.
Speaking outside court, HSE principal inspector James Goldfinch said Ferris “lost his life due to the failings of two leading companies in their field. The fact lessons had not been learnt from a near-miss the year before makes what happened on that day all the more galling.
“For a window to fall once was quite extraordinary; for it to fall again was simply criminal.
A spokesperson for St James said: “The death of Mick Ferris in 2018 was tragic. Our thoughts remain with his family and friends. We acknowledge the court’s sentencing decision and the fine imposed.”

Breadcrumb
UN rights chief says civilians are bearing the brunt of fighting in Yemen
Civilians are being hardest hit by surging violence in Yemen between Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and Iran-backed Houthis, the UN human rights chief said on Thursday.
The latest fighting marks a sharp escalation in Yemen's civil war, which had largely been frozen since a 2022 truce.
Violence has flared along old front lines in recent weeks, including around Taiz as the Houthis swept south along the Red Sea coast, prompting a humanitarian crisis with over 130,000 people displaced and some fleeing to Africa across the Red Sea.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said his office has documented the killing of 32 civilians, including 15 children and 3 women, since August in fighting, including drone and missile strikes.
"Civilians are now bearing the brunt of this latest upsurge in fighting," Turk said in a statement, without giving a breakdown of who was responsible for the casualties.
A total of 125 people were documented by his office as killed or wounded in the latest flareup in the conflict. Both sides allege that hundreds have been killed in fighting over the past weeks, without providing details.
The statement said the UN human rights office had documented three attacks by Ansar Allah, the formal name for the Houthi movement, on sites for internally displaced people since August.
It was not immediately clear if the UN toll included any deaths or injuries from those incidents.
Houthi spokesperson Mohammed Abdulsalam said the UN human rights office was no longer impartial, accusing it of ignoring what he described as Saudi bombardment in Yemen that had targeted public facilities.
He cited what he said was the targeting of inmates at a correctional facility in al-Hazm in al-Jawf province, as well as homes and schools in several areas. He said the UN allegations were false and unsupported by evidence.
More than 70 UN staff are being detained by Houthis in Yemen, some of whom have been held for many years. Turk called for their release and urged all the warring parties to protect civilians.
Saudi officials have repeatedly said the country's forces do not target civilians in Yemen. Saudi Arabia's diplomatic mission to the UN in Geneva did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ministry of Defence spending with Scottish industry rose by 13 per cent in real terms to £2.53 billion in 2025/26, which the department describes as the highest level of industry investment in Scotland since records began, the Ministry of Defence stated.
The figure equates to £460 for every person living in Scotland, up from £390 the previous year, and the department says it forms part of its work to rebuild the national defence industrial base, boost readiness and support the reindustrialisation of Britain.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “We cannot strengthen our deterrence without a strong, sovereign defence industry here at home, and Scotland is at the heart of that.
“That’s why we are unashamedly backing British, using the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the Cold War to back jobs and skills in Scotland to build the capability and technology we need to keep us safe in a more dangerous world.”
Douglas Alexander, the Scottish Secretary, said: “The UK Government is delivering a defence dividend for Scotland. Scotland’s defence sector is a powerhouse of innovation and expertise and a key driver for economic growth. With Ministry of Defence annual investment in Scottish industry increasing to £2.53 billion we are backing businesses to grow, supporting the creation of good jobs, driving reindustrialisation and building a stronger economy that creates opportunity.
“From naval shipbuilding on the Clyde and at Rosyth, to our nuclear deterrent and submarine support at Faslane, to our world-leading strengths in cyber, space, advanced radar and electronic warfare, Ministry of Defence investment is directly supporting 12,200 jobs in Scotland and opening exciting career pathways for young Scots.”
According to the department, the figures show rising investment generating jobs and opportunities in towns and cities across the United Kingdom, lifting living standards and increasing household incomes, with the defence industrial base placed at the centre of what it calls national renewal.
The department maintains a substantial footprint in Scotland, supporting 12,200 jobs, with major employers including BAE Systems, Babcock International and Rolls-Royce alongside the military hubs at HM Naval Base Clyde and RAF Lossiemouth.
Much of the Scottish work sits in shipbuilding and submarines, with BAE Systems building the Type 26 frigates at Govan and Scotstoun on the Clyde and Babcock assembling the Type 31 at Rosyth, where four of the five ships are now taking shape. The Norwegian order for Type 26 frigates announced last year is expected to sustain work on the Clyde into the late 2030s.
HM Naval Base Clyde directly employs around 6,000 people across Faslane and Coulport and is home to the Submarine Service, with Project Royal Oak committing £15.1 billion to regenerating the base over the next decade as part of a wider £26 billion programme covering naval base infrastructure.

Israel uproots 400 olive trees in occupied West Bank as harvest season approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:10:03 UTC
00:10:03 KST

Qais Abu Samra, Ikram Kouachi
24 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
The Israeli army uprooted 400 olive trees and bulldozed 31 dunams (3.1 hectares, 7.6 acres) of Palestinian-owned land Thursday in Beit Rima in northwestern Ramallah in the occupied West Bank as harvest season approaches.
Sources told Anadolu that bulldozers cleared the land and uprooted the trees, two days after Israeli authorities issued a military order targeting two areas of land in the town.
They added that the military order demanded “removing wild vegetation and uprooting olive and other trees from the targeted areas.”
The Palestinian Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission said Tuesday that Israeli authorities issued five military orders targeting the uprooting of trees and removal of wild vegetation from 533.5 dunams of Palestinian land in the Jenin, and Ramallah and Al-Bireh governorates in the northern and central West Bank.
Since the beginning of 2026 through Sept. 22, Israel has issued 51 orders to remove trees and vegetation in the occupied West Bank, targeting 2,093 dunams of land, according to data from the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission.
The uprooting operation comes as the olive harvest season approaches. Olive trees are a major source of income for thousands of Palestinian families. Bulldozing and uprooting operations cause losses to farmers and threaten their ability to access and cultivate their land.
Afrah Qadura, 65, from Beit Rima, told Anadolu that residents learned of the military order two days ago and saw a map at the municipality building showing the areas targeted for the removal of olive trees.
He said landowners were given 12 hours to remove trees before the Israeli army would implement the order. “How can we remove trees planted by our fathers and uproot them with our own hands?” he asked rhetorically.
Qadura said the olive trees had been planted over decades, beginning in the late 1960s and continuing through the 1970s and 1980s, as well as trees planted in the 1990s.
He said some of the trees uprooted Thursday had become highly productive for years, adding that olive trees are a primary source of livelihood for residents.
Palestinians in the occupied West Bank are preparing for the olive harvest season, which usually begins in October.
Thousands of Palestinians rely on olive trees and their crops as a source of income, alongside their connection to the land and agricultural heritage passed down through generations.
“We are proud of those trees like our children,” said Qadura, noting the years he and his father spent cultivating the land, caring for the trees and watering them.
He added that he used to bring water from a well to water the saplings and follow their growth during the years. “My father worked hard planting the trees, and we also worked hard caring for them.”
He said his family continued to tend, clean and care for the trees until they became part of their lives. Losing them in this way was, for him, like losing one of his children.
Qadura said uprooting the trees would not force his family to abandon their land, stressing that he and his family intend to replant the trees uprooted by the Israeli army.
“We will continue planting trees like my father did, and our children will continue after us,” he said, citing his family’s connection to the land and its cultivation across generations.
Abdul Rahman al-Rimawi, mayor of Bani Zeid al-Gharbia, which includes Beit Rima and other towns, told Anadolu that everybody was surprised Thursday when Israeli army bulldozers began uprooting mature olive trees in the town in an area of 31 dunams.
Rimawi said the trees “are hundreds of years old,” and that uprooting them not only destroys the trees, but also affects the livelihoods of Palestinian families that depend on them.
He said the operation comes as the olive harvest season approaches, describing it as part of “arbitrary Israeli practices against people, trees and stones.”
Rimawi said the residents of Beit Rima “are not isolated from this people” and what Palestinians are subjected to in terms of harassment, killings, displacement and the uprooting of olive trees.
 
He implored international institutions and relevant parties to work to halt the decision to uproot the trees, noting that there is ongoing communication with the Colonization and Wall Resistance Commission to that end.
Rimawi said Israeli authorities had not, according to him, explained the grounds for implementing the decision, and that what is happening represents “Israeli practices against all members of the Palestinian people” in the occupied West Bank.

What the World Owes the Marshall Islands
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:09:08 UTC
00:09:08 KST

This week, the U.N. General Assembly affirmed that statehood endures the loss of land. My country, the Republic of the Marshall Islands, will persist despite rising seas. The question is how Marshallese people go on living here safely.
Our nation consists of narrow strips of land on 29 low-lying coral atolls scattered across more than 750,000 square miles of the central Pacific Ocean.
For many, adapting to rising seas may mean moving communities to higher ground. In the Marshalls, we have no higher ground to move to. That fundamental difference shapes what climate adaptation means for us and how we must act.
As we prepare for another El Niño, our people know its rhythms well, but the severity with which these forces now arrive is worsening.
First, the rains come heavily. Then they stop. Water tanks empty, wells run dry, crops fail, and ocean conditions shift. We begin shipping water to communities with none.
These changes are the reality behind the historic diplomatic achievement taking place this week. The U.N. General Assembly will very likely adopt the first Sea-Level Rise Declaration by consensus. In a year of fractured diplomacy, that is worth celebrating.
The Republic of the Marshall Islands has never wavered in its position. Sea level rise will not alter the statehood, sovereignty, or maritime zones of any state. But while the legal status, rights, and maritime zones of my country and its people are now secure, our physical safety is not.
That distinction must guide what comes next. The world must respond to the impact of sea level rise on coastal communities, heritage, and cultures, and the lands that have nourished our ancestors for generations. We must start by preventing as much sea level rise as we can.
Island nations have long fought for climate action. The Alliance of Small Island States, the High Ambition Coalition (which the Marshall Islands convenes), and other progressive forces fought hard for the 1.5°C temperature limit within the Paris Agreement.
And last year, inspired by a campaign led by Pacific youth, the International Court of Justice affirmed in its advisory opinion on climate change that every country's emissions reductions must align with 1.5°C. The Court also affirmed that the continued licensing, subsidy, production, and consumption of fossil fuels may constitute internationally wrongful acts.
Yet earlier this month, the United Nations Environment Programme released a report indicating that an overshoot of 1.5°C is now almost certain. Crossing the threshold cannot be an excuse to abandon the target. Every fraction of a degree means greater risks, higher seas, and more lives and livelihoods lost. Our responsibility is to make that overshoot as small and short-lived as possible.
In the Pacific, we know that fossil fuel dependency hurts not only the planet but also our health, security, and economies. That is why, earlier this month, Pacific leaders set out our vision for a fossil fuel-free Pacific.
If the world does not follow science, international law, or the Pacific by phasing out fossil fuels as swiftly as possible, the harm to the roughly one billion people who live on the world’s coasts will be devastating. What’s more, the costs of adaptation will rise exponentially. For the Marshallese people, the desire to stay in the land of our ancestors is deeply felt. We demand action from major emitters as we also adapt to rising seas.
Adaptation is a huge technical challenge. We are mapping our atolls from the air, meter by meter, because available satellite elevation data has a margin of error nearly three times the height of most of our nation. We cannot determine which land to raise or whose drinking water can survive a drought from inaccurate data. Precise information is also essential to develop credible proposals and access climate finance.
We know what practical adaptation looks like. Our National Adaptation Plan is complete; funding it is not. Effective adaptation costs money—$310 billion to $365 billion per year to manage worsening climate impacts—which is why the call in the Declaration on Sea Level Rise to streamline and simplify access to finance matters. Pacific leaders in Palau put it plainly: what this region needs is climate finance, and finance that actually reaches people on the ground. We need states to invest in helping communities adapt, protecting livelihoods, allowing people to remain safely on their lands for as long as possible, and ensuring that those who move can do so with dignity.
The Marshall Islands is proud to lead the champions launching the Rising Nations Institute, which aims to translate the principles we have fought for into practical solutions for communities confronting rising seas.
Despite geopolitical challenges, UNGA’s Sea-Level Rise Declaration shows that the world is committed to climate action and to the protection of countries threatened by sea level rise. We now have legal frameworks capable of enduring physical change and inspiring action. The next challenge is to ensure that our systems of finance, planning, and adaptation can do the same.
We cannot completely hold back the rising seas. But we can do a lot more to limit that rise and to choose how we meet it.

Dangerous surf, heavy rains hit Mexico as Hurricane Polo tracks offshore
Sept 24 - Heavy surf and rain lashed southwestern Mexico as "extremely powerful" Hurricane Polo crawls northwest offshore the mainland, the US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said in a bulletin on Thursday.
With maximum sustained winds near 160 miles per hour (260 kph), Polo is a Category 5 storm, the highest level on the Saffir-Simpson scale. It could see some near-term strengthening and is expected to remain a major hurricane for the next few days, said the NHC.
The NHC said that Polo's outer rainbands are spreading onshore and producing heavy rains. Tropical-storm-force winds are likely occurring along the coast of southwestern Mexico, it said.
Polo's hurricane-force winds extend outward up to 40 miles (65 km) from the center and tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 125 miles (205 km).
Rainfall totals of 4 inches to 6 inches (102 mm to 152 mm), with isolated maximum totals up to 8 inches, are expected across coastal areas of Mexico's Guerrero state on the Pacific coast through Thursday, possibly triggering life-threatening flooding and mudslides.
Coastal areas of the Mexican states of Michoacan, Colima and Jalisco are also forecast to experience heavy rains, while swells generated by Polo will affect portions of the coast of southwestern Mexico during the next couple of days.
"These swells are likely to cause life-threatening surf, rip currents, and coastal flooding," said the NHC.
Polo is expected to remain offshore of southwestern Mexico on Thursday before moving further out to sea and is expected to approach the Baja California Peninsula early next week as a hurricane. REUTERS

Ukraine’s Draft 2027 State Budget Envisages UAH 1.67 Trillion Deficit, KSE Institute Says

The Draft State Budget 2027 envisages a UAH 1.67 trillion deficit, while Ministry of Defence spending is set to rise to UAH 3.76 trillion – KSE Institute analysis
Ukraine’s Draft State Budget for 2027 is based on the assumption that the full-scale war will continue throughout next year. The Government expects real GDP growth of 1.3%, average inflation of 8.6%, and an average exchange rate of UAH 47.1 per US dollar. The framework depends heavily on the timely receipt of $91.6 billion in external financing. The Government also acknowledges that the forecast approved in early June does not yet fully reflect the impact of the destruction caused over the summer and may be revised ahead of the second reading. These findings are presented in KSE Institute’s analytical review, “Draft State Budget 2027: Priorities, Risks, and Opportunities.”
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Defence and security remain the top priority. Spending under the Ministry of Defence’s budget programs is planned at UAH 3.76 trillion — UAH 318.3 billion, or 9.2%, more than under the amended 2026 plan. The increase was made possible primarily by incorporating the second €45 billion tranche of the Ukraine Support Loan (USL) into the budget. At the same time, the allocated funding may prove insufficient if decisions are made to increase military pay, introduce additional financial incentives for military service, or expand procurement of military equipment and weapons.
Kremlin Says Too Early to Discuss Putin’s G20 Trip After Welcoming US Invitation
State budget revenues are expected to rise to UAH 5.65 trillion, including UAH 2.86 trillion in tax revenues and UAH 2.49 trillion in international assistance. UAH 117.3 billion in projected revenues still depends on amendments to tax legislation, while another UAH 64.9 billion is expected from reducing customs duty evasion and will reach the special fund only if customs revenues exceed the target.
The state budget deficit is expected to rise to UAH 1.67 trillion, or 15% of GDP, compared with an estimated UAH 1.25 trillion, or 12.4% of GDP, in 2026. State and state-guaranteed debt could reach 113.9% of GDP by the end of 2027. Of the $38.7 billion in external loans planned to finance the deficit, $32.6 billion currently has no confirmed financing sources or corresponding commitments from partners. A shortfall in the required volume of external financing therefore remains the main risk to fiscal stability.
Local budget resources are expected to increase to UAH 1.06 trillion in 2027, while the share of interbudgetary transfers in local budget revenues is expected to rise by 5.5% to 33%. The Government also proposes reducing the share of personal income tax allocated to local budgets from 64% to 60% and providing a targeted UAH 18.2 billion subvention to cover accumulated tariff differences. Under the adverse scenario, an energy supply deficit of 30–50%, a 20–40% decline in goods exports, and a loss of 350,000–450,000 employed people could reduce real GDP by 4.1–6.8%, while consolidated budget tax revenues could fall UAH 140–230 billion below the baseline forecast.

Canada studied ‘extreme’ US military scenario – Carney

Canada studied ‘extreme’ US military scenario – Carney
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has revealed that his government carefully examined the possibility of US-led military action against his country, despite President Donald Trump having ruled out using force against America’s northern neighbor.
In an interview with the New York Times published on Wednesday, Carney described such a scenario as an “extreme tail risk” – an event considered highly unlikely but serious enough to warrant contingency planning.
“That’s just risk management,” he said, adding that “it would be irresponsible not to [prepare].” Carney declined to discuss what that preparation involved.
Trump has repeatedly floated making Canada the 51st US state but explicitly ruled out using military force to achieve it, stating in January 2025 that he would apply “economic force” instead.
The US president has long accused Ottawa of unfair trade practices, particularly on dairy and automobiles, and has imposed a series of tariffs on Canadian goods since early 2025. Washington escalated the dispute in August 2026 with additional 50% duties on a range of Canadian products.
Carney’s disclosure comes just days after he traveled to the EU to deepen ties with the bloc.
Addressing the European Parliament last week, Carney argued that economic integration was increasingly being “weaponized,” with tariffs used as leverage and supply-chain dependencies exploited as vulnerabilities – remarks widely seen as an implicit reference to Washington’s economic pressure on Ottawa.
Defense was also part of Carney’s talks in Strasbourg, where he and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen discussed expanding Canada-EU military cooperation and joint procurement to strengthen what Carney called their “strategic autonomy.”
That cooperation is already taking shape through the EU’s €150 billion ($170 billion) SAFE defense procurement program, in which Canada has become the first non-European country to participate. The initiative is part of Brussels’ wider militarization under its Readiness 2030 strategy, aimed at countering an alleged threat from Russia – something Moscow has repeatedly denied.
Ottawa is also seeking closer ties with European military structures beyond the EU. Last week, it formally applied to join the UK-led Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), a ten-nation rapid-response military grouping that complements NATO and operates primarily across the Arctic, North Atlantic, and Baltic regions – key parts of the bloc’s northern flank, which stretches toward Russia’s borders.

7 Fall Yard Habits That Help Pollinators Survive Winter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:04:12 UTC
00:04:12 KST

A few years ago, Katie Costanzo and her students went curbside shopping for trash. They collected eight bags of leaves that homeowners around Buffalo had raked up for disposal, then sifted through them to see what—if anything—was hiding inside.
The bags were anything but empty. They contained insects from more than 25 families, representing every stage of life from eggs and larvae to pupae and adults. There were bees, wasps, lacewings, hoverflies, beetles, and more—all tucked into material their human landlords had deemed garbage. The class exercise was later published in American Entomologist.
That’s the problem with what we call “fall cleanup.” Costanzo, an ecologist and entomologist at Canisius University, wishes people would stop viewing leaves, stems, and wood as trash. “This is part of the ecology of our system,” she says. “This could be habitat or resources.” Much of what looks dead, messy, or finished for the season is still serving as food, shelter, or a nursery. And leaves are only the beginning.
Queen bumblebees may be tucked just beneath the soil in your yard. Native bees and ladybugs can shelter inside hollow stems you might otherwise have snipped and stuffed into a yard-waste bag. Beetles, flies, and other insects hide in spent flower heads, while birds return to those same plants for seeds. Once cold weather arrives, a yard might look like it’s closed for the season, but “all this business is happening” through the winter, says Mary Phillips, head of native plant habitat strategy at the National Wildlife Federation.
Pollinators are animals that move pollen from one flower to another, allowing plants to reproduce. In an American yard, that group includes native bees, butterflies, moths, beetles, flies, and some wasps—not only the honeybees most people picture. The same habitat also supports plenty of beneficial creatures that aren’t technically pollinators, including predators and decomposers that help keep an ecosystem functioning.
Kim Eierman, an ecological landscape designer and author of The Pollinator Victory Garden, encourages homeowners to think differently about even the smallest patch of land. “You have an ecosystem,” she says. “It may be a really tiny one. Maybe you’re lucky and have a lot of land—but you have an ecosystem, so we need to start treating our landscapes that way.” That means reconsidering some familiar features, including the closely cropped lawn she calls a “green desert.”
Here are seven fall habits pollinator experts practice in their own yards—and how to make each one manageable.
Choose one corner where cleanup stops
Before you pick up a rake, divide your yard mentally into zones. Continue maintaining the high-traffic areas where kids play, pets run, or people gather, as well as walkways and other spots that need to remain clear. Then identify one quieter space—under a tree, behind shrubs, alongside the house, or at the back of a garden bed—where leaves, stems, and a few branches can remain.
Costanzo does this in her own yard. “You don’t have to manage your entire property the same,” she says. Her family keeps recreational areas usable and designates other spots for pollinator gardens and small piles of natural material. Someone with a suburban lot might preserve only a few sticks and one bed of leaves. That still counts. “Anything—any change—is good change,” she says.
If you’re worried that neighbors will mistake habitat for neglect, put up a sign explaining what you’re doing. “I have a pollinator sign. I have a native-plant sign,” Eierman says. “It’s a clue to neighbors and passersby that we’re gardening a little differently—and we’re gardening with a purpose.”
The same zoning strategy applies to the lawn: “I start to cut back—not cut the lawn back, but cut back on how often I mow,” Phillips says of the turf her family still uses. As growth slows in the fall, she spaces out mowing and leaves the grass a little taller. A patch set aside as habitat is different: Once insects have settled in, leave it undisturbed through the winter rather than mowing it down.
Rake leaves into beds instead of bags
Eierman would like to rebrand “leaf litter” as “nature’s gold.” Fallen leaves insulate bumblebee queens near the soil surface where they hibernate and shelter butterflies, moths, caterpillars, and many other invertebrates. As the leaves break down, they also return nutrients to the soil, suppress weeds, and become free mulch and compost. “Nature knows what it’s doing,” Costanzo says. “We don’t have to clean it up.”
The most practical approach isn’t necessarily to leave every leaf exactly where it lands. The National Wildlife Federation recommends moving leaves off turf, pavement, driveways, and other places where a thick or slippery layer would create problems. Rake them beneath trees or into garden beds, aiming for a layer about 3 to 5 inches deep. If you still have extras, pile them in a little-used corner and let them slowly become leaf mold. Lightly spray newly placed leaves with a hose to keep them from blowing away on a windy day.
If you plan to shred fallen leaves with a lawn mower and leave the pieces on the grass, do it early in the season, before many insects have settled in for winter, Eierman says. “If you leave all those leaves and then start chopping them up, you’re chopping up lots of invertebrates, too,” she says. When you send occupied leaves to the curb, “you’re throwing away a part of your ecosystem,” Costanzo adds.
There are exceptions: Diseased plant material and invasive plants may need to be removed; ask a local extension office how to dispose of them. Leaf litter can harbor ticks, so keep it away from play spaces and heavily used paths, and follow local public-health guidance. In wildfire-prone regions, habitat advice never outranks defensible-space rules. For example, CAL FIRE advises removing leaves and other combustible debris from the first 5 ft. around structures and maintaining additional cleared zones beyond that. Regional rules vary, so check with your local fire authority.
Leave stems and seed heads standing
When an aster, ironweed, Joe-Pye weed, or native grass turns brown, resist the urge to shear it to the ground. Hollow and pithy stems can serve as nesting or overwintering sites; flower heads shelter small beetles, flies, and weevils; and seed heads become winter buffets for birds. Eierman has watched goldfinches descend on the plants in her yard to pry out seeds.
“They look dead to you,” she says. But they haven’t clocked out yet.
The easiest option is to leave most plants standing through the winter. Phillips’s Joe-Pye weed grows so high that they’re “taller than me,” she says. To keep those lanky stalks from toppling, she gathers them with twine, transforming them into an architectural feature rather than a botanical pileup.
You can shorten especially unruly stems, but don’t cut them all the way down: Leave at least a foot standing. Eierman trims only some hollow or pithy stems and varies their heights, creating openings for stem-nesting bees of different sizes. Leave plenty untouched, too. The point is variation—not precision pruning with a ruler.
Diseased plants are the exception. Remove affected material rather than preserving it alongside healthy stems, and use local extension guidance to determine whether it should be trashed, burned where legal, or processed another way. Normal browning at the end of the season isn’t itself a disease.
Uncover a little bare ground
Bee housing doesn’t always resemble a charming wooden hotel. Many native bees nest in the ground, burrowing a few inches into exposed soil and spending much of their lives there. A landscape sealed beneath thick wood-chip mulch offers them fewer entrances.
Look for a quiet spot where you can pull back the mulch and leave a modest patch of soil exposed and undisturbed. It doesn’t need to dominate the garden. Even small openings between plants can help, especially when they aren’t covered with plastic sheeting, landscape fabric, or another barrier. The Xerces Society offers guidance on recognizing and preserving ground-nesting habitat.
If you like mulch because it suppresses weeds and looks polished, keep using it where you need it; just don’t smother every square inch. “Everybody’s situation is different,” Costanzo says. The goal is to create access, not a moonscape.
Save a few logs and branches
A fallen limb doesn’t automatically need to leave the property. Decaying logs, sticks, and small brush piles provide structure and shelter for insects and other wildlife; birds also forage there for food. “Keep some of the sticks, keep some of the larger pieces of wood,” Costanzo says. “It really does provide structure and habitat that’s so important in the winter.”
That doesn’t mean every branch must remain exactly where it lands. “You don’t leave them where they fall necessarily,” Phillips says. She moves dead branches, logs, and brush into a corner of her yard—like behind shrubs, where they’re less conspicuous. “Sometimes a pile like that can be really helpful,” she says.
Start small: Place a log along the back of a garden bed, tuck a few sticks beneath a shrub, or build one restrained brush pile in a low-traffic area. Keep dead wood away from the house, and don’t leave a damaged tree standing if it could fall on a person, building, power line, or neighboring property. The National Wildlife Federation has additional guidance on dead wood and wildlife habitat.
Plant one native species this fall
Fall isn’t only a season for leaving things alone. In many parts of the country, it’s an excellent time to plant: Cooler temperatures can reduce stress on new plants, and nurseries may discount perennials that look tired but have perfectly viable roots. “Here in the Northeast, our optimal times for planting are September, October,” Eierman says. “That’s what I’m doing right now.” The ideal window varies, so check local recommendations and leave enough time for roots to establish before the ground freezes.
Start with one or two species rather than redesigning the entire property by sundown. Choose plants native to your region and suited to the site’s sunlight, soil, and moisture. Costanzo’s family has added everything from oaks, dogwoods, and redbuds to Joe-Pye weed and black-eyed Susans. “We’ve seen such a difference,” she says. “We have so much diversity.” Last year, seven bird species nested on their property.
Some plants pack an especially powerful ecological punch. “The oak tree is the superstar,” Phillips says: Across the U.S., oaks support hundreds of species of butterfly and moth caterpillars. If you don’t have room for a giant tree, native shrubs, grasses, and flowering perennials still count. Enter your ZIP code into the National Wildlife Federation’s Native Plant Finder to see locally useful options. The right list will look very different in Pennsylvania than it does in Arizona or Oregon.
Native plants can be pricey, but fall bargain-hunting may pay off. Phillips looks for end-of-season markdowns at nurseries that carry them. “They may not look good, to be honest,” she says. You might put one in the ground and immediately cut it back—but “then they’ll come back the next year.”
When shopping, ask whether a cultivated variety still produces pollen, nectar, and seed. “You don’t want sterile plants,” Eierman says. “You want plants that actually produce seed.” Some cultivars provide nectar for pollinators but no seeds for birds, making them less useful than they first appear.
Fall is also seed-collecting season. Gather mature seeds from native plants you already grow and spread them elsewhere on your property. Phillips does this with plants she wants to expand into other parts of her yard. Some seeds, including those of many milkweeds native to cold-winter regions, need a period of low temperatures before they germinate. Plant them in fall, Phillips says, and winter will handle the chilling for you.
Stop spraying just in case
Treat the problem, not the calendar. Pesticides and herbicides should answer a specific need—not arrive automatically with the turning leaves.
Broad-spectrum insecticides don’t distinguish between a mosquito and the many insects you want to keep. Costanzo recommends using them “in response to something rather than proactively,” and only when truly necessary. “They kill every insect,” she says. “They’re not specific.”
Herbicides create a different problem: They eliminate clover, violets, dandelions, and other plants that can provide food for insects. “Your lawn doesn’t have to look like a carpet,” Costanzo says. Keep turf where you need it for recreation, but consider allowing more plant diversity elsewhere.
That doesn’t mean never treating a genuine infestation or health threat. Identify the problem first, then use the most targeted approach available rather than spraying preventively across the entire property. Follow the label exactly. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency recommends using pesticides only when necessary and treating only the specific area that needs treatment.
Also reconsider the assumption that every nibble is damage. A chewed leaf can be evidence that a native plant is feeding the ecosystem exactly as intended. When Costanzo notices signs of hungry insects, she reminds herself: “I’m supporting the ecosystem. I’m so glad these insects are finding a resource here.” A few holes usually won’t kill a healthy plant, she adds—and flawless foliage isn’t much use to a caterpillar.
These changes benefit the gardener, too. In an August 2026 National Wildlife Federation survey of more than 1,000 wildlife gardeners, 96% said the practice had improved their mental health, and 93% reported physical-health benefits. Respondents most often described the joy of seeing wildlife, a lift in mood, and the satisfaction of knowing they were making the world a little better. Unlike many long-term environmental problems, the payoff can appear surprisingly quickly. “Within a season, you’re seeing the wildlife come,” Phillips says. “You’re seeing the butterflies. You’re seeing the birds; you’re hearing the birdsong.”
For Eierman, that ability to take action—and see it rewarded—is part of the appeal. “There are very few things we have control over in our lives—particularly the ones that give us a lot of pleasure,” she says. “This is one. The effort that you put into it comes back to you in a big way.”

PARIS — Far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen still wants to take France out of NATO’s integrated command — but won’t do so while Russia's war in Ukraine still rages on.
"As long as there is a war on Europe's doorstep, this is not the time to take action in that regard, but of course my will to do so remains," the National Rally leader told POLITICO on Thursday at the Playbook Paris Live summit.
Le Pen is the front-runner in next spring’s high-stakes presidential election to replace Emmanuel Macron, according to polls.
Advertisement
She and far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon both want Paris to leave the military alliance, raising alarm bells at NATO headquarters about France's future defense policy.
The National Rally has long advocated withdrawing from NATO's integrated command, but Le Pen's comments indicate a slight shift in her position. Back in May, she said France would pull out during her first term, without referring to the war in Ukraine, while the party's president Jordan Bardella wanted to wait for a peace agreement between Kyiv and Moscow.
Le Pen and Bardella are campaigning as a ticket that would see the 31-year-old become prime minister.
Le Pen also said that France should not enter into a war with Russia, a nuclear-armed power, and rejected the notion that it is currently in a conflict with Moscow despite the Kremlin's hybrid attacks against European nations.
By publishing a statement condemning Russia last week, Le Pen and Bardella sought to fend off attacks from center-right and center-left opponents who have frequently portrayed the party as an ally to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
However, Le Pen repeated her pledge Thursday to stop financial help to Ukraine if she wins next year's presidential election.
Advertisement
“We can train their soldiers and their military leadership, and provide them with military aid. We can no longer provide financial assistance to Ukraine, and we regret that,” she said.
However, she did not push back against the Coalition of the Willing, a group led by France and the U.K. that aims to provide a military presence in Ukraine once the war ends.
"A potential peacekeeping force that’s actually quite similar to UN peacekeepers seems entirely feasible to me. And if the Coalition of the Willing is one of the conditions for negotiating a ceasefire, then I would obviously be in favor of moving forward with this proposal," she told POLITICO.

European economy lost 113 bln euro this year due to summer heat — research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:01:17 UTC
00:01:17 KST

BERLIN, September 24. /TASS/. The anomalous summer heat in Europe led to a decline in total European production by 113 billion euro this year, with Germany suffering the second-largest damage after Italy, said the international insurance company Allianz, citing the results of its own Climate Risk Tracker study.
According to the company, Germany's losses amounted to 25 billion euro, while Italy lost 28 billion euro. France ranks third, with a projected GDP decline of 20 billion euro. Economic losses in this context refer to production halts and reduced value added. This is driven by falling labor productivity, as well as longer breaks and missed workdays. Therefore, total European losses could amount to nearly 0.5% of the expected economic output for the current year.
The study was based on weather data and damage statistics on one hand, and modeling of expected economic implications on the other. In addition to the heat-induced decline in economic performance, there are also actual losses caused by storms, floods, and other natural phenomena. Allianz estimated these at 50 billion euro for Germany over the last five years. Annual losses turned out to be on average twice as high as during the comparative period from 2000 to 2019. However, on a global scale, damage from natural disasters has increased by 54%, according to Allianz, with Norway leading the list of the most affected countries.
Allianz experts are not overly optimistic about next year either, due to the El Nino weather phenomenon. This cyclical warming of water in the eastern Pacific Ocean, which occurs every few years, can influence weather on land even in very remote regions.

Guidance: Scotland firing times
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
16:00:57 BST
00:00:57 KST

Scotland firing times
Firing times for ranges in Scotland including Barry Buddon, Kirkcudbright, Garelochhead, Tain, Cape Wrath, Fort George, Blackdog, Castlelaw Ranges and Dreghorn
Documents
Details
As seen in the Security Defence Review, the Army are at heightened readiness due to a new era of threat. This has placed greater demands on the Defence Training Estate across the UK, which is being used for training more regularly and at shorter notice.
As such, the firing time notifications published on Gov.UK have been standardised to show the daily timings for when live-firing is permitted on the UK DTE. This is a change from the previous method of showing when training bookings had been made in advance.
This to ensure safety of all users, as it is not possible to change Gov.UK notifications at short notice. Broadly, the only guaranteed safe times for access are before or after the firing times provided on this page, however there may be exceptional circumstances where extensions have been requested.
If you wish to use the DTE for recreation, please always refer to onsite safety warning signals to understand if the site is safe to access before doing so.
Your safety
Danger - When warning signals are displayed, regardless of the timings, do not cross the range boundary.
Warning signals are red flags by day and red lamps by night; range boundaries are marked by red and white poles.
Red flags and red lamps indicate that live firing is taking place within the range boundaries.
Do not enter the danger area when in use, this could result in loss of life.
Do not touch any military debris, it may be dangerous. Please note the location and inform a Training Safety Officer (TSO) via 07717542336 or the police.
Learn more about accessing MOD training areas

OpenAI Gives Ukraine Daybreak Cyber Tool to Defend Critical Infrastructure From Cyberattacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:00:45 UTC
00:00:45 KST

- Category
- World
OpenAI Gives Ukraine Daybreak Cyber Tool to Defend Critical Infrastructure From Cyberattacks
OpenAI will provide Ukraine with access to its Daybreak cyber defense program to help protect hospitals, power plants, and other civilian infrastructure from cyberattacks, the BBC reported on September 23.
According to the BBC, the initiative is being carried out in cooperation with Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation. OpenAI announced the partnership on September 23 on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The BBC reported that Ukrainian teams will receive access to advanced AI tools designed to identify software vulnerabilities and develop and test fixes more quickly.
Verified Ukrainian teams will also receive training and technical support, according to OpenAI, helping cyber defenders identify weaknesses in their networks and respond to threats faster.
Under the initiative, Ukraine will also receive access to GPT-5.6 Sol, an advanced OpenAI model, the BBC reported.
The outlet noted that Daybreak can help cyber defenders review older software, investigate suspicious activity, identify and validate vulnerabilities, and test potential fixes.
“Protecting civilian infrastructure means defending it against both physical and digital attacks, so people can continue to live, work and access essential services,” George Osborne, Head of OpenAI for Countries, said, according to the BBC.
The BBC reported that Ukraine’s national cyber incident response team, CERT-UA, handled nearly 6,000 cyber incidents in 2025. The incidents included attacks affecting hospital systems, the energy sector, and telecommunications.
Rafe Pilling, senior director of threat intelligence at cybersecurity firm Sophos, told the BBC that Russian offensive cyber operations have been a key component of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine since 2014.
According to the BBC, Pilling said that any initiative strengthening Ukraine’s already capable but heavily burdened cyber defenses “could provide a valuable force multiplier.”
Jamie MacColl, a senior research fellow specializing in cyber at the Royal United Services Institute, told the BBC that Western technology companies have supported Ukraine for some time.
MacColl described their motives as partly altruistic and partly practical, noting that companies can gain valuable data and intelligence from an active war, the BBC reported.
He added that access to Daybreak would be useful given the scale of Russian cyber operations, while noting that Ukraine already has access to AI tools from other companies, including Google.
The initiative comes amid Russian-linked hackers' growing use of commercial AI models against Ukrainian targets.
A cyberespionage operation disclosed on September 10 targeted more than 20 organizations, primarily in Ukraine and Europe.
The group scanned email and remote-access systems belonging to more than two dozen Ukrainian government bodies and exported mailboxes from at least two drone component manufacturers.

Sexual objectification does not erase the perceived humanity of OnlyFans creators, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:00:34 UTC
00:00:34 KST

People who create content on the digital platform OnlyFans are heavily sexually objectified by observers, yet they are simultaneously viewed as capable individuals with free will. These findings challenge the traditional psychological assumption that sexually objectifying someone automatically strips them of their perceived autonomy and humanity. The research was recently published in The Journal of Social Psychology.
Sexual objectification occurs when a person is reduced to their body parts or physical appearance, primarily to satisfy the desires of others. Psychologists have observed that this reduction typically leads to dehumanization. When observers focus entirely on a target’s physical form, they tend to ignore the target’s internal states and mental capacities.
A primary casualty of this psychological process is agency, which is the capacity to think, plan, and act with intention. Prior research has consistently shown that sexually objectified women are viewed as passive and lacking the ability to make independent choices. This loss of perceived agency is a core component of dehumanization, effectively reducing a person to a mere tool for someone else’s gratification.
The rise of new digital media platforms has altered how people present themselves online. OnlyFans allows creators to share personalized explicit content directly with paying subscribers. Unlike traditional media, the creators retain control over their scheduling, content style, and pricing.
Researchers Chiara Pecini and Alessandra Sacino from the University of Genoa led a team to investigate whether the traditional rules of objectification apply in this modern digital environment. They wanted to know if observers can objectify a person while still recognizing that the person is actively orchestrating their own sexualization. The research team designed four distinct experiments to capture these social perceptions.
In the first experiment, 220 male participants reviewed fictitious survey responses supposedly written by a young woman. Half the men read a profile of a woman who actively used and enjoyed creating content on OnlyFans. The other half read about a woman who did not use the platform.
The researchers measured how much the men intended to sexually objectify the woman, alongside how much agency they attributed to her. The men reported higher intentions to sexually objectify the content creator compared to the woman not on the platform. However, the men did not rate the creator as having any less capacity to make choices or exercise self-control.
To see if this pattern held up against another highly sexualized role, the team conducted a second experiment with 253 men. This time, participants compared an OnlyFans creator to a motorsport umbrella girl, a traditional occupation where women stand alongside racecar drivers to shield them from the sun. The participants also viewed artificial intelligence-generated photos of the women in either highly sexualized or casual clothing.
The men reported higher intentions to sexually objectify the digital content creator than the umbrella girl. Despite this higher level of objectification, they attributed greater free will to the creator than to the umbrella girl. Whether the woman was pictured in sexualized or casual clothing produced results that were not statistically significant, suggesting the occupational role drove the perception.
The researchers then explored whether the creator’s financial success influenced how observers perceived their autonomy. In a third experiment involving 188 men and women, participants evaluated a creator who earned either a high monthly income of 4,000 euros or a low income of 120 euros. The photos again varied between casual and sexualized attire.
In this particular test, neither the income level nor the style of clothing altered the participants’ judgments. The differences in attributed free will across the groups were not statistically significant. The research team suspected that financial success alone might not communicate autonomy without understanding the creator’s personal motives.
A final experiment recruited 323 men and women to evaluate a creator’s profile based on a combination of income and their motivation for joining the platform. Some profiles stated the creator was intrinsically motivated, meaning she enjoyed showing off her body and feeling appreciated. Other profiles indicated an extrinsic motivation, stating she joined purely out of financial necessity.
The researchers evaluated self-determination, which is a specific facet of agency centered on a person’s ability to direct their own life free from external pressures. The participants rated the intrinsically motivated creator as having a higher level of self-determination than the extrinsically motivated one. A high income also slightly elevated the creator’s perceived self-determination.
Female participants were more sensitive to the motivation details than male participants. Women adjusted their ratings more sharply based on whether the creator enjoyed the work. Men tended to view the creators similarly regardless of their underlying motivations.
The results indicate a modern form of objectification where the target retains their perceived humanity and ability to choose. This attribution of agency can be a positive shift, but the researchers note it may rely on an illusion of total control. Once digital content is distributed, creators often lose the ability to dictate where their images end up, exposing them to nonconsensual sharing and harassment.
Observers who assume creators have complete autonomy might also engage in victim-blaming if that creator experiences online abuse. When society views these creators as entirely responsible for their sexualization, people might be less sympathetic when the creators face privacy violations. Fictional profiles in a controlled experiment also lack the interpersonal dynamics of a real digital exchange.
The participants in these experiments were familiar with the platform but were not active paying subscribers. Future studies will need to test whether people who regularly purchase explicit digital content perceive the creators differently. The researchers also hope to see if these attitudes apply to other forms of digital sex work.
The study, “Objects and Agents? Social Perception of OnlyFans Content Creators,” was authored by Chiara Pecini, Alessandra Sacino, Bianca Tallone, Roberta Rosa Valtorta, Gian Antonio Di Bernardo, and Luca Andrighetto.

TikTok drops appeal over £12.7m fine for not keeping under-13s off platform
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:00:34 UTC
00:00:34 KST

TikTok will pay a £12.7m fine to the UK’s data watchdog after dropping an appeal against a ruling that it did not do enough to keep children below the age of 13 off the platform.
The video app was punished by the Information Commissioner’s Office in 2023 for inadequate checks of who was using the platform and failing to remove underage users.
When issuing the fine the ICO said TikTok had done “very little, if anything” to address underage use of its service.
TikTok has a minimum user age of 13 but failure to enforce that limit resulted in up to 1.75 million UK children under 13 using the service in 2020, said the ICO. TikTok also failed to provide users with how their data was being collected and used, as well as neglecting to obtain parental consent.
Emily Keaney, the ICO’s deputy commissioner, said: “Our successful action against TikTok shows how important it is for companies to have the right protections in place, including to prevent access by children who are not old enough to be using their services.”
Chinese-owned TikTok said it still disagreed with the ruling but had decided to pay the fine because it related to a period between 2018 and 2020, after which it had implemented “many youth safety measures and policies”.
TikTok, which has more than 30 million users in the UK, has also withdrawn an appeal against an ICO request for information about how its algorithm processes teenagers’ personal data – and serves potentially harmful content. The ICO said it would now resume the investigation.
At the time the fine was issued, the then information commissioner, John Edwards, told the Guardian that TikTok was “not doing enough” on multiple fronts.
“Our findings were that TikTok were not doing enough to prevent under-13s accessing their platform, they were not doing enough when they became aware of under-13s to get rid of them, and they were not doing enough to detect under-13s on there,” he said.
Age-checking measures at tech platforms will be at the vanguard of the government’s new under-16 age limit for accessing social media platforms, which comes into force next year.
The UK’s communications watchdog, Ofcom, has warned that “more action from the tech industry is needed” on enforcing age limits as the ban approaches. The country’s eSafety commissioner has said a “substantial proportion” of under-16s in the country have kept their accounts, managed to create new ones or bypassed age-gating systems.

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Russia will consider the full range of circumstances when deciding on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s participation in the G20 summit, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov told reporters.

Meet the newest living cat species, the first described in 100 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Attention cat lovers: There’s an adorable new addition to the feline family tree.
Meet Leopardus tilcayo, a pint-size tiger cat discovered in Bolivia in the Yungas forests of the central Andes Mountains. L. tilcayo, reported September 17 in Current Biology, is the first new living cat species described and named by scientists in more than 100 years. The last one was the Uruguayan pampas cat (L. fasciatus), described in 1923.
L. tilcayo has a slender body, spotted fur and a ringed tail. It weighs roughly two kilograms, about as much as a two-month-old domestic kitten. For such a tiny cat, L. tilcayo has made a terrific splash, pouncing into headlines around the world. “I did not at all expect attention at this scale,” says Jonas Lescroart, an evolutionary biologist at the University of Antwerp in Belgium.
Lescroart and his colleagues hadn’t set out to discover a new species. They were looking to untangle one branch of the cat family tree. Until now, scientists didn’t have a good sense of how many tiger cat species existed. These small cats live in the tropical regions of the Americas and tend to look alike, Lescroart says.
The researchers analyzed the genetics of 38 species of the Leopardus genus, which includes tiger cats as well as more widely known animals like the ocelot. They expected to find two, three or even four distinct species of tiger cat. Instead, Lescroart and his colleagues’ analyses pointed to five separate species, including one that scientists had never before described: L. tilcayo.
The new species is based on two specimens: a female that was treated briefly for injuries at a sanctuary in Bolivia and released to the wild and a male that still lives at the sanctuary. His name is Tigrino. Lescroart’s colleague, Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz, met Tigrino at the sanctuary and noticed that he looked a little different from the cats she expected to see in the region. Nogales-Ascarrunz, a cat conservationist and National Geographic Explorer, genetically tested Tigrino and then connected with Lescroart’s team to share data.
The researchers’ work suggests that there’s diversity hiding even among well-studied animals like cats. “I don’t know if you’ll have to wait another 100 years for a new species,” Lescroart says. Though at the moment, the team doesn’t have any other cryptic kitties on the radar.

"This project reimagines spatial experience as a means of supporting emotional recovery and well-being in modern life.

"Extending beyond these senses, a sixth sense, an interior garden, creates a contemplative landscape that encourages connection, pause, reflection and inner clarity.
"Ultimately, the project envisions interior architecture as a non-verbal form of therapy, where sensory perception becomes a gentle guide toward healing and balance."

EU sanctions Xenia Fedorova for brainwashing France with Russian propaganda
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:59:02 UTC
23:59:02 KST

The EU agreed to sanction the former head of the Kremlin media outlet RT France, Xenia Fedorova, on Sept. 24, for spreading pro-Russian narratives and supporting Moscow's hybrid war on Europe.
Fedorova ran RT France from 2017 until it was forced to shut down by EU sanctions.
Since then, she has "continued to disseminate in French media such as CNews, Europe 1, and Le JDNews, narratives aligned with those promoted by the Russian authorities," reads an EU press release announcing the sanctions.
"Our determination is total: those who think they can carry out hostile moves against our democracy with impunity will face consequences," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot wrote on social media as the new sanctions were adopted.
Fedorova portrayed European support for Ukraine as prolonging the war; presented Russia as seeking peace with a confrontational Europe; cast doubt on Russia's abduction of Ukrainian children; and portrayed European and NATO policies as threats to European security, reads the official EU sanctions listing.
French authorities also said that her "conduct undermines the fundamental interests of the state," and her continued presence on French territory "therefore constitutes a particularly serious and immediate threat to public order, in a July deportation order to Fedorova."
The sanctions mean that Fedorova's assets in Europe will be frozen, and EU citizens and companies are forbidden from making any funds or economic resources available to her.
Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI) by propagandists such as Fedorova has become an increasingly important issue for EU policymakers as Russia steps up its hybrid war on Europe.
In addition to the 101 actors sanctioned so far by the EU for FIMI efforts, the bloc has partnered with Ukraine to analyze Russia's attempts to distort the information space; established a Hybrid Rapid Response Team to help third countries counter FIMI — most recently deployed in Armenia; and is setting up a Center for Democratic Resilience to protect democracy in the EU.
Concerns are high, especially for 2027, when many EU countries, including France, Spain, Italy, Poland, and Greece, are set to hold elections.
And the campaign for France's presidential election, not set to take place until April 18, 2027, is already underway, with candidates making support for Ukraine a key issue.

He started as a driver. Now he pilots Ukraine’s heavy strike drones
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:57:24 UTC
23:57:24 KST

A Ukrainian service member with the callsign Talisman learned to fly four heavy strike drone platforms and now switches between them when conditions demand it, the 808th Dnistrovska Separate Support Brigade reported on 23 September. Before joining the military, he worked in business.
He began his service in a unit in Rivne Oblast, in northwestern Ukraine, starting as a driver and later moving to battalion management tasks. He was then seconded to the 808th Brigade and eventually transferred to its roster permanently. It was there that he retrained as a heavy strike drone pilot.
Four platforms, one pilot
Heavy bombers were just coming into wide use when the unit was moved onto them. They trained for a week at the manufacturer, then practiced in the unit. Everyone started on the Vampire. After nearly a year on it, Talisman tried a second platform. "When you already have the base and the foundation, mastering another platform is much easier," he said.
Talisman now operates four platforms—the Vampire, a hexacopter with six motors, and three quadcopters: the Ares A1, the Heavy Shot, and the Magura Mini. Each type has its own characteristics—some are more resistant to jamming or navigation suppression than others, he said.
"I'd probably single out the Vampire and the Ares. The Vampire is more pleasant to operate, while the Ares is more resistant to various types of jamming. I've had situations where the Vampire wasn't working, and I continued carrying out missions on the Ares," Talisman said.
The Vampire is a six-rotor bomber built by Ukraine's SkyFall, originally codified with a range of up to 20 kilometers carrying up to 15 kilograms. The company says the current range is 35–40 kilometers. The Ares A1, built by Drones of Ukraine, has been in service since 2023 in strike, remote-mining, and resupply roles.
"The hardest thing is when there's no water. For a shower. Positions are all different: for some it's harder to get there, for some it's harder to work with drones. I have this thing—it's important to me that there's water," he said with a smile.
His crews have worked the Donetsk direction, near Lyman, in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, and later on tasks in Sumy and Kharkiv oblasts. In winter they drove in for the night and had to finish the task in that window, some faster and some slower depending on conditions and on Russian jamming, before the next crew took over. In warm weather they stay on position for four to seven days at a stretch, in crews of four or five.
His callsign came from his time serving alongside his fellow soldiers. "We had luck when I was with them. That's how they gave me this callsign," he said.
After the war, Talisman sees himself returning to civilian life. Before military service he was an entrepreneur and plans to go back to it.
Brigade tops remote-mining rating
In June 2026, the 808th Brigade topped Ukraine's DELTA remote-mining rating, which ranks units by how effectively they turn enemy approach routes into traps with drones.

OpenAI’s agent hacking Australia is a warning for governments everywhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:56:42 UTC
23:56:42 KST

On Wednesday Australia’s prime minister revealed that one of OpenAI’s artificial intelligence agents hacked into a health care platform maintained by the nation’s government—and that OpenAI took months to inform the latter about the breach.
Should these kinds of events continue to occur—or if they’ve already happened—they point to a need for stronger controls on private and sensitive data collected and stored by governments and other institutions. “This is a warning for governments and their IT staff to bolster security,” says Rajesh Veeraraghavan, a professor at Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service.
Addressing reporters at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York City on Wednesday, Australian prime minister Anthony Albanese said, “The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files.” An investigation is underway as to whether other government systems were accessed, if any, he said.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The Australian government was alerted to the incident on September 10, but Albanese said the hack occurred months before, on June 18, when an internal OpenAI model was tasked with researching public health spending. OpenAI became aware of the breach in August, according to the prime minister, and proceeded to wait more than a week before it alerted the Australian government through a generic public e-mail—not through any official channel for cybersecurity reporting and disclosure. As a result, the government was further delayed in learning of the event, Albanese said.
“Early evidence here seems to suggest that there was, at best, some communication challenges,” says Michael Horowitz, a political science professor at the University of Pennsylvania.
The breach follows a series of hacks by models owned by leading U.S. AI companies, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Earlier on Wednesday U.S. tech leaders—including OpenAI CEO Sam Altman—stressed their concerns over the pace of AI development in an address to the U.N. Security Council. Illegally hacking a government platform to access records could prove a watershed moment for AI regulation. In his address to reporters, Albanese said the breach was “something that has precedence.”
Details are scant as to what kind of access and information the agent got in the Australian breach. Albanese said no personal information was exposed in the incident. OpenAI did not immediately respond for a request for comment from Scientific American.
Still, Veeraraghavan stresses that responsibility for such incidents should rest solely on the AI companies that made the involved agents. “OpenAI, in this case should be held responsible, even if the ‘intent’ to divulge information may not be clear,” he says.
In his briefing to reporters, Albanese expressed that Australia will take action to respond to the event. “There will obviously be legal consequences on it,” he said. It’s not yet clear what those consequences will be, especially given that a legal case concerning this style of autonomous agent hacking has not been pursued in court yet.
It is perhaps a small relief that this incident happened to a close U.S. ally. “Australia wants OpenAI to be there, so they should be able to figure it out,” Horowitz says. But unless AI labs can learn how to test their models without allowing those models to escape, they may not keep getting so lucky.
Editor’s Note (9/24/26): This is a developing story and may be updated.

Spain’s housing crisis in spotlight with eviction of pensioner, 87
Thousands have protested in outrage at the eviction and a market widely denounced as unaffordable for renters and buyers
The eviction of an 87-year-old from her Madrid home has highlighted a political paralysis that has thwarted efforts to resolve Spain’s chronic housing crisis, fuelling debate before next year’s election.
Maricarmen Abascal’s 70-year stay at her home in upmarket central Madrid ended on Wednesday when she left escorted on a stretcher, flanked by protesters on one side and police on the other – a traumatic event broadcast live on TV.
Unable to afford a 275-per cent increase to the monthly rent imposed by the real estate firm that owned her flat, she has become the cruellest symbol of a crisis that has stalked Spain for years.
Thousands protested in Madrid, Barcelona and elsewhere on Wednesday night in outrage at the eviction and a market widely denounced as unaffordable for renters and buyers – young and old alike.

Man, 105, being investigated over murders at Nazi PoW camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:55:51 UTC
23:55:51 KST

A 105-year-old man is under investigation on suspicion of being an accessory to multiple murders at a Nazi prisoner of war camp, German prosecutors have said.
The case, which is being handled by the public prosecutor’s office in Dortmund, centres on the Stalag 326 VI K camp in western Germany, in what is now the state of North Rhine-Westphalia.
“The 105-year-old suspect is thought to have been a guard at the prisoner of war camp Stalag 326 VI K in the Senne region of western Germany,” prosecutors said in a statement. The man is “accused of being an accessory to multiple murders owing to his activities there”, they said.
The Senne camp housed between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by American troops.
The investigation is the result of an urgent last-minute scramble by the judiciary to prosecute alleged participants in the Nazi killing machine before they die. The judicial efforts stem in part from a recognition that many of the suspects who have escaped prosecution in the eight decades since the end of the second world war on the grounds that they were considered to have played an insignificant role were in fact integral to the implementation of the Hitler regime’s murderous aims.
A judicial precedent was set by the court case of John Demjanjuk, a former guard at the Nazi Sobibór death camp in occupied Poland, who was convicted in 2011 of being an accomplice to the murders of more than 28,000 Jews that took place in the time he worked there.
Prosecutors had sought Ukraine-born Demjanjuk’s extradition from his Ohio home to Germany for years, arguing that he was complicit in the crimes committed at Sobibór despite a lack of evidence that he had directly killed anyone.
Demjanjuk died aged 91 in March 2012 awaiting an appeal due to his age and frailty, which meant he did not go to prison.
The Demjanjuk case lowered the bar for proof of complicity, paving the way for other nonagenarians and more recently centenarians to stand trial.
The most prominent trial of recent years, and representative of what Hannah Arendt, a political theorist, described as a Schreibtischtäter (desk perpetrator, or bureaucratic mediator), was that of Irmgard Furchner, who worked at the Stutthof concentration camp between 1943 and 1945 as a secretary to the camp commandant. She was given a two-year suspended sentence for her role as an accessory to murder.
Her trial was, contrary to normal rules, filmed for historical purposes. Furchner made headlines after running away from her retirement home on the scheduled opening day of her trial.
Josef Schütz, a former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp north of Berlin, was sentenced for being an accomplice to murder to five years in prison in June 2022. He died the following year, aged 102.
In April last year an alleged former guard at Sachsenhausen died before he was able to face trial over charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people.
A separate investigation was opened last year by Dortmund prosecutors into a 100-year-old former guard at a PoW camp in Hemer, North Rhine-Westphalia, which also held mainly Soviet prisoners. He is suspected of participating in executions of prisoners between December 1943 and September 1944.
The new investigation was initiated by the Central Office for the Investigation of National Socialist Crimes in Ludwigsburg, in the southern state of Baden-Württemberg, which passed its preliminary investigation into the man to public prosecutors along with that of another former guard. The other suspect has since died, according to German media.
If the trial goes ahead, like other recent cases it is expected to throw light on the Stalag system in general and on Senne in particular, drawing survivors and historians to give evidence. Up to 5.7 million Soviet prisoners were held captivity in Germany. More than half did not survive.

Unknown Publisher
