Lithuania to let Belarusians apply for residence permits in Armenia, Georgia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:40:00 UTC
23:40:00 KST

Belarusian citizens will be able to apply for temporary residence permits in Lithuania through external service provider offices in Armenia and Georgia starting in November, Lithuania’s Interior Ministry said Thursday.
The measure is intended to allow Lithuanian employers to continue recruiting workers from Belarus after changes to the country’s immigration law take effect November 1.
“To ensure that employers continue to have the opportunity to bring in workers from Belarus where there are labour shortages, Belarusian citizens will be able to submit applications for temporary residence permits at external service provider offices in Armenia and Georgia,” the ministry said.
Without the new arrangement, Belarusian citizens would no longer be able to enter Lithuania for employment purposes after the law changes take effect, the ministry said.
The decision follows Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas’ announcement Wednesday that Lithuania would close external service provider offices in Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan and Bosnia and Herzegovina because of “security concerns”. Applications for Lithuanian temporary residence permits will no longer be accepted at those offices from November 1.
The number of countries with external service providers will consequently fall from 31 to 27. According to the Interior Ministry, applications for residence permits on the basis of employment will be possible in 21 of those countries.
In five countries – India, Cambodia, Ghana, Azerbaijan and Mongolia – employment-based applications are not available. Applicants there are limited to priority categories, including study, highly qualified employment, academic and scientific work, family reunification, intra-company transfers and certain investment-based cases.
The ministry said Belarus currently has no external service provider office authorised to accept applications for Lithuanian residence permits. Belarusian citizens seeking permits for employment therefore currently apply in Lithuania through the Migration Department while legally present in the country.
From November 1, however, foreigners, including Belarusian citizens, generally will no longer be able to submit residence permit applications from within Lithuania, except in specified cases. That would otherwise leave Belarusian citizens unable to apply either in Lithuania or abroad, the ministry said.
The new option in Armenia and Georgia is intended to close that gap.
The Interior Ministry notes that the Migration Department must consider national security interests, foreign policy priorities, labour market needs and institutional capacity when selecting countries where external service providers can operate. It must also consult the State Security Department, the State Border Guard Service and police.
The possibility for foreigners to submit temporary residence permit applications abroad through external service providers was introduced in January 2023.
As of September 1, nearly 227,000 foreigners held valid residence permits in Lithuania, according to Migration Department data. They included about 80,000 Ukrainian citizens, nearly 48,000 Belarusians, 13,000 Russians, a similar number of Uzbek citizens, 9,400 Indians and 7,400 Tajiks.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:39:37 UTC
23:39:37 KST

Rory Stewart has been an Afghan NGO leader, a Conservative leadership candidate, a Harvard professor, a popular podcaster, and the deputy governor of an Iraqi province. This week, he created a moment that drew wider attention than any of them: he fixed a beady gaze on a fellow Newsnight panellist for the longest four seconds in television history.
Stewart, who now co-presents The Rest Is Politics with Alastair Campbell, appeared on the BBC programme on 18 September – but in the last few days, a clip of the moment in question has taken on a life of its own on social media.
Stewart appeared alongside the former Labour leader Neil Kinnock and the New Statesman’s political editor, Ailbhe Rea, to discuss the day’s main news stories, including the race between China and the US to develop artificial intelligence (AI).
After Stewart made his comments, the presenter Matt Chorley asked Rea what Westminster could do about the development of AI. Stewart then swivelled around in his chair and stared directly at the journalist with an expression – and posture – of absolute focus.
Chorley told the Guardian the behaviour hadn’t appeared overly strange in person: “I didn’t notice Rory looking particularly intently at anyone during the course of the programme.”
He only became aware of what had happened when several friends texted him. “You know a moment from Newsnight has cut through when friends and family who don’t normally watch it are suddenly sending me clips,” he said. “But it is just quite a funny moment.”
He added that as it was the first Newsnight episode to move to the programme’s new earlier slot at 7pm, it had been “quite manic” in the runup. He had even joked to the panellists: “Anything that can be used to go viral, maybe a punchup or whatever, a tiff at the table, if you want to do that, that’d be great.”
Chorley observed that Stewart was “used to this”, after another clip of him taking his tie off during a Tory leadership debate had gone viral in 2019.
“It’s not the first time that something he’s done has gone wild online. I think he was genuinely probably just intently listening to what Ailbhe had to say. But there was something about the camera angle and his very direct look,” he said.
Many behaviours that appear normal in person can look strange on screen, Chorley added. He said he had learned to “remember you’re always on” and to control his naturally emphatic hand movements, which can “look crazy” on screen. He also recalled an early Newsnight episode which had surprised viewers when Tim Stanley, a columnist at the Telegraph, winked at the camera.
“This is just the beauty of live telly,” he said. “It’s a reminder that even when the camera is on the person who’s talking, you might be in shot.”
Rea, who was on the receiving end of the stare, posted the clip on X to joke that she would “please like attention levels like this on my latest interview” after sharing a link to her most recent reporting.
The clip has turned into a meme online, with commenters imagining situations in which the stare could have taken place.
The Larry the Cat social media account posted: “When HR tells you that you need to listen better to female colleagues.”
Total Politics Group’s chief executive, Mark Wallace, compared Stewart’s behaviour to the comedian Kevin Eldon’s surreal style, writing: “There’s a high degree of Kevin Eldon energy to this. Magnificently strange.”

105-year-old investigated for crimes at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:37:34 BST
23:37:34 KST

105-year-old investigated for crimes at Nazi PoW camp in Germany
- Published
German prosecutors are investigating a man aged 105 over allegations that he was an accessory to multiple counts of murder at a Nazi prisoner of war camp in World War Two.
The suspect is alleged to have been a camp guard at Stalag 326 VI K in Senne in northwestern Germany.
A similar case had also been under way involving a second former camp guard at Senne, Dortmund public prosecutor Sonja Frodermann said in a statement.
That suspect died a few months ago at the age of 99, she said.
No further details about the two former guards have been made public, however the two cases highlight the difficulties faced by prosecutors who continue to investigate Nazi-era crimes, with most of the remaining suspects already dead.
More than 5.3 million soldiers from the Soviet Red Army were held in German captivity during World War Two and half are thought to have died. Many of those who did survive were treated as traitors on their return home.
But the PoW camp, or Stalag, at Senne was one of the biggest.
One in three Soviet PoWs entering Nazi Germany between 1941 and 1945 went through the complex at Senne, according to the memorial site, and they often ended up doing forced labour in the wider region.
Living conditions at Stalag were horrific, and prisoners faced appalling mistreatment and malnutrition.
Of the 180,000-200,000 Soviet prisoners of war registered there, many died and tens of thousands are buried there. PoWs from France, Poland, Serbia and Belgium were also held at Senne.
The prosecutor made clear the investigation surrounding the 105-year-old was still under way and that the allegations of being an accessory to multiple murders related to his activities at Stalag 36.
There has been no statute of limitations in Germany for either murder or accessory to murder since 1979, to enable the prosecution of Nazi-era crimes.
Another centenarian camp guard from the Hemer Stalag VI A camp is also said to be under investigation.
However, bringing perpetrators to justice more than 80 years after the war is now fraught with difficulty.
Four years ago a 101-year-old concentration camp guard was given a five-year jail term for complicity in murder at Sachsenhausen. Josef Schütz was the oldest Nazi criminal ever brought to justice.
He never served time in jail and died in 2023 while appealing his sentence.
A former Nazi concentration camp secretary was convicted in 2022 of abetting murder and given a suspended jail term. She died last year aged 99.
Although prosecution of Nazi crimes is handled by the public prosecutors in the western city of Dortmund, cases are initially taken on by the central office for Nazi crime investigations in Ludwigsburg in the south-west.

France says ICC warrant posed no obstacle to Netanyahu overflight
PARIS, Sept 24 - France defended its decision to let Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's plane cross its airspace en route to the United Nations on Thursday, saying international law did not require action despite an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against him over alleged war crimes.
France is a signatory of the ICC's founding Rome Statute and is formally bound to cooperate with the court, including arresting suspects who enter its territory. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux told reporters the clearance was "in full conformity with international law".
"The Rome Statute does not impose any obligations regarding overflights of its territory by a state plane which has a passenger who is targeted by an arrest warrant," Confavreux said.
Netanyahu is unable to travel to many countries because of an International Criminal Court arrest warrants issued against him and his then-defense minister as well as the then-military commander of Hamas in 2024.
Israel rejects the jurisdiction of the Hague-based court and denies war crimes in Gaza, where it waged a military campaign it says was aimed at eliminating Hamas following the deadly attack on Israel by the militant Palestinian group on October 7, 2023. It is contesting the warrants against Netanyahu and his former defence chief Yoav Gallant.
Flight-tracking app Flightradar24 showed Netanyahu's plane flew over Greece, Italy and France. A spokesperson for Italy's Foreign Ministry said they could not immediately answer whether Israeli authorities had sought permission for an overflight.
Last year Netanyahu flew a circuitous route to New York to skirt the airspace of several European countries, including France, media reported at the time.
Washington has announced a campaign to isolate the court. US President Donald Trump this week urged ICC members to quit what he called an "out of control institution". France has said it condemns the threats against the court.
Netanyahu was making an unusually short visit to the US for his address to world leaders at the UN General Assembly. He arrived in New York around 9 a.m. ET (1300 GMT) and was expected to fly back later in the day after delivering his speech. REUTERS

"The fund's participants are either current or former Eximbank employees. The total amount of obligations accrued and fulfilled by the fund exceeds UAH 200 million, including almost UAH 100 million in lump-sum pension payments.
Ukreximbank established the fund in 2005 as part of its corporate employee pension program, and it began operating in April 2006.
The fund follows a conservative investment strategy. Its main investment areas are government securities, instruments of state-owned and largest Ukrainian banks, and corporate bonds of major Ukrainian issuers.
Two bills on reforming non-state pension provision are currently registered in the Verkhovna Rada. The main bill, No. 15570, "On Voluntary Pension Funds," provides for a transition from the current model of non-state pension funds (NPFs) to voluntary pension funds that may be established exclusively by pension companies. Existing NPFs would have 10 years to decide whether to terminate through reorganization or liquidation.
The National Securities and Stock Market Commission (NSSMC) supported the package of bills Nos. 15570, 15571 and 15572 on updating the voluntary pension provision system. The proposed changes concern, among other things, corporate governance and internal control, risk management, internal audit, introduction of the "prudent person" principle for investing pension assets, and disclosure of information to participants. Separate bills in the package regulate tax and civil law issues.
Serdiuk said the proposed model would mean that employers would lose their status as founders of corporate pension funds.
"At present, we have clearly separated functions for managing and overseeing the fund. We have the fund's founder, the fund's board, an administrator, an asset management company, a custodian bank – in our case Raiffeisen Bank – and an auditor. (...) A great many questions arise when all of this is concentrated in pension companies," the banker said.
An alternative bill, No. 15570-1, "On the Non-State Pension Provision System," would allow existing NPFs to remain alongside new voluntary pension funds. Under its transitional provisions, existing NPFs would have 10 years to decide whether to reorganize or liquidate, but the bill would not make this mandatory.

Marineland dolphin dies at aquarium in Spain in latest death after rescue
A dolphin rescued from the troubled theme park Marineland Canada has died weeks after it was taken to an aquarium in Spain. Several other animals from Marineland, including three beluga whales, have died at their new homes in recent weeks.
Oceanogràfic València, Europe's largest aquarium, said Thursday that the dolphin, known as Echo, arrived from Marineland with "serious vision problems" and other health issues, including blindness, that "required individualized attention."
Echo was taken to the facility's medical pool and cared for by veterinarians after beginning to exhibit respiratory problems and difficulty swallowing, the aquarium said. Her health "deteriorated rapidly" throughout Wednesday before she died that night, the aquarium said.
The aquarium said its staff and pathologists from a nearby university will conduct an autopsy to determine the cause of death.
Echo is one of four dolphins rescued from Marineland Canada. The facility said the other animals are "still progressing favorably" under the care of Oceanogràfic València staff.
Another beluga whale rescued from Marineland, known as Jelly Bean, died at Oceanogràfic València in July. The facility said it is still investigating what caused the whale's death.
Marineland Canada shut down in 2024 after its owners died, but remained in possession of its animals, including dolphins and 30 beluga whales. In October 2025, the theme park warned it would have to euthanize the animals if they couldn't be relocated.
In July 2026, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration announced an international relocation plan that would send 28 beluga whales to accredited aquariums in the United States. The other two beluga whales were sent to Oceanogràfic València.
Several other animals rescued from Marineland Canada have died in recent weeks. Three beluga whales taken from Marineland to the Shedd Aquarium in Chicago died within a month of each other, raising questions about how medically fragile the animals were when they were rescued. A fourth beluga whale, a longtime member of the Shedd's beluga pod, also recently died at the aquarium.
Even before Marineland Canada closed, it was under scrutiny for its treatment of animals. Twenty whales, including 19 belugas, have died there since 2019. Inspectors previously declared that all animals in the theme park were in distress due to poor water quality. In a letter to American aquariums, NOAA noted that the whales from Marineland "are health-compromised."
Staff at the Shedd Aquarium are also conducting investigations and medical exams to determine the whales' cause of death.

Grave of Guilford soldier missing since 1918 identified

Grave of Guilford soldier missing since 1918 identified
A rededication service for Second Lieutenant (2nd Lt) Frank Fleming, from Guildford, was organised by the UK MOD’s ‘War Detectives’ in Belgium
The previously un-named grave of an officer from Guildford, Surrey, who served with the Seaforth Highlanders been identified and rededicated in his name 108 years after his death on 22 September 2026.
A rededication service for 2nd Lt Frank Fleming was organised by the UK MOD’s ‘War Detectives’ at CWGC Voormezeele Enclosure No. 3, Belgium. The service was supported by soldiers from 4th Battalion The Royal Regiment of Scotland.
JCCC Caseworker, Nicola Nash, said:
  More than 100 years after his death, it was an honour to be there today to pay tribute to Frank’s bravery and sacrifice.
Frank Fleming was one of three sons of Alexander and Mary Fleming, and all three would ultimately lose their lives during World War 1.
Born in Guildford, Surrey, on 15 October 1894, Frank grew up on his family’s farm before moving to London to work as a market clerk. He later joined the Army and was commissioned into the Seaforth Highlanders.
During the German Spring Offensive in April 1918, 2nd Lt Fleming was attached to the 7th Battalion and took part in fierce fighting near Hollebeke, Belgium. While leading his men in an attack against German positions on 11 April, he was seriously wounded. Displaying remarkable courage and selflessness, he ordered his men to withdraw to safety and refused to let stretcher-bearers risk their lives attempting to rescue him. Unable to be recovered, he was later listed as missing and was commemorated on the Tyne Cot Memorial.
Subsequent research submitted by a member of the public has now shown that 2Lt Fleming was actually buried in the Hollebeke area of Belgium and moved to Voormezeele Enclosure No. 3 after the war.
His headstone, replaced by Commonwealth War Graves Commission, now carries his name and the service today has commemorated his loss.
Catherine Nell, Identifications Manager at the Commonwealth War Graves Commission, said:
  It has been a privilege for the Commonwealth War Graves Commission to be involved in Second Lieutenant Frank Fleming’s identification. We shall continue to care for his grave, alongside his comrades, in perpetuity.

Germany and Spain clash over who gets into ‘Made in Europe’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:35:18 UTC
23:35:18 KST

BRUSSELS — Germany and Spain have pitched competing views on the scope of a “Made in Europe” push to favor European companies in public procurement, setting the stage for more hard bargaining over a flagship EU industry bill.
The European Commission unveiled the Industrial Accelerator Act in March aiming to channel the EU’s vast government spending on green technology, energy-intensive industry and autos toward European companies, helping them compete against China’s dominant exporters.
Six months on, the bloc’s 27 governments are still struggling to find common ground. Position papers from Germany and Spain obtained by POLITICO ahead of a meeting of EU industry ministers on Thursday reveal divisions among the bloc’s big economies over where to draw the line.
Advertisement
A core question is how many countries should be admitted to the Made in Europe club, which would give their products privileged access to public contracts for everything from wind farms to the steel and cement used in highways and metro systems.
Germany, the bloc’s export powerhouse, is pushing for a broad “Made with Europe” group broadly in line with the original Commission proposal. That foresees admitting partners that have free-trade or public procurement agreements with the EU, or are in a customs union with the bloc. The eligible pool could run to as many as 80 countries.
“Germany rejects protectionism and discrimination,” the German paper reads. “The EU must remain a reliable partner for its free-trade partners and uphold its legal obligations.” It also calls for an “opt-in” possibility to include other third countries that give the EU reciprocal treatment.
No other EU countries have signed up to the German paper, however. France, the bloc’s second-largest economy, is meanwhile pushing in the opposite direction and advocating a more restrictive approach.
While not denying that Europe has to remain open to its trading partners, French Industry Minister Sébastien Martin emphasized that public money must be directed toward production in Europe.
“In the future, it will still be possible to have products with some of their added value coming from elsewhere, but production must take place in Europe in order to qualify for public support,” Martin said as he arrived for Thursday’s meeting in Brussels.
Advertisement
Rule of three
In an attempt to make the European preference concept workable, Spain has proposed a three-tier structure that would give EU-made products the strongest preference, according to its paper.
“A more granular and risk-based approach could improve both the effectiveness and the political acceptability of the text,” the document reads.
The EU’s 27 member countries would make up the first tier, while the second would include European Economic Area members and other “trusted” partners.
A third tier would be reserved for countries that have a free-trade agreement, customs union or procurement agreement with the EU. Their status could be upgraded to the second level if they deepen their trade agreements with the bloc, the paper says.
Ireland, which is chairing the talks among EU countries until the end of the year, is working to bridge differences among governments. Dublin will convene a discussion of deputy ambassadors on Oct. 7 and plans to put a new compromise on the table by the middle of the month, Industry Minister Peter Burke told his colleagues on Thursday. It hopes to broker a deal in November.
The differences among EU governments also run through party politics, with the German and Spanish wings of the center-right European People’s Party — the largest group in the European Parliament — similarly split over the industry act.
Advertisement
Lead MEPs are scheduled to discuss their draft report at a meeting on Sept. 28, while lawmakers can file amendments — or suggestions for changes — by Oct. 7. The deadline was pushed back by a week at the request of the EPP.
Only when both the Council and the Parliament adopt their respective positions on the bill will it be possible to launch talks among the EU institutions to hammer out a compromise that can become law. With the legislative timeline showing signs of slipping, the Commission’s ambition to strike a deal this year is looking increasingly unrealistic.
The argument over who gets into the club is being followed particularly closely across the Channel.
The EU’s tortuous legislative process is complicating efforts by the U.K. to renew its reset of relations with Brussels, after former PM Keir Starmer’s resignation in June forced a planned summit to be canceled.
New Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government has brought its concerns about a possible exclusion from Made in Europe into the discussion. EU officials have replied that they can’t pre-empt the outcome of the legislative process for the Industrial Accelerator Act.

Grave of Angus soldier missing since 1918 identified in Belgium
A rededication service for Private George Pert from Ferryden was organised by the UK MOD’s ‘War Detectives’ at CWGC Harlebeke New British Cemetery, Belgium
The previously un-named grave of a soldier from Ferryden, Angus, who served with the Seaforth Highlanders been identified and rededicated in his name 108 years after his death on 22 September 2026.
A rededication service for Private George Pert was organised by the UK MOD’s ‘War Detectives’ at CWGC Harlebeke New British Cemetery, Belgium.
JCCC Caseworker, Nicola Nash, said:
  From a fishing village on the banks of the River Esk to the battlefields of Belgium, George Pert’s journey reflects the sacrifices made by ordinary people during the World War One. It was an honour to be there to pay tribute to his life and service.
Private Pert grew up in Ferryden, a traditional fishing village on the bank of the River Esk, before joining the Seaforth Highlanders.
Just a month before the end of the war the Western Front saw a massive and rapid Allied advance that forced the German army into continuous retreat. It was on the 20 October 1918, during intense fighting around Harlebeke, that Private Pert lost his life.
His body was never recovered, and he was officially recorded as missing. However, subsequent research submitted by a member of the public has shown that Private Pert was buried east of Harlebeke and moved to Harlebeke New British Cemetery after the war.
The service was supported by serving soldiers from The Royal Regiment of Scotland. Pert’s headstone, replaced by Commonwealth War Graves Commission (CWGC), now carries his name and today’s service commemorated his loss.
Polly Brewster, Commemorations Case Officer at CWGC, said:
  More than one hundred years after he made the ultimate sacrifice, CWGC are honoured to have supported the identification of Private George Pert’s final resting place. The personal inscription chosen by his family, “Gone too soon, but not forgotten,” serves as a moving tribute to the profound loss experienced by his loved ones. His rededication service today reaffirms the Commission’s enduring commitment to preserving the memory of all those who fell during the two World Wars.

Abbas warns about settlement expansion, 'Greater Israel' plan
Abbas also warned that the E1 settler project announced by the current government will "separate the northern West Bank from its south, isolate east Jerusalem from its Palestinian surroundings, and prevent the realization of a geographically continuous Palestinian State."
He then demanded immediate intervention by the United Nations Security Council and the implementation of Resolution 2334, which established that Israeli settlements in the West Bank have no legal validity and constitute a violation of international law.
He the asked the assembly: "What is the world waiting for to protect the Palestinian people, ensure their continued presence on their land, end the Israeli occupation, and implement the two-state solution?"
"This solution guarantees peace for all, instead of the threat emanating from Israeli extremism, which seeks to expand their colonial project towards establishing the so-called greater Israel," he added, warning about "Israeli attacks" reported in eastern Jerusalem's Al Aqsa Mosque, the Holy Sepulcher and Hebron's Cave of the Patriarchs.
He also claimed that "settler terrorism is escalating under the protection of the occupying forces, while the crimes of land theft, checkpoints and raids continue," and is also isolating Palestinians in eastern Jerusalem, with the area "being fragmented and Judaized."
"We highly appreciate the measures taken by the UK, as well as other twelve countries, to protect the two-state solution, and the call launched by the leaders of France, the UK, and Canada to convene a summit in New York on this matter," Abbas pointed out.
"Furthermore, we call on US President Donald Trump to fulfill the commitments that he made to the leaders of the Arab and Islamic states last September, to prevent the annexation of Palestinian land and prevent displacements," he continued.
Abbas claims reforms must allow for independent state, release of funds
Later in his speech, Abbas pointed to the reforms the Palestinian Authority has pushed in the last year. "We have fulfilled our pledge. We completed the national reform program that we had committed to. We strengthened institutional governance, public financial management, transparency, anti-corruption measures, and the rule of law," he said.
"We established a unified, needs-based national system for social protection and social welfare, abolished the previous laws in the area, and obtained an independent international audit confirming the validity of our measures," he added, and detailed that the education system has been "developed in accordance with international standards."
"We are demanding the release of all our withheld funds. The guarantee of their regular and full transfer. And the lifting of the financial and economic restrictions and the blockade imposed on our people, in accordance with the Paris Economic Protocol agreed upon in the Oslo Convention," he also demanded from the Israeli government.
Abbas also called for the acceleration of the establishment of the second phase of Trump's Gaza Peace Plan. "The transitional period must not be allowed to become a permanent or open-ended situation without any clear time-bound political horizon. Rather, it must lead to the reunification of the Gaza Strip and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, under the authority of the State of Palestine," he explained.

Where the Harvest Has Nowhere to Go
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:33:00 UTC
23:33:00 KST

In the Kherson region, where shelling is relentless and anti-drone nets cover the roads, Russian attacks on export routes are driving a wedge between the value of grain abroad and what farmers can earn at home. The consequences extend beyond individual livelihoods to the survival of rural communities and the prospects of the next generation.
South of Kyiv, heading toward the Black Sea, the country opens into broad expanses of farmland. Wheat, barley and sunflowers stretch into the distance on either side of the lightly traveled highway toward Odesa. It is watermelon season, and harvesting is under way. The sheer extent of cultivation gives a sense of the country’s agricultural reach, supplying markets far beyond its borders.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
                                                                                                                                                                         
As checkpoints begin to punctuate the road, damaged and abandoned houses become a familiar sight in the villages, their facades scarred by shrapnel. Fragments of rockets and drones lie along the streets, in courtyards and back gardens, while unexploded ammunition and mines remain scattered across land still being farmed. On the highway between Mykolaiv and Kherson, anti-drone nets enclose stretches of the route, extending onto the country lanes that lead toward the farms.
Kernel Pilots Modular Grain Storage to Cushion Export Disruptions
Some 30 kilometers (20 miles) outside Kherson, in the village of Posad-Pokrovske, a tractor is plowing a field beside one of these narrow roads. The front line once ran through this area; beyond it, toward the neighboring hamlet of Soldatske, Russian troops held the land until the Ukrainian advance that liberated Kherson in November 2022.
I wait at the edge as the tractor approaches, then climb into the cab when the driver stops. His name is Vyacheslav Dolholutskyi. Short and stocky, with a full beard and a weathered face, he is dressed in shorts and sandals. His broad hands, thick fingers resting on the steering wheel, guide the machine back across the field.
The noise is loud and the view restricted; the 38-year-old explains that he neither sees nor hears Russian drones while working.
“You’re watching the machinery, the instruments,” he says. “There’s no time to think about whether something is flying above you or not.”
Nowhere to hide
Vyacheslav, known as Slava, farms roughly 100 hectares (245 acres) scattered across smaller plots around Posad-Pokrovske, working largely on his own. A second job maintaining the canals of the Inhulets irrigation system, which supplies water to farmland in southern Ukraine, provides a regular government-paid income. “I combine it. After work, on weekends, sometimes when they let me take leave during the harvest.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
That job also brought him equipment he now uses on his farmland: a drone detector, issued to canal workers as Russian drone activity increased around the villages of Stanislav and Oleksandrivka, closer to the front. He describes watching for his own position in the drone’s camera feed on the detector’s screen – the view available to its operator. “If you see yourself, you have 30 or 40 seconds to jump out of the tractor and hide.”
But out on the exposed farmland he cultivates, even an early warning can leave him with nowhere to go. He recalls continuing to work after the detector picked up drone activity nearby. “How can I hide in the middle of the steppe?”
Vyacheslav points out a crater in a nearby wheat field, where a Shahed drone once came down and broke apart. It is a consequence of interception he wants people to understand: wreckage still falls somewhere, sometimes into crops that have taken months to grow. “A lot of wheat has burned in people’s fields.”
Beyond the threat to the harvest, military activity is woven into the working day: aircraft overhead, military vehicles passing through, strikes on neighboring settlements. He recalls glide bombs hitting nearby villages and attacks around fuel facilities, in daylight as well as at night. “Here, basically every day, you can understand that military operations are going on.”
Taking back the land
Vyacheslav learned to drive a tractor while he was still at school. Around the ninth or tenth grade, he began working for a local vegetable grower to earn some money. “I started little by little around 2008 or 2009 — half a hectare, then a hectare of vegetables.”
Today, he grows mainly winter wheat and winter barley, which he considers best suited to the region’s dry conditions. He plans to continue with both, possibly devoting more land to wheat.
Back in February 2022, Russia’s full-scale invasion interrupted his preparations for spring planting. “Literally the day before the war started, I bought fertilizer.”
He, his wife Liudmyla, and their daughter Zlata stayed at home for roughly a month, sheltering in the basement, before fleeing through Mykolaiv to the Vinnytsia region. “When they started shelling the village, we understood that we had to leave.”
For Vyacheslav, the former front runs through the geography of his own farmland. “Here was the contact line, and there was the canal. The Russians were there, and ours were here.”
After the Ukrainian counteroffensive drove Russian forces back across the Dnipro, the family returned to a village without electricity or running water. “There was patriotism. We believed in a quick victory, as they say – not in a prolonged war.”
As the land had not been professionally cleared, he bought a metal detector and checked access roads and fields on foot before bringing in machinery. “It was the gray zone,” he says. “Everything was mined.”
Over the years, he had worked through one setback after another, reaching a point by early 2026 where he hoped a successful season would allow him to formally register and expand his farm – only for the war to place another obstacle in his path.
A harvest without a market
At the end of the field, Vyacheslav turns the tractor and begins another pass.
“I thought harvesting would be the problem, with the shelling and so many fields burning. But now it turns out the problem is selling the grain.”
In roughly two weeks, he says, the price he was being offered for wheat fell from $150–160 per metric ton to around $90. Barley has fared no better. “Five days ago it was $148. Two days later, $97.”
The figures reflect local prices, while those at export terminals or on international exchanges can be considerably higher. “We managed to grow it. We managed to preserve it. We harvested it. And now there is nowhere to sell it.”
Farther west, he reasons, a farmer might store the harvest and wait for a better price. He lacks the money for a storage facility – and even if he had it, the investment would be a gamble. “You can build a warehouse – and it can be destroyed.”
He gestures toward the wheat still standing in the surrounding fields. Some farmers, he explains, cannot move their harvest on; even loaded trucks can be left waiting. “There is nowhere to put it. There are no vehicles. There is nowhere to take it.” Larger agricultural companies, he says, can afford to wait longer, drawing on their own grain stores, financial reserves and better access to aid.
The bottleneck at sea
The ports are central to Vyacheslav’s explanation. A farmer may own the grain and have someone willing to buy it in principle, but the transaction depends on trucks, warehouses, terminals and ships continuing to work beyond his field. “Ships are afraid to enter,” he says. “People are killed, ships are damaged.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Access to Ukraine’s Black Sea ports deteriorated sharply over the summer. By mid-July, the Ukrainian Agrarian Council estimated that Russian attacks had reduced grain-export capacity by about a third, to roughly 4 million metric tons (about 4.4 million tons) a month. Four major terminals had stopped purchasing grain. Freight costs were rising, while shipment delays and storage shortages carried the disruption inland.
On July 13, a Russian strike hit a Togo-flagged merchant vessel carrying mineral fertilizer in the Odesa region, killing five crew members and injuring ten. Less than two weeks later, another ship carrying nearly 2,800 metric tons of corn – about 110,000 bushels, or roughly a 100-truck convoy – was hit twice and set ablaze as it left a port in the region.
In early August, the agriculture ministry estimated that continued restrictions on maritime trade could cost the sector $1.5 billion to $3 billion. More than 90% of Ukraine’s grain exports had been moving through its seaports.
A proposed rail route through Moldova to Romania’s Constanta port could carry an estimated 4.5 million metric tons (about 5 million tons) a year – roughly a tenth of the country’s originally forecast annual grain exports. “Trucks and trains are small compared with what goes through the Odesa ports,” Vyacheslav says.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Cargo diverted to the Danube faced congestion, low river levels and further Russian attacks on ports including Izmail, in southwestern Ukraine near the Romanian border. In the first twelve days of August, grain exports were already down 76% from the same period a year earlier. By the end of the month, about 80 vessels were waiting near Romania’s Sulina Canal to reach Ukrainian river ports. A shortage of pilots, frequent air alerts and limited inspection capacity compounded the delays.
The attacks continued into September, threatening the land routes as well. On Sept. 9, Russian drones struck the Starokozache border crossing with Moldova, killing two civilians and injuring three. Further deadly strikes hit Odesa itself in the following days.
Earlier that month, the agriculture minister said favorable conditions might allow monthly agricultural exports to reach 2 million tons, still only around 40% of the volume needed. The river and land routes were moving cargo, but they were not replacing the capacity lost at sea.
The breadbasket paradox
The shortfall reaches countries that depend on Ukrainian harvests, including buyers in Africa whom Vyacheslav sees as an important market. “We are the breadbasket. We play a major role.”
That dependence is reflected in international markets, where disruptions to Ukrainian exports can drive prices higher even as grain piles up inland.
By Aug. 20, Chicago wheat futures – a benchmark for wheat prices – had risen more than 17% since early July, while domestic quotations in Ukraine fell by roughly 15% for both wheat and barley between Aug. 3 and Sept. 7.
For now, Vyacheslav’s irrigation salary helps pay for electricity, gas, water and groceries, keeping the family going when grain provides no reliable income.
Still, he is preparing for another sowing season, hoping exports will recover. But by the end of the year, he fears he could reach a limit. Without enough money from the harvest to buy fuel and fertilizer, he may struggle to finance the next crop.
Whether farming can still provide a living is becoming harder for him to judge. “Honestly, I don’t even know.”
“There will be no village”
I climb out of the tractor and look across the farmland. In a region so dependent on agriculture, a harvest that brings in too little money threatens livelihoods far beyond Vyacheslav’s own household.
Under that pressure, communities rely all the more on mutual help. A friend brings a crate of tomatoes from the next village. Someone a couple of streets away has watermelons to share. When a car will not start, a neighbor helps repair it; when a job needs more hands, others lend theirs.
For Vyacheslav, helping one another extends to sharing the fieldwork with other farmers. “They help me with their combines; I plow or disk their fields.” To him, family farms are part of what holds these communities together. “If we don’t have small farmers, there will be no village.”
From dawn to dusk
Back on the main highway between Mykolaiv and Kherson, dubbed the “Road of Death,” I come to a field worked by Fedor Shpak, right beside the route.
The sun is low as he shuts off his tractor’s engine. Behind him, smoke rises above a neighboring village a few kilometers away.
                                                                                                                                                                         
Shpak cultivates 100 hectares (about 247 acres), growing wheat, barley, sunflowers and peas. “We do not grow vegetables because there are no people. There is no one to do it.”
He links the labor shortage partly to military mobilization. More capable machinery would help him manage with fewer workers, but he lacks the money to replace what he has. “We are working with old wrecks.”
Like Vyacheslav, the 49-year-old combines farming with work for the Inhulets irrigation system, where he operates an excavator for its canal administration. He lives with his wife, Aliona, and their 11-year-old daughter, Bohdana. He works from dawn to dusk, relying on both incomes to keep the family afloat. “Up at five, and off you go,” he says, a brief smile crossing his face.
Out in the fields, he relies on what he can see or hear to detect approaching drones. Farmers across the area call to warn one another, but there are times when the danger forces him to stop work altogether and leave the field.
He shows me metal debris he has collected at the edge of the field – remnants of earlier attacks that cultivation still brings to the surface. “You work it for a year, and it still comes out of the ground.”
“This is our home”
At the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, Fedor’s family and their neighbors took shelter in a nearby cellar. His wife and daughter left as the strikes drew closer, while he stayed with his father-in-law until an impact close by prompted them to leave too. “I left on March 23. Thank God, we made it to Mykolaiv. Shelling started at the bridge, but we got through, thank God.”
Five months passed before he saw his wife and daughter again in Zakarpattia, in western Ukraine. Yet after just three days together, he returned to Posad-Pokrovske. “You had to work. There was rent to pay. Everything had to be paid for.”
Nine months after fleeing, the family was finally reunited in the village. “When we came back, we were shocked. They had taken everything, even out of the house and the garages. We had to start from scratch.”
He had grown up here and invested years of work in the property. Elsewhere, the family had no equivalent place or established life. “It is ours. This is our home. We traveled around – who needs us? Nobody needs us.”
                                                                                                                                                                         
Beyond the next harvest
Fedor faces the same squeeze affecting farmers across the Kherson region: rising costs for fuel, seed and agricultural chemicals. Nitrate fertilizer alone, he estimates, has roughly doubled in price. “Grain, on the other hand, is getting cheaper. It has become much cheaper.”
Beyond the price, there is the question of who will collect his harvest. “Practically nobody wants to come, because it is dangerous. You can understand people not coming.”
His frustration extends to the lack of support for small farmers. He says he has received no meaningful compensation or benefits to help cover the costs of rebuilding and keeping the farm running. “The fighting is not far away. We cleared all the metal out of the fields ourselves, and we still pay taxes. I cannot understand it,” he says.
What troubles Fedor is the future awaiting Bohdana here. With no functioning school or kindergarten in the village, his daughter’s lessons take place online. New educational facilities were supposed to be ready in 2025, he says, but not even the foundations have been laid. “They keep promising.”
Vyacheslav shares that concern for his own daughter. After Kherson’s liberation, she too had wanted to come home. Now he describes a harder life than the family had hoped for, with Zlata missing out on everyday school life and activities with other children.
As a father, he has begun considering whether housing compensation or a housing certificate could help them buy a home somewhere safer, where the 9-year-old could attend school in person.
                                                                                                                                                                         
In the meantime, he is still preparing the land. Farming offers him a measure of peace. “When you work, you rest mentally. You forget about the war.”
Vyacheslav finds a simple satisfaction in seeing a crop through to harvest. “You made it with your own hands. You grew it.”
The sun is setting over the countryside outside Kherson. Pink spreads along the horizon above the yellow-green fields. Houses with damaged facades stand among trees still thick with leaves. Along the road, the drone nets remain overhead. Across the region, the shelling continues.
For now, the last light falls on grain still waiting to be harvested.

Europe misses out on €120 billion in investment a year, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:31:37 UTC
23:31:37 KST

Different national rules and systems for transport, energy, technology and skills are holding back investment across Europe, a new study argues.
Europe’s struggle to build on successful national models across borders could be costing it at least €120 billion a year in missed investment.
That is the estimate of Italian think tank The European House–Ambrosetti (TEHA), in a study produced with Amazon.
The study, published on Thursday, analyses successful national examples across a wide range of sectors—from railway networks to AI, from energy to smart regulation—and argues that Europe does not need to imitate foreign models, but rather integrate leading examples at the European level.
“Europe does not need to look elsewhere for answers. Some of the most compelling investment models are already operating within the EU. They simply have not been connected or scaled,” TEHA senior consultant and the study’s author Diego Begnozzi said in a press statement.
The €120 billion estimate, however, could be even higher as it refers only to additional direct investment. It does not count any wider economic benefits, the report says.
According to a 2024 report on competitiveness led by former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, Europe needs between €750 and €800 billion in additional annual investment to remain competitive in the global economy.
The European Commission is working on recommendations from Draghi’s report and a separate report by former Italian Prime Minister Enrico Letta on how to complete the EU’s single market. Both call for changes to make it easier for businesses to operate across national borders.
Where the costs lie
The study estimates how much more investment Europe could attract with better-connected national markets.
As high energy costs are increasingly threatening the output of the European industry, the report says, “European businesses paid around 2.8 times more for electricity than US businesses in Q1 2025, while greater Single Market integration of national energy systems could generate up to €43 billion annually by 2030.”
On transport, it says that “cross-border train services are 23.4% slower than comparable domestic routes, despite nearly 40 years since the start of railway liberalisation, limiting the value of the Single Market’s physical infrastructure.”
It identifies similar barriers in AI, digital infrastructure, tax rules, education, the labour market and the justice system.
One reason, the report argues, is that national governments have little incentive to pay for projects that benefit other countries too. The EU budget is much smaller than their combined budgets, limiting what it can fund across borders.
The EU budget currently represents around 1% of the EU’s gross national income, a figure the study’s authors consider too low to fund major cross-border investments.
The study compares €170.5 billion in EU spending with €8,856.8 billion spent by member states in 2024. It argues that this leaves the EU with limited scope to make up for a lack of national investment in projects that would benefit several countries.
What Brussels is doing
The EU is working on changes to capital markets rules and measures to support industry. It has also proposed EU Inc., a set of common rules intended to make it easier to start and grow a business across the bloc. The Commission has called for agreement on EU Inc. by the end of 2026.
Two years after the publication of the Draghi report, the Joint European Disruptive Initiative (JEDI Draghi Tracker) said that Europe was falling short in implementing his agenda, as policymakers were moving too slowly to approve and implement legislation.

Forever Chemicals: Ground Zero
Pervasive, persistent and poisonous: How one US company helped pollute the world with forever chemicals.
When scientists discovered a new class of chemicals in the 1940s, they knew they had struck gold. Polyfluoroalkyl substances, known as PFAS, are nearly indestructible – resistant to heat, cold, oil and water. They’ve been used in everything from cookware to cosmetics and from pizza boxes to pesticides. But they also don’t biodegrade in the environment, and some of them are toxic. US corporate giant 3M was the first to mass-manufacture PFAS and allowed them to pollute the environment around its facilities for decades despite being aware of their harmful effects.

🔴 Live: Palestinian President Abbas calls on UN General Assembly to 'not allow another Nakba'

Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas called on the UN General Assembly on Thursday to “not allow another Nakba”. Abbas addressed the assembly via a prerecorded speech from his office in Ramallah. The United States denied him a visa to attend the gathering for the second year in a row. Follow our liveblog for all the latest updates.
Threat to 'life and existence': Major takeaways from Palestinian president's UN speech
France 24's Kethevane Gorjestani takes a look at some of the main takeaways from Abbas' turn on the rostrum at the UN general assembly.

Five EU states push Brussels to ease carbon costs for industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:28:40 UTC
23:28:40 KST

Austria and four Central European countries want more flexibility in the EU carbon market, warning high decarbonisation costs risk driving investment and production overseas.
Austria, Czechia, Hungary, Slovakia and Poland are pushing for changes to the EU's carbon market to give European industry more time and flexibility to cut emissions without losing competitiveness, according to a document seen by Euronews.
The five countries argue that companies face enormous costs to decarbonise factories while competing with producers outside Europe that are not subject to the same carbon price.
"We need something like an 'export discount' because we have a huge problem when we start doing business outside," Austrian Industry and Energy Minister Wolfgang Hattmannsdorfer told reporters on Thursday.
The appeal came as EU industry ministers gathered in Brussels amid debate over the European Commission's proposed revision of the Emissions Trading System (ETS) — added to the Competitiveness Council agenda because of its impact on industry, the Austrian minister said.
Under the ETS, companies in carbon-intensive sectors such as steel, cement and chemicals must buy allowances for their emissions. The more carbon they emit, the more they pay.
Hattmannsdorfer called for "economic patriotism" to keep industries and jobs in Europe, arguing that maintaining European production is crucial for regional wealth, welfare and environmental standards.
EU ministers have warned Brussels that industry needs incentives and flexibility to decarbonise, particularly as factories already face high electricity costs. Businesses similarly argue that if production becomes too expensive in Europe, they could shift elsewhere.
Austria's central bank highlighted the pressures in late 2025, describing the country's export industry as "under pressure on several fronts". Weak German industry, US tariffs, high wage and energy costs and growing competition from China were all weighing on exports.
The outlook has since worsened as the war against Iran has pushed up energy costs, adding further pressure on Austria's – and Europe's – industrial competitiveness and green transition.
Basics before green investment
The five governments argue that factories should only be required to make major decarbonisation investments when basic conditions are in place – including affordable electricity, sufficient grid capacity, hydrogen supplies and infrastructure to transport and store captured CO2.
Removing protection from carbon costs before those conditions exist could have the opposite effect to that intended by Brussels, the document argues. Rather than investing in cleaner European production, companies could move manufacturing elsewhere.
"European industry is being asked to undertake multi-billion-euro investments in electriﬁcation, hydrogen, CCS/CCU and new production processes. These investments require aﬀordable electricity, functioning grids, hydrogen as well as adequate input materials availability and CO2 transport and storage infrastructure," the document says.
Alex Eggert, head of the steel trade body Eurofer, said the industry would reach climate-neutrality while producing in Europe.
“We need an ETS that rewards first movers while supporting the decarbonisation of the whole industry. Withdrawing carbon leakage protection too quickly risks undermining the very investments needed to make the transition,” Eggert said.
The ETS has helped cut emissions from covered sectors by more than 50% since 2005 while generating more than €270 billion in revenues, according to European Commission figures.
But plans to revise the bloc's carbon market have proved highly divisive among EU governments, with several countries pressing Brussels to soften the system's impact on European industry.

Russia plans higher taxes on passive income and foreign online purchases as budget deficit continues
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:27:37 UTC
23:27:37 KST

Russia plans higher taxes on passive income and foreign online purchases as budget deficit continues
Russia’s Finance Ministry has submitted a draft 2027 budget, along with spending plans for 2028 and 2029, to the government.
The budget also would tax passive income — including dividends, interest on deposits, proceeds from property sales, securities transactions, and other income — at rates ranging from 13% to 22%, up from the current 13-15%. The Finance Ministry justified raising the top rate as a “standardization of tax levels.”
“The proposed standardization will affect no more than 6% of the population that has taxable income, or about 4 million people,” the Finance Ministry said.
The tax rate will depend on the amount of income, not the method or source by which it was earned. Deposits up to 1 million rubles and the income of “participants in the SVO” will remain tax-exempt.
The draft budget also includes:
- a 22% VAT rate on purchases made through cross-border e-commerce, with online marketplaces acting as tax agents responsible for paying it
- a customs fee of 100 rubles per parcel for personal-use goods worth up to 200 euros sent from abroad by mail
- indexing insurance pensions twice in 2027 — by 6.8% starting February 1 and by another 3.3% starting April 1. The average old-age pension is expected to reach 29,904 rubles by the end of 2027.
The budget will run a deficit in all three years, about 2% of GDP annually. “The draft budget was designed to be balanced. It will allow the government to fulfill all of its obligations and preserve macroeconomic stability under any possible changes,” Finance Minister Anton Siluanov said.
The Finance Ministry named “financing the country’s defense and security needs, and providing social support to SVO participants and their families” as the budget’s strategic priority.
The previous three-year budget, covering 2026 and the 2027-2028 planning period, also was drafted with a deficit. Among other things, it called for raising the base VAT rate by two percentage points, to 22%.

After so long in Trump’s sights, hopeful Greenlanders breathe a collective sigh of relief
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:27:35 UTC
23:27:35 KST

Greenland’s prime minister, Jens-Frederik Nielsen, and Múte B Egede, the foreign minister, received a hero’s welcome when they landed back in Nuuk from New York on Wednesday night – and a nation took a collective sigh of relief.
Colleagues, friends and members of the public turned out to greet them at an airport where, just 20 months ago, the landing of a Trump-branded plane containing Donald Trump Jr had kickstarted a geopolitical crisis that the people of Greenland now hope is over.
To cheers and applause, and waving red and white Erfalasorput flags, the politicians were credited with saving the nation thanks to a new defence agreement between Greenland, Denmark and the US signed this week at the UN in New York. It comes after an unprecedented period of turbulence in which Donald Trump repeatedly threatened to invade the Arctic island and almost tore apart Nato in the process.
“Welcome home,” the speaker of Inatsisartut, the Greenlandic parliament, Kim Kielsen, said. “Welcome to a country that we were about to lose. You have ensured that we have a future here.” Like many Greenlanders, for the last year-and-a-half he said he had been holding his breath.
Nielsen, who became prime minister last year in the middle of the crisis, told the crowd: “We can be calm. Our land will not be taken. Our land will not be bought. The road has been long, and it has been very difficult and dangerous.”
Hundreds then attended a celebratory coffee party at Katuaq, the Greenlandic capital’s cultural centre. Aqqalukkuluk Fontain, 38, who was there with his girlfriend, Stella, and their youngest daughter, Aura, who is three, said the collective release of tension was palpable. “It was a joyous moment. It’s going to linger for a while,” said the IT manager, who earlier this year organised a protest outside the new US embassy in Nuuk.
He cautioned he could not entirely relax – concerned that, after the midterms, Trump could change his mind and relations could “take a turn for the worse” – but hailed the deal with the US as a moment of pride for Greenland and a stroke of “strategy genius” from Greenlandic and Danish negotiators. “Trump is trying to angle it that he made a great deal. But he wanted total control, ownership of Greenland. He didn’t get that,” he said.
Its full text contains some key differences from the 1951 defence agreement it is intended to update – for example, the US gets underwater access to Greenland and specific permission to construct a missile defence system – but is a far cry from Donald Trump’s original threat to annex the Arctic island. And in terms of tangible outcomes, the biggest winner is arguably Greenland, where it is seen as a potential stepping stone to future independence.
When the 1951 agreement was signed, Greenland was still a colony of Denmark. Now, it is a largely autonomous territory that has signed an agreement alongside Denmark with the US that it played a central role in negotiating.
A big question hanging over Greenland independence was what would happen to its status within Nato and relationship with the US.
The new agreement answers that question. It stipulates that if it did become independent, the governments of Greenland and Denmark would “together ensure that the independent Greenlandic state will agree to remain in Nato, including by applying to become a member if necessary”.
The centrality of Nato to the agreement is also seen as a boost for an alliance that was creaking under US claims against one of its fellow members’ territory.
Greenlandic politician Qarsoq Høegh-Dam, who earlier this year became the first member of the pro-independence party Naleraq to be elected to the Danish parliament, said there was still considerable work to do in terms of gaining independence but that “a lot of what ifs” have now gone.
“It’s a point of relief for Greenlanders,” he said. “They can lower their shoulders a bit, so we can talk about domestic issues, the road to independence more freely, instead of the search of what if?”
Much of the agreement already existed in practice, he said, but now “it is written in ink” with Greenland’s explicit involvement. “It’s a continuation of an agreement since the 1950s. The difference is now that Greenland has some say in it. They want to agree for themselves instead of a country overseas agreeing on behalf of them,” he said. “That’s the difference first and foremost and it is significant.”
He said, however, there were still questions about what the words will equate to in practice, for example on investment. “It’s a good foundation, but the details are missing,” he said.
Given that just a few months ago Trump was threatening to invade Greenland, and a few weeks since he posted a map of Greenland covered with the US flag to social media, in many ways the very fact that a diplomatic agreement has been reached is a victory in itself.
Ulrik Pram Gad, a senior researcher at the Danish Institute for International Studies (DIIS), said: “For Danes and Greenlanders, it’s a win to be able to force Trump into doing something diplomatically. And if this actually puts the Greenland crisis to rest, it will be felt as a win for Greenland, Denmark and Europe because then we can concentrate on real problems and trying to find ways to work with the US on that.”
Aviaja Fontain, 41, a student from Nuuk, said the agreement puts to rest months of anxiety. At one point, amid government warnings about preparedness, she thought Nuuk was being attacked by the US during what turned out to be a power cut caused by a storm. “Many of us have been afraid that Trump will use force, but now I can feel relief,” she said. Now she feels she can finally relax. “We don’t have to think about getting attacked and just live our peaceful life again.”

State Real Estate Ltd. puts former Tallinn Music High School properties up for auction
State Real Estate Ltd. (RKAS) has announced a public online auction for properties in Tallinn's Nõmme district that housed Tallinn Music High School from 1961 to 2022. The starting price is €6.09 million.
The property portfolio for sale comprises developed properties in the block between Vabaduse puiestee and J. V. Jannseni tänav (Vabaduse puiestee 130a, J. V. Jannseni tänav 38a / Vabaduse puiestee 130 and J. V. Jannseni tänav 38), with a total area of 33,127 square meters. RKAS said in the sale listing that it is one of the largest and greenest contiguous development sites in the area.
There is no detailed plan currently in force for the land being sold. Under the Nõmme district comprehensive plan, the properties at J. V. Jannseni tänav 38 and J. V. Jannseni tänav 38a / Vabaduse puiestee 130 are in a mixed-use development area, allowing for residential and commercial space or a mixed-use neighborhood combining the two. The property at Vabaduse puiestee 130a is in an area designated for public and social facilities, making it primarily suitable for educational, civic or community activities.
Bids can be submitted through RKAS' official sales platform where detailed terms of participation, documentation and drawings are also available. The auction deadline is October 22.
The school merged with MUBA and moved to the city center
The complex in Nõmme has stood vacant since summer 2022 when Tallinn Music High School ended operations there after more than six decades.
On September 1 that year, Tallinn Music High School, Georg Ots Tallinn Music School and Tallinn Ballet School were merged to form the state-run Tallinn School of Music and Ballet (MUBA). The new school began classes in a newly completed building on Pärnu maantee in Tallinn.

Relaxed planning rules allow for 4,000 new Zurich flats
Thousands of flats that had previously been blocked by urban planning restrictions can now be built in the Swiss city of Zurich.
The recently amended federal ordinance has lifted a construction freeze on around 4,000 flats in Zurich. This was reported by Swiss public broadcaster SRF on Thursday.
More
Zurich: Welcome to the world capital of housing shortages!
The government’s decision is of great significance for Zurich. Martin Schneider, deputy director of the Office for Urban Development, told SRF that it was a huge relief. “This decision is a very important breakthrough for us,” he said.
It represents the solution to a problem that had caused a great deal of difficulty.
In the past, the strict application of planning regulations meant that many building projects in Zurich were blocked. According to Schneider, the inventory applied not only to historic sites and buildings, but to three-quarters of the city’s total area.
Even small projects, such as the construction of an underground car park or a solar panel installation, provided grounds for appeals. Many affordable cooperative flats, which are urgently needed in the city, were also affected.
+ Buy or rent? Find out where you can afford to live in Switzerland
To boost the stagnating housing construction and promote densification, the government has now amended the ordinance. The new provisions are intended to simplify and speed up planning and approval procedures without disproportionately restricting the protection of urban areas.
The revised regulations will come into force on November 1, 2026. In Zurich, planning applications can be submitted in accordance with the new rules from that date onwards.
The city expects that, in future, many projects will be able to be approved within half a year to a full year, without the previous restrictions.

Saudi Arabia 'threatens to quit Quad' amid US-Sudan UN visa row
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24

Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia 'threatens to quit Quad' amid US-Sudan UN visa row
Saudi Arabia has threatened to withdraw from the Quad mechanism for Sudan amid tensions over Washington's refusal to grant Sudanese army chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan a visa to attend the United Nations General Assembly, according to a report on Thursday.
Washington's refusal to issue the visa was part of an apparent attempt to pressure al-Burhan into accepting a ceasefire proposal, The Africa Report reported.
According to the report, Riyadh criticised Washington's actions, accusing US officials of engaging in "political blackmail" and attempting to besiege Sudan's leadership.
The dispute reportedly prompted Saudi Arabia to threaten to withdraw from the Quad, a diplomatic grouping aimed at mediating an end to Sudan's war that also includes the US, UAE and Egypt.
Riyadh also reportedly threatened to reject decisions "that have thwarted diplomatic efforts and undermined joint action from within".
The report said Saudi criticism was followed by condemnation from UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres and UN member states, amid accusations that Washington was exploiting its position as the UN host country to settle political scores.
However, the Saudi government has not publicly confirmed that it threatened to leave the Quad or announced any decision to withdraw.
Neither the Sudanese government nor the US State Department has commented on the report regarding the alleged Saudi threat.
The claims emerged as the Quad met in New York on Wednesday alongside the Quintet, which comprises the UN, African Union, European Union, Arab League and Intergovernmental Authority on Development (IGAD), the regional body covering the Greater Horn of Africa.
Reports first emerged on Tuesday that Washington had withheld a visa from al-Burhan, who had been scheduled to address the General Assembly in New York on Thursday.
Al-Burhan's army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since April 2023, in a war that has killed tens of thousands of people and triggered the world's largest displacement and hunger crises.
He has addressed the General Assembly twice since the conflict began.
According to reports, Washington made the issuance of al-Burhan's visa conditional on his acceptance of a 90-day ceasefire proposed by US Senior Adviser for Arab and African Affairs Massad Boulos.
AFP, citing two diplomatic sources, also reported that Washington had refused to issue the visa. One source described the move as a "clear violation of the UN's agreement with the US", while another said the visa had been "conditioned" on al-Burhan accepting the three-month truce.
Meanwhile, Reuters reported that Sudan's UN ambassador, Al-Harith Idriss Al-Harith, had written to Guterres requesting the UN's "immediate intervention" with US authorities.
In a statement, Stephane Dujarric, a spokesman for Guterres, said the UN chief was "deeply concerned" that the visa had reportedly not been issued.
He said the UN Secretariat had urged the US, as the host country, to ensure visas were issued in accordance with its obligations under the UN Headquarters Agreement and in time for al-Burhan to participate in the General Assembly.
The State Department issued a statement on Tuesday questioning al-Burhan's legitimacy but did not directly address whether his UN visa was being withheld.
Spokesman Tommy Pigott said neither the Sudanese army nor the RSF "nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan".
He added that the US would "seek to raise the cost of continued conflict on all belligerents".
Sudan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs responded on Wednesday by calling on Washington to engage positively with the country's government.
Any peace initiative, it said, must "be grounded in respect for Sudan's sovereignty, unity, territorial integrity, and legitimate national institutions".
"It must also address the root causes of the war's continuation – foremost among them, negative foreign interference," the ministry added.
Dispute over US ceasefire proposal
Introduced in June, the US plan called for an immediate 90-day humanitarian truce, followed by negotiations towards a permanent ceasefire and a civilian-led transition.
However, the Sudanese army has objected to the proposal, particularly over the terms governing the RSF's withdrawal from territory it controls.
The army has demanded that the RSF withdraw from all cities it has occupied since May 2023, rather than making the more limited withdrawals outlined in the US proposal.
Al-Burhan has also rejected what Sudanese officials describe as a take-it-or-leave-it approach, arguing that previous pauses in fighting allowed the RSF to regroup.
The disagreement spilled over into the UN General Assembly as al-Burhan prepared to travel to New York.
Washington has also refused visas to Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas and some members of Iran's delegation to the UN.

Iryna Lutsak and Pavlo Illiusha won bronze medals at the European Championships in Sofia. Both Ukrainians lost to their opponents in the semifinals.
Ukrainian boxers Iryna Lutsak and Pavlo Illiushа won bronze medals at the European Amateur Boxing Championships in Sofia. Both athletes lost to their opponents in the semifinals. This was reported by the National Olympic Committee of Ukraine, writes UNN.

The first medals for the Ukrainian national team were won by Iryna Lutsak and Pavlo Illiushа in the up-to-80 kg weight categories
In the quarterfinal, the Ukrainian defeated Bulgaria’s Aleyna Mehmed and secured a bronze medal. In the semifinal, Iryna faced Ireland’s Lisa O’Rourke. By a judges’ decision (0:5), the Irish boxer won, so the Ukrainian finished on the third step of the podium.

Pavlo Illiushа, who already has a winning record of appearances in the professional ring, made a successful start at the continental championships. Naturally, these expenses include transport and so on. Nevertheless, for the city, a foreign tourist represents a completely different financial scale," he said.
The deputy minister noted that 95% of tourists from Asia and the Middle East visit local cafes and restaurants while traveling in Russia. Furthermore, about 80% of guests from India and the UAE rate Russian catering and dining establishments highly.
At the same time, 57% of Chinese tourists perceive Russian cuisine as "heavy" food. "Therefore, it is important to adapt even traditional Russian cuisine to the habits of foreign guests," he remarked.

A 6-year-old girl set a world record for solving a Rubik’s Cube
Kyiv • UNN
Lian Yunzhi solves a 3x3x3 cube in an average of 4.27 seconds. The girl trains for 2–3 hours every day and knows more than 1,300 algorithms.
A six-year-old girl from China has set the women's world record for solving a Rubik's Cube. She solved a 3x3x3 cube in an average of 4.27 seconds. UNN reports this, citing The Washington Post.
Details
Lian Yunzhi first recorded an average time of 4.52 seconds at a World Cube Association-certified competition in Wuhan on September 13.
Three days later, after five attempts, she recorded an average time of 4.27 seconds at a similar competition in Guangzhou, China's state broadcaster CCTV reports.
What is known about the girl
Yunzhi, who is from Chengdu, learned to solve a Rubik's Cube at the age of four and spends two to three hours a day training to maintain her mastery of more than 1,300 cube-solving algorithms, her parents told CCTV.
According to the World Cube Association, the record for solving a single 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube belongs to Poland's Teodor Zajder, who solved it in 2.76 seconds in February at the age of nine.
American speedcuber Tommy Cherry set the record for solving a single 3x3x3 Rubik's Cube blindfolded—in 11.56 seconds.
