French-Lebanese man sues over Israel uprooting 600 olive trees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:17:28 UTC
23:17:28 KST

Breadcrumb
French-Lebanese man files legal complaint over Israel's uprooting of 600 olive trees
A French businessman of Lebanese origin has filed a legal complaint against unknown individuals over alleged war crimes, accusing the Israeli military of uprooting 600 centuries-old olive trees owned by his family, his lawyers told AFP on Wednesday.
The 37-year-old Frenchman, who has not been publicly named, said in the complaint that some of the trees were up to 500 years old and had been uprooted from land cultivated by his family for 250 years in the village of Zawtar al-Sharqiya, his birthplace in southern Lebanon.
According to the civil complaint, filed over theft, destruction and damage to property that it alleges amount to war crimes, the trees were uprooted from the ground.
The plaintiff, who states in his complaint that he is "not a member or supporter of Hezbollah" – the armed group fighting Israel – said he suspects the trees were transported to Israel. The complaint adds: "There is no evidence to indicate that Hezbollah was using the house or agricultural fields for military purposes".
Israel has often claimed that its attacks in southern Lebanon, Beirut’s southern suburbs or other parts of the country are targeting Hezbollah bases and operatives. Close to 9,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks on Lebanon since the conflict erupted in October 2023.
According to the plaintiff, a digital entrepreneur, his family home was completely destroyed in an Israeli airstrike just hours before a ceasefire was announced in southern Lebanon in April 2026.
He said that the Israeli army took full control of his village a few weeks later, followed by the uprooting of the olive trees, after Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement in late June, which Israel has failed to uphold.
The complaint argues that "the destruction and uprooting of olive trees is evidence of war crimes committed by Israel in southern Lebanon," citing in particular a report by Amnesty International.
"These events are part of a broader context of ethnic cleansing and the destruction of numerous villages by Israel in southern Lebanon. Our client expects the French justice system to do everything in its power to identify those responsible and bring them to justice," his lawyers told AFP.
Lebanese officials, NGOs and local residents have condemned the systematic destruction of farmland, particularly through burning, by Israel in southern Lebanon.
The Israeli military has used white phosphorus, banned under international law.
Southern Lebanon is home to a significant share of Lebanon’s olive groves, an important part of the country’s agricultural sector, which has been significantly impacted by the war.
Since invading Lebanon in October 2024, just a year after the start of hostilities with Hezbollah, Israel has widened its occupation to include large swathes of the south along the entire border.
Dozens of towns and villages have been razed or largely devastated in the so-called "Yellow Line," a security zone established by the Israeli military which it says is to push Hezbollah back from the border.
Despite a lull in fighting since the June agreement, Israeli attacks have continued across the south, including home demolitions.
Other complaints have been filed in Paris against the Israeli military over alleged war crimes in Lebanon, including one brought by French-Lebanese artist Ali Cherri, who lost his parents in an Israeli airstrike on a residential building in Beirut in April, and another filed in July by a French-Lebanese man who lost his mother, sister and two nephews in Israeli airstrikes.
Israel conducted more than 100 strikes in 10 minutes on Beirut and across Lebanon on 8 April, a day after the US-Iran ceasefire was announced, massacring more than 350 people in what has become locally known as 'Black Wednesday'.
Israel has refused to leave Lebanon before Hezbollah is fully disarmed, but the Iran-backed group has refused to surrender its weapons as long as the occupation continues.

Unknown

23:17:07 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. Russian shipping group Fesco has redirected its container shipments originating in Ankara from the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk to St. Petersburg, the group said.
"FESCO Shipping Group (within the managed perimeter of Rosatom State Corporation) has redirected its intermodal container shipments going from Ankara from Novorossiysk to St. Petersburg," the company noted.
The route includes scheduled rail shipments from the Turkish capital to the port of Gebze, followed by sea delivery to St. Petersburg by the group's maritime services. The first cargo batch of 40 TEUs (20 ft container equivalent - TASS) was dispatched from Ankara on September 19. Upon arrival in Gebze, the containers were loaded onto a Fesco vessel bound for St. Petersburg. The estimated transit time for the entire voyage is around 20 days.
The intermodal route also operates in the reverse direction to transport Russian exports to central regions of Turkey, the operator noted.
"We have adapted the logistics scheme for shipments from Ankara, keeping the rail leg to Gebze and changing the port of destination in Russia to ensure stable deliveries from central Turkey for our clients. Today, FESCO is the only container operator offering direct intermodal delivery from the Turkish capital to St. Petersburg," said German Maslov, the Deputy CEO of Fesco.

====================================================================================================

Difficulties with digital ruble, inflation, price stability: statements by Nabiullina
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:15:39 UTC
23:15:39 KST

ST. PETERSBURG, September 24. /TASS/. High inflation has been a concern for the Russian Central Bank and Russians for many years, so the regulator must ensure price stability, Central Bank Governor Elvira Nabiullina said at the International Banking Forum.
She noted various difficulties with the introduction of the digital ruble, adding that market participants are addressing them.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the regulator’s chief.
Digital ruble
There are various challenges with the introduction of the digital ruble, though market participants are addressing them: "Clearly, there are some issues, certain technical challenges, and cases with clients lacking understanding. The client’s way should be improved, which is natural for projects of such a scale. But I would like to say that all participating banks are working very promptly with us to resolve those situations."
The Bank of Russia is "not chasing" large amounts of funds to be stored in digital ruble wallets.
Stability of prices
High inflation has been a concern for the Russian Central Bank and Russians for many years, so the regulator must ensure price stability: "Not only the Central Bank has been concerned about high inflation for many years, price growth is what our citizens are worried about. This is why we should ensure price stability."
State of Russian economy
Profits to GDP in the Russian economy are currently at a healthy level comparable to that of 2017: "If we look at profits to GDP in the economy, the figure indicates the scale of profit the economy is generating. In terms of this indicator, we are currently at the level of 2017-2019 with steady economic growth and low inflation. This means the economy is generating profit."
Labor shortages, access to technology, and the investment climate are factors constraining the Russian economy: "We see among the factors holding back economic and investment growth are not so much the impact of interest rates, but rather labor shortages, access to technology, and the investment climate. There are sectoral issues, including structural deterioration in conditions for our export industries. This all should be taken into account in building our credit policy, of course."
Banking sector
There are no problems with banking liquidity on the market, this is a "far-fetched" issue, which is being "whipped up for some reason": "There is no shortage of banking liquidity. Banking regulations are responsible for this. Banks are meeting them with a comfortable margin, and we are keeping an eye on it."
The Central Bank’s banking regulation measures are not aimed at influencing monetary policy, but at ensuring the long-term stability of banks: "We do not aim to influence monetary policy. The instrument we use to influence monetary conditions is the key rate. This is our key tool we use. We apply regulations to ensure the stability of the banking system."
National Payment Card System
It is not required that only financial institutions be National Payment Card System (NSPK) shareholders: "We would like to attract not purely financial investors interested in returns from monopolistically set payment service fees. Our goal is to attract a high-quality investor, essentially a partner."
The Bank of Russia is actively discussing the sale of "a fairly large stake" in the NSPK with market participants: "We plan to start consultations with potential buyers as early as October."
In preparing for the NSPK sale, the regulator "assessed the possibility of reducing existing fees for banks," and it intends to gradually lower them: "After we reviewed the situation, we made a fundamental decision to gradually reduce fees for banks."
The Central Bank believes the NSPK should "remain profitable, self-sustaining, and capable of investing in development projects."
Demand for cash
The Bank of Russia sees a certain rise in demand for cash, but its share has risen only slightly and the situation is stabilizing: "We see an increase in demand for cash, but we need to have a broader, macroeconomic view of the economy. The money supply is also growing. Indeed, the share of cash in the money supply structure fell significantly in previous years because banks offered very attractive rates. As the rate is going down the situation is returning to normal to some extent. The share of cash in the money supply structure has risen slightly.".

Trust in the president and the Defense Forces has declined
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:15:00 UTC
23:15:00 KST

Trust in the president and the Defense Forces has declined
According to public‑opinion monitoring commissioned by the Government Office, Estonia's most trusted institutions remain the police and the president.
The most significant changes are the seven‑percentage‑point decrease in trust in the president and the five‑percentage‑point decrease in trust in the Defense Forces.
Of the institutions included in the survey, residents trust the police the most (83 percent trust fully or rather trust) and the president (69 percent).
An equal share of residents (66 percent) trust the Defense Forces and Estonian Public Broadcasting (ERR).
NATO is trusted by 60 percent of residents, up three points; trust in the European Union remains stable at 51 percent. Confidence in the Riigikogu (36 percent) and the government (39 percent) has also remained largely unchanged.
Economic sentiment shows little movement: 47 percent believe they can cover household expenses over the next six months. Overall coping has weakened, falling from 70 percent to 66 percent, with difficulties concentrated among residents of other ethnic backgrounds and people with lower education and income. 69 percent of residents are rather or very satisfied with life, unchanged from June.
Personal security assessments have improved: 61 percent feel safe living in Estonia, up three points. By contrast, only 38 percent believe the state itself is secure. Anxiety remains widespread, with 36 percent frequently feeling worried about global and domestic events.
Concern about energy shortages has risen to 70 percent, while 68 percent remain worried about the war in Ukraine. Fear of a possible conflict in Estonia or Europe has increased to 67 percent.
Support for aiding Ukraine remains high. Eighty percent condemn Russia's military actions, and 47 percent agree Estonia should not rule out military support. Humanitarian aid continues to be backed by 66 percent, and 57 percent support sanctions on Russia even if energy and food prices rise.
Support for the green transition has increased to 41 percent, with significantly higher backing among residents under 50. Among residents of other ethnic backgrounds, support has risen from 26 percent to 39 percent.
1,288 respondents were surveyed, including an additional sample from Ida‑Viru County. Data were collected from 3 to 8 September by Kantar Emor.

Polish Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Radosław Sikorski stated that Poland will not escalate a recent Russian military airspace violation if Moscow issues a formal apology, Polish news agency PAP reported on September 23.
He also warned that the Polish Armed Forces remain prepared to defend national sovereignty against intentional threats.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The diplomatic reaction follows an incident reported by the Operational Command of the Polish Armed Forces, in which a Russian military helicopter violated Polish airspace near Braniewo along the border with Russia’s Kaliningrad region, penetrating approximately 300 meters for 42 seconds before being tracked and exiting Polish territory.
Speaking to reporters in New York following his address to the UN Security Council, Sikorski made clear that Warsaw expects official accountability from Moscow regarding the border breach, according to PAP.
“Such things happen between neighbors, and if the Russian side says 'we are sorry, ' we will not make a big deal out of it,” Sikorski stated.
“If the Russian side says 'we’re sorry, the pilot made a mistake, ' we won’t make a big deal out of it. But whoever is at fault must feel guilty,” he continued.
PAP wrote that, when questioned about whether Poland would shoot down intruding Russian aircraft in future incidents, Sikorski affirmed that operational decisions rest entirely with military commanders under the Polish Constitution.
“If our Air Force Command and Operations Commander determine that this is intentional and that it threatens the property, health, and lives of our citizens, then our constitution is clear: the Polish Army defends the homeland,” Sikorski said, noting that Polish airspace is continuously monitored and guarded alongside NATO allied aircraft and radar networks.
Sikorski’s call for a firm response was mirrored in Warsaw by Presidential Minister Marcin Przydacz, who urged the government to adopt a tougher stance against Moscow to prevent further provocations, PAP reported.
“We need to take a tougher stance towards Russia in a way that doesn’t pose a risk to Poles or their security,” Przydacz stated, adding that an “appropriate military response” managed by the Operational Command is necessary. “If we don’t react, our adversaries will certainly become even more active, even more aggressive.”
During his remarks in New York, Sikorski also addressed recent insults from Russian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova, who suggested Sikorski required psychiatric medication after he discussed personal crisis preparedness in an interview. Sikorski pointed out the hypocrisy in Kremlin rhetoric given recent statements from Russian officials, according to PAP.
“Just a few days ago, Vladimir Putin’s influential advisor, Mr. Patrushev, threatened us with nuclear annihilation. And Ms. Zakharova suggests that such a fear of Russian aggression is a mental illness,” Sikorski remarked to reporters. “So I suggest that Ms. Zakharova and Mr. Patrushev should agree on a position.”
Additionally, Sikorski commented on reports concerning a potential US invitation to Russian leader Vladimir Putin for the upcoming G20 summit in Miami.
According to PAP, Sikorski argued that if he were US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, he would make inviting Vladimir Putin to the G20 summit in Miami strictly conditional on a ceasefire in Ukraine.
Sikorski added that Putin’s potential attendance would create an “image problem” for invited leaders, including Polish President Karol Nawrocki. He referenced a recent meeting of G20 finance ministers in Asheville, where Polish Finance Minister Andrzej Domański and other European delegates forced organizers to exclude Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov from the official group photograph.

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Nobody is talking about hundreds or thousands. Hundreds are being gathered, one or two missiles at a time,” Zelenskyy stated, as quoted by Suspilne.
The Ukrainian leader described the process as extremely complex. He said that securing even batches of two, three, or five missiles requires decisions made directly by partner countries’ leaders.
Requests handled only between lower-level teams produce no results, he added, because the missiles are scarce and expensive.
Zelenskyy identified the US as the only country capable of providing missiles on a significantly larger scale. He said he was asking US President Donald Trump to help meet Ukraine’s needs despite global shortages and depleted stockpiles caused in part by the war in the Middle East.
Suspilne added that Zelenskyy stressed Ukraine continues to work with all of its partners.
The plea to Washington comes after weeks of strained deliveries of Patriot interceptors.
US President Donald Trump reportedly declined Zelenskyy's request for several hundred additional Patriot missiles during talks in the Oval Office on July 28.
He cited depleted American stockpiles and Middle East commitments.
On August 5, Ukrainian air defenses failed to stop any of the 28 missiles Russia launched, including 24 ballistic missiles, in an attack that killed 17 people in Kyiv and the surrounding region.
Three days later, Zelenskyy announced that the US had agreed to monthly Patriot deliveries, without disclosing volumes, while cautioning that the supply would not be sufficient.

IDF rebukes police over West Bank tunnel report, says only shafts found
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:11:33 UTC
23:11:33 KST

The IDF on Thursday took the unusual step of publicly contradicting an Israel Police announcement that security forces had discovered a tunnel near the West Bank city of Qalqilya, saying an investigation found two deep shafts but no underground passage connecting them.
The IDF also sharply criticized the previous day's announcement, describing reports that a tunnel had been uncovered as “official and irresponsible” statements.
Police said Wednesday that officers and Border Police forces operating in Qalqilya had discovered a “tunnel in the process of being dug” that was at least 25 meters, or 82 feet, deep and contained numerous weapons. Police also said a second tunnel had been found in the initial stages of excavation and that four suspects had been arrested.
The military presented a substantially different account Thursday.
According to the IDF, troops, Border Police officers and Israel Police personnel operating under the Ephraim Brigade entered Qalqilya overnight following intelligence about weapons in the sector. They discovered two shafts about 12 meters, or 39 feet, deep and found an M16 rifle, a hunting rifle, a handgun and ammunition nearby. The weapons were confiscated.
Combat engineers from Yahalom, the IDF's elite unit specializing in tunnels and other underground threats, were called to examine the shafts.
“Contrary to official and irresponsible statements that emerged on the matter, following an examination of the shafts, the presence of a tunnel route was ruled out. It was also determined that the shafts were not located in proximity to the area of the security barrier,” the military said.
The IDF did not name the police in its criticism, but the statement was a clear reference to the police announcement issued the previous night.
The “seam zone” refers to the area along Israel's West Bank security barrier, separating much of the West Bank from Israel. Qalqilya lies immediately east of the barrier and close to several communities inside central Israel, making reports of a possible underground infiltration route particularly sensitive in the aftermath of the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel.
Security forces arrested four people suspected of involvement in terrorist activity during the operation. The detention of two Israeli citizens was extended until Tuesday, while two Palestinian suspects were expected to appear before a military court.
Security forces were continuing extensive searches in the area Thursday for additional shafts and weapons, the IDF said.
‘A tunnel here would change everything’
Before the military issued its clarification, the police announcement had prompted alarm among residents and local officials in the southern Sharon region, which lies just across the security barrier from Qalqilya.
“I didn't fall out of my metaphorical chair last night when they announced they had found a tunnel or weapons cave in Qalqilya,” said R., a farmer from one of the Israeli communities near the seam zone. “It even brought a cynical smile to my face.”
“It was only a matter of time and luck,” he added. “We're lucky they caught it in time, but everyone who said in the past that we were exaggerating when we assessed that they were planning something here too should apologize today.”
Roni, a student from northern Israel who lives in Kfar Saba, an Israeli city immediately west of Qalqilya, said the initial report had frightened her.
“This is supposedly a quiet city in central Israel,” she said. “You think it isn't like the north, where Hezbollah is on the border — or at least was before the war — and suddenly you discover that terrorism is here and raising its head. Now is the time to stop it before it's too late.”
Eran Beck, a farmer from Moshav Tzofit, about 1.5 kilometers, or less than a mile, from Qalqilya, said he had not been surprised either.
“Everyone expected it, and it shows us that what seems far away is getting closer quickly,” Beck said before the IDF ruled out the tunnel. “Who knows if there aren't more tunnels?”
He said several Israeli communities are only a short distance from Qalqilya and expressed concern that an armed cell crossing the barrier could reach communities such as Nir Eliyahu or Neve Yamin within minutes.
The residents' comments reflected the anxiety generated by the police announcement, even though the military later determined that no tunnel had been found.
Local officials said they, too, initially learned about the reported discovery through the media before receiving additional information from security officials.
Kfar Saba Mayor Rafi Saar, who also heads a forum representing Israeli communities along the seam zone, urged residents not to panic.
“It is important for me to reassure the residents of Kfar Saba,” Saar said. “We are prepared, we are in continuous contact with the security forces and there is no change in the instructions. There is no reason for panic. We are continuing our routine responsibly and calmly.”
Saar said he first learned of the incident from media reports and later spoke with military officials in the area, who told him that the situation differed from the initial description.
“From what I understood, it's more of a pit than a tunnel,” he said.
But Saar said the possibility of an underground infiltration from Qalqilya remains part of local emergency planning.
“The scenario of a tunnel beginning in Qalqilya and terrorists emerging from it in Kfar Saba is a scenario we think about all the time, just like a drone scenario or an infiltration above ground,” he said. “A tunnel here, in a seam-zone community, would change everything.”
Saar said residents should remain calm but vigilant and argued that communities along the West Bank barrier require security resources comparable to those provided to Israeli communities near the Gaza border.
“The state must treat us like the Gaza border communities,” he said. “That includes increasing the resources, as I said even before Oct. 7. We warned about this in the past.”
He said security in the area had improved because of increased military activity but called for additional equipment and resources throughout the region.
Local officials criticize conflicting accounts
Oshrat Gani Gonen, head of the Drom HaSharon Regional Council, welcomed the IDF's conclusion that no tunnel had been found but said the sharply conflicting official announcements exposed a broader coordination problem.
“First of all, we're very happy that the suspicion of a tunnel was ruled out,” she said. “I wish every security concern troubling our residents ended this way.”
“But we cannot ignore what happened here over the past 24 hours,” she added. “Yesterday, an official Israel Police announcement said there was a tunnel 25 meters deep. Today, after an examination by the IDF and Yahalom, we're getting a different picture: two shafts, weapons, four suspects in terrorist activity, but no tunnel route and no proximity to the seam zone.”
Gani Gonen said the discrepancy demonstrated the need for closer coordination among the military, police, local authorities, community security coordinators and civilian emergency squads operating near the West Bank barrier.
“When two Israeli security bodies give the public such different information about the same incident, it only illustrates what we have been saying for years: Along the seam zone, there must be full coordination,” she said. “Everyone needs to see the same picture, share information and work as one system.”
She stressed that her earlier comments on the incident had been based on the official information released by police.
“Once updated information was received from the IDF, it is right and important to set the record straight,” she said, adding that the discrepancy between the two announcements required examination and better coordination, particularly in such a sensitive security area.
Hod Hasharon Mayor Amir Kochavi, meanwhile, said the incident should be viewed as part of a broader problem involving Palestinians crossing through gaps in the West Bank security barrier.
“The state allows the illegal and unregulated passage of Palestinians every day,” Kochavi said. “Most come here to work, and that is supposedly good for the state because of the labor shortage, so it turns a blind eye. Most Palestinians who cross the fence come to earn a living, but there are also those involved in crime and those planning the next attack.”
Kochavi called for a coherent government policy on crossings, whether through tighter restrictions, regulated entry into Israel or a combination of the two.
“It's good that they uncovered what they uncovered, but you have to look at everything holistically,” he said. “When the state turns a blind eye, only bad things can happen.”

UN General Assembly: Which Arab leaders are missing and why?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:10:05 UTC
23:10:05 KST

Breadcrumb
UN General Assembly: Which Arab leaders are missing and why?
The UN General Assembly (UNGA) kicked off on Tuesday, with around 130 heads of state and government gathering in New York for high-level debates and speeches.
UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres opened the session, held under the theme "Restoring trust, managing transformation: a United Nations that delivers for all".
Other high-level meetings are being held on issues including climate action, rising sea levels, pandemic preparedness and the elimination of nuclear weapons.
While several speeches have already focused on the wars in the Middle East and the genocide in Gaza, some prominent Arab leaders have been notably absent from the stage.
The New Arab looks at who they are and what is known about the reasons behind their absence.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi was absent from the UNGA in New York for the fifth consecutive year, prompting speculation over why he has once again stayed away.
Sisi's decision not to attend is particularly noteworthy as he previously attended UNGA sessions, while delivering speeches virtually in 2020 and 2021 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.
Since then, Egypt has instead been represented by officials including Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, former Foreign Minister Sameh Shoukry and current Foreign Minister Badr Abdel-Aty.
Some analysts have previously attributed Sisi's absence to strained relations with US administrations, while others have pointed to the possibility of protests over Egypt's human rights record.
Earlier this month, Sisi attended the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India, where he met Russian, Iranian and Indian leaders.
His continued absence from the UNGA has therefore attracted attention, with some commentators speculating that he may be seeking to avoid possible confrontations with US President Donald Trump, pressure over US demands concerning Gaza or involvement in the war on Iran.
Relations between Washington and Cairo have faced fresh tensions in recent weeks after the US Treasury Department imposed sanctions on branches of Banque Misr in the UAE over allegations that they helped finance Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The US Congress has also refused to approve a deal for F-15 fighter jets for the Egyptian military since 2022 and has not supplied Egypt with AIM-120 missiles for its F-16 fighter jets, which the country's air force has relied on for years.
No official reason has been given for Sisi's absence. Speculation has ranged from Egypt's economic crisis and domestic pressures to regional tensions involving the Red Sea, Gaza, Yemen, Sudan and Iran, as well as potential threats to Egyptian security and the Suez Canal.
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas
Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas is also absent from the gathering after the US barred the Palestinian delegation from attending the UNGA in New York in person.
Abbas was denied an entry visa for the second consecutive year.
The State Department did not give specific details on the decision but said the visa restrictions were imposed over actions by Palestinian officials to "internationalize the Israeli-Palestinian conflict", including pursuing cases against Israel at international tribunals.
At least 152 countries voted for a resolution last week calling on the US to reverse its decision. The US, Israel and Paraguay voted against the resolution, while Colombia, Honduras, Panama and Peru abstained.
The countries supporting the resolution argued that preventing the Palestinian delegation from attending constituted a violation of the UN Headquarters Agreement.
The agreement between the UN and the US requires Washington, as the host country, to facilitate the entry of diplomatic delegations, member states and observers attending General Assembly meetings.
Abbas is expected to use his address to press for international recognition of Palestinian statehood, highlight Israel's war on Gaza and push for renewed momentum towards a two-state solution.
He is also expected to address Israeli settler violence in the occupied West Bank and the continued expansion of illegal settlements on Palestinian land.
Sudanese Armed Forces chief Abdel Fattah al-Burhan
Sudanese Armed Forces chief General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan is another prominent Arab figure absent from New York after the US refused to grant him a visa.
Burhan's army has been fighting the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) since 2023 in a devastating conflict that has displaced millions.
The US State Department said neither the army nor the RSF, "nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan".
UN chief Guterres was "deeply concerned" that Burhan had not been issued a visa, according to his spokesperson.
Sudan rejected the US decision and called on Washington to engage positively with Khartoum.
The foreign ministry said on Wednesday that Sudan "upholds its national sovereignty" and strongly rejected the State Department's position questioning the legitimacy of the Sudanese Armed Forces in relation to constitutional governance.
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia threatened to withdraw from the Quad, a diplomatic grouping involving the US, Egypt, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, in protest at the visa decision, according to The Africa Report on Thursday.
Morocco’s King Mohammed VI
Morocco’s King Mohammed VI did not attend the UNGA, sending instead Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita to deliver the national address.
Bourita included the king’s strategic vision on global stability and international law in his speech.
King Mohammed has skipped the UNGA for several consecutive years, having last attended in September 2012 for the 67th session.
Since then, he has not attended in person and instead has sent other representatives, such as his brother Moulay Rachid or the foreign minister.
There have been various reports about why the king has long been absent from the UNGA, with some reports stating it is due to underlying medical conditions. In 2018, he underwent a heart operation in Paris for an irregular heartbeat.
He has also reduced his public appearances, with reports noting that he has appeared visibly frail since 2025.

One year ago on 25 September 2025, the Huthi de facto authorities in Sana’a arbitrarily detained prominent lawyer and human rights defender Abdul Majid Sabra. In response, Diala Haidar, Amnesty International’s Yemen Researcher, said:
“Abdul Majid Sabra, a lawyer who dedicated his career to defending those detained based on the peaceful exercise of their human rights, continues to be arbitrarily detained at the Huthi-run Security and Intelligence detention centre in Chamlan. He was arrested from his office a day ahead of the anniversary of Yemen’s 26th of September Revolution, a date the Huthis oppose celebrating. According to a relative, he was interrogated about his social media posts marking the anniversary and about his profession as a human rights lawyer. To date, he has not been formally charged.
“Abdul Majid Sabra’s case is emblematic of the Huthis’ broader authoritarian practices to target critics, lawyers, human rights defenders and human rights and civil society workers in their attempt to control civic space and silence dissent. Their complete disregard of international human rights law, the rule of law and fair trial rights has made a mockery of the judiciary system under their control.
“The Huthi de facto authorities must immediately and unconditionally release Abdul Majid Sabra and all those arbitrarily detained solely for peacefully exercising their human rights and end their campaign against dissent.”
Background
Abdul Majid Sabra was arrested on 25 September 2025 from his office in Sana’a by a group of Huthi armed forces and armed men in civilian clothing. His arrest was part of a broader pattern of arrests of people publicly commemorating the 26th of September anniversary of the establishment of the Yemen Arab Republic in 1962. The anniversary is traditionally marked by celebrations that include torch-lighting ceremonies and people taking to the streets carrying the flag of the Yemeni Republic. Amnesty International has previously documented the Huthi de facto authorities carrying out a wave of arrests and rounding up scores of people who gathered to peacefully commemorate the anniversary of Yemen’s 26th of September Revolution.

Father of Latvian PM candidate Jūlija Stepaņenko owns a company in the Moscow Region that made “dragon’s teeth” for the Russian military

14:09:08 UTC
23:09:08 KST

The Insider has found that the father of Saeima deputy Jūlija Stepaņenko, Sergei Fedotov, is the majority owner of two companies in the Moscow Region. One of them produced concrete anti-tank barriers known as “dragon’s teeth” for the Russian military. According to public declarations for 2022 and 2024, Fedotov has given Stepanenko nearly 240,000 euros and an apartment in Riga worth 180,000 euros since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The father of Jūlija Stepaņenko, the leader of Latvia’s Sovereign Power (Suverēnā vara, SV) party, is Russian businessman Sergei Fedotov. He owns majority stakes in two companies in Solnechnogorsk, outside Moscow — Forma ZhBI LLC and PLK Forma LLC. Both are family businesses. Sergei’s wife, Irina Fedotova, and his daughter, Anna Makarovskaya, are also listed as shareholders.
Stepaņenko previously said that her father lives in Russia and provides financial support to her family, but she did not disclose his identity. Her financial declarations list two large gifts from him worth a combined 419,598 euros. In October 2022, she declared 239,598 euros in cash, and in January 2024 she was gifted an apartment in Riga from her father worth 180,000 euros.
The Insider identified Stepanenko’s father as 72-year-old Sergei Alexeievich Fedotov, a businessman from Solnechnogorsk.
Fedotov owns 73.45% of PLK Forma and 72.68% of Forma ZhBI. The latter manufactures concrete, mortar, reinforced-concrete products, and landscaping elements, while PLK Forma is involved in construction and in the management and leasing of commercial real estate, including industrial, warehouse, and office space.
It is a sizable family business. From 2021 through 2024, Fedotov’s two companies generated annual revenue of 550 million to 680 million rubles ($6.9 million to $8 million). In 2024, they earned nearly 120 million rubles ($1.4 million) in net profit. However, the figures fell sharply in 2025, when combined revenue dropped to 235 million rubles ($2.8 million) and a small loss replaced the previous profit.
Fedotov’s businesses were not limited to civilian construction. At the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Forma ZhBI reported that it had produced around 2,000 “dragon’s teeth” and tetrapods — concrete anti-tank obstacles. They were sent to Russian-occupied parts of Donbas and Russia’s Belgorod Region, which borders Ukraine and saw multiple incursions by Ukrainian-backed armed groups in 2023 and 2024. The company also said it supplied stoves to the Russian military.
In August, Fedotov’s company was visited by Viktor Bout, an arms dealer who was convicted in the United States in 2011 before being released in a 1-for-1 prisoner swap for WNBA player Brittney Griner in 2022. The visit took place during Bout’s campaign for the State Duma as a candidate from the nationalist Liberal Democratic Party of Russia (LDPR). Footage aired by Russian television showed Fedotov giving Bout a tour of the business and sitting beside him. During the visit, Bout said Russia was “sometimes in a hybrid war, sometimes in an open war” and called for bureaucratic obstacles to be removed so that important infrastructure could be protected.
In an interview with The Insider, Fedotov confirmed that he is indeed Jūlija Stepaņenko’s father. He also confirmed that he transferred all of his Latvian assets to his daughter after the country’s border was closed to Russian citizens.
“I honestly bought an apartment [in Riga] so I wouldn’t have to bother my daughter and so I could see my grandchildren more often. I paid taxes, but when it became impossible to travel there, I gave the apartment to my daughter,” Fedotov said.
“I would like to remind you that I was born in Latvia, lived there for almost 25 years, graduated from university, worked under the [Soviet] job-assignment system and was drafted into the army by the Riga military enlistment office as a reserve officer. I served in military construction units and built purely civilian facilities.
After that, there was nowhere to return to because the political situation had changed. For some reason, I had already become an occupier and so on. So I was forced to stay here in the Moscow region and start my own business, which is what I still do today.
All that time, I traveled to Latvia without any problems. I had a long-term visa. My parents, grandparents, and aunt are buried there.
Today I have been deprived of the ability both to see my daughter there and to visit the graves of relatives.”
On Sept. 5, The Insider tried to speak with Stepaņenko at a campaign tent in Riga. She declined to comment, saying she gives interviews to national media but that, given the current geopolitical situation, she needed to consider whether she should speak to a foreign outlet.
Stepaņenko has led Sovereign Power since 2022 and is the Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Union alliance’s candidate for prime minister. She campaigns on “family values,” opposes financial aid to Ukraine, and has said both sides in the conflict bear responsibility for the start of the war.
In its 2025 report, Latvia’s State Security Service (VDD) named three parties that it said had worked most actively to deepen the isolation of Russian-speaking residents: Stability!, Sovereign Power, and the Latvian Russian Union. The VDD assessed that their activities contributed to Russia’s strategic objectives.
Latvia’s parliamentary election is scheduled for Oct. 3. According to the latest SKDS poll, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ United List leads with 15.2%, followed by Stepaņenko’s Sovereign Power/Young Latvians Union alliance with 11.8%. The Progressives, Latvia First, New Unity, and the National Alliance follow.

Bentley launches its first EV, and it could be its cheapest model
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24

23:08:59 KST

Bentley’s first fully electric car tests wealthy buyers’ appetite for luxury EVs, and it comes with a €408 million investment in its Crewe factory. The launch supports existing jobs at a time when several high-end rivals have delayed or dropped plans for electric models.
After more than 100 years, British luxury carmaker Bentley has launched what it calls "one of the most significant new Bentleys in the company’s long history": its first fully electric model.
The Torcal is Bentley’s fourth model line and its first test of wealthy buyers’ appetite for a fully electric Bentley. The stakes are high for the Volkswagen-owned carmaker: Bentley delivered 4,200 cars in the first half of 2026, down 13.6% from a year earlier.
Bentley has also completed a £350 million (about €408 million) investment in its Crewe factory. The investment covers wider upgrades, including a new production line for the Torcal. UK Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said it would support 4,000 existing jobs at the site.
Electric car sales are growing across the EU, but luxury carmakers disagree on how quickly their buyers will make the switch. Porsche has delayed some electric models, Lamborghini has dropped plans for an electric Lanzador, and McLaren says its customers are not yet asking for an EV.
Ferrari unveiled its first EV, the Luce, in May. Its design drew criticism, but Ferrari’s chief executive said in July that orders were progressing in line with expectations, including from new customers.
Bentley is making a different bet: that a familiar-looking SUV, positioned at the entry end of its range, can attract younger buyers as well as existing customers. The Torcal is reported to start at £173,300 (about €202,000) in the UK.
This is below the starting prices listed for Bentley’s other three model lines: £181,365 (about €211,000) for the Bentayga, £207,120 (about €241,000) for the Flying Spur and £239,320 (about €279,000) for the Continental GT.
Bentley says the SUV can travel up to 600 kilometres on a charge. The more powerful Torcal S can accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in 2.9 seconds. Bentley has also created a sound inspired by its traditional V8 engine to preserve some of the familiar driving feel.
The all-new Torcal, "in every aspect of its design, technology, craftsmanship, materials and sustainability, it is a template for future Bentleys, regardless of powertrain," said the company in a statement.
The launch comes after Bentley pushed back its original 2030 deadline for going fully electric to 2035 — and later said that even the 2035 target could be extended.

Gucci is selling new models of luxury sneakers labeled &quot;Made in China&quot; — how much they cost and why they are being criticized
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
17:07:55 EEST
23:07:55 KST

Gucci is selling new models of luxury sneakers labeled "Made in China" — how much they cost and why they are being criticized
Kyiv • UNN
Gucci has started selling Chinese-made Drip sneakers and slip-ons for up to $1,000. Experts fear a blow to the brand's image.
Fashion brand Gucci has begun selling new models of luxury sneakers bearing the label "Made in China". This marks a departure from the brand’s Italian manufacturing traditions. In the view of some industry experts, the move could harm Gucci’s image as a luxury-goods manufacturer at a time when the company is trying to win back middle-class shoppers, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The publication notes that the decision highlights the complexity of the task facing Gucci designer Demna: he needs to create innovative products while controlling costs in order to attract so-called "aspirational" shoppers—the core mass of luxury-goods consumers, who are more price-sensitive than ultra-wealthy clients.
On Friday, Demna will present his new collection at a show in Milan. His success is crucial for parent company Kering and its CEO Luca de Meo, who took over the group last year with the aim of turning it around; however, this year, an initial rise in the share price has given way to stagnation.
Sales at Gucci—the flagship brand of the Kering group—have halved over the past three years, resulting in lower margins and forcing the group to close dozens of stores.
In a style reminiscent of his work at Balenciaga, Demna created a futuristic sneaker model called the Drip. According to information on Gucci’s website, the footwear bears the label "Made in China". Reuters also spotted Drip models with the same label at a Gucci store in Paris.
In a statement, Gucci said that Italy "will always remain at the heart of the manufacturing model and the brand’s identity," but the company decided to work with a Chinese manufacturer—just as it had previously worked with Swiss and Japanese suppliers to produce watches and eyewear.
"The chosen partner offered the technological know-how and manufacturing capabilities that best matched the quality and performance standards we sought to achieve," the company added.
A Gucci representative said there were no broader plans to move Gucci’s production outside Italy.
In addition
The Drip model, which Gucci’s website calls "Demna’s first sneakers for Gucci," went on sale last month as part of the designer’s Primavera collection.
These sneakers cost around 800 euros in Europe and $1,000 in the United States; they are cheaper than many other Gucci footwear models, although they remain in the luxury-goods category. The laceless model is made of nylon, sturdy fabric (canvas), or suede. The Drip differs from Gucci’s more traditional lace-up white leather Ace sneakers; its sock-like shape evokes associations with Demna’s chunky sneakers for Balenciaga—a street-fashion hit of the late 2010s.
According to information on Gucci’s website, another laceless sneaker model (slip-on) from the same Primavera collection also bears the label "Made in China". A brand representative said that this model was made in China for similar technical reasons related to the footwear’s design.
All other Gucci footwear for which the website specifies the country of origin is made in Italy.
The media outlet notes that China is the world’s center of sneaker manufacturing, and local manufacturers have earned a good reputation among both mass-market brands and premium-goods producers. However, some analysts point out that in Gucci’s case, abandoning the "Made in Italy" label could provoke a negative reaction.
"In our view, this creates a potential contradiction between the product’s origin and the brand’s positioning in the luxury segment, which Gucci is seeking to restore," says an analytical note from Berenberg.
Simon Whitehouse, a Milan-based consultant in the luxury industry, put it more bluntly: "The ‘Made in China’ label does not look ideal."
Two sources at Kering told Reuters that the brand has also begun lowering prices on certain products (including in China) as part of measures to regain market share.
Barclays analyst Carole Madjo said the price cuts came as a surprise to some investors, who are now closely watching for any further moves that could affect Gucci’s image in the eyes of shoppers.
"Some are asking themselves: should they continue buying Gucci if prices are falling? — she says. — The presence of Chinese-made products could fuel the debate about the relationship between the brand’s price and value."

Iran threatens to hit back at countries that ban its airlines
Iran's national security chief has threatened to hit back at countries that cooperate with US attempts to cripple its aviation industry as route cancellations gather pace.
A handful of countries have suspended Iran-operated flights in recent days after the Trump administration threatened to target them with sanctions if they continued to deal with Iranian airlines.
"If you stand by America, we will not simply watch you … your airports will have no flights," Mohsen Rezaei, the head of the Supreme National Security Council, said on state TV on Wednesday.
The US earlier this month imposed sanctions on 27 Iranian airliners, including state-owned Iran Air and Mahan, Iran's largest carrier, as part of its efforts to crush the country's economy.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week that any organisation that continues to work with airlines after 23 September would be frozen out of the dollar financial system. That includes any company that provides services, such as ground handling and ticketing, as well as airport operators.
Several countries have suspended flights operated by Iranian carriers since the announcement, including Turkey, Oman, Azerbaijan and Georgia.
The most recent was the United Arab Emirates, which Iranian media said on Thursday had cancelled all flights operated by Iranian airlines.
As of Thursday, Mahan was also no longer listing flights to India and Malaysia. Neither of the countries has officially announced that flights would be suspended.
A handful of countries have yet to comply with the sanctions, including China and Iraq.
Beijing has opposed the sanctions, calling them illegal under international law.
Iraq, among the top destination countries for Iranian travellers, has not officially announced that it would ban Iranian airlines, though anonymous government officials have said flights would be suspended. As of Thursday morning, Mahan was offering tickets to Najaf and Baghdad.
The airline is also continuing to list flights to Russia, Pakistan and Thailand.
International travel was already heavily restricted for Iranian passengers before the latest sanctions. Flights to key destinations in the region such as Turkey and the UAE had been curtailed by the war, and many major international carriers had suspended routes to Iran.

The Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the rebel group at the centre of Ethiopia's 2020-2022 war, has said that it had launched an attack against the Ethiopian army in the country's north.
In a statement, the TPLF-led Tigray regional government said federal forces had launched an attack on Wednesday and that its forces had been ordered to enter what it described as a “defensive” war.
The group also claimed that federal forces had launched a large-scale offensive from several directions, using infantry and mechanised units as well as drones and other air assets.
Local media reported clashes between federal forces and TPLF-affiliated forces in parts of Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.
Getachew Reda, a former head of Tigray's interim administration who now serves as a federal government adviser, accused the TPLF leadership of launching a large-scale attack on government positions in Afar and Amhara.
Speaking at the UN General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, Ethiopian President Taye Atske Selassie said his country had exercised “immense restraint” despite what he described as interference by “adversarial elements.”
Renewed fears of war in Tigray
The latest escalation follows reports that TPLF forces had taken control of Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray.
Ethiopian Airlines suspended flights to Mekelle, Axum and Shire in the Tigray region from Wednesday, citing the security situation.
The African Union called for restraint as military tensions increased, saying the Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement, signed in November 2022, remains the foundation of the peace process.
The United Nations also expressed concern over the deteriorating situation.
Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged the parties to de-escalate tensions and return to dialogue under the 2022 Pretoria agreement.
The TPLF and Ethiopia's federal government fought a two-year war that began in November 2020. The conflict, which was centred in Tigray and drew in forces from neighbouring regions, is estimated to have killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions.
The war ended with the Pretoria agreement, which halted major fighting but left several issues unresolved, including the status of disputed areas in western Tigray, the return of displaced people and the disarmament of TPLF forces.
The TPLF, which dominated Ethiopia's political system for decades before Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed came to power in 2018, has remained a major political and military force in Tigray.
Last week, seven armed and political groups from different parts of Ethiopia, including the TPLF, announced that they had allied to coordinate their opposition to the federal government led by Abiy.

Rubio warns of Iraq ‘Balkanisation’: Is that a real threat?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:04:43 UTC
23:04:43 KST

Rubio warns of Iraq ‘Balkanisation’: Is that a real threat?
The US secretary of state’s warning comes after he and Trump met the Iraqi PM on the sidelines of the UNGA.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has warned that Iraq risks “Balkanisation” unless its armed factions are brought under state control.
He made the remarks to reporters at the Palace Hotel in New York City on Wednesday, on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, after meeting Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi Tuesday night.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran cancels Baghdad, Muscat flights as US aviation sanctions take effect
- list 2 of 4US, Iran hold mediated UNGA talks on ending war, opening Strait of Hormuz
- list 3 of 4US aviation sanctions disrupt Iran flights, push travellers overland
- list 4 of 4Turkiye agrees to gradual handover of Bashiqa base to Iraq
Rubio said Washington had no doubt about al-Zaidi’s commitment to disarming Iraqi armed groups, but called it a massive and difficult challenge.
He said at least three armed groups had disarmed and joined the national government, while at least one had been far less cooperative.
Bringing all weapons under state control, he said, would mean Iraq no longer had “independent forces operating and balkanising the country”.
So what does Rubio really mean? And is the breakup of Iraq a real threat? Here’s what you need to know:
What does ‘Balkanisation’ mean?
It means a country breaking up into smaller, rival units, usually along ethnic or religious lines.
The term comes from the fragmentation of the Balkans as the Ottoman Empire collapsed in the early 20th century.
In Iraq’s case, it has often been used to describe concerns that the country could split along ethnic and sectarian lines.
However, what Rubio was pointing to was “fractures within the Iraqi state system” caused by Iran-aligned armed groups, Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East Security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told Al Jazeera.
These groups act as rivals to one another, “but also by serving as arteries for pro-Iranian regime interests inside Iraq by wielding parallel economic channels, political influence, and oil smuggling networks”, she said.
Is Iraq at risk of breaking up?
Not imminently, although interpretations differ on how seriously to take Rubio’s warning.
“Balkanisation as Rubio framed it means more that Iraq risks failing to become a centralised, stable state that can wean off Iranian interference – not that it faces imminent territorial partition,” Ozcelik said.
She described the armed groups as a “festering, now structural” challenge, and said they have “operated inside federal Iraq with near impunity”.
Zeidon Alkinani, a Middle East political analyst and founding director of the Arab Perspectives Institute, was more sceptical.
He told Al Jazeera that Rubio’s remark could be read “either as a pressure tactic to push the Iraqi government forward on the disarmament process, or as a sign of the administration’s limited understanding of Iraq and the wider region”.
He said disarmament was “a major turning point” in Iraq’s post-2003 politics, but “far from the greatest challenge Iraq has faced”, pointing to the 2003 United States invasion, the sectarian strife of 2006–2007, the war against ISIL (ISIS) from 2014 to 2017 and the 2017 Kurdish independence referendum as far graver threats to the country’s unity.
What do we know about Trump and Rubio’s meetings with al-Zaidi?
Very little.
Rubio told reporters he first met with the Iraqi prime minister, and then US President Donald Trump met with him on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York on Tuesday evening.
Al-Zaidi’s office said in a statement that they discussed political, economic and investment cooperation as well as regional security.
Why is the timing of the meeting important?
It was the second meeting between the two leaders since July, when al-Zaidi promised at the White House that armed factions would have no justification after September 30.
That deadline has since slipped; al-Zaidi told The New York Times that disarmament would now run until June 30, 2027.
Alkinani said that the government is in “a highly delicate position”, as many Iraqis strongly support disarmament, having long seen armed groups outside state institutions as a central pillar of corruption, and as a way to curb Iranian influence.
That could give Baghdad “some breathing room” from both Washington and Tehran, he said, but “it remains an extremely difficult transformation that demands patience and political sensitivity; without them, the process could quickly unravel”.
The meeting also came days before the remaining few hundred US troops are due to leave Iraq on September 30.
Rubio told reporters on Wednesday that “there’s been no discussion” on extending that timeline.
Who are Iraq’s armed groups?
Most of Iraq’s armed groups come under the umbrella of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), a mostly Shia body formed to fight ISIL (ISIS).
The PMF was formally brought into Iraq’s security forces a decade ago, but many of its factions keep their own command structures and maintain close ties to Iran.
Several groups say they have complied with the government’s push.
Saraya al-Salam, Asaib Ahl al-Haq and Kataib al-Imam Ali have reached understandings with Baghdad to hand over their weapons or regularise their status.
Saraya al-Salam, the armed wing linked to Shia leader Muqtada al-Sadr, was formally integrated into the security forces at a ceremony in Samarra in June.
But Ozcelik cautioned that “full disarmament of any group has not really been fully, successfully implemented yet”.
The most powerful Iran-aligned factions have refused. Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba say they will keep what they call “resistance weapons”.
Hadi al-Amiri, the leader of the Badr Organisation, one of the oldest and largest factions, said last month that bringing weapons under state control was an Iraqi decision, not one imposed from outside, and ruled out any clash between the state and “the resistance”.
Ozcelik said the challenge now is “discerning which of these groups – they have their own sets of interests, pockets, and incentives – can credibly be incorporated and which cannot by the disarmament deadline”.
A key test, she added, will be whether al-Zaidi can “Iraq-ify these groups, meaning a transition to an Iraq-first or Iraqi-Shia identity”.
Have the armed groups played a role in the Iran war?
Yes.
Kataib Hezbollah and Harakat al-Nujaba have both previously targeted US forces in Iraq and have attacked Gulf states during the US-Israel war on Iran.
On Wednesday, Rubio said recent strikes on energy infrastructure in the region were probably carried out in part by Iran-backed armed groups in Iraq, not only by Yemen’s Houthis.
“Pro-Iran militias have directly played a destabilising role in the US-Iran confrontation,” said Ozcelik, citing reports that Saudi Arabia’s East-West Pipeline was targeted from southern Iraq.
Are Iranian airlines still flying to Iraq?
Not entirely.
New US sanctions threaten to cut off any airport or company that refuels, services or sells tickets for Iranian airlines.
Iran says Baghdad has stopped accepting its flights and is trying to reroute them to Najaf, where flights to Iran are continuing, and no suspension order has been received.
Najaf, home to the shrine of Imam Ali, is a major destination for pilgrims, and local travel companies depend heavily on routes to Iran.

Feature: China-supported project helps improve livelihoods in Sudan
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:04:39 CST
23:04:39 KST

ROME, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- For families living through conflict, a small amount of assistance can go a long way.
Liang Xiao has seen living proof of this through her work with the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) headquartered in Rome, where she has helped coordinate a poverty reduction and agricultural assistance project in Sudan's Red Sea State.
Supported by China and launched in Suakin in May 2025, the project provides much-needed assistance to local communities while helping them build more sustainable livelihoods. So far, more than 40,000 people have benefited from the project, including a family in Red Sea State who made a living by raising sheep.
Years of drought had degraded local pastures and made livestock feed increasingly difficult to find. The conflict made things worse, disrupting markets and livelihoods. When the family could no longer afford animal feed, they had to give their sheep sorghum stalks and other crop residues.
Through the project, the family received 100 kilograms of concentrated animal feed so that the sheep could produce milk for the children. Any extra milk could be sold at local market, bringing in some income for the household.
"What may look like just a bag of seeds or animal feed can seem insignificant to many of us," Liang told Xinhua. "But for a family affected by a conflict, it can become a turning point, helping them resume production, improve their livelihoods and rebuild confidence in the future."
The project also focused on helping women. It provided small cold-storage units for 200 women who earn a living by selling fish, according to Liang. This allows the women to keep fish fresh for longer and sell it farther afield.
The project has also trained women to make fishing nets, providing them with another skill and a potential new source of income.
"The project didn't just give me a fishing net. It gave me dignity," said one of the women.
Many of these projects, Liang said, are "small yet impactful". Instead of large infrastructure projects, they focus on practical needs in agriculture and people's daily lives, including production supplies, technical training and livelihood support.
Carrying out the project in Sudan has been far from easy. The ongoing conflict has disrupted transport and markets and pushed up procurement costs, while differences in local social and cultural practices have also brought challenges. Project teams have had to adjust their plans, find alternative ways to deliver supplies and work closely with local organizations to make sure that assistance reaches those who need it.
"China has funding, technology and development experience that can help meet the needs of developing countries," Liang said. "FAO provides a platform to bring them together."
"We hope more people can benefit from these projects and that they can contribute to better production, better nutrition, a better environment and a better life," she added. ■

China Focus: China to build on inbound tourism boom with easier travel, richer experiences
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
22:04:15 CST
23:04:15 KST

The State Council Information Office (SCIO) holds a press conference on promoting high-quality development of culture and tourism during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 24, 2026. (Xinhua/Cai Yang)
BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- As more overseas visitors come to experience China firsthand, the country plans to make inbound travel easier and offer more ways to explore its culture over the next five years, a senior culture and tourism official said Thursday.
China recorded 154 million inbound tourist trips in 2025, up 17.1 percent from a year earlier. Spending by inbound travelers surpassed 130 billion U.S. dollars, up nearly 40 percent from the previous year.
During the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030), authorities will continue to improve inbound tourism services, making visas, payments, tax refunds, guided tours, accommodation and transport more convenient for international visitors, Vice Minister of Culture and Tourism Wang Jianhua told a media conference.
Authorities will also develop more travel experiences that combine traditional culture with modern life, while expanding cultural programs overseas. Wang said the aim is to help foreign visitors travel more conveniently, enjoy more comfortable stays and gain a closer view of contemporary China.
China has steadily expanded measures to facilitate inbound travel in recent years. Since December 2023, when China launched a trial policy granting unilateral visa exemptions to visitors from six countries, it has expanded unilateral visa-free entry to travelers from 50 countries, allowing eligible visitors to stay for up to 30 days.
In a separate move, authorities extended the visa-free transit period for certain countries from 72 or 144 hours to 240 hours in December 2024. Kyrgyzstan and Vietnam were added to the program last month, bringing the number of eligible countries to 57.
In March, Chinese authorities released a package of measures to improve tourism services, including optimizing departure tax refund services, encouraging everyday service apps to offer multilingual versions and further improving visa procedures.
In July, China set its inbound tourism goals. The country's 2026-2030 tourism development plan proposes attracting 190 million inbound tourist visits a year by 2030, with annual inbound tourism spending exceeding 150 billion U.S. dollars.
Beyond policy measures, China's appeal as a travel destination has also been gaining visibility overseas. Video clips and other online content about traveling in China and experiencing the Chinese lifestyle have gained traction, with hashtags such as "China Travel" and "Chinamaxxing" going viral.
GLOBAL CULTURAL COOPERATION
The push to attract more international visitors comes as China's domestic tourism market reaches new highs and its cultural industry continues to grow.
Domestic travelers made a record 6.52 billion trips and spent 6.3 trillion yuan in 2025, Wang said. The cultural industry generated 20.8 trillion yuan in revenue, averaging 8.4 percent annual growth from 2021 to 2025.
The country also staged 640,000 commercial performances last year, generating 61.6 billion yuan in box-office revenue. Both figures rose by more than 6 percent year on year.
Wang said China will also deepen cultural and tourism cooperation with countries around the world through bilateral and multilateral mechanisms, guided by the Global Civilization Initiative.
The ministry will make greater use of the six Silk Road international alliances covering theaters, museums, arts festivals, libraries, art museums and tourism cities, as well as platforms such as the China International Travel Mart, to promote cooperation among cultural institutions and tourism businesses, he said.
China will also strengthen cooperation with international organizations, host a UNESCO conference on intangible cultural heritage, pursue nominations for world heritage and intangible cultural heritage listings, and support more Chinese villages in seeking recognition under the UN Tourism Best Tourism Villages initiative, Wang added. ■

BANGKOK, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Thailand unveiled its first national semiconductor strategy on Thursday, aiming to attract about 80 billion U.S. dollars in cumulative investment by 2050 as it seeks to move beyond chip assembly into design and front-end manufacturing.
The plan, approved by the National Semiconductor and Advanced Electronics Policy Board, targets annual industry revenue of about 150 billion dollars and more than 230,000 new jobs over 25 years under the "Made in Thailand" chip initiative.
Through a three-phase roadmap, Thailand will strengthen and upgrade its assembly and testing base by 2030, draw major investors in chip design and wafer fabrication by 2040, and build a fully integrated supply chain with homegrown "local champions" by 2050.
According to the Thailand Board of Investment (BOI), five mechanisms will support implementation: financial incentives, high-skilled workforce training, upgraded chip-design research and foreign-Thai partnerships, investment-ready infrastructure, as well as regulatory reforms and business facilitation.
The board also approved a workforce program, coordinated by the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation, alongside universities, research institutes, industry, and global partners.
Targeting the training of 86,600 individuals by 2030, the program seeks to develop 84,900 high-skilled professionals and around 1,700 senior researchers via tailored coursework, corporate internships, overseas training, and specialized development for academic and technical staff.
From 2023 to June 2026, the BOI received investment-promotion applications for 879 projects in semiconductors and advanced electronics worth about 909 billion baht (about 27.2 billion dollars), encompassing multi-stage chip manufacturing, printed circuit boards, hard disk drives, and artificial intelligence servers, among others.
The strategy is a key step in laying a comprehensive foundation for the Southeast Asian country's semiconductor industry, from chip research and design, upstream to downstream manufacturing, and assembly and testing, to bringing Thai businesses into global supply chains, said BOI Secretary General Narit Therdsteerasukdi. ■

====================================================================================================

Greece sounds alarm over fake eye therapies: From iridology to 'no-glasses' exercises
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
14:04:10 UTC
23:04:10 KST

The Hellenic Ophthalmological Society (HOS) is sounding the alarm, urging the public not to trust unproven, non-evidence-based practices.
The death of Giorgos Mazonakis — one of the most popular Greek singers of the past three decades — has set alarm bells ringing in the Greek scientific community, which sees "revolutionary" practices putting patients' lives at risk.
Prompted by the recent tragic events that shocked public opinion and brought to light the dangers of using unsubstantiated "treatments", the Hellenic Ophthalmological Society (HOS) is sounding the alarm and urging people not to trust practices that lack scientific backing.
The HOS warns that so-called "miracle" therapies, pseudo-diagnostic methods and unproven procedures are not merely ineffective. In some cases, they can lead to wrong diagnoses, delays in receiving appropriate treatment, serious complications or even permanent damage to vision.
In the sights of the HOS are, among others, "iridodiagnosis", "exercises" that promise to do away with glasses, various unapproved preparations and "regenerative" therapies advertised online, as well as cosmetic interventions performed on healthy eyes.
Iridodiagnosis: a method with no diagnostic value
The so-called "iridodiagnosis" or "iridology" claims it is possible to detect diseases of various organs of the body from the appearance of the iris of the eye.
However, according to the HOS, controlled scientific studies have repeatedly shown that the method does not have diagnostic accuracy greater than would be expected by chance.
The risks, as the Society points out, are significant: a false "diagnosis" can cause unjustified fear and lead to unnecessary or potentially dangerous "treatments". Conversely, false reassurance can delay the diagnosis of a real and serious disease.
"Exercises" that promise to eliminate glasses
In the same vein, the HOS warns about "eye exercise" programmes promoted as a way to treat myopia, presbyopia or astigmatism.
These particular claims are not supported by scientific evidence, as refractive errors are linked to the anatomical and optical characteristics of the eye and cannot be corrected by such exercises.
There are, of course, specific orthoptic exercises used in certain disorders of binocular vision. These, however, form part of targeted management and are recommended only after an appropriate diagnosis and medical assessment.
"Miracle" treatments and products from the internet
The HOS urges particular caution regarding "treatments" that promise spectacular or "miraculous" results without having been evaluated in controlled clinical trials and without the necessary approval from the competent authorities.
Among these are, for example, the so-called "regenerative" injections and various products advertised as capable of "reversing" ageing of the eye.
At the same time, the HOS discourages buying eye products online without prior medical assessment and prescription, where one is required.
Even pharmaceutical substances with proven action, such as certain eye drops that can temporarily improve near vision in people with presbyopia, are not suitable for everyone. Prior ophthalmological examination is necessary, as in specific patients they may cause serious adverse effects.
Changing eye colour: not a simple cosmetic procedure
Particular care is also required with procedures that promise permanent cosmetic changes to eye colour.
As the HOS stresses, these are not simple aesthetic interventions but surgical procedures on healthy eyes. Some techniques, such as the placement of cosmetic intraocular iris implants, have been linked to serious and irreversible complications.
Anyone considering such an operation must first receive full information from an eye surgeon about the potential risks and complications.
Good vision does not mean healthy eyes
The HOS also reminds the public that a full ophthalmological examination is a medical act carried out by an ophthalmologist in a legally operating clinic.
A simple measurement of visual acuity does not equate to a comprehensive eye examination. Good vision, moreover, does not rule out the presence of serious eye disease or even systemic illness.
Conditions such as glaucoma, age-related macular degeneration, diabetic retinopathy, retinal detachment and eye tumours can coexist with satisfactory visual acuity and go undetected without a full ophthalmological check-up.
Finally, the HOS urges people to treat with particular scepticism any promise of a "miracle" cure, rapid recovery or abolition of the need for glasses when it is not backed up by reliable scientific evidence.
When it comes to eye health, information should come from ophthalmologists and authoritative scientific sources, not from advertisements, social media posts or websites promoting unproven "treatments".

BRATISLAVA, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Slovakia has issued a 10-year government bond worth 2.5 billion euros (2.84 billion U.S. dollars), with a coupon rate of 4.25 percent, the country's Debt and Liquidity Management Agency (ARDAL) said on Thursday.
According to ARDAL, the final yield of the new bond stood at 4.309 percent. It was the second and final syndicated bond issuance by Slovakia this year.
The bond was priced at a spread of 77 basis points above the interest rate swap rate, equivalent to 81.3 basis points above the yield on a German government bond maturing in August 2036.
More than 120 investors participated in the issue, with total demand exceeding 4.5 billion euros (5.11 billion dollars). Banks and private banks accounted for the largest share of allocations, at 45 percent, followed by asset and investment fund managers with 31 percent.
The issue attracted investors from a broad range of regions. Investors from Germany, Austria and Switzerland accounted for 22 percent of the allocation, followed by Britain with 21 percent. Meanwhile, Southern European countries accounted for 11 percent, while the Nordic countries, Central and Eastern Europe, and the Middle East each accounted for 10 percent.
"The transaction marked a historic milestone for the Slovak Republic, as it was the first-ever Slovak 10-year benchmark bond issue denominated in euros. This result highlights a significant strengthening of Slovakia's relative value position within Europe," noted ARDAL. ■

On Sept. 18, while a CCG vessel was conducting legitimate law-enforcement operations near Xianbin Jiao, a Philippine vessel ignored repeated warnings from the Chinese side, deliberately altered course and suddenly accelerated to cut across the bow of the CCG vessel, leading to a collision.
The context of the incident is clear and evident, leaving no room for misinformation from the Philippine side, Jiang noted, stressing that such action seriously threatened the safety of the Chinese crew and vessel, and violated international law and the basic norms governing international relations.
The Chinese side will continue to take effective measures to resolutely safeguard territorial sovereignty and maritime rights and interests, and uphold peace and stability in the South China Sea, Jiang said.
Regarding the Philippines' efforts to co-opt other countries into a joint military exercise near China's Huangyan Dao in the South China Sea, Jiang said the move is an act of provocation and propaganda in the name of security cooperation, undermining regional peace and stability.
Jiang reiterated that Huangyan Dao is an inherent part of China's territory. China has indisputable sovereignty, sovereign rights and jurisdiction over Huangyan Dao and its adjacent waters.
He urged the Philippine side to stop its infringement attempts, and to play a constructive role in promoting dialogue and cooperation among countries in the region and safeguarding peace and stability in the South China Sea.
In response to Taiwan's plan to send a retired vessel to the Philippines, Jiang urged Manila to abide by the one-China principle, refrain from any form of official contact or military ties with the Taiwan region of China, and stop sending wrong signals to "Taiwan independence" separatist forces.
The Taiwan question stems from China's civil war fought between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT) about eight decades ago. The unresolved civil war, combined with foreign interference, has kept the two sides of the Taiwan Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation. However, the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. ■
