Iran warns war could spread to Indian Ocean if US attacks resume
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:35:00 UTC
18:35:00 KST

An adviser to Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei warned Thursday that Tehran could expand the Middle East war to the Indian Ocean if the U.S. attacks again.
"Since the conflict has spread from the Persian Gulf and Strait of Hormuz to the Red Sea, it is possible that, in response to more war, the front will expand even further, reaching the Indian Ocean and perhaps beyond," said Yahya Rahim Safavi in a video released by Iran's Fars news agency.
Yemen's Houthis, fighting Saudi-backed government forces, recently took control of the Red Sea coastline, tightening their grip on the strategic Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which links Asia to Europe via the Suez Canal.
Iran has long provided military support to the Houthis but denies any involvement in the Yemen conflict.
The Islamic republic has also locked down the Strait of Hormuz off the Iranian coast, in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli strikes that triggered the Middle East war at the end of February.
Iran and the United States are now vying for control of Hormuz, through which much of the world's oil and gas passed before the war.
Iranian officials had already threatened to expand the geographic scope of the conflict if U.S. strikes resume.
But Thursday's warning is the first time an adviser to Iran's supreme leader explicitly mentioned the Indian Ocean, home to a strategic U.S.-British military base at Diego Garcia, nearly 4,000 kilometers from Iran.
Officials from both countries held talks in New York this week on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly in a further attempt to end the conflict.
Iran has put forward its conditions for ending the war, including the lifting of sanctions targeting its economy and the unconditional release of its frozen assets abroad.
In an exclusive interview with AFP Tuesday, a spokesman for Iran's Revolutionary Guards, Hossein Mohebi, also mentioned ending the war in Yemen.
Mohebi said that Iran had hardened its conditions for ending the war with the United States following the collapse of a June deal, adding Washington now had "no choice" but to accept its demands.
Iran had previously agreed with the United States to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.
"They broke the agreement and committed another vicious act. We have therefore toughened our conditions," Mohebi told AFP in a rare exclusive interview in Tehran, noting that if the US persisted with its current course, "they will only make things difficult for themselves".
"We are not their playthings, and they cannot unilaterally violate an agreement they signed whenever they please."
During the interview, Mohebi outlined Iran's view of the nearly seven-month Middle East war and the prospects for ending it as diplomatic efforts stall.
"We believe we have won this war, and we are currently consolidating that victory into a total deterrent force," he added.
The June memorandum of understanding included Iranian demands on the lifting of US oil sanctions, removing its naval blockade on Iranian ports, unfreezing Iranian assets abroad, and ending the war on all fronts, including Lebanon.
Since it fell apart, however, Mohebi said Iran had toughened its demands, including by seeking the release of the full $24 billion in frozen Iranian assets up front before negotiations, rather than in stages.
Meanwhile, top Pakistani and Iranian diplomats met in New York to discuss the latest developments, following recent talks between Washington and Tehran, an official statement said Thursday.
The meeting between Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar and his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi was held on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly, a statement from Pakistan's Foreign Ministry said.
It comes a day after the U.S. and Iranian negotiators held hourslong talks in New York to discuss ways to reopen Hormuz and revive the long-stalled direct talks under the Islamabad Accord.
The two counterparts discussed bilateral relations and exchanged views on regional and international developments.
Dar underscored the importance of dialogue, diplomacy and sustained engagement in promoting regional peace and stability.
Both sides agreed to remain in "close" contact, the statement concluded.

US returns stolen antiquities worth more than $5 million to Syria
US officials announced Wednesday the return of 36 stolen antiquities to Syria, including a stone trafficked during the Islamic State group's destruction of the ancient site of Palmyra.
Authorities seized the items, collectively valued at more than $5 million, from New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art and several ancient art collectors.
"Repatriation ceremonies are a powerful reminder that preserving cultural heritage transcends any border or nationality," said Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg.
The Palmyran stone was removed from the UNESCO World Heritage site Palmyra before Islamic State members destroyed much of the city from 2015 to 2017, according to a press release.
Weighing more than 450 kilograms, the carved limestone sculpture depicts a reclining male surrounded by a woman and three children.
The United States has returned looted antiquities over the years to several countries, including China, Greece and Italy.
Mohammad Kanatri, Syria's charge d'affaires in Washington, said the transfer demonstrates how "a shared commitment to protecting cultural heritage can build lasting bridges between our two countries."
"Through Syrian-American cooperation, a part of Syria's history is finally returning home thanks to the efforts of the Manhattan District Attorney's Office," he said in a statement.
Four of the antiquities were seized from American collector Michael Steinhardt, who in 2021 returned about 180 items stolen from around the world as part of a deal with the US government. The pieces had a total value of $70 million.
The Manhattan District Attorney's office said the 13 items seized from the Met were among 402 antiquities valued at $98.7 million that it has taken from the cultural institution since 2017.

Zelensky: Air Defense Intercepted 60% of Ballistic Missiles in Russian Attack on Kyiv
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:31:49 UTC
18:31:49 KST

Ukraine’s air defense intercepted 60% of the ballistic missiles launched during three waves of Russian attacks on Kyiv overnight on September 24.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky reported the figures. A video of his remarks was published by Novyny.LIVE.
According to Ukraine’s Air Force, Russia attacked using Zircon and Iskander missiles, along with various types of strike drones. The main targets were areas in the Kyiv and Odesa regions.
“It is important. We would like to see more missiles intercepted, of course… But it was not 10% or zero – it was 60%. And this year, there have been moments when the figure was zero,” Zelensky said.
The military reported that four Zircon missiles and three Iskander missiles were intercepted. The State Emergency Service of Ukraine said that two people were killed and at least eight others were injured as a result of the massive attack on Kyiv.
During his current visit to New York to attend the 81st session of the UN General Assembly, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed strengthening Ukraine’s defenses against Russian ballistic missiles with Donald Trump.
Ukraine and the United States are also continuing work on launching the production of Patriot interceptor missiles in Ukraine and developing a winter air defense package.
In New York, Zelensky also discussed Ukraine’s ballistic missile defense with U.S. senators and members of the House of Representatives.
Intercepting ballistic missiles is one of the most difficult tasks for air defense systems because of their high speed, steep flight trajectory, and the very short time between detecting the target and intercepting it.
To counter such missiles, Ukraine primarily uses Patriot air defense systems. However, their effectiveness directly depends on the availability of interceptor missiles.
Ukraine has already received Patriot missiles from its partners this year. In particular, Poland and the Netherlands delivered air defense missiles for these systems in April, while Poland later officially confirmed the transfer of PAC-3 missiles. Spain has also said it will continue supplying missiles.
Meanwhile, Ukraine is contracting around 1,000 Patriot missiles using EU funds, although most of them are expected to be delivered over the coming years.
Ukraine also has an agreement with the United States for monthly deliveries of Patriot missiles. However, Volodymyr Zelensky has emphasized that the current supply levels are not sufficient.

To the victor belong Venezuela’s spoils: Delcy Rodriguez’s UNGA about-face
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:31:15 UTC
18:31:15 KST

To the victor belong Venezuela’s spoils: Delcy Rodriguez’s UNGA about-face
Seven years after using the UN stage in New York to warn of US regime change and the seizure of Venezuela’s resources, the country’s interim president returned to thank the man who delivered both.
Venezuela’s interim President Delcy Rodriguez took to the stage yesterday at the United Nations General Assembly meeting in New York City to deliver a rather bland speech, in which she thanked United States President Donald Trump for resuming “diplomatic relations and cooperation” with Venezuela.
This was a different vibe, to be sure, than the one she opted for at the same venue in September 2019, when, as vice president under Nicolas Maduro, she accused the US of perpetrating “economic terrorism” that did not require the use of bombs “but rather through banks and insurance companies”.
Denouncing the global superpower’s militarisation of international relations and punishment of millions of innocent people “in order to apply regime change doctrines and steal other nations’ resources”, the Rodriguez of 2019 went on to cite Venezuelan economic losses to the tune of $130bn between 2015 and 2018 alone on account of US sanctions.
She additionally offered her opinion that the domination of the US political system by “plutocratic minorities” made the country unqualified to impose its model on other countries.
Seven years later, US plutocracy is going strong with Trump at the helm – the same Trump alongside whom a grinning Rodriguez appeared in a photograph taken in New York on Tuesday, less than nine months after he oversaw regime change in Venezuela by kidnapping Maduro.
The kidnapped president is now also in New York, albeit in jail, and is scheduled to stand trial in June 2027. This despite his attempts to remind everyone that, as a sitting head of state, his prosecution in a foreign court contravenes international law.
Then again, abducting other countries’ presidents is also pretty glaringly illegal. But Trump has made it clear that he alone is in charge of deciding what is and is not permissible on any given day.
The abduction took place on January 3, when the US military launched air attacks on Venezuela, killing some 100 people and whisking Maduro and his wife away.
He is accused of an array of misdeeds, including being the leader of the “Cartel of the Suns” – which, mind you, does not actually exist – and engaging in “conspiracy to possess machineguns and destructive devices”.
This is quite the accusation coming from the country that just used all manner of destructive devices to bomb Venezuela and kill a bunch of people.
Anyway, bald-faced hypocrisy is nothing new in the land of the “plutocratic minorities”.
Now, the waning corporate media interest in Maduro’s fate amounts to another coup for US impunity, as folks go about more or less forgetting that there is a foreign head of state sitting in a Brooklyn prison.
But Maduro’s disappearance works out well for Rodriguez, as she goes about enabling the very theft of resources she once decried.
Rodriguez took the stage at the UN the day after Trump, who used the platform to pat himself on the back for the trampling of Venezuelan sovereignty that conveniently culminated in last month’s announcement from the White House of the “biggest oil deal in world history”, securing US majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves.
Speaking to his international audience, Trump boasted: “To the victor belong the spoils. You’ve all heard that.”
Never mind that you’re not technically supposed to admit that you attacked a country just to get its oil. (You’re also not, in polite company, supposed to threaten to annihilate Iran – another of Trump’s UN talking points.)
Since January, the US has lifted many coercive economic measures against Venezuela (including against Rodriguez herself), easing the brutal sanctions regime that as of 2020 was estimated to have already killed 100,000 Venezuelans, according to former UN independent expert Alfred-Maurice de Zayas.
But trading sanctions for de facto colonialism isn’t a great deal, either.
Meanwhile, Trump’s continued manic bombing of vessels in the Caribbean and Pacific, which a recent UN report warned may constitute crimes against humanity, suggests the US is nowhere near to kicking its old habit of terrorism – and is all the more reason that Rodriguez might have refrained from thanking the US leader for his “cooperation”.
As Gregory Wilpert, founder of the Venezuelanalysis website and author of Changing Venezuela by Taking Power, diplomatically put it to me: “One cannot help but wonder whether Delcy Rodriguez is over-complying with Trump in some aspects of her negotiations with him.”
Noting that Rodriguez is “in a highly vulnerable position”, Wilpert ran through a few of the options she faces, such as “the possibility that the Trump administration could treat her as it treated Maduro – by attempting to kidnap her – or as it treated Iran, by targeting the country’s highest levels of government”.
Or, Wilpert said, there is always the Cuba approach, which would entail “the kind of economic siege” that is undertaken “with the aim of starving an entire country”.
In her UN address, Rodriguez promised that Venezuela would hold elections at some unspecified point in time – not that the US, for its part, really cares about democracy as long as the right people are in power.
And although it’s still too early to tell, Rodriguez might just be one of those people.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Government supports conclusion of the European Union–Indonesia economic partnership agreement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:30:59 UTC
18:30:59 KST

The main objectives of the agreements between the European Union and Indonesia are to enhance and strengthen the rules-based international trading system, deepen bilateral trade and investment relations, improve access to the Indonesian market for European Union companies, and create a more transparent legal framework for trade and investment. “Moving forward with these agreements demonstrates that, even in a challenging geopolitical environment, the European Union continues to build its network of partnerships in order to strengthen open markets and thereby support Estonian companies,” said Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna.
Indonesia is Southeast Asia’s largest economy and the EU’s 30th-largest trading partner. In 2025, EU exports to Indonesia amounted to €10.2 billion. Estonia’s total exports of goods and services to Indonesia amounted to €13.6 million last year. Under the agreement, tariffs will be eliminated on more than 98% of tariff lines, covering almost all EU–Indonesia trade by value.
According to the foreign minister, opening the market and reducing trade barriers will improve opportunities for Estonian companies to export machinery, electrical equipment and electronic products to Indonesia, as well as, for example, wood products, processed food products and environmental technology solutions. “By increasing the transparency of trade rules and simplifying customs procedures, the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement will have a positive impact on the EU business environment. For Estonian companies, however, the most significant impact in the Indonesian market lies in services and digital trade, as the agreement will, among other things, facilitate the cross-border flow of data and support the development of digital commerce,” Tsahkna explained. He added that, from the perspective of economic security, the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement will improve the EU’s access to critical raw materials, including nickel.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Coast Guard Administration has begun stationing newly built 100-tonne patrol vessels at Dongsha Island on a long-term basis, after completing a pier renovation project in July.
Due to the old pier’s limitations, 100-tonne patrol vessels only docked for special operations targeting Chinese illegal fishing, the Coast Guard said, per Liberty Times. Now that the larger ships can permanently dock, they will strengthen deterrence against Chinese fishing vessels and Chinese coast guard ships.
To curb illegal Chinese fishing, Taiwan has strengthened law enforcement strategies by allowing detentions and confiscating tools used in illegal activities, the coast guard said. The aim is to raise the cost of violations and enhance deterrence.

The coast guard said it has increased patrols near Matsu Island ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival. Personnel are targeting Chinese vessels entering restricted waters, contraband smuggling, and the risk of African swine fever.
During an operation between Sunday and Monday, officers inspected four Taiwanese fishing boats, drove away three Chinese vessels, and arrested one wanted person.
Coast guard personnel stationed on Matsu have driven away Chinese vessels 287 times, detained four vessels, and responded to three marine conservation or coastal oil-pollution cases.

Taiwan updates soil liquefaction maps for 6 cities and counties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:29:27 UTC
18:29:27 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Geological Survey and Mining Management Agency has updated soil liquefaction potential maps for six cities and counties, expanding the analysis to provide more detailed assessments of geological conditions.
The Ministry of Economic Affairs agency announced the update Thursday, covering Taipei, New Taipei, Taoyuan, Yilan County, Hsinchu County, and Hsinchu. The update also includes maps showing the distribution of weak soil layers and information from soil liquefaction monitoring stations.
The agency said the number of geological boreholes used in the analysis increased from 3,571 in the previous version to 11,731, while the analysis area expanded by about 96 square kilometers to 909.8 square kilometers. The additional data provides a more complete picture of geological formations and groundwater conditions.
More than 80% of the areas reviewed retained their previous liquefaction potential classifications. Liquefaction potential increased in Hsinchu City’s North and Xiangshan districts and decreased in New Taipei’s Banqiao District.
Soil liquefaction occurs when earthquakes cause loose, water-saturated sandy soil to compact and temporarily behave like a liquid. It can reduce the ground’s ability to support buildings, causing structures without anti-liquefaction measures to settle, tilt, or collapse, according to the Geological Survey and Mining Management Agency.
The soil liquefaction potential map is a regional assessment based on natural geological conditions. Being located in an area classified as having high potential does not mean a building is unsafe, the agency said. It added that ground improvement, structural reinforcement, and proper engineering design can reduce liquefaction risks.
The updated data came from government soil liquefaction assessment and housing resilience programs. Local governments conducted field drilling surveys and provided the results, while the Geological Survey and Mining Management Agency integrated the data.
The agency has held local forums, public briefings, and sessions with local governments and disaster-prevention agencies to explain how to use the updated data. Drilling density in metropolitan areas reaches four boreholes per square kilometer.
The agency's updated soil liquefaction potential maps are available through its Soil Liquefaction Potential Inquiry System, where users can enter an address to check the potential classification and related information. The agency said it will update the maps on a rolling basis as more geological data becomes available and as groundwater levels change with seasonal conditions and climate change.
The soil liquefaction maps were first developed after the 2016 Meinong Earthquake, when the central government ordered nationwide mapping, per Liberty Times. The first nationwide version was released at the end of 2021.

What is Netanyahu's lawyer doing at Serbia's new Elbit drone factory?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:29:00 UTC
18:29:00 KST

Unveiling Serbia's first factory producing Israeli drones, President Aleksandar Vucic took to Instagram on September 17 to tout the 100 jobs it had created and the "most modern equipment" it would supply to the Serbian army and "the armies of some other countries".
The press wasn't invited, with Vucic citing the sensitivity of the project.
In its own Instagram post, the Israeli embassy said Ambassador Avivit Bar-Ilan had attended the event and hailed the "cooperation between Serbia's local defense industry" and Israeli defence sector giant Elbit Systems.
What neither mentioned, however, was the involvement of Zion Amir, a prominent Israeli lawyer currently representing Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu before the Israeli Supreme Court.
The lawyer's role, revealed here for the first time, comes via the Serbian-based company SDS Technologies, of which he is a director.
The factory premises, in Belgrade's Makis neighbourhood, is emblazoned with the SDS brand name, as were the clothes worn by employees demonstrating the drones to Vucic at the opening, in a video the president posted on Instagram.
In Serbia's business registry, the company name 'SDS Technologies' appeared within hours of the factory's opening, not as a new firm, however, but as the new name of a company previously called CUPA Enterprises. The very same day, September 17, Amir was formally appointed as a director of SDS.
Vucic said previously that ownership of the drone venture would be shared equally by Serbia and Israel. The ownership structure of SDS Technologies, however, does not reflect this.
SDS is in fact owned by London-registered CUPA Limited, itself majority-owned by Greek national Athanasios Ramos. On September 21, four days after the factory opened, CUPA Limited changed its name to Blue Liberty International Ltd.
Elbit System, the designer of the drones, told Haaretz/BIRN it "collaborates with local companies in several European countries as part of localisation processes and efforts to tailor its offerings to customer needs". It denied any link to SDS, however, or to Amir. It stressed it does not own, nor is a partner in, any drone facility in Serbia.
BIRN reporters first visited the Makis factory site several months ago, for an exclusive story about Serbia's plan to open a drone factory with Elbit.
Situated alongside several other businesses and warehouses, the factory gates were branded with the name SDS Technologies. At the time, there was no such company in Serbia's business registry.
Today, SDS Technologies has three directors: Greek national Maria Kardamaki, Lebanese-born US citizen George Antoine Elghossain, and Amir.
Amir has represented Netanyahu and his government before the Israeli Supreme Court in five petitions against the government's decision to dismiss Ronen Bar as head of Shin Bet, Israel's domestic security service. According to Haaretz's reporting, Bar had warned Netanyahu of a potential attack on Israel in a phone call before the Palestinian militant group Hamas struck on October 7, 2023, triggering Israel's devastating war in Gaza.
Israel's state prosecutor argued that Netanyahu's removal of Bar was unlawful, given the conflict of interest arising from the fact Shin Bet was investigating the alleged involvement of Netanyahu associates in the paid promotion of Qatari interests in Israel, so-called 'Qatargate'.
One of those associates is Srulik Einhorn, who has also advised Vucic.
Amir declined to answer questions about his involvement in SDS Technologies and the new drone factory in Serbia.
The website of SDS Technologies is little more than a homepage, offering no other information.
The domain was registered on January 18 this year; the domain owner's information in the WHOIS registry - a platform that allows access to basic registration data - is hidden. Historical data shows the same domain was registered before and used by an IT firm offering web and software services. According to archived snapshots on the Wayback Machine, the firm listed Chandigarh, in northern India, as its address.
BIRN sent questions to the official email address of SDS Technologies but received no reply. Calls to the phone number listed on the website also went unanswered.
Haaretz/BIRN previously reported that Elbit Systems would hold 51 per cent ownership of the drone production facility in Serbia; 49 per cent would be controlled by Serbian state-owned arms trader Yugoimport SDPR.
Indeed, photos from the factory opening this month do feature Ran Kril, Elbit's executive vice president for international marketing and business development since 2015.
Elbit was also named as a partner in the project by the Israeli embassy, and Vucic named three types of Elbit drone that would be assembled at the Belgrade site and later also manufactured: the Lanius-X drone, the FireFox-X attack drone, and the Magni-X reconnaissance drone.
In its statement to Haaretz/BIRN, however, Elbit wrote: "Elbit holds no ownership stake in, nor is it a partner in, any UAV manufacturing facility in the country [Serbia]."
Vucic was gushing about the Lanius-X, saying it "literally has eyes and ears, chases the target, waits for the target in an ambush".
"You simply can't defend yourself against it," he said.
Autonomous and AI-powered, a Washington Post story in 2022 quoted experts as warning the drone represented a "nightmare scenario". Lanius comes from the Latin for 'butcher'.
Last year, a report by UN Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese mentioned Elbit as one of the companies behind the drones, hexacopters and quadcopters that she said had become "omnipresent killing machines in the skies of Gaza".
Undeterred, Serbian arms cooperation with Israel has boomed over the last three years. The value of ammunition and weapons exports from Serbia to Israel has increased as much as 42-fold since 2023, reaching 114 million euros by the end of last year, despite numerous appeals from UN experts to halt the sale of military equipment to Israel.
In April this year, the Serbian parliament adopted a security agreement on classified data between Serbia and Israel in the defence sector. The urgency of its implementation, as stated in the document obtained by BIRN, stemmed from the expected delivery of military equipment from Israel to the Serbian army.
Early last year, Elbit sold Serbia advanced PULS artillery systems and Hermes 900 unmanned combat drones worth a total of $335 million. In August, another contract was signed, worth $1.6 billion, covering the delivery of drones, long-range missiles, electronic warfare systems, and a range of other military equipment to Serbia.
BIRN previously also reported that the Belgrade-based company Edepro, which describes itself as "a regional leader in propulsion system solutions" for rockets, drones and missiles, exported military goods to IMI Systems, a company owned by Elbit since 2018.
Serbian government plane's Tel Aviv trips
According to open-source aviation data, an aircraft used by the Serbian government flew twice to Tel Aviv last week. On September 14, it flew from Belgrade to Tel Aviv and immediately returned to Serbia. The same plane repeated the route on September 17, taking off from Belgrade several hours after the factory opening, and returning to Belgrade in the evening.

Trump’s diesel export threat meets a shrug in fuel-strapped Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:27:57 UTC
18:27:57 KST

BRUSSELS — European authorities have downplayed threats that the United States could temporarily ban all exports of U.S. diesel, despite warnings that such a ban would have "very serious" consequences for the continent's energy supply.
On Wednesday POLITICO reported the White House was preparing a 90-day ban on exports of diesel, a move that would blow a huge hole in Europe's supply of the fuel that's used in heavy transport and industry. The ban puts U.S. President Donald Trump at odds with industry and some in his own circle, including Energy Secretary Chris Wright who opposes the ban.
Last month, the U.S. supplied 420,000 barrels of diesel to EU member countries and the U.K., accounting for more than half of total imports that month, according to Kpler. Europe's reliance on the U.S. for diesel has increased in recent months after the closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent imports from Qatar, Kuwait, Oman and the United Arab Emirates plummeting.
Advertisement
“Given the precarious situation that Europe currently finds itself in, any further restrictions on fuels available to the EU at this stage could quickly become very serious,” said a person in the industry who closely follows the market situation and was granted anonymity to discuss the sensitive situation openly.
“Diesel inventories in particular are under pressure, and the EU has become increasingly reliant on supplies from the U.S. as it’s had to diversify first from Russia and then from the Middle East. Beyond this, Europe currently has few limited, easy replacement options.”
But European officials either downplayed the risk, said it was unlikely to happen, or weren’t even aware of the threat.
Czech trade minister Karel Havlíček said he believed the ban “will not actually materialize, given the potential negative indirect impact on world markets. Therefore I welcome the latest statements of U.S. Energy Secretary Wright.” Wright on Wednesday said the "blunt tool of banning diesel exports definitely doesn’t work."
Havlíček added that direct U.S. diesel exports to the Czech Republic were “insignificant.”
A German government spokesperson declined to comment on the specific U.S. threat of a ban on Wednesday, saying that Berlin was “doing everything it can to maintain security of supply, as it always has done in the past; this also applies to refineries that are operating at good capacity utilization.”
Advertisement
Germany last month imported 30,000 barrels of diesel from the U.S., according to Kpler. This year U.S. imports have so far accounted for about 18% of Germany’s imports, according to industry association en2x.
The United Kingdom, the biggest importer of American diesel in Europe at 108,000 barrels last month according to Kpler, had a similar official line to Germany. “Forecourts in the U.K. are being supplied with petrol and diesel as normal and we have a diverse and resilient supply,” a U.K. government spokesperson said.
But one British lawmaker wasn’t so sanguine. “If the U.S. restricts our supply of diesel it would be a big concern for drivers,” said Bill Esterson, a U.K. Labour MP and chair of the House of Commons Energy Security and Net Zero Committee. “Prices are already sky high because of the war in Iran.”
France, which imported 42,000 barrels last month, did not respond to a request for comment. The European Commission also declined to comment. Multiple other European officials, granted anonymity to discuss Trump's threats openly, downplayed the threat.
Since the war in Iran began, diesel imports from Qatar have completely dried up, according to the Kpler figures. Imports from Kuwait, Oman and the United Arab Emirates also fell to zero for a while, though they have picked up again in the last couple of months. Still, they are nowhere near U.S. levels.
Aude Le Gentil and Nicholas Earl contributed reporting.

At least 158,000 people have been displaced, according to Yemen’s Executive Unit for the Management of Displaced Persons Camps.

Prospects for CTBT’s entry into force unclear, primarily due to US — diplomat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:26:22 UTC
18:26:22 KST

MOSCOW, September 24. /TASS/. The prospects for the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty (CTBT) entering into force remain unclear, primarily due to the US position, Russian Foreign Ministry Spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a statement marking the 30th anniversary of the document’s opening for signature.
"Despite the fact that 179 of the 188 signatory states have ratified the treaty, the prospects for the CTBT’s entry into force remain just as unclear. This is due to the position of several countries, primarily the US, which was one of the treaty’s initiators but has nevertheless failed to take effective steps toward ratifying it over the past decades," the diplomat emphasized. "US officials’ statements that the relevant bill will not pass Congress do not stand up to scrutiny. We see how quickly legislation that is of great importance to the American political establishment is passed on Capitol Hill," Zakharova pointed out.
US position threatening moratorium
Washington’s statements are causing particular concern, the spokeswoman emphasized.
"US President Donald Trump’s executive order of October 29, 2025 to begin preparations for nuclear tests is not just rhetoric, but in fact a direct threat to the relevant moratorium that is preventing the world from sliding into a new round of the nuclear arms race. Attempts by the Americans to accuse other countries of activity allegedly incompatible with the Treaty look totally unsubstantiated.
As we know, whenever such statements come from Washington, it means that the Americans are once again looking to withdraw from their international commitments," Zakharova stressed.
According to the diplomat, Russia was the first of the "Nuclear Five" (P5) to accede to the CTBT on the day the treaty was opened for signature, September 24, 1996. "For more than 20 years, we maintained this status even when Washington failed to make any progress toward ratifying the treaty. But this could not go on forever," she noted. "In 2023, Russia withdrew its ratification, restoring parity with the US in terms of international legal obligations in this area," the spokeswoman said.
Russia’s responsible stance
"Russia remains a party to the CTBT with all the rights and obligations that this entails. We continue to work responsibly within the Preparatory Commission for the CTBT Organization. In December 2023, we completed construction of our national segment of the International Monitoring System - the second largest in the world - with 32 facilities certified and operational," Zakharova emphasized.
"Russia continues to observe its voluntary moratorium on nuclear testing, which was introduced by the USSR back in 1990. On November 5, 2025, Russian President Vladimir Putin unequivocally stated: 'Russia has always strictly adhered to and continues to adhere to its obligations under the CTBT, and we have no plans to deviate from them. Nevertheless, if the US or other states parties to the treaty conduct full-scale nuclear tests, then Russia, too, will have to take appropriate countermeasures.’ We are strictly following this approach," the diplomat concluded.

Despite broadcaster AVROTROS maintaining its concerns over Israel’s participation and the war in Gaza, the Netherlands will return to Eurovision in 2027, with the country’s entry now being coordinated by the NPO.
The Netherlands will return to the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027, despite the broadcaster previously responsible for the country’s participation (AVROTROS) continuing to oppose a return.
Dutch network AVROTROS withdrew from the 2026 contest and has said it would also not take part in 2027, arguing that the competition could "no longer be considered neutral" amid Israel’s participation and the war in Gaza.
"It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the Contest, undermining its neutral character. The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division," said Taco Zimmerman, Director-General of AVROTROS.
The NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the Netherlands, has now taken responsibility for the country’s entry. Coverage of the contest will be provided by broadcaster NOS, while "an independent team of experts" will select the Dutch act.
Jurre Bosman, NPO's director of media, said: "It is important that, as a public broadcaster, we remain part of this unifying European event at this moment in particular."
Eurovision director Martin Green said in a statement: "We are delighted to welcome the Netherlands back to the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027. We value the constructive conversations we have had with NPO and look forward to working together to reinforce the Contest as a place that truly reflects the spirit of 'United By Music'."
The decision comes as Eurovision continues to face widespread controversy over Israel’s participation. Five countries - Iceland, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Spain - withdrew from the 2026 contest over the issue.
Ireland has already confirmed it will boycott Eurovision for a second year in 2027, citing the "appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza".
Spain is also considering extending its boycott. RTVE president José Pablo López said this week that he would recommend that Spain remain out of the 2027 contest, saying it was “deeply painful” that Israel’s public broadcaster would remain eligible to compete "despite everything, and given this situation that is still being experienced in Gaza." A final decision has not been made by RTVE yet.
Next year's Eurovision Song Contest is being held at the Arena Burgas in Burgas, Bulgaria.

‘Partial satisfaction’: Sri Lankans hail 2019 bombings ruling with a caveat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:22:27 UTC
18:22:27 KST

‘Partial satisfaction’: Sri Lankans hail 2019 bombings ruling with a caveat
As 15 Muslim men are given unusually long prison terms, a father who lost his teenage daughter still wants to know if it was a political conspiracy.
Colombo, Sri Lanka – On the morning of April 21, 2019, tuk-tuk driver Indika Rohan took his wife and daughter to the local church for the Easter Sunday mass.
He dropped them outside St Sebastian’s Church in the Katuwapitiya area of Negombo, a scenic Christian-majority town north of Sri Lanka’s capital, Colombo.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Sri Lanka court convicts 15 over deadly Easter Sunday bombings
- list 2 of 4Fifteen guilty in 2019 Sri Lanka Easter bombings: What the verdict says
- list 3 of 4Two ex-Sri Lanka officials sentenced to death over 2019 Easter bombings
- list 4 of 4Sri Lanka’s former intelligence chief arrested over 2019 Easter attacks
As he went back to his tuk-tuk parked near the church, he heard a huge explosion.
A suicide attacker had detonated himself inside the church in a coordinated attack inspired by the ISIL (ISIS) group in two other churches and three luxury hotels across Sri Lanka, killing 279 people, including 45 foreigners, and injuring more than 500 others.
It was Rohan’s last ride with his 13-year-old daughter, Kanishka Hirushi, who was among 110 people killed at St Sebastian’s Church. His severely injured wife, Nilanthi Pushpakumari, 50, spent weeks in the ICU recovering.
“My daughter went to the church by tuk-tuk, but returned home by hearse,” he told Al Jazeera on Wednesday, as he welcomed a court verdict that convicted 15 men over the Easter Sunday bombings – the deadliest in Sri Lanka’s history.
All the men directly involved in the attacks were believed to have died. Authorities later arrested 25 suspects accused of planning the attacks – all of them Muslims.
On Tuesday, a three-judge bench of the High Court in Colombo found 15 of them guilty of more than 23,000 charges, including murder, conspiracy to commit terrorist attacks, and possession of firearms and explosives.
They were given long prison terms – five receiving 200 years, five others 220 years, four 240 years each, and one receiving 260 years, based on their involvement in conspiring and aiding the attacks.
Nine others were acquitted of all charges, while one accused died during the trial.
Rohan, 56, said he waited for justice for more than seven years.
“My siblings and niblings always express sadness over the loss of our daughter,” he told Al Jazeera. “Most of them reside abroad, and they always asked about the development of the trial against the accused.”
‘Hold masterminds accountable’
After the bombings, a Sri Lankan parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials had failed to prevent the attacks despite repeated intelligence warnings.
In 2023, the country’s Supreme Court ordered former President Maithripala Sirisena, former Inspector General of Police Pujith Jayasundara, State Intelligence Service Director Nilantha Jayawardene and National Intelligence Director Sisira Mendis to pay compensation to the blasts’ victims for their failure to prevent the attacks.
The same year, a whistleblower told the British network Channel 4 that Suresh Salley, a former intelligence chief and retired army major-general, had allegedly met the bombers and that he had links with them.
The whistleblower claimed the attack was allowed to happen to boost the popularity of Gotabaya Rajapaksa ahead of the 2019 presidential election. Rajapaksa, who denied the charge, declared his candidacy two days after the attacks and won the election.
Salley was arrested in February this year. He is being treated in hospital while under police custody.
In July, Jayasundara and former Defence Secretary Hemasiri Fernando were sentenced to death for criminal negligence over the bombings. But Sri Lanka has not carried out any executions since 1976.
Case against Salley ‘very significant’
Rohan said he was closely following the case against Salley “with serious concern”.
“The verdict against the accused men gives me only partial satisfaction. We will be fully satisfied when the verdict for this [Salley] case is announced,” Rohan told Al Jazeera.
Ruki Fernando, a Sri Lankan rights activist, said the case against Salley in a lower court is “very significant and needs to proceed to the High Court”.
“It [case] has the potential to hold those who may be the masterminds accountable,” he said.
The Easter Sunday bombings also revived memories of Sri Lanka’s 26-year-long civil war involving the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), a disbanded separatist group that once fought a bloody conflict to establish an independent state for the ethnic Tamil minority.
After the historic Gen Z-led protests in 2022, which ousted the powerful Rajapaksa family, Sri Lanka elected Marxist-leaning Anura Kumara Dissanayake as president in 2024.
Two weeks after his victory, Dissanayake visited St Sebastian’s Church and met the families who had lost their loved ones in the attacks. He promised a thorough investigation into the attacks and to expose any alleged political backing behind them.
“There seems to be some progress in the continuing investigations into the Easter attacks and the government appears to be committed to it,” activist Fernando told Al Jazeera.
Rohan says he trusts the government to act on its promise. “We hope it is able to deliver justice.”

Australia says rogue OpenAI model hacked into its healthcare system, admonishes Sam Altman
A rogue OpenAI model bypassed safeguards during training and hacked an Australian government website, the country's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said Wednesday, admonishing the ChatGPT creator over an "obviously unacceptable" breach.
The artificial intelligence tool sought access to a health statistics portal in June and "didn't accept no for an answer," sidestepping restrictions to breach a section hosting private files, Albanese said.
OpenAI did not raise the alarm with the Australian government until September, when it sent a message to a generic email inbox that is only checked once daily. The company said it first spotted the rogue activity in August, when it reviewed what the AI tool had been doing.
Global worries about the power of advanced AI tools are mounting after a string of hacking incidents involving models from both OpenAI and rival developer Anthropic.
"Today, I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident," Albanese told reporters in New York on Wednesday. "I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred."
"It took until September 10 before there was any notification at all — and the notification was an email sent to just the public mailbox," he said.
The AI tool accessed public and non-public files hosted on an old health statistics website. Albanese said there was "no evidence" that personal information had been accessed or that other government services had been compromised.
"Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," he said.
The breach occurred in June as OpenAI ran training exercises to rate the performance of its AI models. It asked the model to trawl the internet for data showing how much the Australian government spent on medicine, Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher told reporters.
"Smart enough to kill us"
Australian Defense Minister Richard Marles said the AI model had "scaled the fence."
"It asked a question, the information was not given and rather than leaving at that point, it scaled the fence," he said.
Australia has launched a rapid review of the incident, which will include the national intelligence agency responsible for cybersecurity.
OpenAI said it spotted the breach while carrying out an "extensive review" of its AI models.
"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation," the company said. "In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend."
Altman and other tech CEOs addressed a special meeting of the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday about AI risks.
More than 100 organizations around the world, including OpenAI and Anthropic, signed an open letter last month calling for a global effort to "strengthen cyber defenses" against AI-powered cybersecurity threats.
It came after two OpenAI models escaped from a closed testing environment and broke into the internal systems of Hugging Face, a site that AI developers use to store and share code.
Anthropic recently discovered that its models had gained unauthorized access to three unidentified organizations during testing that was supposed to keep them away from "real-world" systems.
Google's consumer AI model Gemini hacked multiple systems by guessing login credentials, the company said last week.
Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon told CBS News earlier in September that AI could soon grow "smart enough to kill us."

Nick Clegg plays down fears ‘godlike’ AI could exterminate humanity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:19:28 UTC
18:19:28 KST

Nick Clegg has dismissed fears over AI’s “godlike power to exterminate humanity”, calling it a sign that tech bosses are “breathing their own fumes”.
The former UK deputy prime minister said that tech bosses should focus on addressing known specific threats such as cybersecurity and bioweapons rather than the “slightly hand-wavy view that this technology is unavoidably going to develop some godlike power which is going to turn on us and exterminate humanity”.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, he said: “I think it is perhaps accidentally self-serving, because it sort of implies that we can only be made safe by having everything controlled, in effect, by an oligopoly of a small number of companies, and I think it slightly paralyses the political debate.”
Clegg, who was formerly the president of global affairs at Meta and owns more than 917,000 shares in Nscale, a UK-based datacentre, and is a cofounder of the AI startup AMI Labs, said he spent “a huge amount of time” with people in the tech industry.
“They don’t agree amongst themselves at all. Of course, we hear the most apocalyptic voices,” he said, noting that one person who runs an AI lab said the current discourse was “totally silly”.
“There is a culture in Silicon Valley – it’s an odd place for those who haven’t been there. It is in many ways the centre of the universe, or at least claiming to shape it. It’s also an oddly parochial place. It’s a strange sort of culture where the engineers can get quite close to the technology and start slightly breathing their own fumes as they wind themselves up into a lather about these things,” he said.
Asked about the autonomous hack conducted by a group of OpenAI agents on a major real-world company, Hugging Face, Clegg said there was a case for “tramlines and greater transparency”.
However, he said this would be unlikely to happen under a Trump administration given its competitiveness on AI. He also suspected China’s cooperation would be limited, since the development of AI technologies was viewed as a “national mission” after the country was “cheated out of the Industrial Revolution”.
He added: “I think there’s a great potential for the big three techno democracies in the world – India, Europe and the US – to collaborate more.”
Asked whether the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, could take a lead on such efforts, Clegg noted the UK was not a world leader on AI: “We need to be realistic about what influence we can and cannot exert.”
Clegg also disagreed with other proposed remedies, such as introducing a “kill switch”, which he said would be unworkable; or only producing closed models, where source code is not made public, which he said were no safer than open source models according to the evidence.
Instead, he suggested: “There is a lot that can be done both voluntarily and through regulation, to enforce far greater transparency on the way in which these models are concocted and how they operate.”

For Pope Leo, the risk of an AI apocalypse is a major concern
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:16:45 UTC
18:16:45 KST

For Pope Leo, the risk of an AI apocalypse is a major concern
VATICAN CITY, Sept 24 - The Vatican warned about the risk of an apocalypse spurred by artificial intelligence years before major American firms sounded the alarm at the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday - a concern that Pope Leo is placing at the heart of his papacy.
Leo, who in May called on world leaders for global rules to oversee the industry, renewed his warnings about AI at a Vatican meeting on Thursday and is expected to do so again on Friday in a speech at the Paris headquarters of the UN's culture and education body, UNESCO.
"This is not happening on day zero for the Holy See," Rev. Paolo Benanti, a leading Vatican advisor on AI issues, told Reuters, referring to recent calls for a slowdown that have been endorsed by the CEOs of AI firms Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI, among others.
"The transformative power of AI ... could produce a magnitude of societal changes that are very hard to predict," said Benanti, an Italian academic who recently took part in the AI summit hosted by Britain's King Charles.
The priest said he could not reveal details about the contents of the summit's confidential discussions.
In a speech to the Pontifical Academy of Sciences on Thursday, Leo said AI can benefit humanity, but it has introduced "new dangers to security and international peace." He urged global leaders to "govern wisely" in overseeing the technology.
CARDINAL: THE FUTURE OF HUMANITY IS AT STAKE
Leo, the first US-born pope, has raised the possible dangers of AI development frequently throughout his 16-month-old papacy and first discussed the issue publicly on his third day in office.
In his May appeal, released as his first major document, Leo warned that AI systems spread misinformation, prioritise conflict and could lead the world down a path of unending war.
Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican's top diplomat, reiterated Leo's call for international regulation of the industry at an event in Rome last week, warning that countries cannot "go it alone" on the technology.
"The future of humanity is really at stake here," Parolin said. The world, he said, needs "everyone's involvement in establishing some common rules that can genuinely govern this phenomenon."
Anthropic co-founder Chris Olah spoke at the Vatican's launch event for the pope's May document, known as an encyclical.
Asked if the Vatican is in ongoing dialogue with any AI firms, Benanti stressed the decentralized nature of the global church and said some discussions are being led by local bishops.
On September 16, the US bishops' conference said it had created a new AI taskforce after several of its leaders met with executives that day.
"The dialogue focused on ways to keep any system of artificial intelligence at the service of humanity and the urgent need to address the real and present dangers such technology presents," a statement said.
LEO WARNS ABOUT AUTONOMOUS WEAPONS
The Vatican began warning about the risks of AI in 2019, hosting two conferences that year on the possible dangers of the technology. The late Pope Francis warned attendees at one of the events that misinformation spread by AI could spark a world war.
The Vatican also teamed with Microsoft, IBM, the UN's Food and Agriculture Organization and the Italian government in 2020 to issue a call for AI development that "does not have as its sole goal greater profit or the gradual replacement of people in the workplace."
Leo has urged oversight especially for the development of weapons systems, such as those being used in the Russia-Ukraine war. He said in his encyclical that such weapons have advanced "practically beyond any human reach to govern them."
The Vatican's advocacy on the global stage against autonomous weaponry goes back decades, Benanti said, likening AI-powered drones to landmines that are indiscriminate with their targets.
The priest compared the Vatican's warnings about the risks of AI to how popes have long called for nuclear disarmament.
"If nuclear weapons can destroy humanity ... the manipulation of generative AI content in social spaces can destroy the capabilities of people to stay together as a society," he said.
"Nuclear weapons have to be stocked inside facilities and you can count and control them. AI is not this visible." REUTERS

Morocco parliamentary election delivers setback to PM’s party
Morocco’s Authenticity and Modernity Party (PAM) has won the most seats in parliamentary elections, overtaking its partners in the outgoing government as turnout fell to its lowest level in nearly two decades.
Preliminary results announced by Interior Minister Abdelouafi Laftit on Thursday gave PAM 97 of the lower house’s 395 seats, up from 87 in 2021. The National Rally of Independents (RNI), which topped the previous election with 102 seats, fell to 66, narrowly ahead of the Istiqlal Party with 65.
Turnout in Wednesday’s vote was 38.02% of the nearly 15.8 million registered voters, according to official data, down from 50.35% in 2021 and the lowest since 2007.
The liberal-centrist PAM needs coalition partners to govern, but its leaders have ruled out another alliance with RNI. Outgoing Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch, a billionaire businessman whose government faced criticism over living costs and unemployment, did not contest the election. He announced his withdrawal in January, citing RNI’s two-term leadership limit and saying the party should choose his successor before the vote.
The vote drew allegations of irregularities in several constituencies. In the northern port city of Tangier, the Left Alliance, which won eight seats nationwide, alleged ballot stuffing and demanded a rerun. Prosecutors opened investigations after a man was arrested carrying ballots at a polling site in Tangier. PAM rejected allegations linking its candidates to the incident, calling them a “political conspiracy,” and backed an investigation.
Founded in 2008 by an adviser to King Mohammed VI, PAM positioned itself as a secular-leaning rival to the Islamist Justice and Development Party, which recovered to 54 seats from 13 in 2021.
The king appoints the prime minister from the party that wins the most seats but retains sweeping authority over defense, foreign affairs, and policy direction. Potential candidates include PAM leader Fatima Ezzahra El Mansouri and Budget Minister Fouzi Lekjaa, who also heads Morocco’s football federation. El Mansouri would become the country’s first female prime minister if appointed.
PAM campaigned on promises of 1 million jobs and greater healthcare and social protection spending.
The election follows youth-led protests last year over unemployment, failing public services, and alleged vast spending on preparations for the 2030 World Cup, which Morocco will co-host with Spain and Portugal. At least three protesters were reportedly killed and more than 400 people arrested during the demonstrations, according to Amnesty International, which accused security forces of excessive force and arbitrary arrests.

From idealists to struggling sceptics: how Labour’s majority depends on five progressive voter types – in charts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:15:01 UTC
18:15:01 KST

A new MRP poll suggests Labour would remain the largest party if a general election were held now, but would fall well short of an overall majority as Reform surged into second place.
Behind those headline figures, research from Survation and 38 Degrees casts new light on five distinct voter groups who are collectively defined as the “progressive majority”. These people share concerns about living costs and the NHS, but differ over immigration, the environment, political trust and the pace of change needed to address the UK’s policies.
To build a parliamentary majority, Labour must hold on to the groups that have remained relatively loyal, while winning back voters drifting towards the Greens, Reform or political disengagement. In short, they need enough of this “progressive majority” to stay within the fold.
Labour strategists – including Keir Starmer’s former chief of staff Morgan McSweeney – have often been wary of a tactic that seeks only to unite the progressive bloc. But while it would result in Labour losing huge swathes of seats that it won in 2024, it may be enough to lock Nigel Farage out of No 10 if there were significant tactical voting.
It also gives a clue to how Andy Burnham might seek to structure his priorities – and why the cost of living will be at the heart of the prime minister’s policy platform at the Labour conference, one with salience for voters considering either the Greens or Reform.
The charts below, which are based on polling of more than 8,000 voters, show how Labour’s support cuts across age, class and geography – and reveal five distinct voter groups with contrasting priorities.
The five groups in the ‘progressive majority’
The researchers identified five groups of people who collectively make up what they call the “progressive majority”.
It is a key group of voters who they argue the Labour government should be targeting if they want to win an overall majority at the next general election.
The five groups are described as:
Rooted traditionalists: Older, economically left-leaning voters who are highly concerned about immigration and less interested in environmental issues. Many moved from the Conservatives to Labour but could shift again, including towards Reform. Cost of living pressures and NHS access provide the strongest common ground with other progressive voters.
Open-hearted idealists: Affluent, highly educated and the most socially liberal, pro-immigration and politically engaged group. They lean strongly towards Labour, the Greens and Lib Dems and are particularly open to tactical voting. Bills, NHS access and progressive taxation matter most, while tougher immigration policies risk alienating them.
Quiet persuadables: The youngest and least politically committed segment, often holding centrist or uncertain views. Their support is spread widely across the parties and they are the most likely to vote tactically. They are potentially winnable, but need a compelling reason to engage with politics.
Trusting optimists: Young, affluent, urban and highly educated, with strong confidence in their finances, the government and the country’s future. Most support Labour and economically progressive policies, but they are also the most socially authoritarian group. Their political loyalty could weaken if their circumstances deteriorate.
Struggling sceptics: The least financially secure, trusting and electorally engaged group, with many believing voting changes little. Although economically left-leaning, their support is divided between Labour, the Greens and Reform. Winning them back could depend on tangible improvements to bills, wages and living standards rather than political messaging alone.
There are clear demographic differences between the groups.
Quiet persuadables are the youngest-leaning group, while very few rooted traditionalists are young; more than a third of them are over 65.
Trusting optimists are twice as likely as voters overall to live in London, while rooted traditionalists are half as likely.
Struggling sceptics are most likely to have no or low-level qualifications. Meanwhile, almost two-thirds of trusting optimists are graduates.
While nearly a third of struggling sceptics are in lower-income households, trusting optimists and open-hearted idealists are the most affluent groups, with most households earning more than £40,000.
Rooted traditionalists are overwhelmingly white, while trusting optimists are by far the most ethnically diverse group.
Rooted traditionalists and struggling sceptics contain the most leave voters, while open-hearted idealists are overwhelmingly remain-aligned.
How the ‘progressive majority’ is intending to vote
These five constituent groups collectively account for nine in 10 current Labour voters.
This is up from eight in 10 at the 2024 general election, showing that Labour’s support has become more concentrated among progressive voters in the last two years.
Open-hearted idealists provide the largest share of Labour’s support at 28%, followed by quiet persuadables at 21%. Trusting optimists have recorded the largest increase, rising four percentage points in the last two years.
At the time of polling, Labour led among all five progressive voter groups – although support ranged from 25% among struggling sceptics to 57% among trusting optimists.
Open-hearted idealists lean heavily towards progressive parties, with the Greens being supported by 23% of this group.
Struggling sceptics are the most fragmented group: Labour leads on 25%, but the Greens and Reform both attract substantial support. Thirteen per cent remain undecided – the highest rate of any group.
Reform performed relatively strongly among rooted traditionalists, whereas the Conservatives reached their highest level among quiet persuadables.
The shifts since 2024 are often down to the fact that, while Labour has lost support across the board, some of these groups are more likely to have found another political home – despite the government switching prime minister.
The Greens have gained the most support among open-hearted idealists, while Reform’s rise is most concentrated among struggling sceptics and rooted traditionalists.
The struggling sceptics are the group among which Labour has lost the most support, falling from 39% to 28%. Both the Greens and Reform have gained among these people, rising to 21% and 18% respectively.
The quiet persuadables and trusting optimists are the groups that have stuck with Labour the most, recording only small drops in support since the general election.
While this is probably due to the stronger financial position of the trusting optimists, who are more likely to trust progressive politicians, the quiet persuadables are less committed to politics and generally don’t hold stronger political views.
Conflicting policy priorities – but ‘manageable’ divides
Looking at the concerns of these five groups reveals conflicting priorities which could be hard for Burnham to bridge.
The cost of living is the dominant concern across every progressive voter group, cited by between 54% and 77%.
Health and the NHS generally ranks second, peaking at 56% among open-hearted idealists, while the economy is a significant but less prominent concern across all groups.
The sharpest divide is over immigration: it is cited by 34% of rooted traditionalists and 28% of struggling sceptics, but just 5% of pen-hearted idealists.
The climate crisis shows a reverse pattern, reaching 29% among open-hearted idealists but only 10% among rooted traditionalists.
Rooted traditionalists are also notably more concerned about pensions, while housing and jobs feature more strongly among trusting optimists and quiet persuadables.
When looking at the salience of different issues among voters as a whole, the research concluded that immigration is the area where Labour is least trusted – but also that this might not be a significant vulnerability.
It is named as a vote-deciding issue by 40% of voters – level with the NHS and second only to the cost of living – but Reform leads Labour on it by 10 points. Thirty-one per cent of the public trust Reform on this issue, compared with 21% trusting Labour.
But the researchers point to the fact that these figures are population-wide, and that immigration is not a driving factor in the votes of most people within the progressive majority. Instead, the cost of living and the economy are bigger drivers of people’s votes.
Across the public as a whole, Labour led Reform on every other major issue, including the NHS, by 12 points, and the cost of living, by six.
Damian Lyons Lowe, the founder and chief executive of Survation, said: “Labour’s potential coalition is best understood as five distinct segments making up a ‘progressive majority’ – those voters that strongly consider voting for one or more of Lib Dems, Labour, the Greens, Plaid and the SNP. They have very different views on social and economic policy – the balancing act is real – but our data suggests it’s more manageable than the conventional wisdom implies.
“The issues that divide these groups, immigration above all, are largely ones where Labour isn’t trusted and where the voters it could win are already spoken for. The issues that unite them – the cost of living, energy, food and housing bills, and cleaning up politics – are exactly where even the most sceptical parts of the coalition trust Labour more than anyone else. The way to build such a winning coalition isn’t to referee their disagreements. It’s to deliver visibly on the concerns every one of them shares.”

====================================================================================================

Venus May Have Devoured Its Moon
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:15:00 UTC
18:15:00 KST

Venus has nearly the same mass, size, and structure as Earth, which has led astronomers to believe it should have a moon, but it doesn’t. It is technically possible that a moon never formed, but scientists have also come up with several scenarios to describe how Venus could have lost its satellite.
One previously presented hypothesis is that Venus’ moon was destroyed by a collision with some massive celestial body. But a recent study by researchers at the University of California, Riverside, suggests a different course of events. It posits that instead of being obliterated by some catastrophic external force, the moon was slowly pulled in by Venus’ gravity and plodding rotation until it fragmented and was completely swallowed.
“Venus didn’t require a catastrophe to arrive at what we can see today,” Steven Kane, an astrophysicist and the paper’s lead author, explained in a press release. “It turns out the gravity of the planet itself combined with the rate at which it spins naturally caused the moon to collapse on top of it.”
A planet’s rotation can either push or pull on its satellites, depending on its speed. The rotation can cause variations in gravitational strength. This is why our moon isn’t in any danger of being eaten. In fact—because our 24-hour days are rather fast in a planetary sense—our moon is currently drifting away from Earth at a rate of about 1.5 inches per year.
And when astronomers say Venus spins slowly, they really mean it. The time it takes for Venus to complete one rotation is 243 Earth days. That’s longer than Venus’ year and makes the bright planet the slowest spinner in our solar system. This protracted rotation, combined with the planet’s gravity, means that even if a moon existed, it would not be pushed outward but would instead be dragged inward.
To verify this mechanism, Kane and his research team built a computer model simulating gravitational interactions between celestial bodies. After verifying the model’s accuracy by faithfully recreating the evolution of Earth’s moon, they ran simulations varying several factors including the time it takes Venus to complete one rotation and the mass of a hypothetical moon, ranging anywhere from 0.01 to 10 times that of Earth’s natural satellite.
The outcomes showed that the moon’s fate depended on Venus’ rotation speed, the lunar mass, and the shape of its orbit. Under many conditions, the satellite spiraled inward, eventually breaking apart and succumbing to the planet’s gravity. “When I made this discovery, I was shocked,” Kane recalled. “I thought surely the broad range of scenarios I was exploring would lead to a variety of results. But it all went pretty much in the same direction.”
In a few instances—such as when the researchers artificially sped up the planet’s rotation to once every 10 to 12 hours and the moon had a mass comparable to that of Earth’s—the simulations indicated a moon could survive for up to 4.5 billion years. But that’s little more than an interesting test of the model. It’s an extremely unlikely reality given our planetary neighbor’s current lethargic speed.
This study does not, however, prove that Venus once had a moon, and finding physical evidence of its existence will not be easy. Venus’ surface is geologically young, the number of craters indicating that top layer of rock is just a few hundred million years old. The planet itself formed at the same time as the rest of our solar system, some 4.6 billion years ago, but extreme amounts of volcanic and tectonic activity have essentially remodeled the surface.
If any evidence of a moon exists, it’s been paved over and may lie deep underground. Seismological surveys penetrating far into the Earth have provided evidence of our moon’s formation—anomalous structures pointing to a massive impact. If similar measurements could be conducted on Venus, it’s possible that traces of a moon that was once absorbed might be found.
The moon’s fate could also provide clues to solving another long-standing mystery: whether Venus once had an environment capable of supporting life. Swallowing a moon would have imparted enormous energy and angular momentum to the planet, which could significantly shift its rotation, geology, and climate—altering the course of the planet’s evolution.
This is not limited to Venus. Scientists seeking to identify habitable worlds among exoplanets have often considered the presence of a moon as a factor influencing habitability. However, it remains unclear whether a large moon is essential for the existence of life.
“My feeling is there are benefits to having a moon, but it isn’t required for habitability,” Kane said. “The moon has definitely changed the way Earth has evolved through time, but we don’t fully know how important that role is.”
This finding that planets with slower rotation speeds are less likely to retain a moon offers a new perspective in the search for Earth-like exoplanets. Even if very Earth-like planets are located, if their rotation speeds are not fast enough, they might come to devour their moons.

Tactical voting at next election could push Reform into fourth place, poll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
09:14:54 UTC
18:14:54 KST

Progressive voters could push Reform UK into fourth place and put Labour within touching distance of a majority if tactical voting is widespread at the next election, a major poll has found.
Andy Burnham is beginning to attract a significant number of left-leaning voters back to Labour, motivated by a desire to stop Nigel Farage, the results suggest.
The poll of more than 8,000 voters, shared with the Guardian, suggests a widespread openness to voting tactically. It also shows the prime minister’s most successful electoral strategy would be to unite the centre and left bloc of voters, while the right remains split.
It would be a marked contrast to the tactics of Keir Starmer’s Labour before the 2024 general election, when the party tried to attract more conservative older voters. Such a tactic would be likely to unsettle some in Labour, given the same strategy was deployed for Ed Miliband’s failed bid in 2015, albeit before Reform’s arrival as a major electoral force.
The poll on the eve of Labour’s annual conference in Liverpool shows a significant shift of left-leaning voters towards Burnham’s Labour and will encourage those in the party who are thinking of gambling on an early election while Reform’s ratings are ebbing and while leftwing parties such as the Greens appear to be losing momentum.
Twice as many voters have returned to Labour from the left as from the right since April.
The previously unreleased research, including a seat-by-seat MRP model, was conducted by Survation and the progressive activist site 38 Degrees in Burnham’s first month as prime minister.
It suggests Labour would be the largest party in parliament if an election took place today, on 272 seats, a four-point lead. This would mean achieving 42% of parliamentary seats with 28% of the vote.
Reform would become the official opposition on 153. This represents 24% of seats – the same as its vote share. The Conservatives would fall to third place with 85.
Two hundred seats are tight marginals decided by under five points, meaning a two- to three-point swing could move about 100 seats that are likely to decide a future election. But in a sign of the volatility of the polls, a far higher percentage of voters are open to tactical voting in those seats when they cite their preferred party.
If voters are prepared to switch to one of the two frontrunners in their seats, rather than their preferred party, then Reform UK’s seat count would fall dramatically, favouring Labour and the Conservatives.
About 18% of voters who live in a seat where tactical voting would make a substantial difference say they are willing to do so but are not yet doing so. If those voters decided to vote tactically, Reform UK would be reduced to 62 seats, giving Labour 319 – six short of a majority.
Of the 91 seats where Reform would cease to be the most likely winner, 46 would go to the Conservatives and 43 to Labour. The projection is unlikely to be exact at this stage in the electoral cycle.
Reform’s chances of winning fell by more than 50 points in 59 seats. Among these are the Wrekin, Torridge and Tavistock, and North West Cambridgeshire – all of which have Reform as the most likely leader under the “normal” assumptions but lose out to the Conservatives under a scenario with more tactical voting.
In 2024, the now-chancellor, John Healey, held Rawmarsh and Conisbrough with 49% of the vote, with Reform in second place on 28.6%. The base modelling of the MRP indicates that Reform could win a tight race in the seat, with a 51% chance, but this plummets if tactical voting increases, with a 76% chance of Labour holding the seat in this scenario.
In Bassetlaw, Reform could lose even as its own vote share rises from 35% to 40%, because tactical voting would lift Labour further – from 32% to 40%. The Conservatives, Liberal Democrats and Greens would lose supporters if this switching took place. The forecast estimates that the winner would shift from Reform, with a 77% chance, to Labour, with a 58% chance.
Newark, held by the Conservative-turned-Reform MP Robert Jenrick, is forecast to flip to the Conservatives under both scenarios, although under heavier tactical voting the chance of a Conservative win increases from 68% to more than 99% should Labour backers vote Conservative to stop him.
Damian Lyons Lowe, Survation’s chief executive, said: “Estimating tactical voting is a complex consideration, but the mechanics here are simple. Four in 10 voters are currently backing a party that can’t finish in the top two where they live and are willing to vote tactically.
“But when we ask whether they would lend their vote to the stronger local contender in a two-horse race, around half said yes. That gap – worth some 18 points of the national electorate – is an enormous untapped reservoir for parties looking to squeeze voters.
“Should these voters act as they say, our model shows Reform falling from second place to fourth, losing around 90 seats, despite its own vote share actually going up. Reform-leaning Conservatives will consolidate too. Reform doesn’t collapse; it risks being outnumbered, seat by seat, by voters coordinating around whoever is best placed locally on the left and right.”
The prediction is also complicated by the sheer number of seats Labour won in 2024 from the Conservatives where the party has been polling as low as third over the past year. Progressive voters living in seats such as Labour-held Southend would be unlikely to opt to vote for the Conservatives, even if they were technically the best placed to beat Reform at the next election, showing the limitations of predictions around tactical voting.
The poll also suggests Labour is gaining considerable numbers of voters back from other leftwing parties, but not from Reform. The share of Labour’s lost 2024 voters going to the Greens, Liberal Democrats, Plaid Cymru or the Scottish National party has fallen from 60% to 46%; but on the right, of those lost to Reform or the Tories, it has fallen from 27% to 24%.
Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, said the polling indicated a far more optimistic public mood than before the Labour conference last year, but there was also significant expectation that Burnham needed to deliver.
“There are signs of optimism and even hope, but what has not changed is the way voters are crying out for bold action, fast,” she said. “The results show a huge amount of common ground between voters, especially when it comes to the cost of living. Voters who have moved in different directions since the general election two years ago are united by the fact that action on the cost of living crisis will have the single biggest bearing on their future vote.”
