Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:40:45 UTC
17:40:45 KST

Netanyahu takes UN stage with one eye on Israel’s election
As criticism of Israel intensifies, Israeli PM Netanyahu heads to the UN with his own political future in focus.
When Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu takes to his feet at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York later on Thursday, he does so at a critical point in both his political career and in his country’s long and fractious relationship with the international body.
Israel has faced repeated accusations of genocide at the UN, as well as systematic war crimes in Gaza and the occupied West Bank. Those criticisms continue to shape the country’s fractious relationship with the body.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Do Israelis feel any safer now than they did on October 6, 2023?
- list 2 of 4Why United Nations says US boat strikes may be ‘crimes against humanity’
- list 3 of 4US senator condemns Netanyahu as a ‘chronic liar’ ahead of UNGA visit
- list 4 of 4Despite flurry of New York diplomacy, US-Iran deal remains elusive
For Netanyahu, appearing in front of the UNGA for the 15th time, the stakes have rarely been higher. Addressing a domestic Israeli audience that polls show to be losing faith in him and his Likud party in the run-up to crucial elections later this year, Netanyahu has already pitched himself as Israel’s primary voice on the international stage.
Nevertheless, analysts say Netanyahu’s address could prove a pivotal moment domestically, amplified by international criticism of Israel and expected to dominate headlines and be carried live across the country’s television networks.
“This is a regular fixture for him,” former Israeli consul general in New York and ex-government adviser, Alon Pinkas, told Al Jazeera. “It’s his way of being seen in Israel as standing up against the world and of telling members that he will never give up or surrender. He’s also turned the event into some kind of national holiday in Israel, with everyone sitting down to watch the address on television. He’s brainwashed people in Israel into believing his speech is somehow an announcement of policy, stated in defiance of the [rest of the world] who don’t believe a word he says.”
A history of hostility
Israeli leaders have long framed their stance towards the UN as one of defiance in the face of hostility. The UN has long been a platform for critics of Israel’s illegal occupation of Palestinian land and repeated attacks on its neighbours. It has included attempts to censure Israel over what UN investigators have described as apartheid in the West Bank, as well as accusations of genocide and pogroms across the occupied Palestinian territory since October 2023.
There have been numerous UNGA resolutions criticising Israel’s conduct – nearly all dismissed by Israeli lawmakers as evidence of institutional bias – culminating in Israel declaring UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres persona non grata and severely restricting the operations of the UN’s agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
“Generally speaking, many Israelis tend to see the UN as anti-Israeli,” Nimrod Goren, the president of the Israeli Institute for Regional Foreign Policies, Mitvim, said.
Against that background, criticism from New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani – already cast as anti-Israel in the Israeli press – has drawn greater public attention to the event. Underscoring the sense of hostility towards Israel are stories within the country’s media suggesting that Netanyahu’s visit to New York has been curtailed due to unspecified security concerns, with the Israeli premier expected to fly out of New York on the same day as his arrival.
In response, Israel’s ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, who has repeatedly accused the organisation of waging “diplomatic terrorism” against the state, called for Mamdani’s arrest for what he said was the mayor’s incitement against New York’s Jewish community before Netanyahu’s visit.
“Netanyahu is going into his UNGA speech with not one but both eyes focused firmly on the upcoming Israeli election,” Goren said. “The speech is usually treated in Israel as a major event, receiving broad coverage and dominating the news cycle. Netanyahu will likely try to leverage this to bolster his image as a close ally of the US and to talk up the threat posed by Iran.”
US backing
Some have interpreted US President Donald Trump’s apparent lack of availability to meet Netanyahu during this trip as a sign of waning support. But US backing for Israel at the UN has remained steadfast since the October 7 attack and has contributed to growing frustration within the UN over what they see as Israel’s ability to resist international censure.
Alongside the creation of the Board of Peace, which shifted significant responsibility for Gaza’s future from the UN to the Trump-founded organisation, Washington has repeatedly used its veto at the UN Security Council (UNSC) to shield Israel from resolutions it opposes. The US has vetoed at least six UNSC resolutions on Gaza since October 2023, most of them demanding an immediate ceasefire.
“There seems to be genuine frustration within the UN General Assembly over the body’s failure to play a significant political role in Gaza and the West Bank, but also in its failure to protect its own staff and agencies,” Chatham House Associate Fellow Zizette Darkazally, who previously worked with the UN, said.
“However, it’s worth remembering the context the UN operates within in the occupied territories and the important humanitarian role it plays. The UN continues to get aid and medical support into Gaza and the West Bank, which are both areas where Israel has absolute control over access,” she said. “It’s also worth remembering that the UN is only as strong as the commitment of its member states.
“That, combined with a system of veto that’s more than 80 years old, has left the organisation weaker now than it had ever been,” she said of the confrontations between the UN and Israel. “And we’re seeing the effects of that, not just in Palestine, but in Yemen, Sudan and Iran, where the UN is playing next to no political role.”

Employer representative Chiu I-che (邱一徹) said many small- and medium-sized businesses, traditional manufacturers, and service companies still face weak demand and higher material, energy, and labor costs. He urged the committee to focus more on inflation and what different industries can afford, per Economic Daily News.

L3Harris wins $876 million for Growler radar jammer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:38:52 UTC
17:38:52 KST

- The U.S. Navy added $876.4 million to L3Harris' Next Generation Jammer Low Band contract for the EA-18G Growler, with work running through fiscal 2031.
- The Royal Australian Air Force obligated $23 million at award, compared with $3.65 million from the U.S. Navy.
The U.S. Navy has added $876.4 million to L3Harris Technologies’ contract for the Next Generation Jammer Low Band, a radar-jamming pod for the EA-18G Growler electronic attack jet flown by the U.S. Navy and the Royal Australian Air Force, the U.S. Department of War announced.
The award is a modification to the $587.4 million contract Naval Air Systems Command gave L3Harris in August 2024 to take the jammer through engineering and manufacturing development, the final stage before production. The new money is larger than that original award.
It pays for continued development of the pod, tooling, equipment and labor needed to build it, and delivery of test pods for system demonstration. It also covers additional cybersecurity work, along with logistics, testing and software support for both air forces. Work is scheduled to finish in fiscal 2031.
The modification is undefinitized, meaning the Navy authorized the work before the final terms and price were agreed. It is a cost-plus-incentive-fee deal, which reimburses L3Harris’s costs and pays a fee tied to performance targets. The Navy did not compete it.
Australia is putting in more money up front than the United States. At the time of award, the Navy obligated $3.65 million in fiscal 2026 research and development funds, while the Royal Australian Air Force contributed $23 million in cooperative funds.
Most of the work, 43%, will take place at L3Harris’s facility in Salt Lake City. The rest is spread across sites in Alabama, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Colorado, California, New York and Texas, with 3.4% performed in Australia.
The Growler is a modified F/A-18F Super Hornet built to jam and disrupt enemy radars and communications, clearing a path for other aircraft. Its main jamming system has long been the AN/ALQ-99 pod, first fielded in the 1970s. The Navy is replacing it with a family of Next Generation Jammer pods, each covering a different part of the radio spectrum.
RTX’s Raytheon builds the mid-band pod, the AN/ALQ-249, which already flies with the fleet. L3Harris’s low-band pod targets lower-frequency search radars. Those radars track targets less precisely than higher-frequency systems, but they can spot aircraft at long range and cue long-range missiles toward them.
L3Harris says the pod will let Growler crews suppress enemy air defenses with high-power jamming from standoff ranges, keeping the aircraft farther from the threats they are attacking.
Suppliers are already delivering hardware. In July, CPI Aerostructures of Edgewood, New York, received a $13.6 million contract from L3Harris to build pod structures for operational prototypes that will go to the Navy for fleet assessment and to extra test units for airworthiness and design checks. The company said it had delivered its first test article. Honeywell Aerospace joined the program in June 2025, and Marotta Controls announced contracts to support it this month.

Alarm bells sound in Brussels as EU sales of Chinese hybrid cars rocket
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:34:46 UTC
17:34:46 KST

Sales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry.
In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU. However, after Brussels imposed anti-subsidy tariffs on fully electric cars from China in 2024, sales of hybrids have shot up to 160,662 in the first seven months of this year.
Eurostat figures show that sales of Chinese-made plug-in hybrid vehicles – models popular for longer driving distances that can recharge via both the fuel engine and an external power source – have also soared, rising from 56,706 sold in 2022 to 217,764 from January to July this year.
The volume of Chinese hybrids on the roads is now spooking the car industry and Brussels, which has asked China to voluntarily reduce its hybrid exports to the EU or face safeguards, likely to be quotas.
On Thursday the German car industry for the first time indicated it would be willing to consider tariffs on Chinese hybrids specifically.
The German Association of the Automotive Industry, VDA, called on the European Commission to carry out a comprehensive assessment of the impact of any trade safeguards, which can range from quotas to price floors and tariffs.
It said: “The EU must also have an effective and up-to-date set of trade defence instruments at its disposal. Where unfair conduct is proven, the use of WTO-compliant trade defence instruments must be considered; these are legitimate and tried-and-tested means of achieving a level playing field and safeguarding fair conditions of competition.”
According to new figures released by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), hybrid cars now account for almost 37% of the overall market, with electric cars making up just over 21% of the market.
The ACEA figures show three Chinese manufacturers – BYD, Chery and Leapmotor – making significant inroads with triple-digit growth in the EU.
A fourth firm, Geely, has had a steady 8% increase in the first eight months of the year and remains the most popular Chinese brand in the EU, with 205,000 cars sold in the first eight months of the year. Its brands include Sweden’s Volvo and Polestar, the EU’s only all-electric car manufacturer.
BYD is catching up with Geely, with sales rocketing by 163% year on year with 177,000 units sold.
Both firms, along with a fifth Chinese manufacturer, SAIC, are now firmly ahead of Elon Musk’s Tesla, which sold 142,000 cars across the bloc in the first seven months of the year.
European car manufacturers still dominate, with the Volkswagen group selling 2m cars in the first eight months of the year.
Sales of electric cars are also growing fast in parts of Europe including Germany, up 75% to 69,000 units in August, and in France, where sales are up by 112%. In Slovenia, sales have increased by 266%. This compares with the UK, up 27% in August to 28,000 EVs sold, and Ireland, up just 7% to 2,200 units.
Earlier this month, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, described the now €1.18bn-a-day trade deficit between the bloc and China as having reached an unsustainable “tipping point”.
The EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao will meet on 8 and 9 October to try to build a truce.
Also hoping for a trade truce are Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, who meet in their third summit in 12 months in Washington on Thursday.
Trump agreed in South Korea last October to drop tariffs on certain Chinese imports in exchange for a suspension of China’s export restriction on rare earths, critical to the car industry across the US, EU and the UK.
Some believe a deal may not have been reached yet and the suspension may not be announced until the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference next month.

Our specialists, in cooperation with other Rostec companies, are constantly enhancing production processes to ensure the necessary pace of aircraft manufacturing," said UAC CEO Vadim Badekha, as quoted by the press service.
The state corporation noted that the Su-57 stealth multirole fighter aircraft was designed to perform a wide range of combat missions. It is capable of engaging air, ground, and sea targets. The aircraft can be deployed around the clock, including in adverse weather conditions and electronic countermeasures.
"To fulfill the objectives of supplying the troops with highly sought-after weapons and military equipment, the Aerospace Forces’ crews have accepted the Su-57 aircraft in their new technical configuration. I would like to thank the plant representatives and all employees of Rostec’s United Aircraft Corporation who participated in the design, assembly, and preparation of this aircraft for their professionalism. The aircraft has already proven itself in the special military operation. The new technical configuration will help broaden the range of missions for which this type of aircraft is deployed. "The advanced capabilities built into the aircraft weapons system allow for the use of new types of aerial weapons," said a Su-57 pilot of the Aerospace Forces, whose remarks are quoted in the press release.

Ukraine handed over to South Korea two North Korean soldiers whom Ukrainian forces had captured during fighting in the Kursk region, Russia.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky made this statement on September 23 during his address to the general debate of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly in New York.
One of the North Korean servicemen attempted to take his own life after being captured.
Ukrainian soldiers took two North Korean soldiers prisoner on January 11, 2025, during combat operations in the Kursk region.
The Ukrainian president later said he was ready to hand them over to Kim Jong Un as part of a possible exchange for Ukrainian prisoners of war.
South Korea had previously expressed its readiness to accept North Korean servicemen captured while fighting on Russia’s side in the war.
This is also related to South Korea’s constitutional framework. The country’s fundamental law defines the Korean Peninsula and its adjacent islands as the territory of the Republic of Korea, which affects the legal status of North Korean residents.
North Korean POWs asked to be transferred to South Korea.
Militarnyi previously reported that in April 2026, North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un effectively confirmed a policy under which servicemen are expected to avoid capture at the cost of their own lives while participating in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
In early 2025, servicemembers of Tactical Group № 84 of the Ukrainian Special Operations Forces, working alongside Air Assault Forces units, captured two North Korean servicemen fighting on Russia’s side in the Kursk region.
This was not the first attempt to capture servicemen from North Korea. At the time, North Korea had not yet officially acknowledged its involvement in the war, so Russian and North Korean troops would typically finish off their wounded and do everything possible to prevent evidence of another country’s involvement in the war against Ukraine from being left behind.
According to the prisoners, they served in the Reconnaissance General Bureau (정찰총국) under the General Staff Department of the Korean People’s Army. One of the prisoners, a 26-year-old serviceman, is named Ri, while the other, a 21-year-old, is Paek. They served as a reconnaissance sniper and a rifleman, respectively.
According to Ri, he arrived in Vladivostok on October 10, 2024. Before that, he and his fellow soldiers spent about a month in Chagang Province, where they helped eliminate the aftermath of flooding.

Autumn begins but summer heat lingers in Portugal, catching tourists off guard
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:30:41 UTC
17:30:41 KST

Autumn has arrived in Portugal, but the summer heat is still being felt. In Lisbon, 36 degrees surprised tourists who did not expect such atypical temperatures for this time of year.
Autumn has begun, but summer is stubbornly hanging on, with much of Portugal still sweltering in unusual heat and thermometers reaching 40 degrees in some inland areas.
In downtown Lisbon, tourists were caught off guard on Wednesday, the first day of autumn, by temperatures of 36 degrees. Expecting cooler weather in September, they had packed clothes for a milder climate.
"I wasn’t expecting this heat. In fact, I even brought a coat because I thought it would be cooler and similar to Canadian autumn weather, around 21, 23 degrees Celsius, and I told my friend the same thing: 'Bring a coat'. And now I feel I’ve got slightly thicker socks than I would have brought if I’d known it was going to be this hot, to be honest," said Shamminaz Polen, a tourist from Canada visiting Lisbon.
To avoid being out in the sun during the hottest hours, there are a few tricks that help these unprepared tourists.
"First of all, we carry bottles of water. If there’s air conditioning, we go into a shop, do some shopping, or take a break to eat or drink something and then walk again. Another trick is to find an alleyway with shade and always walk on the shaded side of the pavement," the same tourist explained.
"It’s very dry, obviously it’s quite pleasant here in the shade and in the shops and so on, but when you’re walking in the sun it can get really very hot," said Fletcher Shepard, another tourist from the United Kingdom on holiday in Lisbon.
Despite the scorching heat, Fletcher Shepard still finds the warm weather pleasant for a few days while sightseeing, given that in England temperatures are currently hovering around 20 degrees Celsius.
The Portuguese weather service IPMA has issued a heat warning for some regions of the country until the end of Thursday and local authorities have also warned of a high risk of forest fires in some inland areas. Temperatures are expected to fall slightly from next week.

Who has the upper hand in financial markets, the US or China?
Against the rising resilience of Chinese markets, the sharp reappraisal of US debt and dollar risks makes the answer far from clear-cut
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Nicholas Spiro is a partner at Lauressa Advisory, a specialist London-based real estate and macroeconomic advisory firm. 
As Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington for his much-anticipated summit with US President Donald Trump, it is clear which country emerged stronger from the tariff shock. Last month, China’s exports rose 25 per cent in annualised terms, causing the country’s trade surplus to swell to US$119 billion and putting it on track to exceed last year’s record of US$1.2 trillion.
Moreover, China’s surplus with the US rose 44 per cent to US$29 billion, the widest gap since Trump returned to the White House. Not only has China’s export machine roared ahead, Beijing’s weaponisation of rare earths showed it has the power to severely disrupt the global economy. When it comes to the trade war, China “has the cards”, as Trump likes to say.
In financial markets, however, things are less clear-cut. On the face of it, comparisons between the US and China are inapt. The US accounts for almost two-thirds of the market capitalisation of the MSCI All-Country World Index, a leading gauge of global stocks. It also constitutes 40 per cent of the global bond market.
Furthermore, the dollar is the world’s pre-eminent reserve currency, while America boasts the deepest, most liquid and most transparent capital markets.

Zelenskyy says Ukraine sent two North Korean POWs to South Korea
The president criticised North Korea for using citizens like ‘currency’ to aid Russia in its war against Ukraine.
Ukraine has transferred two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in an address to the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA).
“Recently, we sent two North Korean prisoners of war to the Republic of Korea,” said Zelenskyy in his speech on Wednesday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items

“These guys are not easy to capture alive,” Zelenskyy said. “One of them, when he realised he was going to be taken prisoner, tried to kill himself. And he was shocked that fate did not let him die.”
He strongly criticised Pyongyang’s involvement in the conflict, questioning why North Korean soldiers were giving their lives in a war against Ukraine.
“Kim Jong Un uses them like currency and gets something in return,” Zelenskyy said, adding that “countries across Asia have likely already noticed North Korea’s enhanced ballistic missiles and significantly advanced drone capabilities”.
Ukrainian and South Korean estimates indicate North Korea has deployed approximately 15,000 soldiers to support Russia’s war effort since 2024, primarily in the Kursk border region.
Zelenskyy provided no further details regarding the transfer.
Ukrainian forces captured the two North Korean soldiers in Russia’s Kursk region in January 2025, in the first known apprehension of Pyongyang’s troops since their deployment to the conflict in 2024. Zelenskyy had previously stated he would consider returning the soldiers to North Korean leader Kim in exchange for Ukrainian prisoners of war held by Russia.
Human rights groups, however, urged him to repatriate them to South Korea, citing the risks of punishments the soldiers faced. South Korean media reported that the two captured soldiers had expressed their desire to defect to South Korea.
South Korea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs did not deny Zelenskyy’s remarks, but it also declined to confirm operational details of the transfer, citing individual safety and family protection.
The issue was a key topic during a July summit in Ankara, Turkiye, where President Lee Jae Myung met Zelenskyy.
Senior presidential spokesperson Kang Yoo-jung stated afterwards that both leaders agreed to resolve the status of North Korean POWs in Ukraine in accordance with international law and humanitarian principles, while respecting the free will of those involved. This built on a prior agreement reached during the South Korea-Ukraine foreign ministers’ meeting in March, where both nations pledged to cooperate on the POW issue under the same humanitarian framework.

Germany news: Bundestag to discuss opt-out organ donation

Germany news: Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid
Published September 24, 2026last updated September 24, 2026
What you need to know
- Berlin has confirmed reports that it is withdrawing its bid to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics.
- Lawmakers debate whether to introduce an opt-out scheme for organ donation
- The Bundestag will also examine government proposals to grant intelligence agencies a wider scope to counter manifold security threats
- German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has warned of Russia's growing aggression against Europe
- The first-ever Islamic theology faculty in Germany is to open in Münster
Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Thursday, September 24, 2026:
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Far-left German activist Lina E. freed again after refusing to testify
A German woman convicted of attacking far-right activists will be released from detention following a ruling by the Federal Constitutional Court.
A court spokeswoman confirmed that the woman, identified only as Lina E. due to German privacy laws, will be released pending a final decision.
Lina E. was originally sentenced to five years and three months in prison in May 2023 for serious assault and forming a criminal association. She and her accomplices were accused of carrying out several attacks against suspected members of far-right groups in the eastern states of Saxony and Thuringia between 2018 and 2020.
Her conviction sparked outrage among left-wing activists and led to riots in several cities across Germany, most notably in Leipzig.
After serving two-thirds of her sentence, she was released on probation in May in a ruling by the Federal Court of Justice.
However, in June, she was jailed for six months by a Dresden court after refusing to testify in a case involving the far-left Antifa-Ost group.
German Defense Ministry declines comment on reported CIA drone warning
A German Defense Ministry spokesperson declined to comment on media reports that the CIA had warned of potential Russian drone attacks targeting Spain, France and Italy.
Asked by DW what the warning means for Germany, the spokesperson said the ministry generally does not comment on media reports. However, the spokesperson said European Union (EU) and NATO members routinely share intelligence through bilateral channels, EU operations and NATO's integrated air and missile defense framework.
German military units and institutions also contribute on an ongoing basis to creating a shared situational picture, the spokesperson added.
Citing a source close to the Lithuanian Ministry of Defense, Spanish newspaper El Mundo reported that the US intelligence agency has warned Russia is preparing to carry out drone strikes in Europe targeting France, Spain and Italy from the sea.
It comes in the wake of a string of drone incidents near sensitive sites elsewhere in Europe, including Belgium, Germany and Denmark.
IN DEPTH: Could Berlin expropriate large real estate companies?
The socialist Left Party won the Berlin election partly on the promise to implement the city's 2021 expropriation referendum to address the city's rent crisis. But can it really happen?
German business confidence up in September — Ifo
The monthly business climate index put out by the Ifo economic research institute has risen 1.1 points to 89.9 points, the highest level in more than three years.
The index, Germany's most important economic barometer, has been rising constantly over the past five months, indicating that the country is slowly returning to economic health after years of struggle.
The business optimism comes despite an energy price shock that has pushed fuel costs to record highs.
"The German economy continues its recovery," said Ifo president Clemens Fuest.
The gauge of business expectations accompanying the index rose to 90.4 from 89.1 in August, while companies also gave a rosier assessment of their current situation than the month before, improving to 89.5 to 88.5 points.
Ifo said, however, that the automotive sector was still in "difficult terrain."
The index is based on a monthly survey of 9,000 companies.
The news from Ifo comes as the country's five leading economic institutes presented a joint fall forecast raising 2026 GDP growth expectations to 1.3% from 0.6%.
105-year-old suspected Nazi POW guard under investigation
German prosecutors said on Thursday that they were investigating a 105-year-old man over crimes that might have been committed during his alleged time as a guard at a Nazi prisoner-of-war camp during World War II.
In a statement seen by the AFP news agency, they said the man was "thought to have been a guard at the prisoner-of-war camp Stalag 326 VI K" in the Senne region of western Germany.
The man is "accused of being an accessory to multiple murders through his activities there," the statement said.
The Stalag 326 VI K camp held between 180,000 and 200,000 Soviet prisoners of war between 1941 and April 1945, when it was liberated by US troops, according to the memorial at the site.
Some 30,000 Soviet POWs are believed to have died at the camp.
The age of the suspect is a reminder that time is running out to prosecute people who committed crimes as part of Germany's Nazi regime.
In April 2025, for example, an alleged former guard at the Sachsenhausen concentration camp near Berlin died before he could face trial on charges of complicity in the murder of more than 3,300 people.
Berlin officially withdraws Olympics bid
Berlin has confirmed reports that it is withdrawing its bid to host the Summer Olympics and Paralympics.
The decision means that only Munich and the western Rhine/Ruhr region are still in the running as potential hosts, with Hamburg having pulled out in May after failing to win support at a referendum.
The withdrawal comes after the socialist Left Party's victory in Berlin's elections on Sunday. The party's lead candidate and potential mayor, Elif Eralp, said she did not support Berlin's bid.
The current mayor, Kai Wegner of the conservative Christian Democrats (CDU), told reporters: "Today is a sad day for Berlin, because the Olympic and Paralympic Games would have been a tremendous opportunity."
"When Ms. Eralp stated that the bid was effectively off the table ... the leading sports associations made it clear: We cannot give you our approval under these circumstances," he said, adding: "I deeply regret this."
Kaweh Niroomand, the volleyball manager who led the Berlin bid, said, "We simply could not offer the political stability required."
On Saturday, the German Olympic Committee (DOSB) is to choose a preferred region as part of a bid to the International Olympic Committee to host one of the 2036, 2040 and 2044 Summer Games.
The Summer Olympics have been held twice on German soil.
Berlin hosted the Games in 1936 in then Nazi-ruled Germany and Munich, then as part of West Germany, was the site of the 1972 Games.
IN DEPTH: Top economic think tanks raise 2026 GDP growth forecasts
Economic experts predicted on Thursday that German GDP will double to 1.3% this year. They also warned of difficulties ahead.
You can read more about their forecasts for Germany's economic future in the next few years in this article: Germany: Economic institutes double growth forecast for 2026
Planned intelligence reforms trigger heated Bundestag debate
The German parliament has held its first debate on government plans to give intelligence agencies more power as national security is threatened by new dangers at home and from abroad.
Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told parliamentarians that the planned reforms would turn Germany's intelligence agencies — the BND (Bundesnachrichtendienst), in charge of international intelligence, and the BfV (Bundesamt für Verfassungschutz), responsible for domestic intelligence — into "true secret services."
He said the agencies would no longer just gather information on threats but be equipped to provide "real defense against dangers, attacks and terror."
Under the plans, the agencies would receive more power to collect, save and automatically evaluate data, as well as permission to react to sabotage or hacking attacks with counterattacks.
Intelligence reforms under fire
Various parliamentarians voiced concerns about the reform's implications in what was sometimes a heated discussion.
Konstantin von Notz from the Green Party said he recognized the need to "update" the powers of the agencies in view of the growing threat from Russia.
But, he said, "the excessive plans for domestic intelligence activities" needed to be trimmed or the the reforms would not survive an appeal to the Constitutional Court.
He said the government needed to take the interests of people professionally entrusted with confidential information much more into consideration, especially psychotherapists.
Clara Bünger of the socialist Left Party accused the government of breaking down the distinction between intelligence agencies and the police that had been a lesson learned "from the crimes of the German fascists."
The far-right politician Gottfried Curio from the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party was strongest in his criticism, saying the government wanted to create a "Stasi 2.0," a reference to the secret service in former communist East Germany.
The reforms would bring about "more than a total surveillance state," he said.
Bundestag set for organ donation debate
The Bundestag will discuss two separate cross-party proposals on Thursday to increase the number of human organs donated for often life-saving transplant operations.
One proposal upholds Germany's current system, under which people who wish to donate organs must actively give permission.
Advocates of the proposal say that the shortfall of donated organs can be remedied by campaigns calling on adults to take part and making it easier to register the desire to donate.
The other proposal calls for an opt-out scheme under which organs can be removed postmortem from anyone who has not expressly rejected being an organ donor.
Backers of this proposal say that although surveys show that most people in Germany are willing to donate their organs, very few actually document this wish.
They also cite statistics showing that countries with opt-out schemes have more donations, with Germany lagging behind in international comparisons.
Altogether 254 of the 630 members of the Bundestag have signed on to the opt-out scheme, and 58 have backed the first proposal to maintain the current national system.
The Bundestag last voted on the issue in 2020, with a majority supporting the opt-in model, even though an opt-out proposal had more signees then, too.
France, Spain and the Netherlands are examples of European countries that have opt-out models in place.

And the university in Münster is to open a faculty of Islamic theology — the first in the country — that will have an equal status with the Catholic and Protestant faculties there.
All this comes amid a bit of good news for the German economy, which experts say will grow twice as much this year as previously forecast.

Police arrest far-right activist Daniel Thomas after ‘dinghy slashed in Channel’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:25:22 UTC
17:25:22 KST

The far-right agitator and anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been arrested on suspicion of criminal damage with intent to endanger life after he filmed himself appearing to slash the side of a dinghy in the middle of the Channel while a rescuer was onboard.
The arrest came as the Home Office recorded 781 arrivals in 10 boats on Wednesday, the highest number for a single day so far this year. Responding to the figures, the government said it would “push further and harder” to crack down on the people organising the crossings.
Hampshire and Isle of Wight constabulary said a 37-year-old man of no fixed abode had been arrested after a boat that had an emergency responder onboard was damaged in the Channel. The man was arrested “on suspicion of destroying ships or fixed platforms or endangering their safety”.
He was also suspected of committing “criminal damage, criminal damage with intent to endanger life, and conduct endangering ships, structures or individuals”. Police said he remained in custody on Thursday.
The force had earlier said it was looking at footage livestreamed by Thomas, in which he could reportedly be seen using a knife to stab and slash an inflatable dinghy in the middle of the Channel after asylum seekers had been helped to safety but a French rescue worker had just got onboard.
Thomas’s footage appeared to show him approaching one of dinghies, which was empty, shouting: “Let’s get rid of that boat.” After the rescue worker got onboard, Thomas shouted: “Get off the boat. You’ve got time to get off the boat.” His footage shows his boat speeding away before the rescue worker climbed back on to the larger boat.
Thomas, who goes by the name Danny Tommo, had spent the afternoon in a boat, filming himself as he tracked two dinghies carrying asylum seekers from France to the UK. The livestreamed footage was watched by more than 200,000 people.
A longtime associate of fellow far-right activist Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, AKA Tommy Robinson, Thomas this summer gathered dozens of nationalist protest groups under the umbrella anti-immigration movement Patriot Platform.
The organisation was behind marches this month in Dover and Portsmouth, when masked men in black gathered and protested over immigration and asylum policy. Thomas repeatedly told his followers they should march silently, without violence, and avoid doing anything that could lead to arrests.
Thomas apparently managed to film and upload footage of his own arrest before police were able to stop him. On Wednesday night a 56-second clip was uploaded to his YouTube platform showing a police officer telling him he was being arrested on suspicion of criminal damage and “recklessly endangering someone’s life”.
Thomas said: “I understand. I knew this was coming.”
The latest Home Office figures put renewed focus on the government’s handling of small-boat arrivals in the UK.
A government spokesperson said: “Our progress this year in tackling small boats is indisputable, with crossings down by 42% and the lowest recorded over the summer months since 2020. But this week’s events show that while the peaks we are seeing are far below those of previous years, we need to push further and harder in order to eradicate this vile trade.”
Wednesday’s arrivals take the provisional total for Channel crossings for the year so far to 18,565. Home Office data indicates this is down 42% on this time last year (32,188) and 26% below the figure at this stage in 2024 (25,165).
This week ministers have also been concerned by two uncontrolled landings from the Channel in two days. Most small boats carrying asylum seekers across to the UK are escorted to shore by rescue services or Border Force vessels, and no unescorted small boats had been recorded since 6 September 2025.
The education secretary, Lucy Powell, said: “You can’t stop everything all of the time,” after 21 people were detained when a boat evaded Border Force to reach the beach of Samphire Hoe in Dover on Wednesday. Another dinghy made an uncontrolled landing in Folkestone on Monday morning.
The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has ordered an urgent review by Border Security Command, describing the failure to intercept the two boats as “not acceptable”.
Speaking on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme, Powell said: “Of course, it’s a concern. That’s why the home secretary has demanded and ordered this urgent review, because this is not what we want to see. This is not acceptable.”

Kiev residents brace for harsh winter amid increased attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:24:41 UTC
17:24:41 KST

In this photo provided by the Ukrainian Emergency Services, a rescue worker checks a car destroyed following a Russian strike on Kyiv, Ukraine, Thursday, Sept. 24, 2026. (Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP)
The first days of autumn chill have only barely set in over Kiev, but winter is already dominating conversations among residents, who are making plans in case Russian strikes once again knock out the energy system.
The shadow of last winter hangs over Kiev, which was plunged into darkness and bitter cold for weeks when Russian forces struck the country’s power and heating infrastructure while temperatures dropped as low as -20 degrees Celsius.
As Russia stepped up assaults on Kiev, the question of what to do this winter is particularly pressing for families with children, said Oleksandra Matveieva, founder of a Facebook group for mothers.
“Now it seems Russians have started bombing Kiev heavily,” she said.
“Immediately, people, mostly mothers, started writing: ‘we’re ready to leave anywhere, as long as it’s not too far and expensive.’”
Travel Mama Club, originally founded for traveling mothers before evolving into an advice forum during the war, has recently seen a surge in publications concerning accommodation in relatively safer western Ukraine, or abroad.
“People are looking for a Plan B, even booking refundable apartments,” she said. “They still don’t know yet whether they will actually leave.”
Russia has over the past month stepped up its attacks on the capital and air raid alerts urging locals to seek shelter due to incoming drones and missiles are now a nightly and, increasingly, daily occurrence.
If it used to target Kiev mainly during the hours of darkness, Moscow now attacks more in broad daylight. The alerts paralyze life across the city, especially in schools and hospitals, which follow strict safety protocols.
The strikes are part of escalating infrastructure attacks by both Russia and Ukraine, which U.N. investigators warn are leaving civilians increasingly vulnerable as winter approaches.
U.S. President Donald Trump said last week that Ukraine and Russia had agreed not to target each other’s energy facilities, but the proposal failed to materialize.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told the U.N. General Assembly in New York on Sept. 23 that “Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us, but in response we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too.”
Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko, who has been criticized by the government for failing to present a clear strategy, has said the city completed 80 percent of its preparations ahead of winter.
Besides heating and energy, there are fears Russia may seek to destroy water supplies, Ukraine’s Energy Minister Denys Shmygal said in August.
Residents are making their own preparations, dusting off the generators, portable batteries and hot water bottles they relied on last year, while making adjustments.
Some hold on to the hope the weather will be milder this year.
“If it’s cold again, as critically cold as it was last year, I will leave,” said Matveieva, who has a daughter.
“I’ll take her and get her out of here.”

Italy puts $5.9 billion toward a new main battle tank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:24:18 UTC
17:24:18 KST

- Italy's Defense Ministry opened a €5.14 billion ($5.86 billion) procurement for a new main battle tank and derivative vehicles on Sept. 21.
- The tank is being developed by Leonardo Rheinmetall Military Vehicles to replace the Italian Army's Ariete.
Italy’s Defense Ministry has opened a €5.14 billion ($5.86 billion) procurement for a new main battle tank and vehicles built on it, according to a record published Sept. 21 in the database of Italy’s National Anti-Corruption Authority (ANAC).
The entry, listed under code BD0D09994D, covers the supply of a new tank and its derivatives for the Italian Army. The contracting authority is the ministry’s Land Armaments Directorate in Rome. The record does not name a supplier, state how many vehicles will be bought or give a delivery schedule.
Italian defense watcher A-129 Mangusta flagged the listing on X on Sept. 22.
The program is known as the New Main Battle Tank, or NMBT, and is being developed by Leonardo Rheinmetall Military Vehicles (LRMV), a joint venture between Italy’s Leonardo and Germany’s Rheinmetall. Earlier coverage referred to the tank as the IMBT, for Italian Main Battle Tank. The two companies agreed in October 2024 to split the joint venture 50:50, with 60% of the work carried out in Italy, including final assembly, testing, delivery and logistics support.
LRMV unveiled an NMBT concept demonstrator at the Eurosatory defense show in Paris in June. The design draws on Rheinmetall’s Panther KF51, but Italy is developing it as a separate tank built to Italian Army requirements. The demonstrator used a Leopard 2A4 hull fitted with a new turret, and LRMV representatives said the production version will get a new chassis with better mobility and protection.
The NMBT will carry a 120 mm smoothbore gun fed by an autoloader holding 20 ready rounds, with an option to switch later to a 130 mm gun. Its secondary weapons include a 12.7 mm machine gun mounted beside the main gun and a remotely operated turret with a 30 mm cannon that can also fire at drones. The demonstrator shown in Paris also had launchers for small loitering munitions, drones that circle a target area before diving onto a target.
Under the joint venture’s division of work, Rheinmetall is responsible for the vehicle platform and Leonardo for electronics and weapons.
The new tank will replace the C1 Ariete, which entered Italian service in the mid-1990s and is now going through a C2 upgrade. Earlier reports put Italy’s requirement at about 132 new tanks, with purchases planned after 2027. The procurement is scheduled to be completed by 2038.
The NMBT is one of two major armored vehicle programs Italy has given to LRMV. The second, the Army Armored Combat System (A2CS), is based on Rheinmetall’s Lynx infantry fighting vehicle and covers more than 1,000 vehicles in 16 versions, including anti-aircraft, reconnaissance and anti-tank models.
In late 2024, an Italian parliamentary committee approved an €8.2 billion ($9.35 billion) plan running from 2025 to 2038 to buy new-generation tanks and modernize the country’s land forces.
The ANAC record lists the tender as active and shows an offer deadline of Sept. 21, the same day the entry was created and published.

Overnight, the Kyiv City Military Administration issued a missile alert in the Ukrainian capital, after which it reported that two warehouses were damaged in the city’s Sviatoshynskyi and Solomianskyi districts, while also reporting damage in other locations.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) said on Telegram on Thursday morning that two people were killed and at least eight others were injured in the attack.
“All necessary emergency services are working at the sites,” the DSNS said, which also reported that two people were injured in the country’s southern Odesa region following overnight Russian strikes.
It said the strikes in the Odesa region caused a fire at a previously attacked shopping center, while a two-story private residential building caught fire at another location, where the injuries occurred.

Microsoft ends cooperation with ICC over US sanctions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:21:33 UTC
17:21:33 KST

THE HAGUE, September 24. /TASS/. Microsoft has ended cooperation with the International Criminal Court (ICC) due to US sanctions, which forced the Court to turn to alternative digital services, lead counsel at the ICC Geert-Jan Alexander Knoops told TASS.
"A company like Microsoft has severed ties with the ICC due to existing sanctions, forcing the Court to switch to other digital services," he said, adding that the move made the work of lawyers involved in court proceedings more difficult.
US sanctions could hamper the work of the Court, Knoops noted. Specifically, the refusal of banks to service the ICC because of the threat of secondary sanctions could jeopardize ongoing investigations and proceedings. The lawyer does not rule out that the European Union’s protective measures to counter US sanctions will even fail to remove the risks for banks.
The US restrictive measures could potentially affect all 900 employees of the Court, complicating their travel and access to their bank cards, he said, adding that in the current situation the ICC is paying salaries to staff and fees to lawyers in three-month installments.
US sanctions against ICC
On September 20, The Wall Street Journal reported, citing US officials and documents, that the US administration was preparing broad sanctions against the ICC that would affect the majority of financial transactions with the court, which could potentially paralyze its operations by prohibiting transactions in dollars and cutting off its access to a large part of the financial system.
The current US administration has already imposed sanctions on the ICC several times. US President Donald Trump signed a decree imposing restrictions on the court’s officials on February 6, 2025. The US has accused the ICC of unlawful conduct against Washington and its allies, such as Israel. The decree allows for the introduction of financial and visa restrictions against ICC employees involved in investigations concerning US citizens or citizens of their allies, as well as members of their families.
ICC and Russia
In 2016, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree stating that Moscow would not become a party to the ICC. According to the Russian Foreign Ministry, the court has not lived up to the hopes invested in it and has not become a truly independent body of international justice.

====================================================================================================

Is the EU undermining its Russia sanctions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:19:14 UTC
17:19:14 KST

The EU's decision to lift sanctions on two prominent Russian oligarchs has raised questions about the credibility of its sanctions regime, as the reasons for their removal bear little relation to the grounds on which the restrictions were originally imposed.
Alisher Usmanov, a Russian-Uzbek billionaire, and Mikhail Fridman, a Russian businessman with Israeli citizenship, were removed from the EU sanctions list after pressure from France and Luxembourg, even as Brussels renewed restrictions on roughly 3,000 other individuals and entities linked to Russia's war in Ukraine.
Luxembourg had sought Fridman’s delisting amid a multi-billion-dollar legal dispute over his frozen assets.
Fridman has brought a roughly $16 billion arbitration claim against Luxembourg over assets frozen under EU sanctions. Luxembourg reportedly feared that removing Usmanov while keeping Fridman sanctioned could weaken its legal position in the dispute. Slovakia also supported Fridman's removal.
With the renewal of the EU's wider Russia sanctions requiring unanimous agreement from all 27 member states, the demands became part of a broader compromise.
In return for the two delistings, the bloc secured a three-year extension of sanctions on thousands of other individuals and entities, rather than the usual six-month renewal.
The agreement preserved the wider sanctions regime but raised questions about whether individual sanctions could increasingly become bargaining chips for member states pursuing their own national interests.
The decision followed difficult negotiations among EU member states, exposing divisions over the use of sanctions in disputes unrelated to Russia's war in Ukraine.
Experts warn that France and Luxembourg's efforts to secure the delistings for their own national interests could undermine the integrity of the 27-member bloc's sanctions regime and set a precedent for similar demands in the future.
While the decision should not be "read as a broader softening of the EU position on Russia" because the sanctions regime as a whole remains in place, the more difficult question is "what kind of precedent this creates," Linas Kojala, CEO of the Geopolitics and Security Studies Centre, tells TRT World.
“When exemptions appear to be driven by political or bilateral considerations, that risks weakening the logic of the whole system. If individual sanctions start becoming bargaining chips in other disputes, then the message is that there may be political ways around the system. That is not helpful for the credibility of sanctions,” Kojala says
Ukraine, which has opposed easing sanctions on Russia and individuals linked to the Kremlin, condemned the EU's decision as "shameful and unjustifiable". Moscow, meanwhile, demanded the removal of sanctions on all Russian businessmen and citizens.
"Moscow is celebrating because it got what it wanted: a sense of impunity, the humiliation of the EU, and division among Europeans," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said on X.
EU ‘credibility’ on the line
The EU's decision to delist the two Russian oligarchs also exposes a "broader contradiction" in Brussels' approach towards Moscow, says Kojala, as European officials and analysts increasingly warn of the possibility of a direct confrontation with Russia.
While European leaders describe Moscow as a major security threat, increase defence spending and prepare for a prolonged confrontation , the possibility of politically negotiated exemptions from Russian sanctions sends "an ambiguous message", according to Kojala.
He acknowledges that removing the two oligarchs from the sanctions list is unlikely to significantly benefit the Kremlin's finances or expand its access to European markets and technology. The bigger issue, he argues, is the EU's credibility in the eyes of both domestic and international actors.
"Sanctions matter not only because of the assets they freeze, but because they create an expectation that restrictions will remain in place as long as the reasons for imposing them remain," he says, referring to the original grounds for imposing sanctions over Russia's war in Ukraine.
At the heart of the controversy is the rationale behind the EU's decision.
Sanctions are generally lifted when the grounds for imposing them no longer apply. In the cases of Usmanov and Fridman, however, the reported reasons for their removal appear unrelated to the original sanctions criteria.
“Their delisting is unrelated to the reason the sanctions were imposed on them,” Oleg Ignatov, a senior analyst on Russia at the International Crisis Group, tells TRT World.
Like Kojala, Ignatov believes the decision could set a problematic precedent for future EU sanctions policy.
The decision also raises questions about whether well-connected oligarchs such as Usmanov and Fridman, who have influence in European capitals, can secure exemptions while others with less political leverage remain subject to sanctions.
“This sets a certain precedent—that sanctions can be lifted without strong reasons related to ending the war. But there have been various precedents like this in the past, it’s just that the figures involved here are quite prominent,” he says.
Yet the controversy also highlights the complexities of decision-making within the 27-member bloc, where competing national interests must be reconciled before sanctions can be renewed.
“Relations within the EU are complex, and decisions are made through compromise. As you can see, in this case, it took EU member states several rounds of difficult negotiations to make this decision,” says Ignatov.
Latvia initially opposed the delisting of Usmanov and Fridman but eventually withdrew its objections after the EU agreed to extend sanctions on roughly 3,000 other individuals and entities for another three years.
Despite the questions surrounding the compromise, the lengthy negotiations also demonstrate "how difficult it is to lift sanctions", according to Ignatov.
"If, for example, there is talk of exchanging some sanctions for certain steps by Russia toward a peaceful settlement, even in that case, it will be difficult to reach a decision within the EU."
While the compromise may raise concerns about the EU's credibility among outside observers, Ignatov argues that such negotiations are an unavoidable feature of the bloc's decision-making process.
"This is exactly how decision-making works in the EU, and there is no other way," he says.
"The extension of sanctions is approved by consensus, and any country can raise objections, which will require negotiations."
But does this mean that not only the delisting of oligarchs, but much of EU politics, is shaped by deals negotiated behind closed doors?
"Well, that's politics," Ignatov responds.

Yoseph Haddad outlines plan to overhaul Israel’s public diplomacy
The No. 2 in Ofer Winter's Amcha Israel; if they enter government Haddad wants to be Israel's public diplomacy minister
Yoseph Haddad is running for Knesset as the No. 2 in Ofer Winter's Amcha Israel; if they enter government he wants to be Israel's public diplomacy minister, he joins i24NEWS's On The Record to lay out his plans.
Haddad is an Arab Christian from Nazareth, he was injured in Lebanon in 2006, and since 2014 has been advocating for Israel in Hebrew, Arabic, and English. Haddad says that while Israel succeeded on the seven military fronts since October 7, it lost on the eighth front: public relations.
His first move as minister would be to provide weekly press conferences in Hebrew, Arabic, and English aimed not just at the foreign press but also at an Israeli audience to keep them updated on government moves.
Haddad says that his aim in Hebrew is to challenge "extremists" in Israel who are parroting the Hamas narrative, while in Arabic he plans to take the fight to the Arabic-language channels that are "twisting the facts in Arabic."
"If they don't come, it's even better, because I will show that those people are not even willing to confront me," Haddad said.
"I want CNN reporters to ask me the toughest questions about what's happening in Gaza, what's happening here in Israel, about Israel being an apartheid state, about ethnic cleansing, genocide, all that nonsense, that they've been telling about Israel for years and years. Bring it on. Let me show you."
When asked why Israel had failed to respond, Haddad said "Israel did not realize the change of tactics and strategic of our enemies."
"Israel knows that no one can beat the soldiers of the IDF. No one. You can temporarily put us on our knees, just like on October 7, where our fighters both female and male, rose up and we will conquer our enemies."
When asked how effective outreach to the Arab world could be, Haddad pointed to the UAE as a success story, but he said that an even better example was Arab Israelis themselves.
"If you ask the majority of Arab Israeli, for instance, no one will deny the Holocaust. No one will actually say that it was a lie. So it's possible."
Haddad said that his own entry into a War Cabinet would be an even better example to counter claims that Israel is an apartheid state.
"So the idea is to strengthen the Jewish community and to strengthen the pro-Israel community through my story and through actually my experience as an Arab Israeli citizen."
"I'm going to take my Middle Eastern mentality to the public diplomacy in the Middle East and bring it to the Middle East," he said. "When they lie, I will expose their lies. But I will expose their lies in my own way, the Arab way, especially if I'm speaking to them in Arabic. That itself will make a lot of noise."
Haddad said that there is already support for such diplomacy in the Arab world. "My idea is to strengthen the relationship with the Lebanese."
"We have an ally in Lebanon. You have about 80-90% of the Christians want normalization and even peace with Israel. You have about 70% of the Sunni Muslims want normalization, 60-70% from the Druze community, even 20-30% from the Shia who are sick and tired of Hezbollah. And they say, 'We want to do something for Lebanon, not for Iran or the IRGC.'"
"We need to capitalize on that," Haddad said. "I want to open that dialog with the Lebanese. There's a better future where Israel and Lebanon are close friends together."
Haddad said US Vice President JD Vance was very dangerous for Israel and that he hoped Vance would not be nominated by the Republican Party. "I really hope Rubio is going to be the next president of the United States."

Reshetnikov stated that not all of these jobs are managerial. While administrative structures operate in Moscow, companies like Aeroflot, Russian Railways, and Rosseti also maintain local staff who directly provide public services.
The economic ministry framed the relocation as a measure to boost efficiency by lowering expenses, citing lower costs for salaries, rent, and office maintenance in regional areas compared to the capital.
Reshetnikov emphasized that the move would offer growth opportunities, jobs, and added tax revenue for regions, noting that several firms are already shifting accounting, IT, and legal divisions outside Moscow.
Among existing transfers, Inter RAO established HR and call center operations in the Ivanovo, Saratov, and Orel regions, while Zarubezhneft set up a corporate service center in the Samara region, The Moscow Times reported.
Russian Post moved over 1,000 IT employees to Tatarstan and plans to reallocate roughly 2,000 more. Russian Railways intends to place up to 2,000 workers in an innovation cluster in the Vladimir region, and Transneft plans to transfer about 1,000 employees out of the capital.
The invitation comes amid Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's visit to the United States, where he met with US President Donald Trump to discuss military support and potential diplomatic pathways to end Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Asked when the company expects to provide the military with ballistic missiles for strikes against Russian targets, Shtilerman said the key remaining step is engine testing.
“Only one thing separates us from that, and that is engine testing. As soon as we test the engine, we begin flight trials,” Shtilerman said.

Baghdad audits PMF to weed out 'ghost employees'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:17:48 UTC
17:17:48 KST

Breadcrumb
Baghdad audits Popular Mobilisation Forces to weed out 'ghost employees'
Iraqi government and political sources told The New Arab that the government, headed by Ali al-Zaidi, has begun a wide-ranging process to inventory and audit the number of members of the Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF), including fighters and civilian employees. The process seeks to match the names registered on payrolls with those actually serving and establish a unified and accurate database for the authority.
"The inventory process is aimed at auditing the numbers and employment data of all members and verifying their places of service and whether they are actually continuing to serve," according to the sources. "The total number of fighters and employees affiliated with the PMF exceeds 250,000, after the authority's numbers increased significantly over the past two years".
The sources further explained that "the importance of the audit process is increasing with the renewed discussion of what is locally known as 'ghost employees', referring to fictitious names or members who are not actually serving despite being included on payroll lists".
They noted that the issue had previously been raised within Iraqi security institutions, pointing to "the discovery, in 2020, of about 82,000 fictitious names on PMF payrolls".
"The inventory process comes alongside efforts to place weapons exclusively under state control, and amid a preliminary agreement stipulating that the PMF will undertake the process of absorbing weapons that armed factions are expected to hand over, rather than the Interior and Defence ministries, in addition to integrating members of those factions through the authority and new directorates," the sources added.
The sources believe that "these developments could lead to an increase in the number of PMF members in the coming period and consequently increase the financial burden on the state treasury".
This makes it necessary to audit membership lists to uncover any fictitious names that may be linked to political parties or factions and receive salaries from public funds without actually performing any service.
Controlling salaries and spending
Security affairs expert Brigadier General Adnan al-Tamimi told The New Arab that "the inventory and audit process being conducted by the government for PMF members represents an important step towards controlling salaries and government spending and determining the actual number of fighters and civilian employees".
Al-Tamimi explained that "the importance of the inventory lies in matching the registered names with those actually serving, verifying their workplaces and financial entitlements, helping to uncover fictitious names or members who do not perform actual service, known as 'ghost employees', as well as preventing the waste of public funds".
"Establishing a unified database and linking it to the relevant government bodies will strengthen administrative and military discipline, and will also be important in organising the PMF file within state institutions," he added.
This is particularly important as discussions continue over placing weapons under state control and reorganising the status of factions and members operating within official frameworks.
Al-Tamimi stressed that "the inventory process must be professional and transparent, and its results should be clearly announced, with any proven violations referred to the relevant oversight and judicial authorities".
"The success of the process will give the state an accurate database that can be relied upon for financial and security planning and prevent manipulation of payrolls in the future," he noted.
Financial audit and accountability for beneficiaries
Meanwhile, researcher and academic Ali al-Jubouri warned, in comments to The New Arab, of "the danger of some political parties and armed factions exploiting the PMF payroll file".
"Any manipulation of the number of members or inclusion of fictitious names to obtain salaries from public funds constitutes an assault on state resources and turns an official security institution into a source of financing activities unrelated to its legal duties," he argued. "The issue of ghost employees should not be viewed as merely an administrative violation, because the presence of fictitious names on payrolls, if proven, means that public funds may have gone to entities and individuals who do not perform actual service".
He added that these funds could be used to finance political, media or commercial activities outside the framework of the state.
He stressed that "there is a need for a genuine audit that identifies the party behind any fictitious names, rather than simply removing the names from payrolls, because what is required is to know how these names were added and who benefited from the money paid to them over the past years".
"The current inventory process must include a parallel financial and administrative audit, matching names with actual service and bank accounts," he added. "The continued presence of any fictitious employees or fighters means that public funds can continue to be used to serve political, partisan and media agendas."
"The PMF is an official institution funded from the public budget, and therefore no political party or faction may treat the salaries of its members as a private resource or a fund for financing its activities," Al-Jubouri stressed. "Any entity proven to have been involved in creating fictitious names or benefiting from undeserved salaries must be subject to legal and financial accountability without exception."
The PMF was formally established in 2016, after parliament voted on Popular Mobilisation Forces Law No. 40.
The prime minister's office announced the same year that that the PMF had been incorporated into the Iraqi armed forces.
In 2020, the salary of a PMF member was standardised with that of an Iraqi army soldier, reaching 1.25 million Iraqi dinars per month, equivalent to about $850.
PMF members were also granted the same allowances related to housing and other benefits, while authorities stressed that they would be distributed according to the military brigade system.
Despite the legal framework regulating the authority's work, the armed factions operating within it still, in practice, retain their names, formations and members, as well as their political and ideological affiliations.
Differences in areas of influence and deployment also continue across Iraq's various provinces.

Swiss interest rate remains at 0%
The Swiss National Bank (SNB) decided on Thursday to keep its key interest rate at 0%, where it has been since June 2025.
The central bank made its quarterly decision as inflation remains under control in Switzerland.
“If necessary, the [SNB] is prepared to intervene in the foreign exchange market to ensure appropriate monetary conditions,” a statement added.
Unlike the United States Federal Reserve and the European Central Bank (ECB), which have recently raised their key interest rates, the Swiss central bank has therefore opted to maintain the status quo on monetary policy.
Despite the slight acceleration in inflation in Switzerland, due to soaring oil prices, the SNB’s monetary policy “is appropriate for keeping inflation within the price stability range and supports economic activity”, it added.
The SNB aims to keep inflation between 0% and 2%.
The Swiss central bank nevertheless warned that “the trade policy environment and exchange rate developments remain sources of uncertainty”.

The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) lowered its 2026 growth forecast for its regions by 0.6 percentage points to 2.5% because of a deep recession in Iraq and tighter financing conditions.
Economic growth across the EBRD regions accelerated to 3.4% in 2025 from 3.1% in 2024 before slowing to an estimated 2.4% in the first half of 2026.
"Excluding Iraq, this year’s forecast has been revised down by 0.1 percentage point, reflecting tighter financing conditions, the impact of drought in Europe and the Black Sea shipping blockade, while the outlook for 2027 is unchanged," the bank said, adding that collapsed oil exports reflected a deep recession in Iraq.
The institution projected the growth rate to rebound to 4% in 2027.
Average inflation across the regions stabilized at about 6% after peaking at 6.7% in April 2026.
Energy costs accounted for approximately a quarter of the headline inflation rate.
Oil prices climbed from around $65 a barrel before the conflict in the Middle East to more than $100 by April 2026, as seaborne crude exports from the region halved, the bank reminded.
The bank noted that oil prices remained 30% to 60% above their pre-conflict levels.

As Neriya Leiter fights for life, sister goes into labor 40 meters away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:13:10 UTC
17:13:10 KST

Israel’s ambassador to the U.S., Yechiel Leiter, arrived in Israel on Thursday and went directly to Jerusalem’s Shaare Zedek Medical Center, where his son Neriya remains hospitalized after being critically wounded in a terror attack at a checkpoint on Route 443.
Neriya Leiter, a reservist from Havat Yair in the West Bank, underwent a complex brain operation that lasted several hours after a terrorist drove a vehicle into him while he was serving at the checkpoint.
Prof. Alexander Yuskovich of Shaare Zedek said Thursday morning that Neriya’s condition had stabilized following a series of examinations and surgeries, though he remained in serious, life-threatening condition.
“After a series of tests and a series of surgeries, we can say that his condition is stable,” Yuskovich said. “His condition is still serious and his life is still in danger, but we are full of hope.”
Leiter thanked the hospital staff treating his son and said the family understood that doctors had faced an exceptionally difficult night.
“When I boarded the plane yesterday in New York, while preparing the prime minister’s visit to the UN, I was afraid I might land without hope,” Leiter said. “Thank God, the doctors managed to stabilize Neriya’s condition. His life is still in danger.”
‘Neriya leads the family’
For Leiter, the crisis has reopened the wounds of another family tragedy. His son Maj. (res.) Moshe Yedidya Leiter was killed in Gaza in November 2023.
“This experience is different from the night when I got the knock on the door nearly three years ago, after my son fell,” Leiter said. “He died immediately. There was no possibility then of bringing him to a hospital and allowing Israel’s senior doctors to work on him.”
“This time, we had the opportunity to gather around Neriya’s bed, say Psalms and mobilize the people of Israel to pray for his recovery,” he added.
Leiter said Neriya and Moshe had grown up sharing a bedroom and were best friends.
“Neriya has led the family since Moshe’s death,” he said.
Sister goes into labor nearby
As the family gathered at the hospital, another dramatic event unfolded only meters away.
Leiter said his eldest daughter, Sarah, whose husband is serving as commander of the Shaked Battalion, had given birth during the war to a daughter named Shaked and later became pregnant again.
“When she came to her brother’s bedside yesterday, her water broke, two weeks before her due date,” Leiter said. “Now she is lying 40 meters from her brother in intensive care.”
Neriya’s mother, Hannah, said the family was still struggling to absorb what had happened.
“His wife started crying and came to tell me,” she told Army Radio. “At first she told me, ‘I thought it was an explosive device.’”
“You can’t get used to this,” she said. “We’re still in shock. His wife keeps saying, ‘I can’t believe this is happening to us.’ She said she was worried when he served in Lebanon, but this close to home?”
Hannah said Neriya had played a central role in holding the family together after Moshe was killed.
“After Moshe fell, he wanted so much to gather all of us together and help us,” she said. “He held our hand. He was amazing. He was close to almost all of us. Whoever needed help, he was there. We cling to life.”
Asked whether Neriya’s children had been told about his condition, Hannah said his wife spoke to them Wednesday.
“Neriya’s oldest is 11,” she said. “His wife told them yesterday. Their friends stayed with them overnight, and she went to tell them.”

Leading institutes double German economic growth forecasts for 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
08:11:00 UTC
17:11:00 KST

Germany: Economic institutes double growth forecast for 2026
September 24, 2026
Several leading German economic think tanks on Thursday announced they had increased their earlier GDP growth forecasts for the country.
New numbers predict an uptick of 1.3% for 2026, more than double that of spring forecasts of 0.6% growth.
In their "Autumn 2026 Joint Economic Forecast," this year titled "Recovery Under Structural Stress — Fiscal Policy on Slippery Ground," five institutes also adjusted their economic outlook for 2027, predicting 1.1% growth.
The picture looks less rosy in 2028, when GDP is expected to slow to just 0.4% growth.
"The economy saw more robust development than expected," said Oliver Holtemöller of the Leibniz Institute Halle (IWH). "Still, that upturn rests on a rather wobbly foundation because high energy prices and structural problems continue to be a burden."
Experts say that the trend is clear but add that recovery is nevertheless weaker than in the past.
Analysts said a strong global economy and the AI boom had in part fueled the trend but added that corporate investment and private consumption remained weak.
Structural problems, uncertainty persist
Looking ahead, economists say they expect dynamism in 2027 as consumer spending recovers and housing construction gains pace.
German institutes are not alone in their positive forecast. The Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) — a group of mostly rich countries — also adjusted its forecast to 1.1% growth in Germany's GDP this year, up from 0.7% in June.
Additionally, the OECD foresees 1.1% growth for Germany in 2027.
One thing that all observers agree on — beyond the need for urgent long-term reforms — is that the US-Israel-Iran war in the Middle East and the great uncertainty that the conflict brings to the global economy is the biggest wildcard in the deck.
Despite the cautious optimism voiced in Thursday's report, many economists have warned that increased government spending on infrastructure and defense — largely financed through new debt — could quickly become a flash in the pan if not coupled with sustainable reforms.
In Berlin, Chancellor Friedrich Merz, who has shown himself to be committed to pushing those reforms through the Bundestag, also recently voiced a bit of optimism over Germany’s economic future, saying, "We're out of the valley of economic recession or decline."
The five institutes that issued the Joint Economic Forecast are: the German Institute for Economic Research, the IfO Institute, the Kiel Institute for Global Economics, the Leibniz Institute for Economic Research Halle and the RWI-Leibniz Institute for Economic Research Essen.

Smart glasses let wearers take photos, film videos, listen to music, make phone calls, translate text or interact with an AI assistant.
The audio-only versions will complement the release of dozens of new smart glasses models that keep photo and video-recording options.
Building in privacy features such as a recording indicator light is "really important," Meta's vice president of AI product, Vishal Shah, told AFP on Wednesday.
"We wanted people to clearly understand that this was something that was recording, and we've only made that light more explicit over time," Shah said.
"We said a lot about that when the glasses first launched, and I think we probably need to keep repeating that more than we have been more recently because none of that's changed," he added.
With nearly four billion monthly active users across its ecosystem, Meta is betting that wearables like smart glasses can become an easy entry point for people to use its AI software.

The company will also soon launch mixed reality glasses that are much lighter than its earlier Quest VR headsets.
Called Meta VR Glasses, they are powered by an external battery and memory pack tethered by a cord, allowing the headset itself to be lighter.
