SIR queries raised, but pertained to draft stage; focusing on some notes while ignoring others gives only one part of picture: EC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:09:42 UTC
07:09:42 KST

Dr. Sukhbir Singh Sandhu, Gyanesh Kumar, Dr. Vivek Joshi
NEW DELHI: Faced with criticism for election commissioners S S Sandhu and Vivek Joshi being cut out of crucial decisions, the Election Commission on Wednesday said the “operational queries, inputs and suggestions” raised over the past 10 months by the two commissioners, including on the special intensive revision (SIR) process, remained limited to the draft stages and were part of the standard administrative practice and decision-making process at the Commission.All decisions taken by the commission in the past one year, including SIR, “are an outcome of the unanimous decisions of the full commission,” EC asserted in a statement rebutting the contention that the chief election commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar was acting unilaterally.EC was reacting to a report in Indian Express claiming that the two election commissioners had objected to steps taken by the poll panel on 14 occasions over 10 months, including the changes made to Form 6 as part of SIR, restricting field officers’ access to electoral roll databases and even regarding postings and foreign tours involving EC personnel.
Focusing on some notes while ignoring others gives only one part of picture: EC
Sandhu and Joshi even wrote to the Cabinet secretary separately on July 29, complaining about redistribution of work by the senior deputy election commissioner (DEC) in charge of administration EC and the resultant centralisation of decision -making , said the report.In its statement, EC said that differing views and observations are a normal part of deliberation in any institution before a final decision is taken.
“Written notes, observations, technical suggestions and internal checks and balances are standard, ongoing practices to ensure transparency, legal compliance and operational rigour." EC said all its actions as well as official orders, decisions and administrative decisions have been in accordance with laws and commission's instructions and carry full legal sanction.
_
"Highlighting certain specific internal notes/observations spread over the period of 10 months while overlooking the much larger body of approvals, decisions, instructions and initiatives give only one part of the picture," EC said adding that its decisions, instructions, 40 new initiatives and conduct of polls in six states/UTs in the past one year were all based on unanimous decisions by the commission in the past one year.Sources in EC said the objections were largely raised in written notes sent by the election commissioners to the deputy election commissioners (DECs), in many cases after they had signed on the concerned file following a unanimous decision; including in the cases of changes made to Form 6. The two commissioners, Joshi in May and Sandhu in August, had argued that changes in Form 6 could be carried out only by the government. However, sources maintained, after they along with the CEC unanimously approved the file relating to SIR orders for Bihar (Phase 1) and then a dozen states (Phase 2), which listed the revised Form 6 and the accompanying declaration on citizenship. In fact, by the time Sandhu objected, the Supreme Court had already upheld the validity of SIR as well as the processes followed by EC, sources said.As part of his case against powers getting centralised and CEC not taking his two colleagues in confidence, Sandhu had raised the issue of who had authorised filing of appeals on EC's behalf before the SIR tribunals in West Bengal. Sources, however, told TOI that this was as per the Supreme Court order dated April 1, 2026, particularly para 9 that stated that appeals may be filed by "persons whose names have been excluded from the voters list" or "by the authorities of the ECI, who may be aggrieved by the inclusion of names by the adjudicatory authorities".On the commissioners’ alleged objection to centralisation of the electoral roll database or ERONet/ECINet, allegedly with restricted access to field officers like the electoral registration officers (EROs) to decide on addition of deletion of names, the Commission said digital platforms such as ECINet operate under strict data security protocols to prevent unauthorised tampering, manipulation, etc. "IT security checks and audit controls are standard cybersecurity measures implemented across national databases. Statutory authorities, including EROs and district election officers (DEOs), function as per statutory powers for registration and deletion under law,” said EC. Sources in EC told TOI that while EROs and DEOs may have faced access issues due to system errors on some occasions, they have full access to electors databases and have been deciding on roll updations during SIR.Sources in the Commission did not contest Joshi's claim that agenda and minutes of EC meetings were not being circulated, but said this has been the norm before the present commission assumed office.Responding to the objections to decision of the DEC (Administration) to change the officer in charge of IT division, sources said that powers to decide appointment, recruitment, transfers and postings of officers above the level of section officer and posting and transfer of personal staff of election commissioners and DECs were delegated to DEC (Administration) in 1997.
Regarding Joshi's April 16 objection to EC officers being sent on foreign trips without the "commission's" approval, sources said the power in this regard has been with the CEC since long.
Reacting to Sandhu's objection that he had learnt of EC's new IT modules, portals etc from the media, sources pointed that both Sandhu and Joshi were present at ECINet's launch on January 22.
Bharti Jain is senior editor with The Times of India, New Delhi. She has been writing on security matters since 1996. Having covered the Union home ministry, security agencies, Election Commission and the ‘prime’ political beat, the Congress, for The Economic Times all these years, she moved to TOI in August 2012. Her repertoire of news stories delves into the whole gamut of issues related to terrorism and internal strife, besides probing strategic affairs in India’s neighbourhood.

NEW DELHI: Supreme Court said Wednesday allegations of Bar Council of India's assets being transferred to a trust created by the BCI chairperson are a matter of concern and it has to be examined. SC also agreed to examine whether it has the power to establish and regulate law colleges and universities.The court was hearing petitions questioning the functioning of BCI-Pearl First Trust and the establishment of law colleges by the trust. It sought BCI's response on the issues within two weeks. A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana asked how BCI can be considered an expert body to regulate legal education when law scholars and academics are better suited to deal with academic matters. "How can BCI regulate law colleges? That's the real question. Their statutory role comes into existence only after one gets a licence. So the issue is whether law schools can be regulated. We'd like to examine whether BCI has the power to control and regulate universities/law colleges," the bench said.
Advocates Prashant Bhushan and Pranav Sachdeva, appearing for petitioner Girish Mittal, said BCI passed a resolution in 2016 and abolished an earlier trust and transferred the funds to a new trust 'Bar Council of India Trust for Promotion of Education, Legal and Professional Reforms and Improvement in Research'.
They said the trust established one law college each in Goa and Andhra Pradesh. BCI, however, said the Bar body has passed a resolution providing that there would be no lifetime trustees and that the tenure of trustees would be coterminous with their membership of BCI.SC had earlier said BCI chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra's position was only "pro tem" until a freshly constituted lawyers' body elects its office bearers. Mishra was first elected as BCI chairperson till 2012. Though he briefly demitted office in 2014, he returned as chairperson in Nov that year and has remained in the post since then.

Integrity Initiative: UK-funded network framed dissent as Russian disinformation for years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:48:28 UTC
06:48:28 KST

Integrity Initiative: UK-funded network framed dissent as Russian disinformation for years
A sprawling network of media influence “clusters” has existed in NATO member states for years, seeking to portray voices opposing the policies of the military bloc and the EU as Russian propaganda, RT America’s Ben Swann and independent investigative journalist Elizabeth Lane have learnt.
Founded in 2015, soon after the Western-backed coup in Kiev, the so-called Integrity Initiative program was designed to counter what it called Russia’s disinformation. It was run by the UK Foreign Office-funded Institute for Statecraft – an organization posing as an independent charity that was founded by Christopher Donnelly, a former adviser to a NATO secretary general, and Daniel Lafayeedney, a former Special Air Service officer.
The definition of ‘Russian propaganda’ developed by the organization, which received funding not just from London but also from the NATO-linked Atlantic Council, was so broad that it virtually included any criticism of NATO and the EU.
“They are not really after Russian disinformation,” Lane said. “They targeted independent journalists. And that’s very clear in their own communications.”
For the Integrity Initiative, Russian disinformation was “any position that is counter to the NATO position,” according to Swann.
Among the most prominent targets of the Integrity Initiative were former Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn and retired Spanish Army colonel Pedro Banos, who lost his appointment as director of national security in the Spanish government in 2018 amid a concerted campaign portraying him as a Russian asset.
The campaigns were focused on “killing the image” of any dissenter to the point where their political careers were ruined, Lane explained. “If you assassinate their image, no one wants to be associated to that person. And that’s what happened with Pedro Banos. That’s what happened with Jeremy Corbyn.”
The network established “clusters” of politicians and journalists it treated like “assets” in virtually all NATO nations, with many of them often unaware that they were part of a media influence network, according to Lane. “They are just given the script and they legit trust the story and they run the story and turns out they are part of the propaganda,” she said.
The Integrity Initiative came into the spotlight in 2018 when hackers, claiming to be linked to the Anonymous collective, leaked a trove of documents revealing the scale of its operations. The revelations led to an investigation into the Institute for Statecraft’s activities by the Scottish charity regulator OSCR, which concluded in 2019 that the organization was violating charity rules.
The institute then formally announced that it was terminating its involvement with the Integrity Initiative in 2019 but continued to operate until August 2023, when it was dissolved several months after being declared an “undesired organization” by the Russian Prosecutor General’s Office over what officials called “aggressive militarist rhetoric” and a “discreditation campaign” against the Russian authorities.

CCA Builders Start Revving Production Rates, as They Await 2027 Funding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:45:16 UTC
06:45:16 KST

General Atomics Aeronautical Systems Inc. and Anduril Industries both say they’re ready to produce Collaborative Combat Aircraft in volume as they wait for a fiscal 2027 budget to fund that work.
General Atomics announced earlier this week it has the capacity to produce its FQ-42A Vengeance drones at a rate of “six aircraft per month to meet USAF goals” and could make more if needed. Competitor Anduril, which started production of its FQ-44A Fury at its new Arsenal-1 facility in Ohio in March, aims to build 150 aircraft annually, its officials said last week at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
The Air Force’s 2027 budget request includes $996.5 million to acquire production CCAs in fiscal 2027, plus another $150 million in advance procurement funds for 2028. But USAF has not specified how many aircraft that might cover.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley declined to tell Air & Space Forces Magazine exactly how many FQ-42s are rolling off the company’s production line right now, but did confirm production is underway. “Some of those aircraft will become company aircraft,” he said, meaning that not all are for its Air Force customer.
Brinkley said the company’s potential production expansion could be used to answer international demand for its Gambit series of autonomous drones, which are closely related to the FQ-42.
General Atomics also said in its statement that it is self-funding FQ-42 production today as it awaits Congressional fiscal 2027 appropriations. The new fiscal year launches Oct. 1, but lawmakers failed to pass a budget for fiscal ’27, and instead passed a continuing resolution that would hold current year funding steady, but provides no new funding. The measure ensures funding through Dec. 11, 2026.
GA’s self-funding will help support the government’s procurement plans and prevent delivery delays, the company said, and building aircraft for its own fleet will help it invest in new technologies that reduce risk and increase capabilities.
The Air Force plans to use CCAs as a complement to crewed fighters in a bid to add combat capacity at a lower cost than convention fighter jets. CCAs are designed to be flown semi-autonomously, at times alongside piloted fighters like the F-22 and F-35 Lightning II, and could eventually carry out a variety of missions including air-to-air or air-to-ground strikes; intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance; or electronic warfare operations. The concept is still comparatively early in its development.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14 that USAF is aiming to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. The Anduril and General Atomics CCAs were selected following a competition in April 2024, andboth companies won initial production contracts in June 2026.
General Atomics said a new FQ-42 was delivered to Creech Air Force Base, Nev., on Sept. 18, for test and evaluation. Creech is home to the Air Force’s Experimental Operations Unit, which has been experimenting with CCAs to develop approaches to how they might be employed in real-life operations.
Jason Levin, Anduril’s senior vice president for air dominance and strike, said Sept. 14 that his firm delivered an FQ-44 to the EOU in August. Prior to that, the YFQ-44A prototype took part in two exercises with the EOU, the first in April and the second in July.
The July exercise at Creech, Levin said, demonstrated that CCA had advanced enough for a single Air Force operator to launch and recover an aircraft on his own after just a few hours of training.
“The Air Force was operating mission autonomy by themselves, which was a first,” Levin said. “They were flying multiple times a day, operating mission autonomy without Anduril personnel—they were on-site kind of helping, but it was really the Air Force operating that.”
Levin said that during the July exercise, Fury flew in the same airspace as crewed fighters and other drones using mission autonomy, helping build Airmen’s trust that CCAs can operate in congested airspace.
The production model of the FQ-44 that will start to roll off the line next year at Arsenal-1 will be able to carry four air-to-air weapons, such as the AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile, or AMRAAM, under its wings.
The FQ-42, General Atomics said, has flown in formation with piloted F-35 Lightning II and F-15E Strike Eagle jets to prepare for future test flights, when fighter pilots will actually command the drones. The FQ-42 represents fifth-generation stealth and operates with an internal weapons bay.
General Atomics previously conducted flights of its MQ-20 Avenger drone, operating as a CCA surrogate, to demonstrate how collaborative control flights might work. The company said its aircraft, including the Vengeance, Avenger, and XQ-67A Off-Board Sensing Station, have flown both semi-autonomously and autonomously using AI pilots and under the collaborative control of human pilots flying in the F-22 Raptor and F-35.
“The CCA program’s rate of progress has been incredible,” said Mike Atwood, vice president of advanced programs at General Atomics Aeronautical Systems, in a company statement. “Every week, the Air Force is pushing forward with new and more impressive accomplishments using Vengeance. It’s amazing to think of how far this program has come in such a short amount of time.”

Palestinian killed after attack wounds Israeli envoy's son
Unknown

Breadcrumb
Palestinian killed after attack wounds Israeli envoy's son
A Palestinian man has been shot dead by Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank after an alleged car-ramming seriously wounded a soldier identified as the son of Israel's ambassador to the US.
The Palestinian health ministry identified the man killed on Wednesday as 29-year-old Mahmoud Mohammed Mahmoud Suleiman, from the Ramallah area.
The incident took place at the Maccabim, also known as Beit Ur, checkpoint on Route 443, west of Ramallah.
The Israeli military said Suleiman carried out a car-ramming attack at the checkpoint and was subsequently shot dead by forces at the scene.
Israeli police said a vehicle had driven towards a police patrol and struck one of its members, who was seriously wounded. Police later said the injured man was an Israeli soldier accompanying the patrol as part of a joint operation.
The soldier was subsequently identified as Neria Leiter, the son of Israel's ambassador to Washington, Yechiel Leiter.
"Neria needs a miracle," the ambassador wrote on X, saying medical staff were fighting to save his son's life.
Leiter said his son had continued serving as a reservist following the death of his older brother, Moshe Yedidya Leiter, who was killed while serving with the Israeli military in Gaza in November 2023.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu also responded to the attack, saying: "My wife Sara and I, together with the entire people of Israel, are praying for a miracle."
The Palestinian health ministry said Suleiman was killed by Israeli gunfire near the village of Beit Ur al-Tahta, west of Ramallah.
The New Arab's correspondent reported that Israeli forces withheld Suleiman's body and prevented Palestinian ambulances from reaching him following the shooting.
Israeli forces also closed the checkpoint and tightened restrictions at several other checkpoints in the northern and western parts of the Ramallah and al-Bireh governorate.
The Maccabim checkpoint connects six Palestinian villages with Ramallah and has been repeatedly closed by Israeli forces in recent days.
Local sources also reported that groups of Israeli settlers threw stones at Palestinian vehicles travelling on the road between Ramallah and Nablus near the Israeli settlement of Shilo on Wednesday evening. No serious damage was reported.
The incident comes amid heightened tensions across the occupied West Bank, where Israeli military raids, arrests and demolitions have intensified.
Earlier on Wednesday, Israeli forces demolished agricultural, residential and industrial structures in several areas of the West Bank, including around occupied East Jerusalem.
Taha Basharat, the mayor of Jaba, north of Jerusalem, told The New Arab that Israeli forces accompanied by bulldozers entered the area and demolished two industrial structures days after issuing demolition orders.

New Zealand's cyber security agency said China was the country's most persistent and capable state-backed cyber threat, as foreign actors targeted government agencies and organizations in sectors including health, education and information technology.
The National Cyber Security Center (NCSC), part of the New Zealand intelligence community, said it had identified activity suspected to originate from foreign state actors that put sensitive New Zealand information at risk.
It linked suspected state-sponsored cyber activity to actors from China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, according to its annual Cyber Threat Report released on Thursday.
"Of these nations, the People's Republic of China is the most persistent and capable state actor undertaking cyber activity in New Zealand," the report said.
The assessment is the latest warning from a Western-aligned intelligence agency over alleged Chinese cyber espionage, which Beijing has routinely denied. It follows a report from New Zealand’s security agency in August that said that China was the only country New Zealand had detected conducting espionage "at scale."
Chinese state-backed actors accounted for 86 nationally significant cyber attacks
The Cyber Security report said 86 of 369 cyber incidents deemed to be of potential national significance in the year to June 2026 had suspected links to state-sponsored actors. The incidents included activity targeting government agencies, health and education organizations, and IT managed-service providers.
The agency warned that geopolitical competition was increasingly playing out in the South Pacific, where it was aware of state-backed cyber espionage targeting governments and infrastructure.
New Zealand has close family, cultural, political and economic ties across the Pacific, and such activity could affect citizens, businesses and civic institutions, it said.
State-backed actors were likely to target organizations that operate infrastructure or networks, provide essential public services, or hold information that could offer a strategic advantage, the NCSC said.
It warned that cyber espionage can be difficult to detect, with actors conducting reconnaissance and positioning access in systems over months or years before using it for intelligence gathering or disruption.
Long-running intrusions could lead to the compromise of operational technology and the loss of corporate and personal data, it said.

Iraq and Turkey have agreed to a framework that will involve Turkish forces handing over a key Turkish military base in Iraq. “Within the framework of the progress achieved by Iraq through security steps, the Turkish forces will gradually hand over the Baashiqa - Zeliqan camp to the Iraqi Federal Government, in accordance with the agreed mechanism and timetable,” Iraq’s Prime Minister’s Office said on September 23.
This is an important step and comes amid many developments in Iraq. Iraq is also trying to rein in Iranian-backed militias. It says this will happen by June of 2027. In addition, the Yazidi YBS armed group has agreed to disarm. The Kurdish Peshmerga also announced a unification of forces this week. As such, Iraq is moving to consolidate federal control over many areas. This will essentially change the landscape of Iraq.
Many of these bases and issues are remnants of the ISIS war. When ISIS invaded Iraq, the Iraqi state collapsed in many parts of Iraq. This was especially true in Sunni areas, as well as in the Nineveh Plains and Sinjar. ISIS carried out a genocide against Yazidis. As a result, the Iranian-backed militias were empowered to fight ISIS. The Kurdish Peshmerga also stepped forward to take up hundreds of miles of the front line. Turkey expanded its role in Iraq.
Turkey claimed to be expanding its role because it was fighting the PKK
Turkey claimed to be expanding its role because it was fighting the PKK. However, the Bashiqa Turkish base was something else. It helped support the Peshmerga from the heights overlooking the town of Bashiqa. It was also working with some Sunni Arab forces. Turkey was also keen to monitor what was happening in Sinjar. Ankara feared that PKK-linked groups in Syria and Sinjar might exploit the vacuum in power. It was also wary of PKK-linked elements at Makhmour camp, a Kurdish displaced persons’ camp near Makhmour.
According to the Iraqi prime minister’s office, “the Prime Minister of the Republic of Iraq, Mr. Ali Falih Al-Zaidi, and the President of the Republic of Turkey, Mr. Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, met in New York on 23 September 2026.” The report says that “the two sides agreed to deepen cooperation in the security field, during negotiations in which the Iraqi and Turkish authorities discussed the strategic relations between the two countries from all aspects; and in this context, they agreed to extend the full authority of the Iraqi state in Sinjar, and to end the presence of prohibited foreign armed elements.”
The result is also a deal for the Bashiqa camp. This camp had several positions near it. The Jerusalem Post covered this frontline near Bashiqa in 2015-2016. The Turkish forces provided fire support against ISIS. The camp was modern and well maintained. “The two sides also agreed to expand the volume of bilateral trade and investment, the immediate implementation of the signed agreements, and the acceleration of joint strategic projects, especially the Development Road project,” the report says.
The meeting will lead to more Iraqi authority in Sinjar. This is a result of YBS saying it will hand over its weapons and integrate with the Iraqi state. Turkey will be pleased. Turkey is involved in a peace process with the PKK. It wants to see all the PKK-linked groups disarmed as part of this process.
This will be important for the Kurdistan Region
Turkey also has numerous bases in the mountains of the Kurdistan region. Bashiqa camp is not in the mountains. It is on land between Erbil and Dohuk, overlooking the Nineveh Plains. Ankara has numerous posts in the mountains near the border, above the city of Dohuk. This is where Turkey was fighting the PKK for several decades.
Rudaw also reported on the handover. This will be important for the Kurdistan Region. The Turkish forces were controversial in several ways. Iranian-backed militias opposed them and conditioned their disarmament on the Turkish forces leaving. Rudaw says “Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan stressed their mutual commitment to pull back Turkish troops from a base in northeast Mosul established in 2015, a joint statement shared by Zaidi’s office said Wednesday, citing the fulfillment of ‘security measures’ that include ending the presence of proscribed ‘foreign armed elements.’”
The deal also comes as US forces of the anti-ISIS coalition are leaving Iraq. As such, many changes are afoot. Iraq is re-asserting its authority.

V'landys steps down as Racing NSW boss to secure firmer grip on NRL
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:32:17 UTC
06:32:17 KST

Peter V'landys has officially been named NRL's executive chairman.
V'landys resigned as NSW Racing chief executive after 22 years at the helm to free himself up for the NRL role.
The ARLC said V'Landys had "unanimous endorsement" for his new position.
Peter V'landys' appointment as NRL executive chairman has been made official after the veteran administrator stepped down as Racing NSW chief executive.
V'landys confirmed this morning that he was ending his 22-year stint at the helm of Racing NSW, following a period of long-service leave that ends in November.
That resignation looms served as the final step in a process of moving into the NRL full time and taking on the most powerful role in rugby league since the Super League war.
"Peter has completely reinvigorated Rugby League during his tenure and the Commission is backing him in to grow the game even further," AR:C commissioner Peter Beattie said.
"Peter inherited a game with limited reserves and no significant assets, one that had needed an advance from its broadcasters just to pay the clubs and players.
"He consistently put the fan first, and the record audiences and the biggest broadcast deal in Australian sport followed."
V'Landys said he was excited to begin his new role and pledged to "take [rugby league] to the world".
Since taking over as ARL Commission chairman in 2019, V'landys has become an increasingly dominant figure in rugby league.
But this move will see his role grow even further, effectively replacing former NRL chief executive Andrew Abdo in his old position while remaining at the head of the commission.
When Abdo announced his resignation in May, V'landys had said only "Superman and Jesus added together" could replace him.
At the time, V'landys refused to speculate whether that figure could be him, but signalled he would take leave from Racing NSW in July to be able to dedicate time to the NRL.
In the months since, the 64-year-old has garnered the support required from both the clubs and the states to allow him to take on the role.
Fellow commissioners have also approved the move, with the appointment now expected to be made official as early as today.
Since the creation of the independent ARL Commission in 2012, no person has held the role of chairman and executive on a full-time basis.
V'landys had been chief executive of Racing NSW since early 2004, after previously spending 17 years as boss of NSW Harness Racing.
He led the racing industry through the equine influenza outbreak, with the creation of The Everest in 2017 among his other key legacies.
"Naturally, this is a very sad day for me. I have put my heart and soul into racing for 22 years. I have been fortunate to work with outstanding, loyal and hardworking boards of directors and staff," V'landys said.
"As a team, we went from a struggling jurisdiction to a world-leading jurisdiction. I take this opportunity to thank everyone who has been in our team. I will miss them greatly, and I wish the industry every success."
In a statement, Racing NSW said V'landys's "many initiatives" had procured $3.5 billion in new funding.
Racing NSW chair Saranne Cooke said his contribution to racing was without parallel.
"Peter V'landys has been, without doubt, the most effective and successful administrator in the history of Australian sport," Dr Cooke said.
"His contribution cannot simply be measured by the extraordinary growth of racing in NSW during his tenure.
"Peter has fundamentally changed the trajectory of racing in this country and made NSW one of the world's leading racing jurisdictions."
Waterhouse says right time to move on
Horse racing legend Gai Waterhouse said it was the right time for V'landys to move on.
Waterhouse came up against V'Landys amidst his failed attempt to sell Rosehill Racecourse in Sydney to the State Government to build residential housing.
The battle saw the two prominent industry figures disagree about the sport's future, with Waterhouse successfully campaigning among Australian Turf Club members not to sell the track, despite Premier Chris Minns and V'Landys pushing to sell the site.
"A lot of money has gone into buying properties that should have been funded back into development of the race tracks and stands," Waterhouse said.
"If we're going to be able to attract people back to the races, they have to be comfortable."
Waterhouse was especially concerned about the state of regional racetracks.
"They've been shockingly neglected over the tenure of Mr V'landys, and they need to have money spent on them," she said.
Waterhouse said his expected move to rugby league from horse racing had come at the right time.
"He's a very strong and very powerful person, but it's time for him to move and he has moved on. So let's move on now," she said.

Moscow’s Ceasefire Bingo Card – What Might the Kremlin Say to Ukraine’s Unconditional Ceasefire?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:31:00 UTC
06:31:00 KST

Ukraine unveiled an unconditional ceasefire proposal on Wednesday, Sept. 23, backed by 50 countries in a joint statement.
Now the key question – how will Russia respond? Russia’s Foreign Minister Lavrov has already ruled out a ceasefire during peace talks – but how will Moscow react to an unconditional ceasefire as a whole?
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Instead of guessing what Moscow will say, here’s a bingo card of what it might say, based on past statements on similar proposals.
Or it could be a combination of different points; who knows.
“Ukraine already violated it”
Russia has in the past moved the starting date earlier, then blamed Ukraine for violating a ceasefire before it was agreed.
The more recent example came in the form of US President Donald Trump’s energy truce, when he claimed both Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to it when, in fact, they had not. Before Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov snubbed it as a “very good idea” a day later, he also accused Ukraine of attacking Russian energy facilities.
But there was never an energy truce, not to mention that Russia had also hit two gas stations in Kyiv the same morning.
Similar patterns were observed in most ceasefire agreements, with both Kyiv and Moscow accusing one another of violations, including the so-called energy truce in March 2025, when Moscow said Ukraine had violated it by moving the starting date, or during Moscow’s May 9 parade, when no one really understood what ceasefire meant on the front.
Russia Must Answer for Crimes in Crimea, Zelensky Says
That’s why the “unconditional” part of the latest proposal matters.
“Good idea. But…”
Here comes the Putin classic – saying yes and meaning no.
One such case happened in March 2025, when Trump pushed for a 30-day ceasefire after his return to office.
In response to that proposal, Putin said the 30-day ceasefire proposal is “good and we absolutely support it but there are issues that we need to discuss” before questioning the effectiveness of the proposal, naming a number of “conditions that need to be studied,” such as the enforcement of the ceasefire along the front.
The result was the 30-day energy truce – see how it worked out in the previous section.
“How about we try something else?”
Remember the Istanbul talks?
A short recap – in the summer of 2025, the EU issued an ultimatum to Putin to move toward an unconditional 30-day ceasefire or face massive sanctions. Putin countered with a plan to resume what he called the Istanbul format, based on early negotiations in 2022 during the first days of the full-scale invasion.
Putin was a no-show and sent a historian in his place who reportedly threatened the Ukrainian delegation. The format, including multiple negotiations, resulted in prisoner swaps but not the ceasefire envisioned.
And good for Putin – without the promised massive sanctions either.
Another example would be August 2025’s Alaska summit, when Trump threatened Putin with massive secondary tariffs, with the two ultimately agreeing to a summit in Alaska instead that earned Putin first-class treatment on US soil after being ostracized since 2022.
Again, no sanctions and tariffs as promised. A win-win for Putin.
“Ukraine doesn’t really want it”
Sometimes it’s as easy as blaming Ukraine for impeding the process without saying how.
“Representatives of the Kyiv regime, the leadership in Kyiv, speak of peace and propose resuming so-called negotiations, but themselves commit such crimes, doing everything to ensure that there is no peace and no negotiations,” Putin told Russia’s Military-Industrial Commission on Sept. 18.
Which raises the question – what exactly should Ukraine do then?
Bonus: Setting out unmeetable conditions
Russia also has a habit of highballing other parties in negotiations, setting conditions that some might consider outrageous.
If the opponents relent and cave in – that’s a win. If they don’t? Blame them for failing to meet the conditions.
A recurring example would be asking Zelensky to come to Moscow for a Putin meeting to settle things once and for all. Another would be to tell Kyiv to withdraw from territories it still controls – that Moscow failed to win for 12 years – as a precondition for peace talks.
Again, this is why the “unconditional” part of the new proposal matters.
“Sure, let’s stop”
If only we had heard this, then perhaps thousands, if not millions, of Ukrainians and Russians would still be alive today.

Is NAZA Zionism's worst nightmare or normalisation propaganda?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:25:36 UTC
06:25:36 KST

Breadcrumb
Is NAZA Zionism's worst nightmare or normalisation propaganda?
The documentary film NAZA (an acronym for Nezek Agavi; “collateral damage” in Hebrew), written and directed by Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, has created a firestorm of controversy. Though few have actually seen the film, it reportedly contains interviews with 24 anonymous Israeli military and intelligence members who attest to the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and automated surveillance into military targeting systems used by Israeli forces during the ongoing Gaza genocide.
They also allege government approval of operations in which thousands of Palestinian civilians were killed as “collateral damage.”
Since its premiere at Venice, where Abraham and Szor received a record 25-minute standing ovation, the filmmakers have faced an escalating campaign of official condemnation and deadly threats. Israeli Culture Minister Miki Zohar called for their citizenship to be revoked, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced plans for legislation targeting those who “defame” Israeli soldiers, and Israel Defence Force (IDF) Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir said the military would use “every tool at our disposal” against the film.
Far-right activists have gone further, with calls for the filmmakers to be hunted and hanged, with more threats directed at their families.
On the surface, however, it is not clear why the film and its creators have become such a target of hatred and condemnation within Israel and the broader Zionist movement. Documentation of Israel’s genocidal criminality has been readily accessible for years, mostly from Palestinian journalists on the ground in Gaza, and the use of AI in targeting civilians has been detailed by Abraham himself in April 2024.
Furthermore, Israeli soldiers have documented themselves shamelessly committing an array of war crimes. So why the thuggish wrath by Israeli leaders, then dutifully echoed by their fascist supporters? This response is akin to Pavlov blowing his whistle at his trained dogs: the whistle sounds, and the conditioned response follows.
What distinguishes NAZA is that it brings allegations of Israeli genocide from the Palestinian “out-group” and its allies into the Israeli “in-group,” opening a potential space for Israeli voices to confront and challenge its normalisation, potentially leading to accountability.
The intensity of the reaction becomes more intelligible when examined through the mechanisms of escalation and normalisation described by the Wired to Steal (W2S) model, a neurobehavioral framework for understanding colonial expansion.
Normalisation of genocide
Since the events of 7 October, in which Hamas led a military operation resulting in the murder and kidnapping of hundreds of Israeli security forces and civilians, Israel retaliated indiscriminately, obliterating the Gaza Strip and even targeting its own people. The genocide, as international experts and organisations have termed it, is but a recent development in an ongoing Zionist genocidal-colonial cycle, in which Israel has expanded oppression and dispossession in response to acts of resistance by Indigenous Palestinians.
Crucially, Zionism is not exceptional. In its foundations and operation, Israel manifests other white European settler-colonial projects in which extraction and greed by a ruling class drive a cycle of manufactured identity, segregation, fear, dehumanisation and rewards for aggression. This sustains a self-reinforcing system of dispossession of designated out-groups, while escalation and normalisation reproduce it.
In contrast to Zionist narratives which decontextualise the events of 7 October to portray Israel’s subsequent actions as defensive rather than offensive, Palestinian resistance can be understood as being instrumentalised as an essential, albeit tragic, trigger for renewed and expanded aggression. It nourishes the ongoing Zionist settler colonial project which predates the establishment of the state of Israel in 1948.
According to the W2S model, resistance is also used to justify theft under the guise of “defence”. Settler society then normalises this through media institutions, social norms, incentives, and everyday conditioned behaviour, rendering the resulting construct a perceived reality.
In this way, normalisation expands the moral boundaries of what is considered acceptable, and who is considered human, thereby increasing the resources available for theft. This is clear to see in the deliberate and cynical blurring of civilian and militant categories, and the designation of Palestinian children as “future terrorists” by Israeli military and political leaders in recent years.
Furthermore, normalisation constructs a façade of so-called “open debate” among “varying opinions” and, consequently, a plurality of tolerated voices within settler society, while shifting attention from the conduct itself to the boundaries of permissible debate and the legitimacy of individual critics. Without it, the tawdry fabric of settler society is threatened.
Abraham and Szor as collateral damage
Zionist propaganda, also known as Hasbara, is one of the most sophisticated forms of state propaganda greasing expansion and theft. As an essential branch of hasbara, normalisation has evolved into an intricate web of deception, particularly utilised in the tropes of liberal Zionism, which presents the Zionist project and Israel as reformable and compatible with human rights. It includes a right-to-left political spectrum, democratic and progressive values, and a desire for peace and justice.
The fallout from NAZA reflects a conditioned reaction casting Abraham and Szor as traitors to the Zionist narrative, with a distinct propagandistic function.
In contrast to Palestinian journalists, who could be racialised and scapegoated as clear members of the out-group and subsequently targeted for elimination as “terrorists,” Abraham and Szor represent a new kind of threat to Israeli society - a threat from within. They have been singled out as in-group targets to be made an example of, using tactics typically reserved for out-group members (though still mild, for now), with the effect of discouraging other potential in-group whistleblowers from coming forward. Fearmongering and social rewards for their harassment are utilised, while simultaneously clarifying the internal boundaries of Zionist identity.
Thus, rather than approaching the film as new evidence for Israeli criminality, the firestorm around NAZA can be understood as an internal struggle within the Zionist movement over how to respond to evidence of genocide without challenging the underlying Zionist project.
Some liberal Zionists have embraced NAZA as a vehicle for bringing criticism of Israeli conduct in Gaza into Israeli public discourse and encouraging greater scrutiny of existing policies. Establishment Zionists have pushed back against such claims, in part reflecting concerns that their wider acceptance could contribute to a broader crisis of Israeli social cohesion.
In this sense, the debate in its present form serves to normalise Israel’s actions since 7 October: genocide is recast as something “debatable,” maintaining Israel's impunity for the worst crimes against humanity and war crimes, with the identities of those responsible remaining obscured.
Will the Zionist regime permit the film to screen in Israel? The full extent of NAZA's impact is yet to be determined. Already, its reaction should encourage all to adopt the nonviolent Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement against Israel for its oppression of freedom of speech and the targeting of the filmmakers.
Clearly, for it to have lasting moral impact, NAZA and its creators must give other whistleblowers the courage to step forward. Abraham, Szor and their colleagues can do more than hail the 24 Israeli military personnel featured in the film as courageous. They should urge them to come forward publicly from anonymity, which currently gives opponents an easy basis for dismissing the allegations without addressing their substance. Otherwise, NAZA risks becoming a discredited, normalising propaganda tool at the hands of the very forces it set out to hold accountable, and Abraham and Szor may also be swept into the gruesome machinations of Israel's genocide of Palestinian people as mere collateral damage.

As Trump and Xi meet, Chinese automakers could be a Pandora's box for U.S. auto industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:25:01 UTC
06:25:01 KST

DETROIT — As President Donald Trump meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping this week, U.S. politicians as well as the global automotive industry are warning that allowing Chinese automakers to enter the market could be a Pandora's box.
Trump earlier this month said he might be "OK" letting Chinese automakers into the U.S. if they produced vehicles domestically, leading a consortium of auto trade groups representing every major facet of the American auto industry to urge him to rethink that position.
It was an uncharacteristically unified message from automakers operating in the U.S., franchised dealers and suppliers. More than two dozen Democratic lawmakers followed that push with their own letter, urging Trump to keep in place U.S. restrictions against Chinese automakers.
"It's not at this point a partisan issue," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., told reporters Wednesday. "It's about whether we want to make cars in America and whether we want a manufacturing base that can pivot when we need it. If we want that, we shouldn't let them in our country."
Trump is scheduled to host Xi and a delegation from China on Thursday and Friday that reportedly could include Wang Chuanfu, founder of BYD, China's largest automaker, and Robin Zeng, founder of CATL, the world's top battery maker for electric vehicles.
Michael Dunne, an expert on China's automotive industry and a former General Motors executive, said even the potential that those two executives could attend underscores the importance of Xi's trip for the U.S. auto industry.
GM CEO Mary Barra is also expected to be among the attendees at Trump's state dinner for Xi, Reuters reported Wednesday, along with several other U.S. executives, including Tesla CEO Elon Musk.
As for America's other largest automakers, Ford Motor declined to disclose whether CEO Jim Farley will be attending after the Department of Transportation criticized the company for its Chinese ties, including a licensing deal with CATL. Reuters reported Chrysler parent Stellantis said CEO Antonio Filosa is out of the country and not planning to attend.
Industry insiders and onlookers have expressed concerns similar to those raised by automakers and lawmakers as bipartisan bills to ban Chinese automakers from the U.S. move through Congress.
The pressure campaign comes as Chinese automakers have been rapidly expanding outside of their domestic market, especially to Europe and Central and South America. There's fear among global automakers that Chinese rivals, like BYD and Geely, which are heavily subsidized by their governments, could flood global markets, undercutting domestic production and vehicle prices.
Dunne said he doesn't believe those concerns are overblown. He said Chinese automakers would "quickly overwhelm America's auto industry, just as it is now ravaging Europe."
Global market share for Chinese brands jumped nearly 70% from 2020 to 2025, according to market research and consulting firm GlobalData. The automakers' market share in Europe was virtually nothing in 2020 but hit 12% in August, according to Germany-based Dataforce.
"China's scores of automakers are currently engaged in a fight-to-the-death price war at home," Dunne wrote in a post Monday. "There's red ink everywhere. Access to the U.S., by far the most lucrative car market in the world, is like a giant tank of life-saving oxygen."
'Attacking very aggressively'
For much of this century, China was one of the largest and fastest-growing markets in the world. Non-China automakers flocked to the historically enclosed country with hopes of massive sales and profits.
But after years of success for automakers such as GM, the Chinese automotive sector has rapidly changed from an insular industry to the biggest exporter of vehicles globally.
China's growth has been fueled by government funding for companies as well as a culture of innovation and speed the country has instilled in its workers, experts said. The decision to ramp up exports has come on the heels of a slowing Chinese market and plant underutilization.
Christian Meunier, Nissan Motor chairman of the Americas, described competing against Chinese automakers as a "hell of a challenge" in countries outside of the U.S.
"They have decent product but it's all dumping," he told CNBC during a recent interview. "We know we're not competing with [automakers], we're competing against the governments. … They're attacking very aggressively."
Meunier said the Japanese automaker has been trying to battle the Chinese as best as it can through growing scale globally to lower costs and become more efficient.
"We need to get ready for the day when they come to the U.S. because it will happen one day. Hopefully not tomorrow, but it will happen one day," he said.
Dunne said China's ambitions and ways of doing business are vastly different from those of U.S. allies, which makes it different from allowing imports from Japan, South Korea and other countries.
"As Xi Jinping has alluded to many times, the goal for China is to 'make other countries more dependent on China and China less dependent on other countries.' That's not a friendly posture," Dunne said.
— CNBC's Justin Papp contributed to this report.

Lidl banned from selling copycat Birkenstock sandals, Dutch court rules
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
22:25:01 BST
06:25:01 KST

Lidl banned from selling copycat Birkenstock sandals, Dutch court rules
- Published
Lidl must stop selling copycat versions of Birkenstock's famous sandals in the Netherlands, a Dutch court has ruled.
The discount supermarket chain faces a fine of €5,000 (£4,200) per day if it fails to comply and must also hand over sales data to Birkenstock, according to the ruling.
Lidl must also compensate Birkenstock and pay its legal fees, with the amount to be decided in separate court decisions.
Birkenstock said the judgement sent a clear message that "copycats must not be allowed to free-ride on [our] creativity and innovation". The BBC has contacted Lidl for comment.
The ruling, which can still be appealed against, means Lidl cannot sell its copycat versions of Birkenstock's Arizona, Madrid, Gizeh, Boston, and Florida models across the Netherlands, after the court found the discount grocer infringed on the brand's trademark "footbed design".
It is the latest in a string of court decisions on Birkenstock designs.
In November 2025, a Dutch court order stopped retailer Scapino from selling similar lookalikes in a judgment which is being appealed against.
And in December 2025, Europe's highest court ruled everyday commercial products can hold copyright if they represent creative design choices, a decision which Birkenstock said was relevant to its "iconic" sandals.
However, Birkenstock also faced a setback in Germany's highest court in early 2025.
The sandals may have been cool enough for Margot Robbie to wear in the Barbie film, but the German judges ruled they were practical products rather than works of art – an outcome Birkenstock called a "missed opportunity" at the time.
Following Wednesday's ruling, Birkenstock said it will "continue to defend its rights vigorously and will use all available legal means to combat imitations of its iconic products".
"To protect its retail partners and consumers, Birkenstock will continue to take decisive action against copycats seeking to profit from the company's creative ideas and innovations," it added.
Birkenstock is far from the only fashion brand locked in battles with mass retailers over design mimicry.
Footwear giants like Dr. Martens have repeatedly taken online big-box sellers to court over boot designs, while luxury house Christian Louboutin spent years in global litigation defending its signature red soles against high-street copycats.

US pledges $267 million more to fight Ebola in central Africa
NEW YORK, Sept 23 - The US State Department on Wednesday pledged an additional $267 million toward fighting the Ebola outbreak in central Africa, as health authorities battle to get the deadly virus under control.
Senior State Department officials announced the funding on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, where they hoped other countries would pledge new funds toward a target of $2 billion to deal with the disease, mainly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The outbreak was detected in May and is already the second most lethal on record, behind one in West Africa from 2014 to 2016.
The pledge brings the Trump administration's commitment to tackling the outbreak to $886 million, including $107 million from the Department of Health and Human Services in addition to State Department funding.
The assistance would help countries contain the outbreak at its source, one of the officials said, such as for building treatment facilities, providing diagnostics and medical countermeasures for health workers in the field. REUTERS

OpenAI and Anthropic chiefs warn UN Security Council against single-actor AI dominance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:19:36 UTC
06:19:36 KST

The heads of leading artificial intelligence firms OpenAI and Anthropic have told the United Nations Security Council that no single actor should be permitted to dominate AI, urging coordinated international cooperation to manage catastrophic risks as the technology accelerates.
Addressing a dedicated Security Council session on artificial intelligence and international security, OpenAI Chief Executive Sam Altman framed the era as a historic crossroads: "We have a choice in front of us. AI can either be more like a new renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new industrial revolution of upheaval and disarray."
Altman argued that AI "should be built for people, not simply to turn the crank of the machines faster for their own sake", dismissing hyper-dystopian industry pronouncements as sounding "like the plot of bad science fiction movies."
He insisted that "no one person or company or country should be able to use the most powerful AI models to impose their worldview on everyone else", stressing that governance decisions "cannot be made by labs in San Francisco alone" and must be shaped through democratic, accountable institutions.
Bioterrorism hazards
Anthropic Chief Executive Dario Amodei warned of two acute hazards: rogue misuse by bad actors—including "bioterrorists to create biological weapons"— and the structural danger of "model capabilities accelerating beyond developers' ability to control them".
Amodei cautioned that "if managed poorly", the technology "could be a risk to humanity as a whole".
While pledging Anthropic will "slow down as much as necessary" to verify system safety, he stressed oversight requires "an industry-wide and global scale", demanding common worldwide standards for testing loss-of-control scenarios.
However, Yoshua Bengio, co-chair of the UN International Independent Panel on AI, rejected corporate narratives framing rapid deployment as an unavoidable competitive race.
"Citizens and governments should not accept the companies’ claim that they are trapped in a race," Bengio told delegates, concluding that "the race is not a law of nature; it is the product of choices, choices made by the companies themselves" and poses a threat to every nation.

FBI investigates alleged theft of ‘very sensitive’ employee data
ShinyHunters hackers claim to have stolen data on thousands of FBI employees as the agency probes a portal breach.
The United States Federal Bureau of Investigation says it is investigating a breach of its jobs website by a hacking group that claims to have obtained sensitive data on thousands of employees.
“The FBI is aware of a cybercriminal enterprise group claiming a compromise of the fbijobs.gov portal and alleged impact to FBI employee personally identifiable information,” the agency said in a statement on Wednesday.

“While the point of breach is still undetermined — whether a third -party or the FBI’s enterprise — we are actively and aggressively investigating this matter and working closely with those third-party providers that support fbijobs.gov to mitigate any and all risk.”
Several news outlets, including Reuters news agency, reported they had seen parts of the data, claimed to be part of a larger trove between two and three terabytes by ShinyHunters, a hacking group claiming responsibility for the breach. According to Reuters, the data includes granular detail about scores of bureau officials’s job assignments, including sensitive work against Chinese spies, Russian intelligence, drug cartels and more.
ShinyHunters said on Tuesday that it had breached the FBI and stolen data on a huge number of current and former FBI employees. It said it is holding the data hostage until the bureau rescinds an unflattering statement about the group issued in May. On Wednesday, the group said it was trying to keep the personnel information from circulating widely in the meantime.
An FBI statement in May characterised ShinyHunters as “threat actors” who often harass or threaten victims, using “their real or exaggerated claims of access to sensitive or personal information to prompt payment from victims”.
The group “may falsely claim to have sensitive or compromising information, including embarrassing photographs or videos of victims, which frequently do not exist,” the FBI said.
The FBI has been a common hacking target.
In March, the FBI disclosed that it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that contains sensitive information related to surveillance operations and investigations. Also that month, a pro-Iranian hacking group claimed to have hacked an account of FBI Director Kash Patel and posted online what appear to be years-old photographs of him, along with a work resume and other personal documents dating back more than a decade.
The jobs portal was still offline Wednesday afternoon.

====================================================================================================

'Really serious': Government investigates penalties as OpenAI speaks on Medicare hack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
21:14:37 UTC
06:14:37 KST

In brief
- Anthony Albanese has revealed an AI agent owned by OpenAI hacked Medicare.
- Albanese said public and non-public data had been accessed in the breach.
Government ministers have shared new details about the timeline of a Medicare breach by an OpenAI agent, revealing that OpenAI's notification of the hack was sent to an inbox checked once a day.
Defence Minister Richard Marles and Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher fronted reporters on Thursday after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed an agent linked to the developer of the popular chatbot ChatGPT gained unauthorised access to the public–facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal, administered by Services Australia.
OpenAI said on Thursday that no personal information was accessed during the breach, with the federal government also playing down concerns while stressing the incident was unacceptable — establishing a taskforce to investigate the breach and not ruling out penalties against the tech giant.
Earlier on Thursday morning, it was revealed the incident occurred on 18 June, but the government was not made aware of it until 10 September when OpenAI sent an email to a Services Australia inbox that Gallagher said was typically used by researchers to alert the government agency to possible vulnerabilities in its systems.
The inbox is only checked once a day, Gallagher said, and Services Australia found the email the next day. By 15 September, the government agency had determined the email was legitimate and escalated the incident to the Australian Signals Directorate.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
The government services minister said she was notified on 17 September and then spoke with Marles, Services Australia, and the Australian Signals Directorate.
'Forensic investigation' underway
Gallagher said there had been "quite a lot of work over that weekend to try and get to the bottom of what had happened here".
Asked if the inbox the initial email went to should be more actively monitored, Gallagher said that would form part of the "forensic investigation" into the incident.
Marles said the government had told OpenAI it was unhappy with how the AI juggernaut had handled the incident, and that he had not been notified of it when he met CEO Sam Altman earlier this month.
"What we would expect is that the government be notified in the most timely manner possible, and we have expressed our displeasure that that did not occur in this instance," Marles told reporters.
The government informed the public as soon as it could, Marles said, adding the incident appeared to be "relatively minor" but still "very serious", and unknowns remained.
"We really wanted to firstly assure ourselves that the impact of the specific incident was, as I have said, relatively minor, and we do want to be able to reassure Australians about that," Marles said.
"But the incident itself is obviously very serious. It's very serious that we've got an AI agent having gained unauthorised access into an Australian website."
Agent was 'conducting research into public medicine spending'
Gallagher said the government had a "technical interaction" with OpenAI on Tuesday that had provided a "level of comfort about what the agent had been doing".
She said it had been "undertaking a task by OpenAI to conduct internet–based research into public medicine spending as part of internal capability evaluation".
The Medicare Statistics Reporting Portal is a public–facing portal that contains non–sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending, Gallagher said, describing it as a "legacy system".
"It's not a system of government significance, so it doesn't have the cyber protections that you would expect on that personally held information, but it did have protections in place. Unfortunately, this agent got around that."
The government has stressed that systems containing national security information are protected by far higher levels of security.
Victoria and NSW respond
Three other systems are also believed to have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Statistics and Research, and the Victorian Department of Health.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll and NSW Premier Chris Minns both said they had spoken with Albanese and understood there had been no breach of personal information contained in systems in their jurisdictions caught up in the hack.
Minns said NSW will "be working with Commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it", while Carroll said he would have more to say in due course.
The task force will be led by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet and also involve the Australian Signals Directorate, the AI Safety Institute, the Office of AI, and other government agencies.
Albanese says incident 'unacceptable'
The revelations came as AI bosses for OpenAI and Anthropic, who have recently called for a slowdown in development, told the United Nations Security Council of the risks posed by runaway AI.
OpenAI said the information in the breach amounted to aggregate health statistics and file names.
"Our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation. In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.
Albanese, who is currently in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, said he had a phone conversation with OpenAI's Altman in which he expressed "Australia's extreme concern about this incident".
"I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable," Albanese told reporters.
He said Altman had "clearly accepted" the company had not done enough on the issue.
The government has said it is examining the "legal situation" around the breach, with the possibility of penalties for OpenAI remaining on the table.

Burnham backs lifting restrictions on alcohol at English football matches

Burnham backs lifting restrictions on alcohol at English football matches
- British Prime Minister Andy Burnham supports trialling the lifting of four-decade-old alcohol bans for fans at English men's football matches, calling the restrictions outdated and unfair.
- The ban, in place since 1985 due to football-related violence, has been challenged by a safe trial in women’s football and comparisons to other sports like rugby and cricket.
- The UK Football Policing Unit warns alcohol contributes to violence, urging caution and thorough review before any legal changes to allow alcohol at matches.
AI generated
NEW YORK – British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is considering allowing fans to drink alcohol while watching men’s football live in England on a trial basis, arguing that the four-decade-old restrictions are outdated and unfairly discriminate against fans of the sport.
The consumption of alcohol in the stands of the top five tiers of English men’s football has been banned since 1985, when fighting between rival fans at matches was common. Fans are allowed to drink alcohol when they are away from the pitch.
“I think that legislation dates to an era where football was very different,” Burnham, a lifelong football fan, told reporters travelling with him to New York for this week’s United Nations General Assembly.
“I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination. There are different ways it could be done. It could happen on a trial basis.”
Burnham took over the premiership in July from Keir Starmer, vowing to boost the popularity of the ruling Labour Party in the face of a challenge from Nigel Farage’s anti-immigration Reform UK, which is popular among blue-collar voters.
In response to Burnham’s remarks, a spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit said alcohol plays a significant role in football-related violence and it would be “irresponsible to fuel this” by allowing alcohol consumption during matches.
Limits are a legacy of 1980s football violence
The introduction of all-seat stadiums, tougher policing and closed-circuit television surveillance, alongside football’s commercial transformation, has helped reduce violence at matches since 1985, when 39 people died after fighting broke out before the European Cup final between Liverpool and Juventus at the Heysel Stadium in Belgium.
English clubs were banned from European competitions for five years as a result.
A trial allowing fans to drink alcohol in view of the pitch was held in the English Women’s Super League during the 2025-26 season. A survey of supporters found that 90 per cent said matches remained safe and family friendly.
Allowing fans to drink in the stands on a permanent basis would involve changes to the Sporting Events (Control of Alcohol etc.) Act 1985 that would require a parliamentary majority.
Burnham, a long-time Everton fan who took Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to a game last week, referred to other sports, such as rugby and cricket, where fans can generally consume alcohol while watching a match live.
“I don’t see how it can be fair that some supporters of one sport can be treated differently,” he said.
The spokesperson for the UK Football Policing Unit said football experiences levels of violence not seen in other sports, and it would be “incredibly rash” to make any fundamental changes without a thorough review of the evidence and talks with the police.
Across Europe, there are different approaches to allowing fans to drink alcohol at football matches.
While German fans can buy and drink beer in the stands during games, Spain and France are among countries that maintain restrictions on alcohol sales at stadiums. REUTERS

synesthesia translated into light across audrey wright’s musical body at the MET
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:59:30 UTC
05:59:30 KST

At The Metropolitan Museum of Art, violinist Audrey Wright wears a field of electronics across her body while her husband and creative partner Geoff Robertson stands nearby with a tablet. As Wright plays, Robertson moves through visual programs that send light across the wearable display.
The setup comes from Luminous Being, the project the pair began performing in 2024, but the presentation soon shifts toward something still being built. Together with composer Stephanie Ann Boyd, they are developing PRISMBODY, a new work that takes Boyd’s synesthetic experience of music as its starting point and asks how some part of that personal perception might become visible to everyone else.
designboom spoke with Robertson ahead of the performance, when he described the idea through a surprisingly familiar comparison. ‘It’s like subtitles along with audio on a screen,’ he tells us. The lights are meant to communicate information paired with the music, drawing from Boyd’s own associations between sound and color.
Speaking at the Met, he goes on: ‘Audrey is the audio, and the garment has to be the color version of the subtitles.‘ What begins inside Boyd’s perception passes through a violinist’s body before arriving in front of an audience as light.
Robertson built the first Garment himself, teaching himself electrical engineering and programming along the way. Its 46 display panels sit across Wright’s front and back, with more than 3,000 LEDs distributed across the wearable system.
The Garment carries 47 batteries and generates its own Wi-Fi network, allowing Robertson to connect through a tablet and trigger different visual programs during a performance. An onboard microphone also listens to Wright’s playing and feeds audio values into some of those effects. The whole thing runs at roughly 30 frames per second.
Wright calls the wearable ‘a sensory musical instrument itself,’ and Robertson sees his own role in similar terms. ‘There is a bit of that where I’m actually playing the instrument, kind of in tandem with Audrey,‘ he tells us. His tablet sits at the edge of the performance, yet his timing becomes part of what the audience sees. Wright plays the violin while Robertson plays the visual system around her.
image courtesy Audrey Wright, Geoff Robertson
from multisensory to multimodal
PRISMBODY begins with Boyd’s synesthesia. During the Met presentation, the composer recalls realizing in graduate school that color had always been inseparable from the way she understood music. ‘The color was there all the time, like omnipresent,‘ she says. ‘I couldn’t take them apart.‘
For the new work, she has begun turning those associations into a compositional structure, describing PRISMBODY as ‘a codifying of my synesthesia.’ Different passages move through color fields tied to her own perception, while Wright builds layers of violin through loop pedals.
image courtesy Audrey Wright, Geoff Robertson
For Robertson, this changes what the wearable needs to do. The original Garment has five fixed LED colors on each display panel, which leaves little room for the subtle hues Boyd associates with particular sounds. Garment 2.0 introduces RGB LEDs capable of producing a far broader range.
‘The garment transitions from something that is multisensory to something that is more multimodal,‘ Robertson explains at the Met. His subtitle analogy returns here. The goal is to communicate related information through sound and image at the same time, with enough chromatic precision for Boyd to recognize something of her own perception in what appears on Wright’s body.
image courtesy Audrey Wright, Geoff Robertson
a screen that wraps around the body
The second Garment also expands physically. Robertson is developing transparent display panels that will wrap fully around Wright, replacing the clearer front-and-back orientation of the first version with a continuous visual surface. Each panel will contain individually controlled white LEDs alongside an RGB layer, while additional lights cast color inward across Wright as she plays. The external spotlights are evolving too, becoming sculptural extensions of the wearable display and moving the image farther into the room.
That 360-degree view has been on Robertson’s mind since the first Garment. ‘You have a 360 kind of viewing experience,‘ he tells us, recalling the project’s beginnings during the COVID era, when he imagined performances taking place beyond conventional stages. PRISMBODY takes that idea further.
Boyd’s color associations enter the score, then Wright and Robertson move that material into sound and light. The audience receives an interpretation shaped through each person along the way. At the Met, the work was still visibly in progress. That made its central question easier to see: how do you turn somebody else’s way of perceiving music into an image a room full of people can experience?
This article is part of designboom’s SPECTATOR AND SPECTACLE chapter, asking how wonder gets built, presented in partnership withSolidNature, and how it might return some mystery to a world that has measured most of it away. LoP's presence in panel to pick CEC, ECs 'ornamental': SC judge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:57:44 UTC
05:57:44 KST

It would not be a fallacious metaphor if it is said that since the umpire is picked by the captain of one side ... and his team wins, even if the decisions taken by such umpire are correct, it has the patina of suspicion: Justice Dipankar Datta
NEW DELHI: Deliberating on the validity of the law on appointment of chief election commissioner and election commissioners by a panel of the PM, a cabinet minister and the leader of opposition, Justice Dipankar Datta on Wednesday pointed out drawbacks and said it gave "overwhelming" power to the executive and made the presence of the LoP "ornamental", undermining the appearance of independence in the selection process. He also noted that since independence, govts had tried to control the poll body."Over seven decades, every dispensation wresting office found it convenient to keep institutions which the Constitution envisioned to be independent under their control. To enact a law on the lines empowered by Article 324(2) would have meant freeing the ECI from exclusive executive control and inviting trouble for the ruling regime. To the mind of this court, this has not been the failing of any one party or one period. A consistent trait of political power, discernible over the decades, has been to preserve leverage over the very body that is meant to judge its claim to power," Justice Datta said.He said if free and fair elections were to be ensured, it was axiomatic that the EC must not only be an independent body but also be seen to act independently and it was "painful to note that not a single party in power, entrusted by the people of India to govern this great nation", took the initiative of enacting a law of the nature which Article 324(2) left to the supreme law-making body, ie Parliament, to legislate.
Also read: SC refers law on EC appointment to larger bench; decision comes amid row over EC functioning"Placing its own electoral fortunes in the hands of a truly independent arbiter was not favoured by any political party, for obvious reasons. To remain in power, the consistent pursuit through executive action has indeed been simple - influence the composition of the EC, control the process of appointment of CEC and ECs and, thereby, temper adverse electoral outcomes," Justice Datta said.
Summarising the contentions raised against the law, he added, "The bottom line of the argument runs thus: it would not be a fallacious metaphor if it is said that since the umpire is picked by the captain of one side in a cricket match and his team wins, even if the decisions taken by such umpire are correct, it has the patina of suspicion, for, at the end of the day, the umpire has effectively been chosen by the winning captain."Justice Datta further said, "There can be no gainsaying that free and fair elections, to a large extent, depend on a truly independent EC. It is not enough for the EC to be independent, it must also appear to be independent. The minister nominated by the prime minister, to function as the third member on the selection committee chaired by the prime minister, cannot be expected to defy his own nominator. In such a circumstance, the inclusion of a minister in the selection committee fails to provide the independent counterweight that a neutral selector could and he would merely echo the voice of his leader; and, consequently, the presence of the leader of opposition in the selection committee becomes largely ornamental, without furthering the purpose of his inclusion."
