ASD issues new warning on AI agent attacks
One of the key agencies involved in the investigation into the OpenAI breach is the Australian Signals Directorate — Australia's cyber spy agency.
It's tasked with tracking down what happened, how it happened, and how it could have been prevented.
The ASD hasn't commented specifically on this case, but it has put up a very timely, and certainly not coincidental, warning about "instances of AI misalignment, in which AI agents have undertaken unexpected actions that were not intended or authorised by its operators".
It says this incident is a clear demonstration about the potential for AI agents to breach barriers it really shouldn't.
"There is no indication that this activity represents a broader threat or malicious targeting against Australia," it said in the statement.
"However, this highlights the importance of secure AI deployment practices and maintaining strong cyber security fundamentals."
It also repeats existing warnings for basically any company operating online: keep your cyber security up to date, apply patches when they come, and test your systems against AI-enabled threats.
Key Event
What the government's review of the cyber breach will entail
Australia's "rapid review" of the OpenAI incident will look to determine if existing laws and information-sharing arrangements are "fit-for-purpose" to prepare for and respond to a cyber incident involving AI.
It will focus on five key areas – reporting requirements, internal government information sharing, the obligations on AI firms, enforcement and strengthening systems against AI vulnerabilities.
The review will consider what requirements exist for AI companies to notify of incidents, share information and cooperate during incidents.
It would also look at the Commonwealth’s systems for managing incidents involving AI, including roles, responsibilities and "escalation pathways".
The government is also seeking advice on the adequacy of existing regulation and enforcement frameworks in "deterring" AI-driven cyber incidents, including whether current offences, liabilities, penalties and enforcement mechanisms are sufficient and effective.
It also wants to know what could be done to strengthen the networks and systems of government departments and agencies against AI vulnerabilities.
The review will be led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet in coordination with the National Cyber Security Coordinator, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian AI Safety Institute and Services Australia.
Key Event
OpenAI also tried to hack into NSW govt website
New South Wales Premier Chris Minns says the prime minister called him late last night to tell him that OpenAI had interacted with four websites in Australia.
"It was early morning in New York, and he told me about this breach, his real concerns as it relates to safety and security of information held by government agencies," he says.
One of the websites that OpenAI interacted with was the Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research (BOCSAR).
In a statement, BOSCAR said it was "aware that OpenAI has identified a potential vulnerability that could allow access to the dataset underpinning BOCSAR’s Crime Mapping Tool."
"There is no evidence that the vulnerability has been exploited or that a data breach has occurred," the statement said.
Minns says Cyber Security NSW would work with federal intelligence agencies to look into the incident, describing it as a concern for every government in the world.
"Whilst this might have been contained semi public information that wasn't privacy related, it may get to the point where that information is released."
Another fuel threat looms
US President Donald Trump might be about to send another shockwave through global energy markets.
According to Politico, America may impose a ban on the export of diesel as soon as this week.
There is division among members of Donald Trump's cabinet on the issue but he has publicly indicated support for some sort of restriction.
Energy secretary Chris Wright says no blanket ban on export is being considered but they are looking to at the most efficient way to get more diesel into the US.
The motive is to try to bring record domestic diesel prices down which are hurting the ruling Republican party politically at home. The mid-term elections will take place in early November.
America is the world's biggest exporter of diesel and if it cuts off supply, it will send global prices surging.
The world is already dealing with a supply issue because Russia, which is usually the second biggest exporter of diesel, is currently heavily restricting its exports to deal with its own domestic pressures. Its refining capability has been badly impacted by Ukrainian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
While in normal times Australia doesn't import a lot of diesel from America, it has supplied us at crucial times this year.
Australia's is the world leader in per-capita consumption of diesel, and our economy is heavily dependent on the fuel.
This could get hairy, quickly.
You can keep up with the latest petrol and diesel prices across Australia with our fuel tracker below.
What do we know about the Medicare AI breach?
The federal government is demanding answers after an artificial intelligence agent infiltrated a Medicare website, as well as targeting other government sites.
The OpenAI agent accessed both public and private files as it tried to scoop up data.
The government is stressing nobody's personal Medicare details were accessed, and that crucially, the impact was minor.
But that doesn't mean it's relaxed about this breach — largely because it could be a harbinger of much worse attacks with vastly more serious consequences.
So, what type of information was accessed? What else do we know? And what could this breach tell us about future cyber attacks?

"A US company linked to the Trump administration hacking what is arguably the most valuable and sensitive database in Australia is a serious attack on Australia's sovereignty," he says.
"The US ambassador must be summoned to explain what the US government knew and what policy responses they are taking to this serious attack from a major US corporation."
There's no doubt the government is worried about this incident.
But it's very unlikely to summon the US ambassador over it.
OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman might maintain links to US President Donald Trump's government, but OpenAI is a private company, not an arm of the US government.
Mode of OpenAI's breach notification criticised
The assistant minister for technology and the digital economy, Andrew Charlton, says the way in which OpenAI informed Australia of the data breach was "entirely inadequate".
OpenAI emailed a public mailbox at Services Australia on September 10, three months after the breach occurred.
"This is not the way that this type of incident should be reported to the Australian government. It is not timely enough, and it is not the level of information that we require for this type of serious incident," he said.
Charlton says he believes a human wrote the email, but says the way OpenAI has communicated indicates they are not taking the matter seriously.
"It's extremely concerning that we did not know about this for some time, and that is why, even though no personal information was breached in this incident, it's why the government is taking this so seriously."
Wells defends PM misinformation remarks
Communications Minister Anika Wells has defended comments the prime minister made yesterday linking his government's Digital Duty of Care proposal to rising misinformation and disinformation and polarisation in the political system.
Here's what Anthony Albanese said in New York yesterday, when he was speaking about his efforts to tackle algorithm harms.
"Whilst today we're concentrating on the impact on children, the truth is this is having an impact on our entire society and how it functions with misinformation, disinformation.
"With the increased polarisation that we're seeing as well in the political system, where people are moving away from the centre and more and more to the extremes, be they of the left or the right.
"And that is why we think that this is a very positive move that's being put forward."
But according to Wells, the prime minister "was speaking to the broader online environment".
The Digital Duty of Care exposure draft came under further scrutiny yesterday when US President Donald Trump's government, through its Canberra embassy, raised concerns about the bill, including that it could amount to censorship.
Wells said while the US was "entitled to their position," the purpose of the bill would be to deliver basic online safety standards, echoing remarks from the PM that it wasn't about government control.
Key Event
Timeline of breach
There have been lots of questions about the timing of this breach, with many asking why it took so long for it to come to light. Here's a timeline of how this incident unfolded, based on what we now know:
- June 18: Breach occurs
- August 11: OpenAI becomes aware of this during a review of OpenAI misaligned model activity
- September 1: OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman meets Minister for Defence Richard Marles in San Francisco, but Mr Marles says the breach "wasn't the subject of that meeting"
- September 10: OpenAI emails Services Australia via a public feedback portal used by academics to notify the government if they think weaknesses exist in the website
- September 11: Services Australia sees the email
- September 15: Services Australia notifies the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD)
- September 17: Minister for the Public Service Katy Gallagher is told and seeks further information
- September 19-20: Ms Gallagher holds several discussions with Mr Marles in his capacity as Acting Prime Minister, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, Services Australia and the ASD. The Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his office are informed of the incident.
- September 22: First "technical exchange" between OpenAI and Services Australia
- September 24: Mr Albanese calls Mr Altman and informs the public of the breach
Victoria's health department may have been affected in the breach
Victoria's health department may have been affected by the OpenAI hack of the Medicare system, says the state's premier, Ben Carroll.
Carroll says he spoke to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese late last night about the issue.
He says he's been reassured by the PM that no personal information was accessed.
"The Australian Signals Directorate are now working through this matter and information is coming to hand literally as we speak.
"What he has been able to assure me, though, his initial advice is there has been no compromise of personal private information, but we stress this is early days in the investigation."
Earlier this morning, a Victorian government spokesperson described the hack as "deeply concerning".
"This shows how important guardrails are for artificial intelligence, not just in Australia but globally."
Broader interactions of govt systems with AI to be scrutinised
Acting PM Richard Marles says the government's taskforce will not just examine the current Medicare portal breach by OpenAI, but also how government systems have interacted with external AI more generally.
"But I would really want to reassure Australians that, in terms of the sensitive information that the Government has about Australian citizens but also our most sensitive national security information, that sits in a very secure domain, in a context where it is receiving constant attention and probing, and it has maintained that security through until this day," he says.
"We seek to learn everything we can from this incident. We seek to be constantly improving in an emerging environment. But we are amongst the world's leaders in relation to the way in which we manage cybersecurity, and particularly of government systems, but also critical infrastructure within the private sector – ASD leads that work. And Australians should take a great deal of confidence from that."
Meanwhile Katy Gallagher says the government has a "forensic investigation" underway with Services Australia.
"We don't have all the information yet. We've got another technical briefing that will occur with OpenAI, because Services Australia has sought additional information from OpenAI that wasn't able to be resolved on Tuesday," she says.
Why did it take five days for the email to be escalated?
Katy Gallagher is asked why it took Services Australia five days to notify the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) about the breach.
"That email address is looked at once a day ... we have someone who goes and has a look through, it gets sometimes quite a number of notifications, sometimes many of them are hoaxes," she said.
She said Services Australia told her it checked the inbox on September 11, a Friday. Then there was the weekend, and it had to conduct its own checks on the technical data.
"It took a couple of days to verify that what they'd been alerted to in the email was legitimate, and it was at that point that they engaged ASD."
She was asked if that inbox should be monitored more closely, and said that would be looked at in the investigation.
"This should not have gone to a kind of, an email address. It should have been escalated through ASD's channels or through the senior levels of Services Australia. And my understanding is OpenAI accepted that as well."
Key Event
Govt services minister says portal breached by AI wasn't hugely significant
Government services minister Katy Gallagher doubles down on assurances that no personal information was exposed as a result of the Medicare AI breach.
She says the services portal involved was already a public-facing website, as opposed to other systems of "government significance" that Services Australia runs.
"Of course, the cyber protections associated with that are quite different," she says.
AI agent 'scaled the fence'
Richard Marles has been asked if the public should be worried about the cybersecurity of Australian government systems.
The acting PM has said there are various levels of security relative to how important it is for the information to be protected.
"In this instance, it's not particularly sensitive information. In fact, the information has now been made public," he said.
"The analogy I would give here is that it was behind a fence. The AI agent climbed the fence."
He said when we're talking about the data of Australian individuals within the Australian government system, that's akin to sitting inside a safe.
"When you're talking about our national security, the most sensitive information that we have, it sits behind a fortress," he said.
He said he was confident in the level of security for the most sensitive information.
The Medicare statistics data, he said, "was not sitting behind a particularly high fence".
"This AI agent scaled the fence. But it did scale it. And the point it, it was unintended, it wasn't asked to."
Was the breach illegal?
Richard Marles is not drawn on a question about whether what occurred with the OpenAI agent and Australian government websites was a breach of law.
He says determining that will fall to the taskforce the government just announced.
"This is an unintended access, that's clear, but it definitely does raise questions about whether the law has been broken in respect of this," he says.
"And obviously we will investigate all of that. What the consequences are, if there has been a breach of the law, but also part of the task force is to assess whether or not the legal regime we have in place is fit–for–purpose in a world where we have an emerging AI capability."
Key Event
Govt 'expressed concern' to OpenAI on delayed response
Richard Marles says Australian authorities have made their displeasure about the time it took for OpenAI to notify the government of the Medicare breach known, including in a one-on-one meeting between Anthony Albanese and Sam Altman in New York last night.
"In respect of OpenAI, we have expressed our concern to OpenAI about the amount of time it took for the Australian Government to be made aware of this – I want to make that really clear," he says.
"Again, as we work with OpenAI, and we work with other frontier companies, a key part of that engagement is how we can be notified as quickly as possible."
Marles says it's not good enough that the government was alerted to the breach via a generic Services Australia email inbox.
Services Australia still gathering information from OpenAI
The first time Services Australia was able to put questions to OpenAI was on Tuesday.
Minister for the Public Service and Government Services Katy Gallagher said OpenAI first told Services Australia about the hack via email on September 10.
The Australian Signals Directorate was subsequently notified, and then the minister was told on September 17.
"The first technical exchange between OpenAI and Services Australia happened on Tuesday this week," she told reporters.
"That was when Services Australia was able to ask specific questions and ask for the logs, essentially, and some of the data that OpenAI had.
"There are going to be subsequent meetings of those. They haven't concluded."

First Nations workers in Australia paid 16pc less per hour, report finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:54:39 UTC
05:54:39 KST

Landmark reports finds First Nations workers in Australia paid 16pc less per hour
In short:
An Indigenous-led report has found First Nations workers earn 16 per cent less per hour than all Australian workers on average.
After examining factors including age, experience, qualifications and hours worked, the pay gap remained largely unexplained, with the authors pointing to structural racism.
What next:
The report recommends the Racial Discrimination Act be amended to place a positive duty on employers to prevent racial discrimination, in the same way they must prevent sex discrimination.
A landmark report into the First Nations pay gap has revealed Indigenous workers are on average paid 16 per cent less per hour than the average Australian worker.
The report by the University of Technology Sydney's Centre for Indigenous People and Work (CIPW) and Indigenous Business Australia (IBA) found Indigenous workers earned 84 cents to every dollar earned by Australian workers on average.
CIPW director Professor Nareen Young said the size of the pay shortfall was equivalent to losing a lifetime of superannuation payments or working nearly two months every year for free.
"Nobody would accept that in a contract and no one should have to accept this gap," she said.
Australia's gender pay gap is smaller, with women on average earning 11.2 per cent less than men.
"Obviously we still have a problem but [the gender pay gap] is getting much better because of policy interventions," she said.
"But this research shows that Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people are on average getting paid a lot less for doing the same jobs."
Indigenous women had the greatest pay disparity, earning an average of $41 an hour compared to $52 for all Australian men.
Pay disparities across range of professions
The report found that across all eight major occupation groups, from managers to labourers, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander workers earned on average less per hour.
The largest hourly pay gap was recorded amongst professionals at 19.5 per cent.
IBA chief economist Dr Siddharth Shirodkar said it showed higher-paid or highly skilled occupations were not immune from pay inequality.
"If you've got a post-grad qualification … and you're First Nations, you've got a higher employment rate than non-Indigenous people, but the average annual income for Indigenous people with those qualifications is generally lower."
Dr Shirodkar said the pay gap existed across almost every age category as well.
"That points to systemic issues, structural issues and indeed bias and discrimination," he said.
The report analysed data from 227 occupations and found in three quarters of occupational groups, Indigenous workers earned less per hour than all workers in the same role.
The size of that gap varied, from 34 per cent for environmental scientists to 6 per cent for truck drivers.
"The dominant pattern is persistent underpayment, not isolated anomalies," the report said.
Teachers and machinery operators/drivers stood out as exceptions, earning close to pay parity on hourly wages or even slightly reversed hourly pay gaps.
Dr Shirodkar estimated the pay gap would amount to $170 billion in lost income by 2050, which would have broader impacts on the Australian economy.
"That's not taking into consideration the compounding effect of lower superannuation, lower savings, lower rates of wealth creation as well," he said.
Pay gap attributed to structural racism
The study examined the factors typically given as reasons for pay gaps — such as hours worked, occupation, age and education — and found these could not fully explain the pay gap.
The study found differences in the numbers of hours worked by Indigenous people could only explain about 2 per cent of the gap.
And while Indigenous workers were somewhat more likely to work in lower-paying occupations, the authors said this could only explain 27.5 per cent of the total gap.
Professor Young said that left 70 per cent of the Indigenous pay gap "unexplained".
"We've been told for years that this is about education, about experience, about the sorts of jobs our mob end up in, and we've tested every one of those explanations," she said.
"So what is left is structural racism in the way work is valued and paid.
"What we need to have as an Australian community is a big discussion about the value of Indigenous work."
The report said the gap likely reflected factors such as the legacy of historically discriminatory wage setting, racial bias in recruitment, and limited power for First Nations workers to negotiate salaries and pay increases.
These factors were not directly measured in the report but were identified as potential contributors.
While the report measured pay gaps using average hourly earnings, the authors found strong correlations when examining median pay gaps across occupations as well.
The authors said this meant their findings were unlikely to be skewed by a small number of unusually high or low-income earners but reflected broader differences across occupations.
They said their estimates of hourly earnings were economy-wide figures and should not be interpreted as "like-for-like comparisons of otherwise identical workers".
Employers urged to prevent racial discrimination
The report made several key recommendations aimed at creating fairer pay and employment structures.
The most significant was to place a positive duty on employers to prevent racial discrimination, in the same way they must prevent sex discrimination.
Other recommendations included improving Indigenous employment data collection, and for cultural skills to be valued properly when wages are set.

Turkey and Iraq agree Turkey will turn over military camp in northern Iraq
Unknown

Turkey and Iraq agree Turkey will turn over military camp in northern Iraq
CAIRO, Sept 23 - Turkey and Iraq agreed on Wednesday for Turkish forces to hand over a military camp in northern Iraq to the Iraqi government gradually, they said after talks in New York, adding they also agreed to end the presence of "outlawed armed elements" in northern Iraq.
After Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi and Turkish President Tayyip Erdogan met on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly, the sides said in a joint statement they had agreed to deepen security cooperation.
"Within this framework, they reached an agreement on fully establishing state authority in Sinjar and ending the presence of outlawed foreign armed elements," they said, referring to Kurdish militants, some of whom are based in the mountainous Sinjar area of northern Iraq.
Turkey is continuing a peace process that it hopes will result in the disarmament of those militants from the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) and end a decades-old conflict.
The statement on Wednesday added that "in accordance with the agreed-upon mechanism and timeline" and security measures taken by Iraq, Turkish forces would gradually hand over the Bashiqa-Zelikan base, a military installation in northern Iraq near Mosul, to the Iraqi government.
An Iraqi military commander familiar with the talks said the phased withdrawal of Turkish troops from the Bashiqa camp and another small base near Mosul was expected to be completed by the end of this year. There was no immediate comment from Turkey on the timeline.
Ankara deployed troops near Mosul in 2015, saying they were there to train and protect Iraqi forces and local Sunni Arab, Turkmen and Kurdish fighters preparing to fight Islamic State, which seized Mosul in 2014.
The deployment sparked a dispute with Baghdad, which demanded the troops’ withdrawal, while Ankara said they were supporting the anti-Islamic State training mission. Turkey still has several bases in the region, which it says are there to protect Turkey's national security.
Tom Barrack, US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, welcomed the move, saying "Iraqi sovereignty and Turkish security, both (were) served" by it.
The joint statement said the two leaders also discussed bilateral ties and trade, stressing the need to urgently implement previously signed agreements and speed up "strategic projects." REUTERS

550,000 liters of fuel just allowed into Gaza not sufficient: UN
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
04:47:42 CST
05:47:42 KST

UNITED NATIONS, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Welcoming the latest 550,000 liters of fuel allowed into Gaza, UN humanitarians said on Wednesday that their partners warn the overall volume imported remains short of the bare minimum necessary.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said the fuel allowed in on Tuesday will help keep basic services running but is far from sufficient.
OCHA said last Thursday's allocation of 2 million U.S. dollars from the OCHA-managed humanitarian fund for the occupied Palestinian territory, along with a recent Qatari donation, were stop-gap measures to fund fuel for Gaza's medical facilities.
"Additional funding is urgently needed to sustain the availability of fuel and prevent a dangerous slowdown of health care, water provision, rescue operations, debris removal and other critical services," OCHA said.
The office said its partners report that the current extensive use of backup generators is unsustainable. Approvals for engine oil, spare parts, solar panels, the entry of commercial fuel and the resumption of operations at the Gaza Power Plant are critical.
OCHA said that ahead of the rainy season, its partners working on site management reported that 989 of 1,764 sites for displaced people assessed across Gaza are in areas at medium to high risk of flooding. The sites shelter about 1 million people.
"Many displaced families have remained in deteriorating shelters since last winter, with limited protection, inadequate drainage and shortages of mattresses, blankets and other essential household items," OCHA said. "Partners warn that about 400,000 people may need to relocate once heavy rains begin."
The office said that until then, its partners are improving drainage, reinforcing shelters, delivering essential materials and equipment, and trying to help people already choosing to relocate. Still, resources are limited and very little land remains available. ■

The Hawk T2 aircraft had taken off from RAF Valley on Anglesey before crashing in the nearby Pencarnisiog area. North Wales Police said the two pilots had ejected and were being treated for what were believed to be minor injuries, with no reports of wider damage or injuries.
The RAF said that Hawk T1 and T2 operations had been temporarily suspended as a precaution while investigations into the incident were under way.
North Wales Fire and Rescue Service said a fire at the crash site had been brought under control. Ambulance and air ambulance crew also attended the scene, while Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said further details would be "provided in due course." ■

SANAA, Sept. 23 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Wednesday that more than 400 commercial vessels had crossed the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait between Sept. 11 and Sept. 21, as fighting continued near the key waterway.
In a statement aired by Houthi-run al-Masirah TV, the group said 408 commercial vessels transited the strait over this period, with 196 heading north toward the Red Sea and 212 south toward the Gulf of Aden.
It said daily traffic averaged more than 40 commercial vessels, including container ships, and claimed that international shipping was proceeding normally and safely, except for Saudi vessels, which it said are subject to a maritime ban.
The group added that the latest figure exceeded the 393 commercial vessels recorded between Sept. 1 and Sept. 10, when 199 traveled north and 194 south.
The numbers could not be independently verified. Separate ship-tracking data have shown fluctuations in traffic through Bab al-Mandab since the latest escalation, including periods of sharply reduced daily crossings.
The statement comes amid heightened international attention on the waterway following the Houthis' rapid territorial gains along Yemen's southwestern Red Sea coast. Houthi forces seized the strategic port city of Mocha on Sept. 10 and Mayyun Island in the heart of the strait the following day.
Bab al-Mandab Strait connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and forms part of a major maritime corridor linking Asia and Europe through the Suez Canal, making developments around the strait closely watched by global shipping.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government. Renewed fighting in recent weeks has again brought the conflict closer to the Bab al-Mandab Strait. ■

Breaking: OpenAI agent hacked Medicare portal, PM says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:31:06 UTC
05:31:06 KST

OpenAI hacked Medicare portal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says
In short:
The prime minister has had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman after an AI agent breached an Australian government website.
The company did not notify Services Australia of the incident until three months after the fact, via email.
What's next?
The prime minister has announced a taskforce to investigate further.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has revealed an AI agent hacked into an Australian Medicare data portal earlier this year.
Speaking in New York, Mr Albanese said the OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal administered by Services Australia on June 18.
The AI agent accessed both public and non-public files, but Mr Albanese said it did not appear anyone's personal Medicare details were accessed.
Mr Albanese said he had a "frank" discussion with OpenAI's chief executive Sam Altman, saying the company took three months to notify the government of the breach and, when it did, the notification was in an email sent to the Services Australia public inbox.
"Today I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia's extreme concern about this incident," he said.
"And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred."
He said the "nature" of the notification was also "unacceptable".
"The notification was an email sent just to the public mailbox," Mr Albanese said.
What do we know so far?
OpenAI accessed non-public aggregate health statistics and internal files from an old Australian government website that carried Medicare statistics.
It is understood an AI crawler, which is an automated program that scans websites and collects information from them, was able to find a security workaround to access the data.
Often deployed as a tool by AI agents, crawlers collect data that usually trains AI models, builds datasets or retrieves information for AI systems.
Who knew what, when?
Read more
June 18: A Medicare statistics reporting service portal, administered by Services Australia, is breached by an OpenAI agent
August 11: OpenAI becomes aware of the breach during a review of OpenAI misaligned model activity during training
September 1: OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman meets Defence Minister Richard Marles in San Francisco, but Mr Marles says the breach wasn't disclosed
September 10: OpenAI sends an email to publicdisclosures@ servicesaustralia.gov.au — an address used by academics and researchers to notify weaknesses in Services Australia's systems
September 11: Services Australia sees the email
September 15: Services Australia notifies the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD)
September 17: Minister for the Public Service Katy Gallagher is told and seeks further information
September 19-20: Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and his office are informed of the incident, while Minister Gallagher holds several discussions with Mr Marles, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke, Services Australia and the ASD
September 22: First "technical exchange" between OpenAI and Services Australia
September 24: Mr Albanese calls Mr Altman and informs the public of the breach
The prime minister said OpenAI was conducting research into public medical spending when it found a way to break through privacy protections.
"The AI agent found a way around those blocks, didn't accept 'no' for an answer, if you like," Mr Albanese said.
The prime minister said Services Australia was not notified until September 10.
On September 15, Services Australia reported it to the Australian Signals Directorate's cybersecurity centre.
Last week, Services Australia got in touch with Katy Gallagher, the minister for the public service. Mr Albanese's office was notified over the weekend.
He said there was no evidence any individual personal information had been accessed, but an investigation aided by the Australian Signals Directorate was now underway.
"[The] evidence currently available is there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable," Mr Albanese said.
The prime minister said three other websites may have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the New South Wales Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research, and the Victorian Department of Health.
But Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles later clarified that the interactions on those three websites were "entirely normal" and public information was accessed.
Mr Albanese announced a taskforce would be set up to provide an "urgent and immediate review" of the incident.
The investigation will be led by the prime minister's department and will work with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.
OpenAI says 'several' Australian government websites involved
The prime minister was asked if Mr Altman apologised.
"Yes, he clearly … we can get into word games, but he clearly accepted that the company had not done good enough," Mr Albanese said.
In a statement, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company was "conducting an extensive review of misaligned model activity" during training, and notifying third parties when there was a potential impact on their systems.
"During this review, we identified activity involving several Australian government websites and services as our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation," they said.
"In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend.
"Our review found no evidence of patient records being accessed. The information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names."
The company said the information accessed included aggregate health statistics and internal file names.
"We notified the organisations and are providing technical information to support their investigations and help address potential security vulnerabilities," the statement said.
They said OpenAI's overall review was ongoing and it remained "committed to transparency".
Back in Australia, Mr Marles said the fact a non-human AI agent gained unauthorised access represented "a very serious incident", but the impact on the system was minor.
"For what that's worth, that's relatively minor, and so it's important to assure people of that. No personal information has been accessed here. There's no impact on the system."
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the hack was a "serious warning". He accused the prime minister of "failing to pre-empt" the incident and called on him to focus more on cyber defence.
"I would have thought that cyber defence is the number one issue when it comes to AI," Mr Taylor said.
"It's not the only issue, but it's got to be top of the list, and it hasn't been the focus of the government … It should be, it must be."
Acting Greens leader Mehreen Faruqi said the incident was "disturbing" and called for a moratorium on AI data centres in Australia until further regulations were in place.
"This breach by a foreign AI company on an Australian government database is deeply alarming and brings home the risks that these out-of-control tech corporations pose," she said.
Mr Albanese said the incident was complex and unprecedented.
"It was a shock that it occurred because it was real and serious," he said.
"But it also, I think, was something that had been predicted, including by the AI companies themselves."

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:29:20 UTC
05:29:20 KST

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei addressed the United Nations Security Council on Wednesday and called for international coordination to address the potential risks posed by artificial intelligence.
"In our history, there have been times where countries who compete and don't always like each other very much still come together for shared interests and the collective good in the face of a powerful new technology," Altman said. "We believe this must be one of those times"
Earlier this month, Amodei rocked the tech sector by publishing a proposal to slow down the pace of AI development. Altman, in a rare sign of solidarity with his chief rival, publicly agreed with Amodei on the need to "pace the frontier." The safety practices at both companies have been under intense scrutiny after industry researchers warned about AI's growing potential to cause catastrophic harm.
The executives' remarks on Wednesday came just one day after President Donald Trump gave his own wide-ranging speech to the United Nations General Assembly. Trump criticized what he described as a "globalist scheme" to control AI, and said the U.S. would continue to encourage the technology's progress, "not rein it in."
"I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution," Trump said.
OpenAI and Anthropic's public positions have raised questions about what a slowdown would mean in practice, especially as both companies are gearing up for what are widely expected to be blockbuster IPOs. Neither company has officially disclosed when it plans to debut.
"Beating companies in a competitive race is not a reason to make rash decisions," Altman said Wednesday. "We have unilaterally slowed down in the past. We will do so in the future."
OpenAI opted to temporarily pause some of its research and training efforts after two of its models escaped containment, accessed the open internet breached the developer platform Hugging Face in July. The incident spooked industry researchers and executives, including Anthropic's Amodei, who referenced it in his proposal for a slowdown.
Amodei outlined a three-step plan aimed at slowing the pace of development without "sacrificing commercial advantage or the United States' lead in AI." He acknowledged that some steps will be easier to achieve than others.
The third step of his plan, for instance, calls for coordination between democratic governments and authoritarian governments. Amodei reiterated that position on Wednesday, and he encouraged world leaders to put aside their differences and address the "global opportunity," as well as the "global threat," ahead of them.
"No leader, no company, and no nation can manage this alone," he said. "We commit to working with governments in this room on this urgent work."

See the Taurids light up the fall sky with brilliant shooting stars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:28:21 UTC
05:28:21 KST

Annual meteor showers are always high points of the year, but in fall, we are treated to a two-for-one deal that runs for months. Called the Taurids, these showers dazzle the night sky throughout the season and bring an elevated chance of extrabright meteors—fireballs—to help chase the darkening days away.
The first leg of this epic meteor show is the Southern Taurid shower, which began on September 20 and is expected to last through November 20. Peak fireball activity is predicted to occur around the night of November 4 to 5—just after Halloween.
Meteors, also known as shooting stars, are the visible remnants of bits of debris falling from an asteroid or comet. These pieces burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere, creating a brilliant streak of light. The source of dust and debris that makes up the Southern Taurids is Comet 2P/Encke, a relatively small comet that measures about 2.98 miles (4.8 kilometers) wide, according to NASA.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
This year just 22 percent of the moon will be lit on November 4 to 5, providing “generally favorable” viewing conditions for the Southern Taurids’ peak, according to the American Meteor Society (AMS).
The Southern Taurids’ sister shower, the Northern Taurids, will begin on October 20, overlap with the Southern Taurids for a few weeks and peak on the night of November 11 to 12, according to the AMS.
You can catch the Taurids without any fancy equipment. Go outside and find a safe location with minimal light pollution and a clear view of the sky. Give your eyes about 30 minutes to adjust to the darkness and look up. The showers are named after the constellation Taurus, but the shooting stars can show up near other constellations, too.
“The best time to look for Taurids is after midnight, when Taurus is high in the sky,” according to NASA, “and when the sky is dark and clear, with no moonlight to mask the fainter meteors.”

Federal Judge Weighs Limits of U.S. Reach in Trial of Accused Kingpin Sebastián Marset
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:28:00 UTC
05:28:00 KST

Reported by
A federal judge will decide by Nov. 6 whether to dismiss criminal charges against Sebastián Marset, the self-proclaimed South American drug lord whose defense attorney conceded in court on Wednesday that while his client is a drug trafficker, his illicit empire fell entirely outside United States jurisdiction.
During a detailed two-hour evidentiary hearing in federal district court in Alexandria, Judge Rossie D. Alston Jr. weighed a number of defense motions seeking to dismantle the federal indictment against Marset, ranging from jurisdictional challenges to allegations of improper interrogations and vindictive prosecution.
The allegation of vindication prosecution didn’t sit well with Alston, who called it a “very serious” allegation and noted he personally had presided over cases involving the prosecutors, for whom he had high regard.
Defense attorney Robert Feitel quickly interjected that he wasn’t referencing individuals but the process by which Marset was captured in Bolivia, sent to the United States and interrogated without lawyers present. He sought to discredit Michael Greisen, one of the lead agents for the Drug Enforcement Administration in its efforts to capture Marset.
Prosecutors maintain that Marset, a Uruguayan national who operated in the southern cone of South America, laundered tens of millions of dollars through European banks and their U.S. subsidiaries with the help of financial operatives like Federico Santoro, a Uruguayan broker sentenced to 15 years in prison in 2025.
Marset was initially charged with money laundering counts but was later indicted on drug trafficking and narco terror charges.
In court Wednesday, Feitel indicated his client doesn’t dispute being a drug trafficker but noted he “studiously avoided” drug activities that involved the United States and accused the government of trying to “shoehorn this case into narco terrorism charges” by retroactively connecting Marset to regional syndicates - Colombia’s Clan del Golfo and Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital - whose official U.S. terrorist designations took effect after the events under investigation.
“Those designations are based on the groups’ historic conduct,” said Anthony T. Aminoff, the lead prosecutor, while also pushing back against defense claims that key evidence was seized in Colombian territorial waters rather than international seas.
Marset’s lawyers argued that the initial charge of money laundering is invalid because it involved a single wire transfer that did not involve the servers of a U.S. bank. They called as a witness former Treasury official Kristofer Doucette, a specialist in financial intelligence.
Lawyers, with the help of Doucette, tried to argue that the wire transfer was between two non-U.S. banks and not routed on a U.S. computer server. As part of international rules, it was routed to a server in Virginia and vetted by Bank of America’s compliance officials, who did not halt the transaction. The movement never touched U.S. banks thus was not a U.S. violation, they maintained.
Prosecutors countered they would show at trial that Bank of America servers were involved and key to the movement.
One of the most contentious issues is the claim by Marset’s defense that confessions were improperly obtained, a legal doctrine called “fruit from a poisonous tree.” They allege while Marset was read his rights to remain silent, prosecutors lagged in allowing him to contact his lawyer until they tried to entice him into pleading guilty.
On the stand, the DEA agent, Greisen, acknowledged recording interviews with Marset while on flights from arrest in Bolivia in March 2025 to Lima, Peru, and then on to Virginia. But Greisen admitted that he used discretion in not recording Marset when detained in Virginia in hopes that he could convince the drug lord to become a cooperating witness.
That could prove important. Greisen suggested he did so for the benefit of Marset, since recording those conversations would have produced an evidentiary record that could endanger him if he became a witness.
Judge Alston ordered both sides to submit brief summary filings by Oct. 12 before he issues a ruling. Marset's trial is currently scheduled for early 2027.

Turkish Airlines finalizes deal for up to 150 Boeing 737 MAX jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:26:15 UTC
05:26:15 KST

Esra Tekin
23 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Turkish Airlines finalized an agreement with Boeing on Wednesday covering the purchase of up to 150 737 MAX aircraft, marking the carrier’s largest single-aisle aircraft order from the company to date.
 
The agreement, reached following negotiations that began in 2025, is part of Turkish Airlines’ long-term growth strategy and is intended to strengthen the airline’s short- and medium-haul network while supporting the expansion of its fleet.
 
The deal was finalized in the presence of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
 
Under the agreement, Turkish Airlines will place a firm order for 100 Boeing 737-8 aircraft while retaining options for an additional 50 Boeing 737 MAX aircraft.
 
The agreement also provides the airline with the flexibility to switch to the Boeing 737-10, the largest member of the 737 MAX family.
 
This flexibility will allow Turkish Airlines to adjust fleet capacity according to passenger demand and operational requirements across its network.
 
“This agreement represents an important step in line with our strategy to expand our fleet,” said Murat Seker, chairman of the Board and Executive Committee of Turkish Airlines.
 
“The new Boeing 737 MAX aircraft will bring greater efficiency and flexibility to our operations and support the extensive flight network we serve from our Istanbul hub.”
 
Stephanie Pope, president and CEO of Boeing Commercial Airplanes, said the order reflected the “mutual trust and shared vision” that have shaped the companies’ longstanding partnership.
 
“We are proud to continue supporting Turkish Airlines as it expands its Istanbul-based network, connecting more people to more destinations around the world, while also supporting Türkiye’s aviation ecosystem,” Pope said.
 
- Fuel efficiency and network expansion
 
The new aircraft are expected to strengthen Turkish Airlines’ short- and medium-haul operations, particularly on high-demand domestic and international routes.
 
According to the airline, the Boeing 737-8 offers advantages in terms of range and payload capacity while providing a 20% reduction in fuel consumption and emissions compared with the aircraft it replaces. Turkish Airlines said these characteristics will help it respond to changing operational requirements as it expands its fleet and network.
 
Turkish Airlines and its subsidiary AJet currently operate more than 200 Boeing aircraft, including the 737 MAX, 737 Next-Generation, 787 Dreamliner and 777 Freighter models.
 
The latest agreement follows Turkish Airlines’ order for 75 Boeing 787 Dreamliner aircraft in 2025, further expanding the long-standing relationship between the airline and Boeing.
 
- Broader industrial cooperation
 
Beyond aircraft purchases, Turkish Airlines and Boeing are also pursuing long-term cooperation aimed at strengthening Türkiye’s aviation industry.
 
The two companies signed a strategic memorandum of understanding (MoU) on industrial participation this year, establishing a framework focused on three areas -- capability development, value creation and business opportunities.
 
- 'Big day for Boeing and American manufacturing!'
 
US President Donald Trump on Wednesday highlighted aircraft purchase agreements involving Türkiye and Bangladesh, describing the deals as a boost for Boeing, US manufacturing and American exports.
 
"Big day for Boeing and American manufacturing!" he said on his Truth Social platform.
 
Trump said Türkiye and Bangladesh had announced purchases totaling 111 Boeing aircraft, with options for an additional 50 planes.
 
He credited US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and the Department of Commerce with supporting the deals, saying they would generate tens of billions of dollars in sales and significantly increase US exports.
 
Trump also said the agreements would support tens of thousands of American jobs across the country.
 
“The Market is recognizing what Boeing and I have known all along: When you build in America, export from America, and support American workers, you make your company stronger,” he said.

Berlin airport was closed due to an unidentified UAV
Kyiv • UNN
Due to a drone over Berlin Brandenburg Airport, the airspace was closed and flights were diverted to Dresden. Operations resumed with delays.
At Berlin Brandenburg Airport, a drone was spotted on the evening of September 23, temporarily prompting the closure of the airspace over the airport. This is reported by t-online, according to UNN.
Details
It is reported that the drone was spotted on the northern runway at 8:00 p.m., and twenty minutes later, all aircraft movements over the airport were completely halted.
The restrictions lasted at least 45 minutes in total, and several flights had to be diverted to Dresden.
The airspace was reopened at 9:05 p.m.; however, aircraft takeoffs and landings are still being carried out with delays.
No other German airport recorded as many drone sightings in the first half of the year as Berlin Brandenburg Airport. The control tower in Schönefeld registered 28 such flying objects during the first six months. This is one more sighting than at Germany's largest airport in Frankfurt am Main during the same period
Reminder

According to NDR, WDR, and Süddeutsche Zeitung, the possibility that the device may have been equipped with explosives is currently being investigated.

Kyiv Faces Internet Disruptions as Russian Strikes Hit Data Centers and Communications Infrastructure

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Emergency response teams and specialists are currently assessing the extent of the damage across the local network.
Crews are actively working on repairs to restore regular service and bring stable connectivity back to the impacted areas as quickly as possible.
The Ministry of Digital Transformation has not provided a specific timeline for when full service will be restored to the capital and the neighboring region amid ongoing recovery efforts following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
At least three internet service providers in Kyiv—Pavutyna, UTELS, and Crazy Network—reported service disruptions following a attack by Russian forces. Data centers belonging to Pavutyna and UTELS sustained damage, causing network interruptions.
The attack on a traffic exchange point in Kyiv also led to internet connectivity issues for Crazy Network users in Vinnytsia and the Khmelnytskyi region.
The Russian Ministry of Defense has officially claimed to be deliberately targeting internet communication infrastructure in Ukraine, stating that recent strikes against Kyiv-based internet service providers were aimed at "striking facilities supporting the Armed Forces of Ukraine," according to Ukrainian political analyst, Andrii Smolii.
Russian forces are actively targeting Ukrainian data centers in an effort to disrupt early warning systems and leave civilians without critical safety information, according to Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
By striking data infrastructure, Moscow aims to cut off access to life-saving air raid notifications, compromising the nation's civil defense network and putting more civilian lives at risk during ongoing aerial attacks.
The latest strikes followed another daytime Russian attack on Kyiv on September 22, when Russian forces deployed jet-powered Shahed drones.

Vote counting begins in Morocco's parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:22:09 UTC
05:22:09 KST

Khalid Mejdoub, Mohammad Sio
23 September 2026•Update: 24 September 2026
Vote counting began across Morocco on Wednesday after polls closed in parliamentary elections that will determine the composition of the country's 395-seat House of Representatives.
Polling stations opened at 8 am GMT and closed at 7 pm, according to an Anadolu correspondent.
Morocco's Interior Ministry said voter turnout had reached 28.05% nationwide by 5 pm GMT, adding that voting took place under "normal conditions."
Final turnout in the previous parliamentary election, held on Sept. 8, 2021, was 50.18%.
A total of 3,206 observers, including 200 foreign monitors, oversaw Wednesday's vote.
Official figures show that 15,801,162 people were registered to vote. Twenty-eight political parties competed through 1,850 candidate lists comprising 7,288 candidates, including 2,658 women, for the 395 seats in the House of Representatives.
The Interior Ministry is expected to announce preliminary results in the early hours of Thursday.  
Under Article 47 of Morocco's Constitution, the king appoints the head of government from the political party that finishes first in the House of Representatives election. Cabinet members are appointed by the king on the recommendation of the head of government.
A parliamentary majority requires at least 198 seats, making coalition talks likely if no party secures an outright majority.
The next government will face political, economic and social challenges, as well as major projects linked to Morocco's preparations to co-host the 2030 FIFA World Cup.
In the 2021 election, the National Rally of Independents (RNI) finished first with 102 seats, followed by the Authenticity and Modernity Party with 86 and the Istiqlal Party with 81.
The current government is headed by RNI leader Aziz Akhannouch in coalition with the Authenticity and Modernity Party and Istiqlal.

Why McDonald's is following Walmart and Amazon into the advertising business
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:21:17 UTC
05:21:17 KST

McDonald's on Wednesday announced plans to create its own media network, following in the footsteps of retail giants like Amazon and Walmart.
In August, 450 of its company-owned U.S. restaurants began displaying advertising for other companies on its digital drive-thru order boards as part of a pilot. It is early days for the program, which has not yet rolled out to the franchisees who operate the rest of its roughly 14,000 U.S. locations.
Still, McDonald's hopes that it could eventually grow to be a $1 billion business for the company.
"Commerce media is one of the fastest-growing areas in advertising, and it's expected to reach more than $100 billion in the U.S. alone by 2028," Morgan Flatley, McDonald's global chief marketing officer and executive vice president of new business ventures, said during an investor presentation.
"It's an opportunity to generate revenue for the system with little in the way of additional cost, no operational complexity and no disruption to our customer experience," Flatley added.
The move could eventually bring McDonald's a steady stream of high-margin revenue as costs for key inputs like beef climb and as the chain plans to invest billions of dollars in restaurant upgrades over the next decade.
In the restaurant industry, McDonald's would be a pioneer for creating its own media network. CFO Ian Borden said that the company is uniquely positioned to make it a success.
"We have one of the most valuable brands of any company of our size and scale in any industry," Borden told CNBC. "We serve about 85% of the U.S. population at least once a year, so we have reach that's quite unique, and we have 14,000 locations across the U.S., which means we're in every community, and we're connecting with every consumer."
Retailers like Amazon and Walmart have found success running their own media networks, which tend to be high-margin businesses. Amazon reported $68.6 billion in advertising service sales in 2025, accounting for just under 10% of the company's overall revenue. Amazon's ads appear across its portfolio, from its shopping pages to Prime Video to lockers and live streaming platform Twitch, as well as third-party apps and websites.
Walmart does not share specific sales results for its advertising unit, but the company said that Connect, its U.S. ad business, grew sales 43% in its fiscal second quarter. The retailer's media network shows ads on its app, website and inside its more than 4,600 U.S. stores, plus outside apps like Instagram. It also bought TV maker Vizio in late 2024 with an eye toward its ad business.
McDonald's newest venture was announced as part of the company's investor day, which was hosted at its Chicago headquarters. In addition to the media network, executives shared more details about plans to grow sales through pricey restaurant upgrades and better food quality.

Netanyahu heads to UN for brief visit with few high-level meetings, protests expected
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:19:52 UTC
05:19:52 KST

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is set to arrive in the New York area Thursday for an unusually brief visit to address the United Nations General Assembly, with few meetings with foreign leaders and no scheduled meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump as Israel faces intense international criticism.
Netanyahu is expected to spend only several hours in the United States, delivering his speech, holding a small number of diplomatic meetings and returning to Israel without staying overnight. The abbreviated schedule marks a departure from previous General Assembly visits, when Netanyahu used the annual gathering to meet numerous world leaders on the sidelines.
Israeli officials have made efforts to arrange meetings with leaders of countries considered friendly toward Israel, particularly in South America. Netanyahu is expected to meet Argentine President Javier Milei and Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša during the visit.
A meeting with Trump, however, is not scheduled. A senior U.S. official said the two leaders' schedules do not overlap, with Netanyahu expected to arrive after Trump has already left New York.
Netanyahu is traveling primarily to deliver his General Assembly address before quickly returning to Israel.
A hostile reception at the UN
The United Nations has long been a venue for sharp criticism of Israeli policy, but Israeli officials are preparing for a particularly contentious reception this year.
Officials expect some diplomats could walk out during Netanyahu's address, while others may stage protests inside the chamber, including by displaying signs accusing Israel of genocide. Israel rejects accusations that its actions in Gaza constitute genocide.
An Israeli official said images involving National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and incidents of Jewish extremist violence in the West Bank have further damaged Israel's standing internationally. The official said there was a perception abroad that Netanyahu had failed to restrain far-right members of his government.
Outside the UN, several demonstrations are planned around Netanyahu's appearance, involving Israeli anti-government activists, left-wing Jewish organizations and pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist groups. Major Jewish organizations, meanwhile, organized a rally against antisemitism near the UN on Wednesday, a day before Netanyahu's address.
The demonstrations come amid Netanyahu's escalating public confrontation with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has accused the Israeli prime minister of war crimes and genocide, allegations Netanyahu rejects. Mamdani previously said he would seek Netanyahu's arrest based on an International Criminal Court warrant but later acknowledged that he lacks the authority to do so.
Netanyahu said this week that he intends to use his UN address to “tell the truth” about Israel and its military and respond to Mamdani's accusations.
Netanyahu expected to focus on Iran
Iran is expected to feature prominently in Netanyahu's speech.
In recent days, Israeli officials have held intensive discussions over whether classified intelligence related to Iran could be cleared for public release for use in the address. Netanyahu is expected to present aerial imagery concerning Iranian reconstruction efforts and Tehran's nuclear and missile programs.
He is also expected to refer to a series of recent attacks against Israelis, including the latest attack in which IDF reservist Neriya Leiter, the son of Israeli Ambassador to the United States Yechiel Leiter, was seriously wounded.
The speech comes just over a month before Israel's Oct. 27 election, giving Netanyahu one of the world's most prominent diplomatic stages at a critical point in the campaign.
Netanyahu has portrayed the appearance as an opportunity to defend Israel before an international audience that he says has accepted false claims about the country and its conduct. His critics, however, argue that the speech is aimed at least as much at Israeli voters as at the diplomats in the General Assembly hall.
No Trump meeting, no overnight stay
Netanyahu's official aircraft is expected to land Thursday morning at a military airfield in New Jersey rather than John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York.
Reports about the change have cited a combination of security, logistical and protest concerns. Netanyahu is then expected to travel in a secured motorcade directly to the United Nations.
His wife, Sara, and son Yair are expected to accompany him.
Israel's ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, has worked to arrange diplomatic meetings around the compressed visit.
Netanyahu had sought a meeting with Trump, according to Israeli sources, but none was arranged. U.S. officials have publicly attributed the absence of a meeting to scheduling, saying Netanyahu will arrive after Trump leaves New York.
Israeli officials also believe there is frustration within the Trump administration over Netanyahu's handling of Gaza, though U.S. officials have not publicly cited that as the reason the two leaders will not meet.
Netanyahu had also sought a meeting with Elon Musk in Texas, but the stop was canceled after security and logistical difficulties arose. The planned Texas visit would also have required an additional U.S. landing for refueling. Reports this week confirmed that the Texas stop was dropped from Netanyahu's itinerary.
The prime minister ultimately decided on a lightning visit that will not include an overnight stay at his usual Manhattan hotel, the Loews Regency.
Israel had already reserved three floors at the hotel, however, potentially leaving the government with a substantial bill despite Netanyahu not staying there. Finance Ministry officials are expected to negotiate with the hotel in an effort to secure credit toward a future stay.
The visit comes as Netanyahu faces protests not only from pro-Palestinian and anti-Zionist activists but also from Israelis opposed to his government. The Israeli expat group UnXeptable, which emerged as a prominent organizer during the 2023 protests against Netanyahu's judicial overhaul, is among those planning demonstrations Thursday.
For Netanyahu, the visit will therefore be markedly different from many of his previous appearances at the annual gathering: hours rather than days in New York, a limited diplomatic schedule, no meeting with the U.S. president and an address delivered amid demonstrations both inside and outside the United Nations.

Wired for War: The empire’s propaganda wing honors Palantir
Unknown

Wired for War: The empire’s propaganda wing honors Palantir
Germany’s Axel Springer media monolith is about to award its highest honor to Palantir founder Peter Thiel, in a ceremony illustrating the incestuous relationship between the mainstream media, the defense tech industry, and the US-Israeli order.
Thiel will receive the ‘2026 Axel Springer Award’ at a ceremony in Berlin on Thursday. According to Axel Springer CEO Mathias Dopfner, Thiel “is one of the rare entrepreneurs who does not merely found or finance companies but helps determine the direction of technological development...he reminds us that progress requires courage and nonconformism.”
The ceremony begins at 7pm Berlin time, and anyone curious what Thiel has to say can check out the livestream below.
Previous recipients of the Axel Springer Award include Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky. None of these laureates have proven as controversial as Thiel, however.
According to Status News, employees at Politico and Business Insider – both of which are owned by Axel Springer – have pushed back against the decision. In a letter to management on Tuesday, 120 staffers argued that Thiel, who funded the lawsuit that destroyed Gawker, should not be honored by a company which, in the words of Dopfner, “stands for freedom of speech and a culture of open discussions.”
They’re missing the point. Palantir and Axel Springer are cogs in the same machine. They share an almost identical world view, marked by a devotion to US-Israeli hegemony, a belief that private companies must serve the interests of this hegemony, and a common parent: the CIA.
The CIA connection
During the Cold War, the US saw strategic control of media outlets as key to preventing the rise of socialism and communism in Western Europe. Axel Springer, the anti-communist press baron who gave his name to the company, was a natural ally in this fight. Springer received $7 million in funding from the CIA in 1957, two former agents told The Nation in 1982. Adjusted for inflation, the donation would be equivalent to more than $80 million today.
Although the agents claimed that Springer ended his relationship with the agency in the mid-1970s, declassified documents show that he was still in contact with the United States Information Agency (USIA) – which funded pro-American news outlets – in the early 1980s. In 1982, Springer was introduced to CIA Director William Casey as “a strong supporter of the United States” who “is doing all he can to strengthen the ties between the United States and Europe.”
Thiel, who co-founded PayPal, launched Palantir in 2003 with the stated goal of taking “the approaches that PayPal had used to fight fraud…into other contexts, like fighting terrorism.” The CIA took notice, and invested $2 million in the company in 2005 via its in-house venture capital firm, In-Q-Tel.
“I wish I had Palantir when I was director,” former CIA chief George Tenet – who set up In-Q-Tel – told Forbes magazine in 2013. “I wish we had the tool of its power.”
The Axel Springer investment pays off
In both cases, the CIA’s investments paid off. Axel Springer is now Europe’s largest publisher, and owns Politico, Business Insider, Bild, Die Welt, The Telegraph, and nearly a dozen other outlets. The American deep state continues to finance its operations, with the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and the State Department’s National Endowment for Democracy (NED) pumping just under $34 million into Politico between 2016 and 2025.
In return, Axel Springer has openly pledged fealty to American neoliberalism. Whereas Springer himself described his first newspaper, the Hamburger Abendblatt, as “geared to the underdog and the little man,” staff at Axel Springer publications are today required to adhere to the following code of conduct:
- “We stand up for freedom, free speech, the rule of law, and democracy”
- “We support the right of existence of the State of Israel and oppose all forms of anti-Semitism”
- “We advocate the alliance between the United States of America and Europe”
- “We uphold the principles of a free market economy”
- “We reject political and religious extremism and all forms of discrimination”
In practice, this means that Axel Springer publications will feature lively debate over ‘red versus blue’ politics in the US and Europe, but will never question key tenets of US foreign policy, including America’s alliance with Israel, its dominance over Europe through NATO, and the legitimacy of its proxy war with Russia in Ukraine.
The world according to Palantir
More than two decades after taking CIA money, Palantir is now the largest of the Silicon Valley defense kingpins, and a synonym for the burgeoning surveillance- and military-tech sector as a whole. Palantir is valued at around $427 billion, a figure bolstered by lucrative contracts with the US’ defense and intelligence agencies, including all six branches of the US military, the CIA, FBI, NSA, and DIA.
Palantir’s flagship product is an operating system called ‘Gotham’, which is essentially a data analytics platform for military, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies. Gotham pulls together and analyses existing data that may otherwise take days to sift through. For example, if US Central Command is planning a missile strike in a foreign country, Gotham can combine maps and satellite footage from that country, data from other agencies, including human intelligence from the CIA and signals intelligence from the NSA, and local surveillance data to present CENTCOM with potential targets for military strikes.
Palantir’s international customers include the British, Israeli and Ukrainian militaries, NATO, domestic intelligence agencies in France and Germany, and police departments in Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and the UK, among others.
However, Palantir is not a mercenary company selling its products to anyone with money. According to CEO Alex Karp, Palantir is inseparable from the US deep state, and “was founded to strengthen US national security, to protect Americans and their freedom.”
Because we get asked a lot.
The Technological Republic, in brief.
1. Silicon Valley owes a moral debt to the country that made its rise possible. The engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation.
2. We must rebel…
Earlier this year, Karp set out Palantir’s world view in a manifesto, which RT already covered in depth in our ‘Wired for War’ series. In the 22-point bulletin, Karp argued that “the engineering elite of Silicon Valley has an affirmative obligation to participate in the defense of the nation,” that “free and democratic societies” must pursue AI superweapons to preserve the hegemony of the US, which “has advanced progressive values” more than “any other nation on the planet.”
In separate comments, Karp has described pro-Palestinian protesters as a “cancerous” influence on American politics, while Palantir describes its work with the Israeli state as “in line with our global support of US allies and liberal democracies.”
Critics called Karp’s manifesto “technofascist,” but it differs little in substance from Axel Springer’s code of conduct. Karp’s remaining points wade into US-centric culture war territory, but the core argument of both documents is the same: the US and Israel are a benevolent force and the private sector has a duty to aid their foreign policy goals; by argument, in the case of Axel Springer, and by force, in the case of Palantir.
The incestuous security state
Back in Berlin, the guest speakers at Thursday’s ceremony further illustrate the incestuous relationship between Axel Springer, Palantir, and the US-Israeli order. Before Dopfner hands him his award, Thiel will be lauded by CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss, a self-described “Zionist fanatic” who was appointed head of the network following its acquisition last year by billionaire and pro-Israel megadonor David Ellison, whose family has donated more than $26 million to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) since 2014.
Before the acquisition, Weiss repeatedly complained about CBS’ supposedly “anti-Israel bias.” Once in control of the network, she set about hiring pro-Israel editors and reportedly intervening personally in stories concerning the Jewish state.
Thursday’s ceremony will also feature a questions-and-answers session with PayPal co-founder Max Levchin, a vocal defender of the NSA amid Edward Snowden’s revelations of warrantless wiretapping.
The award is equivalent to an ‘Employee of the Month’ prize from one department of the same company to another. It’s like USAID and CIA agents meeting for after-work drinks, or Weiss congratulating the IDF for its service.
Dopfner, Thiel, Weiss and Levchin understand they’re all on the same team. Anyone who’s followed RT’s ‘Wired for War’ series will grasp this. The only people yet to figure it out, apparently, are the Politico and Business Insider staffers complaining about the threat posed by Thiel to “Axel Springer’s own commitment to freedom.”
Thursday’s ceremony might help them understand the true nature of the power they serve a little clearer.
