No, this video doesn't disprove the 9/11 attack on the south tower of the World Trade Center
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:01:33 UTC
04:01:33 KST

No, this video doesn't disprove the 9/11 attack on the south tower of the World Trade Center
A former British member of parliament implied that a video filmed from a helicopter on September 11, 2001 shows that no planes actually hit the World Trade Center's south tower, but this claim would be unfounded. The plane that hit the south tower hit the other side of the building, which isn’t visible in the video.
A few days after the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks that took place on September 11, 2001, British former Conservative MP Andrew Bridgen cast doubt on the official narrative when he implied that a plane did not hit the south tower of the World Trade Center. In reality, the south tower was indeed hit by a United Airlines Boeing 767 which had been hijacked by al Qaeda terrorists.
The former MP shared a video on September 15, 2026 that he claimed showed proof that a plane didn’t actually hit the south tower. The video, which garnered more than a million views on X from his post alone, was filmed from a helicopter facing the Twin Towers showing the north tower already in flames. The video then shows an explosion taking place in the south tower, but no plane can be seen. "Where was the plane that caused it?” Andrew Bridgen asked.
To display this content from X (Twitter), you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
A plane visible in the full version of the video
Bridgen’s claims, however, are wrong. First, if you carry out a reverse image search (check out our handy guide here to find out how), you will see a longer version of the video Bridgen posted on YouTube. The video was filmed live by Chopper 4, a helicopter belonging to the US channel NBC. In this complete version of the video, you can actually see a plane. It appears as a small dot moving towards the south tower just before the explosion.
While the plane’s collision with the tower isn’t directly visible in the video posted by Bridgen, this is because it hit the other side of the tower, which isn’t visible from the helicopter.
Collision on the south side of the south tower
According to a report by the commission set up by the United States to investigate September 11, United Airlines flight 175 crashed into the south face of the south tower after being hijacked by terrorists. However, as shown when we geolocated the craft, the NBC helicopter was filming the south tower from the north, which meant that the plane's collision was hidden by the tower itself.
The moment when the United Airlines Boeing 767 hit the south tower is actually visible in a number of other videos filmed from different angles on September 11, especially the video filmed by cameraman Evan Fairbanks, who was standing at the foot of the south tower. This video, which became one of the most well-known of the attacks, clearly shows a plane striking the south side of the south tower.

(China Economic Roundtable) Xinhua Headlines: From barbecue to immersive theater, diverse consumption scenarios bring new vitality to China's consumer market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:38:32 CST
00:38:32 KST

* Across China, consumers are increasingly seeking cultural experiences, leisure activities and services alongside goods, creating new opportunities for businesses to meet more diverse demand.
* China's National Bureau of Statistics began releasing the broader indicator of combined retail sales of consumer goods and services in June to provide a more complete picture of the changing consumption market.
* For local businesses, the changing demand is prompting efforts to turn temporary popularity into sustained consumption through improved services and more diverse experiences.
BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- At a barbecue restaurant in Badaju Market in Zibo, east China's Shandong Province, the dining experience now extends beyond sizzling skewers and local delicacies to performances that introduce visitors to the city's history and culture.
"If visitors come just for the food, their visit is too short for them to get to know Zibo better," said Zheng Feng, who runs the restaurant.
The approach is part of a broader transformation at Badaju, a traditional neighborhood market that became an internet sensation in 2023. Since then, it has expanded its offerings to include cultural performances, handicrafts and creative products.
Over the past three years, the market has received more than 18 million visits annually on average, with over 430 merchants offering more than 100 business formats.
Across China, consumers are increasingly seeking cultural experiences, leisure activities and services alongside goods, creating new opportunities for businesses to meet more diverse demand.
In the first eight months of 2026, China's combined retail sales of consumer goods and services rose 2.5 percent year on year, with retail sales of services increasing 4.9 percent, compared with 1 percent growth in retail sales of goods, official data showed.
As incomes rise, service consumption is growing faster than goods consumption, a trend consistent with broader economic development, said Lin Jian, vice president of the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation under the Ministry of Commerce, on China Economic Roundtable, an all-media talk show hosted by Xinhua News Agency.
Lin noted that per capita spending on services accounted for 46.1 percent of China's total per capita consumption expenditure in 2025, up 3.5 percentage points from 2020, and expected the share to surpass 50 percent during the 2026-2030 period.
China's National Bureau of Statistics began releasing the broader indicator of combined retail sales of consumer goods and services in June to provide a more complete picture of the changing consumption market.
For local businesses, the changing demand is prompting efforts to turn temporary popularity into sustained consumption through improved services and more diverse experiences.
Zhang Weihua, deputy head of Shandong's provincial culture and tourism department, said Badaju's continued appeal lies in its combination of consumer trust, local culture and interactive experiences.
The market has introduced clearer pricing, consumer complaint services and infrastructure improvements, while incorporating local cultural traditions into commercial activities and retaining its functions as a neighborhood market.
A similar change is taking shape in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, where small theaters and immersive performances are creating new spaces for cultural consumption.
At the city's Houhu Ximatou theater, an immersive street play titled "Changsha" takes audiences back to the 1990s, telling a story of friendship and entrepreneurship through scenes from the city's past.
Actors interact directly with audiences in recreated neighborhood settings, with some spectators even offering tissues to performers during emotional scenes, said Jin Xingzhou, an actor in the production.
Changsha had established 111 new performing arts venues by the end of June this year, with performances at these venues totaling 14,000 in the first six months and attracting 3.63 million audience visits, according to local cultural authorities.
Zhang Dandan, head of the Changsha New Consumption Research Institute, attributed the emergence of new consumption formats to changing consumer needs, which are driving innovation in products, services and business models.
At the national level, China's consumption expansion plan for the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026-2030) calls for expanding service consumption, upgrading goods consumption, developing new consumption scenarios and improving the consumption environment.
The plan aims to boost China's total retail sales of consumer goods to around 60 trillion yuan (about 8.89 trillion U.S. dollars) by 2030. It also calls for expanding high-quality cultural and tourism offerings, improving the supply of performing arts products, and supporting the development of immersive and interactive venues for consumers.
Efforts similar to Zibo and Changsha are taking shape across China, with 50 cities participating in a national pilot program to develop new consumption formats, models and scenarios.
These cities have a combined resident population of over 480 million and account for more than half of China's total retail sales of consumer goods, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
As of early July, the pilot cities had collected proposals for more than 6,000 projects, with the potential to attract over 300 billion yuan in investment, the ministry said.
Lin said cities should develop distinctive consumption offerings based on their own cultural, ecological and industrial resources, supported by better services, consumption facilities and the business environment.
"Events attract consumers, supply turns interest into spending, and a supportive environment sustains long-term appeal," said Lin.

Feature: Japanese teenage swimmer Ohashi breaks world record at Asian Games
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
23:38:27 CST
00:38:27 KST

By sportswriters Gao Meng, Qian Zheng
TOKYO, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- Shin Ohashi may spend his spare time on his phone, enjoy junk food and, according to his coach, resemble an ordinary Japanese high school student.
In the pool, the 17-year-old is anything but ordinary.
Ohashi broke the men's 200-meter breaststroke world record at the 2026 Asian Games on Thursday, clocking 2 minutes, 4.83 seconds to become the first swimmer to set a world record at the Games.
"I was able to put into the race what I had been training for, so I think it was a perfect race," Ohashi said.
The performance has attracted the attention of some of swimming's biggest names, including France's Leon Marchand.
"I'm scared. I'm very scared of him," Marchand said with a laugh. "He's still so young. His coach is really good. I think his entourage, the people around him, are really good, so I hope he's going to keep improving."
"His breaststroke is amazing, and I'm very excited, also stressed about it, to race him," the Frenchman added.
Ohashi's rise has been rapid. At the Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in August, he clocked 2:08.27 in the 200m breaststroke. Just over a month later, he had lowered that mark by more than three seconds.
His preparation for the Asian Games was far from ideal. Ohashi developed a fever in the days before the competition and subsequently tested positive for COVID-19.
According to his coach Shin Ota, there was no wholesale rebuilding of Ohashi's training program between the Pan Pacific Championships and the Asian Games. Instead, the biggest change came in the teenager's approach to training.
Ohashi had previously been reluctant to undertake some breaststroke training but became more disciplined in his preparation, continuing to complete the assigned work even when his training times were unimpressive.
The plan for Thursday's final had been to control his pace over the first half before maintaining his speed down the stretch. Instead, Ohashi attacked from the start.
"Once I saw that his technique hadn't broken down, I knew his time would be very good," Ota said.
At 1.69 meters tall, Ohashi is relatively small by the standards of elite male swimmers. Ota said his build led the coaching team to identify a high stroke rate as one of the qualities that could become a major strength.
But Ota believes Ohashi's greatest asset lies elsewhere.
"He may look carefree, as if he doesn't think about much, but he really loves swimming, and he really likes to study it," Ota said.
Ohashi regularly analyzes his own swimming, makes adjustments and experiments with different ways of moving through the water. Ota said the teenager often works out technical changes for himself rather than relying on constant instruction from his coach.
Away from the pool, however, the newly crowned world-record holder remains recognizably 17.
Ota said Ohashi enjoys spending time on his phone and eating junk food, adding that "overall, I think he's just an ordinary high school student you could find anywhere."
Ohashi's ambitions are considerably less ordinary.
His immediate goal is gold at next year's World Championships, followed by the 2028 Los Angeles Olympic Games. Asked which swimmer he hopes one day to emulate, Ohashi named Kosuke Kitajima, Japan's four-time Olympic breaststroke champion.
Ota said Kitajima's ability to deliver victories under the weight of expectation was particularly difficult to replicate, and that Ohashi still needs experience and greater mental strength before reaching that level.
For now, Ohashi sees little conflict between the sacrifices required to become an elite swimmer and experiencing life as a teenager.
"Swimming really is my life," he said. "Because of swimming, there may have been times when I couldn't go out and play. But it is also because of swimming that I have been able to get to where I am today. So I don't look at those things so negatively." ■

BEIJING, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's top legislator Zhao Leji has called for efforts to ensure elections of county and township people's congresses are conducted in a law-based and orderly manner and with clean and upright conduct.
Zhao, a member of the Standing Committee of the Political Bureau of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, made the remarks during an investigation and research tour of northeast China's Jilin and Heilongjiang provinces from Monday to Thursday.
Elections of the people's congresses at the county and township levels are a major event in China's political life, Zhao said.
China's people's congress system has a multi-tiered structure, with the NPC at the top and congresses at the provincial, municipal, county and township levels. Deputies are elected at each level every five years to represent the people's interests.
China is currently carrying out a new round of elections of county- and township-level lawmakers. More than one billion voters will directly elect over 2.6 million deputies to the people's congresses at this level.
Stressing the importance of upholding the Party's leadership, Zhao urged solid efforts to ensure that all stages of the elections, including voter registration and voting, are conducted in a law-based and orderly manner and with clean and upright conduct.
During the tour, Zhao also called for efforts to make good use of mechanisms and platforms such as public solicitation of opinions and primary-level legislative outreach offices to build broad consensus on legislation.
Lawmakers should be supported in performing their duties in accordance with the law and maintaining regular contact with the public, he said.
Zhao also called on local people's congresses to properly advance local legislation, ensure that local legislation does not conflict with higher-level laws, has local characteristics and is practical and workable. ■

The research house expects stronger CRESS news flow and deal announcements in the fourth quarter of 2026 and first quarter of 2027, supported by continued expansion of Malaysia's data center sector.
The Malaysian government introduced the CRESS acceleration package, which includes a 30 percent reduction in the System Access Charge (SAC) for firm supply to 0.14 ringgit per kilowatt-hour from 0.20 ringgit, a mandatory ten-year contract between Renewable Energy Developers and Green Consumers, and a requirement for projects benefiting from the special SAC rate to achieve commercial operation by Dec. 31, 2028.
In its recent note, MBSB Research described the package as the most meaningful improvement to the CRESS framework since its introduction, saying the lower charge for firm supply could improve project conversion and expand the pool of commercially viable developments.
The research house said pairing solar generation with battery energy storage systems could smooth intermittency and reduce balancing and reserve requirements on the grid. ■

CAIRO, Sept. 24 (Xinhua) -- An Egyptian archaeological mission discovered a unique pyramid-shaped tomb dating to the Roman period (30 BC-395 AD) in the southwestern province of New Valley, the Egyptian Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities said Thursday.
In a statement, the ministry said the tomb, discovered at the Bir al-Shaghala archaeological site in Dakhla Oasis, was built of mudbrick and used to bury a man and his wife.
The tomb features distinctive architecture and rare funerary inscriptions that shed light on the oasis' burial practices and religious and cultural life during the Roman period, the statement said.
Among the finds were a stone funerary stele bearing a 19-line Greek-language lament, an offering table, a sandstone purification basin, pottery vessels and a bronze coin depicting Roman Emperor Constantine.
The tomb is accessed by a 14-step staircase leading to a sandstone entrance decorated with recessed hieroglyphic inscriptions and funerary spells. Its lintel bears a rare scene depicting the seventh hour of the "Amduat," a major ancient Egyptian funerary text that serves as a twelve-hour map of the underworld recounting the sun god Ra's nightly journey.
The entrance leads to a mudbrick vaulted hall and two burial chambers beneath the pyramid-shaped superstructure.
The funerary stele commemorates a man who may have served as a judge, according to the statement. ■

Video captures ranger's joyful tears on finding rare night parrot chick
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

Rare video of night parrot chick hiding in spinifex tunnel in WA desert
In short:
A young night parrot, one of Australia's most cryptic birds, has been filmed in a spinifex tunnel in remote WA.
The daytime footage captures the elation of a ranger team as they make the rare discovery of the bird in the grassy nest.
What's next?
Rangers for the Ngururrpa Indigenous Protected Area are working with scientists to develop an eDNA program for finding signs of night parrots in waterholes.
Even in the heart of night parrot country it can be rare to actually see one of the world's most cryptic birds.
That is why the discovery of a young night parrot (Pezoporus occidentalis) this year set off an outpouring of emotion in the middle of the Great Sandy Desert in Western Australia.
A new video captures the moment members of the Ngururrpa Rangers and researchers shout-whisper through joyful tears on finding a nestling.
The sighting was even more unique because it happened during daytime, when critically endangered night parrots, as their name suggests, were hidden away.
Night parrots were thought extinct until they were rediscovered in 2013 in Queensland.
While the Ngururrpa Indigenous Protected Area is home to one of the largest populations of the species, this is the first time some rangers have seen a live bird in the area.
Kathryn Njamme, a member of the Ngururrpa Rangers, had previously heard the chime-like call of the bird. She had even seen camera trap footage, an egg and their loose green and yellow feathers.
But she had not laid eyes directly on a living night parrot.
"We was really happy and excited to find a night parrot," Ms Njamme said.
"We all was crying there and holding each other.
"We wanted to show people around the world that there's a night parrot out there in the country."
How the parrot was found
Ms Njamme said during a July trip to the Ngururrpa Indigenous Protected Area she sought help at a spirit tree.
"That's where we asked the Old People to help us find these birds," she said.
"We asked the Old People if they can reveal it for us so we can find them out in the bush when we drew the rain."
A few nights into the trip, there was heavy rain over the desert.
The next morning the rangers went searching among the old-growth mounds of bull spinifex (Triodia longiceps), called "lanu lanu" in Kukatja language, which night parrots are known to use as nests and shelter.
Ms Njamme said that was when ranger Lucinda Gibson found a wet feather in the spinifex.
"She went round to look at that [feather] and she found that burrow [in the grass]," she said.
"That spinifex is a bit grey but she saw little bit of colours on it like yellow and green.
"That's when she noticed that night parrot was in the burrow."
Ms Gibson whistled and gave a hand signal of a flapping bird to Ms Njamme and the rest of the searchers.
Adult night parrots typically sport a coat of green and yellow feathers with black highlights.
But the rangers could see the juvenile bird still had a lot of grey and soft wispy feathers, which helped it blend into the grey interior of the spinifex lump.
Ms Njamme said the parrot may have been perched high in the spinifex because of the damp ground from the rain.
"It was a bit wet on the bottom, that's why he had to move up."
Ngururrpa Indigenous Protected Area coordinator Christy Davies said the parrot was quiet and looked like it was close to the fledgling stage, when a bird learns to fly.
"A lot of young birds and baby birds … unless they're being fed by the parents, they just sit still and don't make a sound," she said.
"So that's what it was doing, just sitting there, not making a sound and relying on its camouflage to protect it."
Turbocharging the search for night parrots
While the moment of finding a juvenile night parrot may seem fortuitous, there is also deep knowledge behind knowing where to look.
By combining what is known about night parrot preferences with cultural knowledge, Ngururrpa Rangers have built a model for finding likely habitat in their region.
The habitat model was developed in a research partnership with the National Environmental Science Program and the Indigenous Desert Alliance.
"A lot of [rangers] have identified areas of likely habitat because they know where that lanu lanu is," Ms Davies said.
"They know where the water sources are and the seasonality of those water sources and where different plants are that form a component of the [parrot] feeding habitats.
"So it's understanding where those different components are that the night parrots need that helps us hone in on particular areas."
Knowing more about where the parrot lives and how many there are will help with conservation efforts to make sure it does not go extinct from threats like feral cats and unmanaged fire.
Rangers are also hoping to use and develop new tools to find the hidden parrots.
An AI tool is being developed to analyse thousands of hours of desert recordings to find likely night parrot calls.
And an environmental DNA (eDNA)analysis technique is in the fine-tuning stage for helping detect if a night parrot has recently used a water source.
Ms Njamme said the eDNA tool could potentially be used by other groups around the country to find and help night parrots.
"We don't see much night parrot, [but] we're trying to look after them."

Mohammad Sio
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Israel’s Central Elections Committee voted Wednesday to bar the United Arab List party, or Ra’am, led by Mansour Abbas, from running in the Oct. 27 Knesset election.
The committee approved Ra’am’s disqualification by 18 votes to five, accepting petitions that alleged “the party rejects Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, incites racism and expresses support for an armed struggle against the country or actions of a terror organization against Israel.”
Earlier Wednesday, the committee also voted 19-5, with two abstentions, to disqualify Knesset member Ofer Cassif from running as part of the Joint List on grounds that he allegedly “denied Israel’s existence as a Jewish and democratic state.”
The panel also voted to disqualify Balad party chairman Sami Abu Shehadeh “on the grounds that he supported an armed struggle or actions of a terror organization against Israel.” Israeli media reported that the decision secured a large majority within the committee.
Under Israeli election law, the disqualification of an individual candidate requires Supreme Court approval before taking effect, while decisions barring electoral lists can be appealed to the court.
The petitions were filed by Israeli parties and organizations, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Otzma Yehudit and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud.
The Supreme Court is expected to review the disqualification decisions ahead of the election.  
There was no immediate comment from Ra’am on the committee’s decision.
Ra’am won five seats in Israel’s 2022 parliamentary election. Polls indicate the possibility of it securing the same number -- or slightly more -- in the upcoming election.
Around 21% of Israel’s population is Palestinian Arab.
The Oct. 27 election is being contested by 38 lists, with parties required to cross the electoral threshold to enter the 120-seat Knesset.
A government must command the support of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-member parliament.
The disqualification decisions come amid heightened political debate over the role of Arab parties and candidates in Israel’s electoral system ahead of the vote.

‘Journalism must be independent’ to remain relevant – Bangladeshi editor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:58:26 UTC
03:58:26 KST

‘Journalism must be independent’ to remain relevant – Bangladeshi editor
Journalism must remain “independent of political power” and offer audiences verification, context and accountability as social media increasingly competes with traditional news, Bangladeshi journalist and editor Khairul Alam has told RT.
Alam, editor of DBARTA24 and former General Secretary of the Dhaka Union of Journalists (DUJ), spoke to RT on Wednesday on the sidelines of the International Forum ‘Dialogue about Fakes 4.0’ in Moscow.
“Rebuilding public trust begins with one simple principle: journalism must be independent of political power,” he said.
According to Alam, media outlets can restore confidence through transparent sourcing, fact-checking, openly correcting mistakes and giving different sides an opportunity to respond. They must also protect reporters from political retaliation and separate journalism from “political activism,” he added.
Alam pointed to Bangladesh’s 2024 political unrest as an example of how social media can both provide information quickly and amplify false or misleading claims.
“The same platforms can spread misinformation, manipulated videos, old footage presented as new, misleading headlines and politically motivated narratives at extraordinary speed,” he said.
The problem becomes more acute when confidence in traditional media declines, Alam argued, pointing to political pressure and legal cases against journalists in Bangladesh.
The 2024 protests began over civil service job quotas before developing into a broader anti-government uprising that led to the ouster of then-Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina. The UN has estimated that as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest. Hasina has since alleged that the US orchestrated her removal after Dhaka refused to allow an American military base on Saint Martin Island.
UN experts raised concerns in 2025 that more than 140 journalists had been charged with murder following the protests. The Committee to Protect Journalists has also documented arrests, criminal cases and other pressure against media workers in the country.
Alam argued that journalists should not face pressure or punishment over their perceived political affiliations, regardless of who is in power.
“Journalism should not become a reward for supporting whoever is currently in power, nor should it become a punishment for having worked under a previous government,” he said.
At the same time, Alam stressed that social media itself is “not the enemy of journalism” and can serve as an important tool for reporters.
Professional media, he said, must instead distinguish itself by providing what social platforms often cannot: “verification, context, responsibility and independence.”

The White House press pool: What is it and how does it work?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:57:50 UTC
03:57:50 KST

The White House press pool: What is it and how does it work?
White House banned CNN, MS NOW, and Politico, after US President Donald Trump complained about coverage.
US President Donald Trump last week announced he would ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House amid coverage that Trump said was unfavourable.
Reporters for the three outlets reported to work over the weekend only to find that their access had been revoked. By Monday, the three organisations had sued the administration, amid allegations the White House violated their First Amendment rights.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4A ‘ban on the free press’: White House bars journalists from three outlets
- list 2 of 4CNN, Politico, MS NOW sue Trump administration over White House ban
- list 3 of 4Rubio defends Trump’s White House ban on CNN, MS NOW and Politico
- list 4 of 4Trump follows in Hugo Chavez’s footsteps to launch his own TV channel
Free speech advocates criticised the White House for yanking their credentials.
“It’s difficult to imagine a more blatant violation of the First Amendment than Trump banning news outlets from the People’s House for criticizing the government. It’s also hard to imagine a dumber move,” Seth Stern, director of advocacy at the Freedom of the Press Foundation, said in a statement.
“The historically unpopular president has been retaliating against the press for years, but it hasn’t helped him. The press keeps exposing his corruption and his failures. These outrageous attacks only demonstrate how scared he is of an informed public.”
The White House has nevertheless defended the decision, with US Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio also supporting the administration’s position.
On Monday, Bryan Boughton, Fox News’s Washington bureau chief and the chair of the rotating TV pool, announced in a memo that the television networks that participate in the pool would suspend presidential pool coverage following CNN’s removal from its scheduled pool duties, according to reporting from Politico.
What is the pool?
The White House press pool is a group of reporters who follow the president in smaller settings when space restrictions prevent the broader press corps from being on location.
Pool reporters share their reporting with other journalists and news organisations. It provides them with raw newsgathering material, including transcripts of news briefings and information about the president’s, and often his staff’s, whereabouts.
Essentially, wherever the president goes, a small group of reporters is there to document what happens and relay that information to the rest of the White House press corps to use as they see fit for their reporting.
Pool coverage is not intended to be editorialised. It serves as a shared newsgathering resource, allowing other news organisations to report on events they could not directly attend.
Often, the details are fairly mundane, such as what time the president’s motorcade leaves the White House or when he arrives at an event, what time Air Force One lands and takes off, and the remarks the president made before boarding.
For television networks, the pool also provides video and audio feeds that other news organisations can use at their discretion.
The system exists in part because of physical limitations, as Air Force One has limited space for members of the press. There are only 13 seats for reporters on the president’s plane.
Each day, different news organisations are assigned pool duties. The television pool rotates among five networks. Those are ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC. Other parts of the pool include print, radio and new media organisations.
How will this impact other outlets?
Subscribers to pooled coverage include smaller television station groups, streaming networks and international news organisations that may not have their own crews with the president.
That also includes organisations such as C-SPAN and other outlets that rely on pooled video and audio to cover presidential events.
The effect was immediately visible Monday during an event at the White House. The president’s remarks were difficult to hear because there was no TV pool crew providing the usual audio feed.
The memo obtained by Politico said the TV pool would continue providing coverage for other parts of government, including Congress.
How has the pool historically been used?
The pool has been at the helm of coverage of some of the biggest events in recent US history.
On September 11, 2001, pool reporters were with President George W Bush during his visit to an elementary school in Sarasota, Florida, when he was informed about the attacks in New York, and they documented his reaction.
Decades earlier, in 1981, pool reporters were present for the assassination attempt on President Ronald Reagan by John Hinckley Jr.
A little less than a decade earlier, the pool also accompanied President Richard Nixon on his historic 1972 visit to China, and in 1963 pool reporters were travelling with President John F Kennedy’s motorcade in Dallas, Texas when he was assassinated.
In 1945, three wire-service reporters who were part of the pool travelled with President Franklin D Roosevelt by train to Georgia and were with him when he passed away there.

“We’re working with our friends to try and deliver that de-escalation,” British Defense Minister Luke Pollard said in an interview Tuesday. The “purely defensive” deployment of an RAF Voyager to Saudi Arabia is intended to “ensure there’s no further escalation in the Red Sea, which could further risk our fuel prices,” he added.
The international assistance comes following weeks of fighting between the Saudi-backed government of Yemen and the Houthis, which shattered a four-year informal cease-fire in the country's civil war. The Houthi rebels have made significant advances along the Red Sea coastline as they seek to tighten their grip on the Bab el-Mandeb, a critical maritime chokepoint that links Asia and Europe via the Red Sea and Suez Canal. With global energy supplies already under strain due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz amid the Iran war, the strangling of another trade route could further impact oil and fuel prices.
“Much of our trade, both in goods and in energy, comes through that part of the world. What happens in that part of the Middle East is absolutely vital for our own national security and our own economic security,” Pollard said, explaining why Britain responded to the Kingdom’s request for help.
When talking to reporters en route to the United Nations General Assembly in New York, ahead of his sit-down with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham also cited the cost of living “pressures” at home as a key reason for the support and said he was “acting to secure the interests of Britain and the wider region.”
Burnham emphasized that it’s a “time-limited agreement in terms of the assistance that we will provide, but we will keep it under review.”
The support extended to Saudi Arabia marks Burnham’s first military deployment since he became Prime Minister in July. However, it’s far from the first time the U.K. has offered assistance to Saudi Arabia, as the two nations share a close military alliance.
How exactly will the U.K. be supporting Saudi Arabia?
The Ministry of Defense on Tuesday confirmed it had agreed to “provide an RAF Voyager air-to-air refuelling aircraft to support Saudi defensive activity” in the region. According to the British Royal Air Force (RAF), a Voyager provides strategic air support by allowing jets and other aircraft to refuel while in flight.
Andreas Krieg, a senior lecturer in defense studies at King's College London, says the Voyager “basically allows the Saudi Air Force to stay in the air over Yemen for longer without having to fly a single sortie and then returning to base.”
“It increases the operational tempo in terms of targeting strikes and being more flexible, and more agile in responding to changing situations on the ground,” he tells TIME.
According to Pollard, the Voyager is set to operate from the British RAF base in Cyprus, which was targeted by Iran earlier this year, and will support the British-built Typhoon jets used by Saudi Arabia. “That will help them with their defensive actions against the Houthis, who have been attacking not just the capital of Saudi Arabia in Riyadh, but also the Republic of Yemen as well,” he said.
Britain has historically held the role of “guarantor for maritime freedom of navigation all around the world,” says Krieg, describing the U.K.’s latest attempt to ease tensions over the Red Sea as an example of the government “stepping up to the plate.”
“We're not just helping a partner in the region,” he adds. “We're also helping ourselves, because the Houthis having the Bab al-Mandeb is not something that the U.K. can tolerate.”
Krieg says the move signifies a small success for Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states as they seek to strengthen bilateral security relationships beyond their traditional reliance on the U.S. This is “the worst security situation the Saudis have been in [for] a very long time,” he notes.
“Gulf states are trying to supplement the existing U.S. capabilities with all kinds of [other] agreements, like the Mecca pact,” he says, referencing a trilateral defense security pact made between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia, and Turkey in August. “The U.K. wants to be seen as being active and being there when a friend is in need.”
The long-standing alliance between the U.K. and Saudi Arabia
The U.K. and Saudi Arabia share an alliance that dates back to almost a century ago.
“It's a very long, strategic partnership,” says Krieg. “It goes back to the early days of the current Kingdom, where Britain, at the time, was still the only superpower in the world, and was controlling the waterways and a lot of the territories in Arabia, including in South Yemen.”
Britain was among the first governments to recognize the independent territories of Saudi Arabia through the Treaty of Jeddah in 1927, which helped solidify the boundaries of the nascent kingdom ahead of the formation of modern Saudi Arabia in 1932.
Decades later, the U.K. supported the Saudi-led military coalition in its campaign against the Houthis from 2015 until the 2022 truce.
According to the Campaign Against Arms Trade (CAAT), the published value of U.K. arms export licenses to Saudi Arabia from the start of the bombing campaign in March 2015 through the April 2022 truce was £7.1 billion ($9.4 billion).
“The two main Western backers of the Saudi Kingdom are the Americans and the British,” says David Wearing, an assistant professor in international relations at the University of Sussex. “From the British and the American point of view, the Middle East is strategically important because it's a huge source of global energy suppliers, oil, and gas.”
In late 2023, the Houthis started disrupted shipping in the Red Sea, targeting cargo ships they said were linked to Israel, in what they described as a show of support for Palestinians in Gaza. Amid concerns over the impact on the world economy, the U.S. and U.K. joined forces in January 2024, striking multiple Houthi targets in Yemen. In April 2025, the U.K. government participated in another joint operation with the U.S. against a Houthi military facility in Yemen.
In March of this year, the U.K. deployed a Sky Sabre, the army’s medium range air defense missile system, to Saudi Arabia to defend the Kingdom against Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The U.K. government's Strategic Export Controls Annual Report of 2025 described the military relationship with Saudi Arabia as a “longstanding” partnership providing “Typhoon, Tornado, and Hawk aircraft, mine countermeasure vessels, and associated munitions, infrastructure, logistics and manpower support packages.”
BAE Systems—a major British defense, aerospace, and security company—said in its own 2025 report that Saudi Arabia was its largest customer by sales in its air business.
How are Saudi Arabia’s other allies responding to the Houthis' advances?
Saudi Arabia has reportedly sought assistance from allies to stave off Houthi advances. France, Pakistan, and Egypt issued strong statements condemning the Houthi attacks, but have not publicly announced new military support for the Kingdom.
Trump is understood to have received requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman to strike the Houthi rebels. According to the New York Times, Trump reportedly considered launching strikes against the Houthis over the weekend, before ultimately deciding against it. TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Asked Tuesday why Washington has held back from striking the Houthis, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it’s “a very dangerous and complex” conflict.
“If it comes down to it, the United States will always stand with Saudi Arabia and support them because we have an agreement with them to do so,” he said, referencing the U.S. economic and defense partnership with Saudi Arabia signed last November, that deepened co-operation between the two countries.
Fears mount over global energy supply as Houthis advance
Global energy supplies have been under increasing strain since the start of the Iran war on Feb. 28, as Tehran has leveraged its chokehold over the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of global oil production flowed prior to the conflict.
In the past few weeks, the Houthis have captured Yemen’s port city of Mokha and the strategic Perim Island, which sits in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. If the Houthis were to assume control of the strait, shipping companies could be forced to travel via South Africa’s Cape of Good Hope—a longer, costlier route.
The volume of crude oil and petroleum liquids moving through the Bab el-Mandeb increased earlier this year, with the route being used as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz. The shipments surged from 5.6 million barrels per day in the first quarter of 2026 to 8.1 million per day in the second quarter, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA).
However, recent crossings have been marred by uncertainty over the potential threat posed by the Houthis. Data shared with TIME by Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, showed an estimated 34 vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb on Sept. 15, a drop from the estimated 53 crossings recorded on July 15th.
A spokesperson for the Houthis on Sept. 11 insisted the waterway will remain free to roam “with the exception of Saudi ships.” Yet concerns among global leaders and shipping companies remain.
Burnham and other U.K. officials have framed Britain’s defensive support partly around the potential economic consequences at home. The average price of petrol rose by 9.1 pence per litre between July and August 2026, compared with a rise of 0.3 pence per litre between July and August 2025, according to data from the Office of National Statistics.
Wearing says that because oil is traded on a global market, supply disruptions in one region can push up benchmark prices worldwide, with those costs cascading through the broader economy.
“What Americans call gas and what we call petrol, if that goes up, think how many goods to market are taken by heavy lorries on petrol. It can push up the price of everything: shipping, road transit, energy, all kinds of industrial production and many consumer products,” he says. “Oil is the lifeblood of the world economy, the longer you restrict the supply, the higher the price goes, the more inflationary pressure there is on everything, and that affects Britain, but it affects the whole system. It's like a heart attack in a human body, suddenly it's not being pumped round."

More Australians than ever lodging workplace sexual harassment complaints
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:53:05 UTC
03:53:05 KST

Human rights commission dealing with record sexual harassment complaints
In short:
Figures reveal a record number of Australians are making workplace sexual harassment complaints, but many are waiting months for cases to be investigated.
The rise is likely due to recent legal reforms and greater awareness of workplace rights, rather than an increase in workplace sexual harassment.
What's next?
There is concern the system cannot keep up with the rise in demand, and more money and expertise are needed to handle cases effectively.
More Australians than ever are lodging workplace sexual harassment complaints.
But behind that rise sits an increasingly urgent challenge: adapting the system so it can respond quickly enough to make a difference.
In 2024, at the age of 19, Heather* thought she had secured her dream career after landing an electrical apprenticeship with a small business in New South Wales.
"I was really thinking about the future and trying to set myself up to buy a house," Heather said.
"I felt it was a stable job that would see me through my life."
But those plans were derailed after Heather said she was sexually harassed by her boss, who she alleged made unwelcome advances, while working away.
Traumatised, she quit the apprenticeship the next day.
Supported by the Electrical Trades Union (ETU), Heather lodged a formal complaint with the Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC).
It took 14 months for her complaint to be formally accepted for investigation and she was only recently assigned a case manager.
"I feel really trapped in the situation,"
"You feel helpless, like it's never going to happen."
Unable to return to an electrical trade, Heather lost nine months of work before eventually finding a new apprenticeship operating heavy machinery.
Her mother, Melissa Unwin, said the lengthy wait has made it difficult for her daughter to move forward, describing the uncertainty as corrosive and damaging to morale.
"You can't see the end in sight," she said.
"I was 100 per cent blindsided. I trusted this guy with my daughter."
Heather's claims are yet to be tested by the commission and are contested by the owner of the business.
System under pressure
The AHRC remains the preferred avenue for many serious workplace sexual harassment complaints, despite lengthy delays there and alternative pathways through state anti-discrimination bodies and the Fair Work Commission.
Employment lawyer Lisa Berton said complainants tolerated longer wait times because the federal system provided access to broader claims, stronger enforcement powers and potentially uncapped compensation.
"If I was acting for an applicant, I would still select the AHRC, even with the delays," she said.
New figures obtained by the ABC show the AHRC received a record 759 complaints under the Sex Discrimination Act last financial year — up 21 per cent on the previous year and 51 per cent over five years.
Of the 460 sexual harassment complaints received in that period, 95 per cent were related to employment.
Complainants waited an average of nearly seven months just to be allocated a case officer.
While the commission had a target to finalise 85 per cent of complaints within 12 months, the latest figures show 49 per cent of workplace sexual harassment matters took longer than a year to resolve.
Data obtained by the ABC also revealed significant differences between jurisdictions.
In Victoria, workplace sexual harassment complaints were typically processed within one to two weeks and resolved in about two months.
By contrast, Queensland reported an average wait of 246 days for allocation and 424 days to finalisation, while in South Australia, complaints were generally allocated within a week.
NSW reported comparatively short delays, with just 84 complaints awaiting allocation and 98 per cent resolved within a year.
The Fair Work Commission received 183 workplace sexual harassment applications in 2024-25.
Monash University discrimination law professor Dominique Allen said the rise in complaints could reflect greater awareness of workplace rights and confidence in reporting, rather than an increase in workplace sexual harassment.
However, Professor Allen said the figures suggested complaint demand was growing faster than the system's capacity to process cases.
"We need more money and expertise put into this so that these claims can be handled more effectively," she said.
The federal government said it had invested $49.8 million in the AHRC since 2022 and would examine the system as part of the upcoming Respect@Work review.
The ETU argued the delays pointed to a deeper problem than growing demand.
The union's NSW/ACT state secretary Allen Hicks said stronger workplace protections only worked if the agencies responsible for enforcing them had enough resources.
"You can have the best laws in the world and if you don't resource the regulatory bodies … then the laws are meaningless," he said.
Unions warn workers walking away
Mr Hicks said the union currently had six members who have been waiting over a year for their AHRC cases to be picked up.
"Young 16 and 17-year-old apprentices who have the courage to stand up and make a formal complaint are put in limbo," Mr Hicks said.
"In construction, witnesses move across six or seven different job sites over 18 months, making it extremely difficult to keep cases together."
Mr Hicks said complaint discontinuance rates at the commission have jumped from 40 per cent to 58 per cent, and a national audit report released in 2025 pointed to delays directly driving workers to give up on their claims.
He said delays threatened broader workforce targets as Australia seeks to add 40,000 more electricians by 2030.
"Stories like this set back female participation by years," he said.
*Heather has been identified by her first name only because of the sensitive nature of the allegations and the ongoing complaints process.

The normalisation process was relaunched following the 2020 Karabakh war and formally resumed in 2022, with a series of confidence-building measures including the launch of direct Turkish Airlines flights between Istanbul and Yerevan, a visa facilitation agreement for diplomatic passport holders, and the completion of bureaucratic preparations for direct trade.
Construction at the Alican-Margara border crossing linking Türkiye's Igdir province with Armenia's Armavir region is now around 90 percent complete, while the two sides have also agreed to restore the Ani Bridge along their shared border, a step diplomats describe as both symbolic and concrete.

The project, if completed, has been seen by supporters and detractors alike as a death blow to future Palestinian statehood.
19 Democrats co-sponsored the bill, which was spearheaded by Chris Coons of Delaware, Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Ron Wyden of Oregon and Ruben Gallego of Arizona.
“As Palestinian civilians face a campaign of devastation and fear from violent extremist settlers, the United States must send a strong message that this behaviour is unacceptable and that it remains committed to freedom, security, prosperity and self-determination for all Israelis and Palestinians,” Coons said in a statement.
The bill will impose sanctions “on any foreign person that the Secretary of the Treasury determines to have been responsible for or complicit in the construction of any Israeli settlements or related structures in the E1 area of the West Bank, including by submitting a bid for E1 tenders”, according to a statement from the lawmakers.
“It would also impose sanctions on those who attempt to organise, direct, finance, or facilitate the transfer of Israeli civilians into E1 settlements,” the statement said.
The move is yet another indication of growing discontent among some US lawmakers over Israel’s policies towards the occupied Palestinian territory, including its genocidal war in Gaza and the state-backed expansion of illegal settlements across the West Bank, where settler pogroms, often under the protection of Israeli forces, has surged in recent years.
The criticism has been particularly acute among Democrats, who are seeking to take control of both the US House of Representatives and the Senate in the midterm elections in November. A handful of Republicans have also increasingly questioned the close ties between the US and Israel and the unconditional military aid provided by Washington.
Beyond Wednesday’s bill, a growing number of Democrats have voted to block arms transfers to Israel in recent months. More than 20 Democrats in the 100-member Senate also recently introduced a resolution calling for an investigation into surging West Bank violence, in which at least nine US citizens have been killed.
‘Unacceptable and destructive act’
Criticism of the E1 settlement project, short for “East 1”, the Israeli administrative name for the area, escalated last month when the Israeli government invited bids for building 1,200 new units.
The move has come shortly before Israel is set to hold elections in October and is considered by some analysts to be an effort to mobilise the right-wing base of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyu by provoking an international response. The project has been spearheaded by far-right minister Bezalel Smotrich, himself from an illegal settlement.
Among those condemning the plan was UK Foreign Minister Ed Miliband, who has called the project an “unacceptable and destructive act”. Countries across the Middle East, North America and Europe have also voiced strong objections.
The United Nations Human Rights Office has described the E1 project as a “grave and unlawful step to consolidate annexation”.
The administration of US President Donald Trump, for its part, has not directly addressed the plan, instead reiterating opposition to Israeli annexation of the West Bank.

Bentley's first fully electric car embraces heritage in a "progressive way"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:47:22 UTC
03:47:22 KST

Bentley's first fully electric car embraces heritage in a "progressive way"
Car brand Bentley has revealed the Torcal, its first fully electric car. Ahead of its unveiling, we spoke to design director Robin Page about how the car balances an electric future with the brand's heritage.
Unveiled today at a launch event in London, the Torcal is a fully electric SUV – the first fully electric vehicle by the luxury car company.
Unlike other luxury car brands – most notably Ferrari and Jaguar – Bentley has not radically overhauled the shape for its first electric vehicle.
According to Page, this was to create an electric car that was clearly modern, but also recognisable as a Bentley.
Page told Dezeen his team began talking about direction four years ago.
"That was when we asked, 'Are we doing a car dedicated to an electric language, or should we do another great Bentley with a more modern language – not directly focused on electrification?'"
"We decided that our best route would be to embrace our heritage and DNA, but in a modern, progressive way."
The Torcal has a long wheelbase with a form that evokes previous Bentleys. Page explained that this form stemmed from Bentley's design principles rather than aerodynamic concerns related to electrification.
"With electrification, what mainly drives the form's language is the aerodynamics and the package proportion – aerodynamics directly relates to range," he said.
"The laws of aerodynamics start to give you quite a moulded form and a certain tail, but we decided that aerodynamics shouldn't lead the design. What's dominated the shape is our design principles, and they are based on our DNA and heritage."
The Torcal takes stylistic cues from previous Bentleys, including a continuous bonnet line, expressed rear arches and a prominent grill.
"Outright elegance, the iconic grill, the endless bonnet line, the resting beast – they're our principles, and we've let them dominate the design rather than aerodynamics," said Page.
Although aerodynamics didn't drive the design, Page highlighted the vehicle's range of 600 kilometres.
The grill, inessential in an electric car, is still clearly expressed.
As with the overall design of the car, Bentley nodded to the past. It referenced the grill of the Continental T, but with a modern twist – it can be illuminated in a diamond pattern.
Page said the team decided it needed a grill and that closing it off would feel "like a hand over a mouth", opting for what it considers an art piece.
"[We] decided to celebrate it, to do a piece of art with light," said Paige.
At the launch, the Torcal was presented in a light, yellowy green, another modern update to the brand's heritage.
"The Bentley green is a much darker, solid green," said Page. "We wanted a colour that showed the form, something a bit lighter, this colour works pretty well."
Inside, the car has a wing-shaped dash and natural materials including timber and Merino wool. It has a modestly sized screen – for a high-end car – and numerous physical dials.
"We didn't want to go down the clinical, super modern material route, because you end up with this quite stark, cold feeling inside," said Page.
"It really captures a place you want to be, rather than something you look at and think, 'that's modern'. It needs to be something that feels fresh, but feels comfortable."
Bentley said its choice to make its first electric car an SUV will open up a new market and offer something that other luxury car brands are not doing.
"The reason we're all doing SUVs is that it's a growing market," he said. "We've had a lot of comments from customers who say they could use this Bentley every day."
When it goes on sale later this year, the Torcal will be the first Bentley to feature the brand's redesigned logo, which was revealed last year.

Unknown

2026-09-23
18:41:23 UTC
03:41:23 KST

Federal prosecutors in New York have opened an investigation into the two co-executors of the estate of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.
No charges have been filed against the co-executors, Epstein's longtime lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn.
The Journal said that in recent months, prosecutors in the U.S. attorney's office for the Southern District of New York have scheduled interviews with potential witnesses and requested documents about those witnesses' dealings with Indyke and Kahn.
The Journal also cited a report it published last year saying the two men "were officers of Epstein entities that obscured transactions, arranged cash for Epstein, made payments to women and facilitated Epstein's immigration schemes."
Indyke and Kahn have denied wrongdoing.
The Journal, citing documents, reported that Indyke could receive $50 million and Kahn could get $25 million from Epstein's estate because they are beneficiaries of a trust that will collect Epstein's remaining assets after claims against the estate are settled.
CNBC has requested comment from a spokesman for the U.S. attorney's office and from Indyke and Kahn about the Journal's report.
Epstein, 66, killed himself in a federal jail in Manhattan in August 2019, weeks after he was arrested on child sex trafficking charges.
Epstein's estate in February agreed to pay out as much as $35 million to settle a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Manhattan that had accused Indyke and Kahn of aiding and abetting Epstein's sex trafficking of young women and teenage girls.
The proposed settlement does not include any admission of misconduct by either Indyke or Kahn. The judge handling the case on Sept. 18 endorsed a proposal by the suit's plaintiff to notify potential class members to submit claims on the settlement by conducting a four-week-long social media campaign on Facebook and Instagram.
The estate earlier established a restitution fund for Epstein victims that paid out $121 million to more than 130 women and has paid or committed to pay $48 million to nearly 60 additional women in separate settlements.
Lauren Hersh, CEO of World Without Exploitation, an advocacy group for Epstein survivors, in a statement Wednesday said, "We welcome the news that federal prosecutors are investigating Darren Indyke and Richard Kahn and asking questions that should have been asked years ago."
"Survivors deserve a full accounting of how Epstein and those in his orbit were able to operate for so long, and accountability for everyone who enabled or participated in their exploitation," Hersh said.
New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez, whose office is conducting its own investigation into Epstein, said in a statement that he was aware of the Journal's report. Epstein maintained a residence in New Mexico.
"While we cannot comment on any potential federal investigation, this reporting only underscores the importance of full transparency and cooperation among all agencies charged with pursuing accountability," Torrez said.
"Our office has repeatedly sought access to the complete, unredacted records that may be relevant to New Mexico's ongoing work. We hope that federal authorities will now be willing to share any pertinent information without further delay," the attorney general said. "Survivors and the public deserve answers, and no institution should withhold information that could help advance justice."
Kahn and Indyke earlier this year testified behind closed doors to the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, which has been investigating Epstein and his connections to various individuals.
"Both Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn reject as categorically false the suggestion that they knowingly facilitated or assisted Mr. Epstein in his sexual abuse or trafficking of women, or that they were aware of that abuse while they provided professional services for him," Daniel Weiner, an attorney for Epstein's estate, told MS NOW in a statement in March.
Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the ranking Democrat on the House oversight panel, said in a statement after Kahn testified in March, "Jeffrey Epstein's massive sex trafficking ring would not have been possible without the consistent payments and services of his long-time accountant Richard Kahn."
"It's not credible that he had no knowledge of Epstein's activities, and his testimony today only raises more questions," Garcia said.

Iran’s Pezeshkian slams ‘terrorist’ US but extols diplomacy in UN speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:36:39 UTC
03:36:39 KST

Iran’s Pezeshkian slams ‘terrorist’ US but extols diplomacy in UN speech
Pezeshkian leaves door open for negotiations, while calling out international community’s double standards.
Iran: Strait of Hormuz won’t be used to ‘impose insecurity on us’
In a defiant speech at the United Nations General Assembly, Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian has delivered a sharp rebuke to a threat by US President Donald Trump from the same rostrum the previous day to annihilate the country, but left the door open for diplomacy to end nearly seven months of war.
“The US president called us terrorists but we are the victims of terrorists,” Pezeshkian said on Wednesday.
During his speech, Pezeshkian held up a picture of former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei – assassinated in a joint US-Israeli strike at the start of the war in February – as well as photos of schoolgirls killed in an alleged US air attack on their school in the southern city of Minab.
“They hit us, but we did not bow our heads or bend the knee,” Pezeshkian added.
As the Iranian president began his speech, an official from the US delegation walked out of the vast hall. The Israeli delegation also boycotted the address.
“[Trump] must know that the resistance of the Iranian people will only grow in the face of sanctions and increased pressure and bullying,” Pezeshkian said.
But Pezeshkian, a relative centrist in the Iranian ruling system, also left the door open for negotiations, saying, “Iran extends its hands towards the world.”
“We invite the world and call to it, not out of weakness, but out of a deep belief in our own power and steadfastness to cooperate and collaborate out of a deep understanding that no one in this region will have security alone,” he said.
‘Very good meeting’
On Tuesday, Trump said his son-in-law Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who are both leading negotiations with Tehran, had held a three-hour meeting with Iranian officials.
“They had a very good meeting, a very productive meeting,” Trump told reporters at the UN, adding that he believed there was “a lot of momentum” towards an agreement. Trump later said talks were continuing and that he believed a settlement would eventually be reached.
The remarks came after Trump used his speech before UN delegates to again threaten Iran’s destruction.
“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before?” Trump said. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”
Strait of Hormuz
Addressing the US naval blockade of Iran and Tehran’s campaign to choke off trade in the Strait of Hormuz, Pezeshkian said Iran would resist what he called US efforts to use the critical sea lane to expand its war on the country.
“In the Strait of Hormuz, we cannot have some free access and gain their independence from that waterway while at the same time use that waterway to impose their aggressions upon us and to impose insecurity upon us; to forbid us access to our own waterways,” he said.
Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow at the US-based Center for International Policy, said the Iranian president’s speech showed usual flashes of defiance, but notably signalled an appetite for a diplomatic off-ramp.
“Iran wants a way out of this war. They’ve kept the door to diplomacy open,” she told Al Jazeera.
“Reading between the lines of the Iranian president’s speech, it seems Iran may even show some flexibility as far as a return to some sort of agreement that may not be exactly along the lines of the June Memorandum of Understanding that US President Trump doesn’t seem interested in returning to,” she said. The memorandum, which has expired, called for a halt to fighting, lifting the US naval blockade and opening the Strait of Hormuz to maritime traffic.
Compromise still a possibility
Drawing parallels between the US and Israel bombing of Iran and Israel’s attacks in Gaza, Pezeskhian said Israel’s genocide in Gaza “revealed the double standards to which Iran is held by the international community”.
“They kill and we are sanctioned and we are punished,” Pezeshkian added.
Joey Hood, a former US diplomat and ambassador to Tunisia, said the speech leaned heavily into familiar Iranian official rhetoric and represented a lost opportunity to seek compromise.
“Instead of coming to the United Nations with something new and bold, we heard the same things that we’ve heard before,” Hood said, adding that a concrete peace offer or proposal posed to the US in the speech might have focused Washington’s attention.
“That would actually put Donald Trump on the backfoot, and he would have to respond. The Iranian president didn’t do any of that,” Hood said.

The Italian Embassy in Muscat celebrated “Italian Sports Day Around the World 2026” today at the Spike Volleyball Club, in the presence of representatives from the Italian community, a large Omani audience, and sports enthusiasts from various countries and cultural backgrounds. 
   Organized annually by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Italian diplomatic and consular network, the Day celebrates sport as a means of bringing people together, fostering intercultural dialogue and social inclusion, and promoting values such as integrity, solidarity, and sharing.
                                    
                                       
				   This year’s third edition is dedicated to boating, sailing, and the sea, in anticipation of the 2027 America’s Cup in Naples, which will be hosted in Italy for the first time. The initiative also highlights the economic dimension of sports and its contribution to the international promotion of Italian excellence.
                                    
                                       
				   In his opening remarks, Italy’s ambassador to Oman, Pierluigi D’Elia, noted that sports represent not only an important component of Italian culture but also a significant economic asset, according to a statement from the embassy. In fact, the Italian sports sector generates approximately 32 billion euros, equal to 1.5% of the national GDP, and involves about 420,000 people, including direct employees and those in related industries. Major Italian brands are present in the main sports centers of Muscat. 
   In Oman, the celebration also highlighted the local public’s growing enthusiasm for Italian sports and the strengthening of sports partnerships between the two countries. Italian soccer enjoys great popularity in the Sultanate, where the activities of academies affiliated with Italian clubs are becoming increasingly numerous. The collaboration also extends to other sports, such as sailing, and the Italian Clay Pigeon Shooting Federation (FITAV) regularly cooperates with the Oman Shooting Federation, including through the annual Friendship Competition in Muscat.
                                    
                                       
				   The celebration at the Spike Volleyball Club served as an opportunity for the Italian and Omani communities to come together, reaffirming the role of sports diplomacy in strengthening relations between Italy and Oman and in developing new opportunities for collaboration.

US open to Cuba talks on government change, Marco Rubio says
Marco Rubio made comments after Trump called Cuba a ‘failed state’ at the UN, prompting Cuban delegation to walk out.
The United States says it is open to speaking with Havana about how it can make a political transition towards new leadership and end a decades-old trade embargo imposed since former leader Fidel Castro‘s communist revolution in 1959 and the US’s recent blockade of the country.
“Cuba has a golden opportunity to place itself on an irreversible path towards a better future,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Wednesday in New York City. “We are prepared to be helpful in that regard if they are open to it.”
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US continues to squeeze Cuban economy with new round of sanctions
- list 2 of 3Cuba says no negotiations with US despite ‘genocidal’ blockade
- list 3 of 3Cuba works to restore power after another major nationwide blackout
Washington has previously said that it wants a change in Cuba’s government. Since earlier this year, the US has additionally imposed an oil blockade that has put the country under severe pressure, dealing with fuel shortages and ongoing blackouts. Cuban officials have also blamed it on problems providing food and other basic needs for its population.
Rubio said Washington was willing to work with some Cuban leaders – those whose “hands are not stained with blood”, he said – but also acknowledged that some were “at least publicly quite recalcitrant”.
Rubio, the child of Cubans who fled the country before the revolution, said businesses and investors from the US, including the Cuban diaspora, were ready to step in and help the country transition its economy if progress was made on political reforms.
Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump called Cuba a “failed state,” and said his administration was willing to use military power against it when necessary, outlining a string of moves it has made in the region to protect Washington’s interests, including the abduction of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro.
“My administration is also seeking a fundamental change in the situation in Cuba,” Trump said. “Where the communist regime is under great pressure, the biggest pressure they’ve ever been under.”
Trump’s remarks prompted the Cuban delegation to walk out of the assembly.
Cuban officials have denied any talks are going on with the US, which has sought to remove the post-revolutionary government in Havana ever since it came to power in 1959.
Earlier this month, Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez called the US embargo against his country a policy of “economic asphyxiation,” and described the blockade as “genocidal”.
The Cuban government says the US embargo cost its economy $8bn between March 2025 and February 2026, the highest figure yet recorded and 7 percent more than in the previous reporting period.
The total does not include some of Washington’s more recent sanctions, including restrictions on the island’s energy supply imposed in January and secondary sanctions imposed in May, said Rodriguez.
Several world leaders at the UNGA criticised the US blockade in their speeches this year, including Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva.
“In Cuba, the world watches in dismay as 10 million people face collective punishment from an illegal economic embargo and energy siege,” he said on Tuesday.
Every year since 1992, the UNGA has adopted by a large majority a non-binding resolution calling for the lifting of the embargo imposed on Cuba by the US.
In July, a vote on whether to hold a debate on the resolution signalled a slight erosion in support for Cuba in the General Assembly, with 136 member states in favour, nine against, and 30 abstentions – including traditional supporters Germany and Canada.

Tesfaye Kasau, father of Haymanot, addressed Lahav 433, the Shin Bet, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
"About ten days ago, we sat at Lahav 433 and asked question after question, and not a single one received an answer. Those who are supposed to provide answers, those responsible for investigating, didn't answer and simply didn't seem to know.
"Do they have suspects? Do they have a direction for the investigation? Is the investigation focused inside Israel or abroad? Were all checks performed, such as phone geolocations and polygraphs for everyone at the absorption center on that terrible night?
"Nothing. Absolutely nothing. How can this be? How is it that the investigation into the abduction of a girl who has already turned 11 is being conducted like this? How can it be that those who are supposed to protect us act as if there is time? As if Haymanot doesn't need us to save her, as if Haymanot isn't important."
He lambasted the government for failing to handle the investigation, asking once again for it to be handed over to the Shin Bet, before asking the people of Israel to "stay with us and continue to support us so that we succeed in our struggle for a proper, equal investigation."
An earlier statement released on behalf of the campaign said, "The investigation is being handled as an afterthought, having already passed through four different hands without a single lead - which is why the demonstration aims to press the ongoing demand to transfer the case to the Shin Bet."
Haymanot’s parents, Tesfaya and Benchi Kasau, have led a public campaign calling for increased efforts to locate her, including protests outside Lahav 433 offices and a march in Tel Aviv.
Shelly Shem Tov, mother of freed Hamas hostage, grateful and ashamed
Shelly Shem Tov, mother of released hostage Omer Shem Tov, came to speak at the demonstration for Haymanot.
She related to the family by recalling the fears and emotions from when her son was in captivity.
"When the hostages were in captivity, we felt the embrace of the Israeli public; we felt that we were not alone. Now I stand here and look at you, a small group of people, and every single one of you is so meaningful to Haymanot's family. Because feeling alone, feeling abandoned, is simply terrible. I want to thank each and every one of you for not leaving Haymanot's family alone."
She continued, saying, "On the other hand, I feel ashamed because I feel that I too had somewhat forgotten Haymanot and her family. And the same goes for the people of Israel. I am certain it is not out of bad intentions, but because there isn't the sheer force of numbers needed to shake up those who need to be shaken up. I want to say that being a mother whose child is not with her is something I wouldn't wish on anyone.
"Haymanot is not where she ought to be - at home with her family and friends. Haymanot disappeared out of the blue. And because this family doesn't have the words to scream in Hebrew so they can be heard, they lack that strength.
"I appeal to everyone who stood with us during our struggle: come and make this family feel they are not alone. The public needs to be here."
