Trump’s trap: Solving Hormuz crisis saves Iranian regime, and threats don't work - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:35:58 UTC
02:35:58 KST

US President Donald Trump has threatened Iran with annihilation so many times over the last year that one wonders how anyone in Iran could still take his rhetoric seriously.
Or, as The Wall Street Journal wrote in an editorial on Wednesday, those threats “would be more credible if we and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps hadn’t heard it several times by now.”
Yet we, and the IRGC, have indeed heard them. And then, in nearly the next breath or at the next photo opportunity, we have heard Trump talk about negotiations and, not in so many words, peace in our time with Iran.
The UN on Tuesday was no exception. On the one hand, Trump threatened to obliterate Iran and “drive them into hell, leaving it no chance of survival and no hope of future greatness for generations.” A few hours later, however, he said the US had held “very good” talks with the Iranians.
Could the tough talk simply be a negotiating move? Of course, it could. But Trump is not the only one who knows negotiating tricks. So do the Iranians.
According to various reports, those warm talks between US and Iranian officials produced a proposal under which Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the US lifting its blockade.
The Iranian ploy is reminiscent of the famous hassidic tale in which a poor man, complaining to his rabbi that his house is unbearably crowded, is instructed to bring more and more animals inside. When he is finally told to remove them, the same house suddenly feels spacious.
That, in essence, is what Iran is attempting to do.
A war never meant to be about the Strait of Hormuz
This war was never meant to be about the Strait of Hormuz. Or, at least, it did not start that way. The Iranians made the strait an issue by mining it and firing at ships and oil tankers passing through. The US retaliated by imposing a blockade on Iran – a blockade that is currently strangling the Iranian economy.
Now the Iranians are proposing that Washington lift the blockade in exchange for Tehran ending a crisis it created. A senior Iranian official reportedly said Hormuz could reopen within seven days if Washington reduced military pressure and lifted the blockade.
Sounds tempting, no? Especially since reopening the strait would allow much more oil onto the world market, lowering gasoline prices at American pumps just weeks before the midterm elections in November.
But such an agreement would solve the crisis Iran manufactured, not the underlying crisis that led to the war.
The central issue is not the Strait of Hormuz. It is Iran’s surviving enriched uranium, its nuclear program, and its ballistic-missile capabilities.
If Washington lifts the blockade to reopen the strait, what leverage will it retain to compel Iran to surrender its enriched uranium and accept limits on its nuclear and ballistic-missile programs?
Very little, which is precisely the problem.
With the blockade, the US essentially has its foot on the neck of the Iranian economy. If continuously enforced, that pressure could lead to the best possible outcome from both an Israeli and American perspective: regime change.
Only will abandon nuclear project with regime change
According to Israeli intelligence assessments, Iran will truly abandon its nuclear project only if its fundamentalist regime changes. As long as that regime remains in power, it will continue seeking to build its nuclear capabilities, which it sees as its ultimate survival guarantee.
The danger for Israel is clear: The US might prioritize reopening the Strait of Hormuz, partly because of domestic electoral considerations, over addressing Iran’s nuclear capabilities.
Iran is offering to cease its actions that were already condemned under international law, and it is demanding sanctions and blockade relief in return. The immediate economic incentive to accept will be enormous, but a deal focused narrowly on Hormuz would reward Tehran for manufacturing the crisis.
Trump said in his UN speech that he did not care about the midterm elections, and that they were not a factor in his decision-making.
“When it comes to Iran, it doesn’t even enter my mind,” he said.
That should be reassuring. The problem is that so many of Trump’s previous threats against Iran have proved hollow, and the skepticism surrounding those threats inevitably carries over to his statements here.
What the Iranians do not realize, Trump said, is that he is not running in the midterm elections. “I’ll be here for two and a half years,” he said.
And therein lies a core issue.
To get the Iranians to show flexibility, Trump must show that his position will not fluctuate before or after the elections. He must convince Tehran that the pressure will remain regardless of oil prices, polling numbers, or the date on the electoral calendar.
Yet even that is not enough.
The American political system – not merely the Trump administration – must persuade the Iranians that preventing them from acquiring nuclear weapons is a lasting American policy rather than the preference of one president.
That is a much more difficult task.
The Iranians are betting first that Trump will avoid drastic measures just before the midterm elections, because he does not want to disrupt the oil market and send gasoline prices soaring.
Their second and more consequential wager is that even if Trump holds firm now, they need only endure another two years. After that, a new administration could enter office with different priorities and a far more conciliatory approach toward Tehran.
This belief that American pressure can always be waited out is central to Iran’s strategy. It is also why lifting the blockade now would be particularly damaging.
It will be difficult for the regime to outlast Trump if the blockade remains in place and the economy continues to crumble. It will be considerably easier if the blockade is lifted, sanctions are eased, and Iran is given the economic oxygen needed to stabilize the regime and rebuild its military capabilities.
Following the 12-Day War of June 2025, Israel changed its objective regarding Iran. The goal shifted from “merely” damaging and setting back Iran’s nuclear and missile programs to establishing the conditions for the eventual fall of the regime – something that Israeli intelligence assessments said would take between one to three years if military and economic pressure was sustained.
That assessment has not necessarily changed. It may, however, if the blockade is lifted, and Iran receives sanctions relief, thereby allowing the regime to rescue its economy.
Trump’s credibility will not be restored by threatening Iran with annihilation yet again. It will be restored by demonstrating that the US will not exchange long-term strategic leverage for temporary calm and cheaper gasoline.
The jury, however, is still out.

Canadian NDP leader slammed for Yom Kippur message claiming Jews failed 'to stop ongoing genocide'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:35:50 UTC
02:35:50 KST

Canadian New Democratic Party Leader Avi Lewis is facing widespread criticism following a social media post published on Monday at the start of Yom Kippur, with critics alleging that he stated that Jewish people failed to do their part to “stop an ongoing genocide” in Gaza.
Lewis posted on X on Sunday, "Tonight Yom Kippur begins, the most somber moment of the Jewish calendar. It’s a time of atonement - a time to grieve those who have been lost, a time to acknowledge and take responsibility for harms we have caused, individually and collectively. For Jewish people, the personal has always been political and the political always personal. This year I'm reflecting on the fact that we failed to do our part to stop an ongoing genocide committed in our name. There are many other fronts where I have to do the work of repair. But nothing on this scale."
Later that evening, news broke that a gunman had opened fire outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ontario, during Erev Yom Kippur services. Constable Jeff Smith was injured during the exchange of gunfire while protecting the community as congregants took cover inside.
Following the shooting, Lewis published a second post on X, stating, "The shooting outside a synagogue in Belleville is deeply upsetting and has traumatized a community that gathered to pray. It is yet another reminder of the work that remains to create a Canada that is truly safe for people of all faiths, including Jewish people – to worship, to come together, to live without fear. Today, I am sending love and solidarity to the Jewish community in Belleville and across the country on this Yom Kippur, the most solemn and holiest day of the year."
The initial remarks drew immediate backlash from federal politicians, advocacy groups, and commentators, who argued that attributing collective responsibility to Jewish people for the actions of the Israeli government violates standard definitions of antisemitism and endangers communities.
'Holding Jews responsible is despicable,' says Liberal MP
Liberal MP Anthony Housefather condemned the remarks on X, writing that "holding Canadian Jews and Jews across the world collectively responsible for events over which they have no control is despicable."
Fellow Liberal MP Ben Carr similarly criticized the post when speaking to CPAC reporters, calling the comments "irresponsible" for a political leader, and warning that "it's dangerous and it's the type of narrative that is actually contributing to the type of threats that we're seeing levied against the Jewish community."
Advocacy organizations also weighed in heavily on the controversy. The Center for Israel and Jewish Affairs (CIJA) issued strong rebukes, pointing out in a post on X that "libels have consequences," and emphasizing that "when Jewish people are collectively portrayed as complicit in atrocities, that rhetoric can become a justification for targeting Jews here at home."
Mike Fegelman, executive director of HonestReporting Canada, criticized the post online as well, writing that "the criticism of @avilewis is entirely warranted. His Yom Kippur message is a near-perfect example of the hypocrisy at the heart of the anti-Zionist movement," and noting that "he is invoking Jews collectively, on Yom Kippur, and assigning them a responsibility to atone for the conduct of a foreign government."
In The Globe and Mail, columnist Robyn Urback published an op-ed arguing that "Avi Lewis's foolish statement on Jewish people should be disqualifying," emphasizing that assigning collective responsibility to a religious group during their most solemn holiday crosses a dangerous line where portraying Jewish communities collectively as complicit serves as a justification for targeting them at home.
Lewis defends his remarks on Jews
Addressing the controversy during a press conference on Monday, Lewis defended his remarks and rejected accusations that he was blaming Jewish people for Israel's military actions. When asked by a reporter to respond to criticism regarding his post on Gaza, Lewis stated: "Yeah, I did not blame Jews for the actions of the Israeli government. That's simply untrue. Holding Jews collectively responsible for the actions of the state of Israel is antisemitic. I've never done it. I think it's dangerous, and that's absolutely not what I did."
Lewis added, "I spoke as a Jewish Canadian from a place of profound sadness on the day of atonement and a day of the deepest and most solemn reflection in our calendar and said what many, many Jews feel and many Jews have said, that we have not done enough as Jewish people among a family of faiths and communities around the world. Humanity has not done enough to stop an ongoing genocide in Gaza."
Lewis also noted, "I just read today as part of my own reflections three Kol Nidre sermons from rabbis over the last couple of years about the failure of humanity and of Jewish people of the Jewish faith to stop an ongoing genocide."
Concluding his remarks on the controversy during the press conference, Lewis stated: "I come from a religious tradition which has a diversity of views which has debate at the center of our practice and our culture as Jews. I'm not going to police how other people reflect on Yom Kippur. And I think it's pretty ugly to see these partisan points being used to score partisan points like that. I won't be doing that. This was a personal reflection that I know is shared by many people. And just one more time, holding Jewish people collectively responsible for the actions of the state of Israel is not something I would ever do. It's antisemitic, and it is wrong."
The NDP did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

The Federal Administrative Court of Switzerland has rejected the asylum application of Iranian refugee and Jewish conversion candidate Behnam Vali Heydarian, also known as Ben Vali, putting him at risk of deportation to Georgia and potentially Iran, Vali told The Jerusalem Post on Wednesday.
Vali previously spoke with the Post in August, describing the violent transnational aggression he said Iran had directed against him while he was in Georgia. A convert to Christianity at the time and a prominent figure in the refugee community, Vali drew the regime’s attention after initially being targeted for distributing Bibles in Iran and later for his pro-Israel advocacy following the October 7 attacks.
After being assaulted multiple times, Vali said he was threatened over his continued pro-Israel advocacy, had his bank accounts repeatedly frozen without warning, and was threatened with deportation by a person he believed was a member of Georgia’s security services.
'He was an active, hardworking, kind, and responsible person'
Mikheil Grishashvili, a Jewish community leader and representative of the Peace Synagogue in Georgia, told the Post that Vali has been an active member of the community since 2023.
“He was an active, hardworking, kind, and responsible person, and he very quickly became part of our community,” Grishashvili said, adding that Vali became increasingly involved in Judaism.
Returning to Iran would likely lead to Vali's execution
Aware that returning to Iran would likely lead to his execution due to his open support for Israel, his conversion and his proselytizing, Vali fled to Switzerland, where he had been granted a business visa.
Though Vali entered Switzerland legally, the country rejected his asylum application, stating that he had entered the country illegally and fled from a “safe” country, despite evidence he provided demonstrating what he described as a clear and present threat in Georgia. Offers from Swiss nationals to provide Vali with employment and housing, so he would not burden the system, also went unanswered.
Ibrahim Alvac, the representative of a Swiss lawyers’ bureau representing Vali, told the Post, “The Swiss authorities have ordered his removal to Georgia because he holds refugee status there and Georgia has agreed to readmit him. His Swiss asylum application was not examined on its merits as a claim concerning persecution in Iran. We challenged the decision to return him to Georgia and sought reconsideration, but we have been unable to persuade the Swiss asylum authorities that his personal circumstances make that return unsafe. The negative judgment of 17 September 2026 has made his situation still more troubling.
“Mr Vali Heydarian is living with the uncertainty of a removal order while trying to make his concerns heard through the legal procedures available to him. He has not hidden from the authorities. He has presented his identity, his history and his objections openly.”
“We appealed the reapplication, arguing that based on my individual risks and the problems I faced, they had to assess, analyze, and examine my individual case and circumstances. But they didn’t,” Vali said. “The final answer was that the State Secretariat for Migration had already done its job and that Georgia is a safe country. You can go back to the safe country and stay there. That’s it. That was the final hope that we had.”
Vali said that the entry ban now in place, preventing him from returning to Switzerland, would stop him from seeking refuge throughout the European Union. He said he has also been attempting to contact Israeli authorities, hoping his pro-Israel advocacy and position as a student of Judaism would encourage some protection, but did not receive a response.

NYT shareholders file lawsuit against paper's parent org. over biased Israel reporting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:35:19 UTC
02:35:19 KST

Shareholders of The New York Times filed a lawsuit against the paper’s parent company Wednesday morning, arguing the paper has failed to follow its own editorial standards.
The suit, filed by the State Board of Administration of Florida (SBA) and the National Center for Public Policy Research (NCPPR) in New York County Supreme Court, requests the Times board of directors to release internal records.
The company has refused to produce the records for four months, the majority of which pertain to the paper’s coverage of the Israel-Hamas war.
Requests were first made by the National Jewish Advocacy Center (NJAC), representing NCPPR, on May 29 following the May 11 Nicholas Kristof column titled “The Silence That Meets the Rape of Palestinians," but the NYT has not complied.
Lawsuit alleges that board failed to establish adequate oversight
The new lawsuit, as reported by The Jerusalem Post, notes that the Times’ reputation for independent journalism is "its most valuable" asset and alleges that the board failed to establish adequate oversight mechanisms to ensure compliance with the company’s own editorial standards.
It cites examples of corrections and disputed reporting, including the October 2023 Al-Ahli hospital explosion coverage, claims about Gaza war reporting errors, and concerns raised by a purported newsroom whistleblower who said internal reporting channels did not resolve her complaints.
The whistleblower, who is not named in the suit but who is said to be a Jewish former New York Times newsroom employee with about a decade’s tenure, said that that in the immediate aftermath of Hamas’s October 7, 2023, attack on Israel, staffers spent weeks searching for evidence that Hamas did not use the tunnels beneath al-Shifa Hospital, even after the Israeli military released its own footage of the tunnels in November 2023.
Whistleblower claimed she raised concerns internally
On November 20, 2023, the head of the video department reportedly referred to the tunnels as "alleged tunnels" in the desk’s morning meeting.
The whistleblower claimed she raised concerns internally about what she believed were violations of the Times’ own editorial standards through internal channels, including EthicsPoint, the Standards desk, Employee Relations, and Human Resources, on at least 15 occasions beginning in 2019.
The filing says the whistleblower’s records include allegations that complaints about newsroom standards were not properly escalated, concerns about bias in coverage were not addressed, and senior leadership was aware of some complaints but did not take corrective action.
According to the filing, the whistleblower alleged that the internal complaint system failed to address her concerns and instead turned against her.
The petitioners argue they are not seeking to direct editorial decisions, but want records showing whether the board monitors compliance with the Times’ own standards and manages reputational risks.

“During the first eight months alone, more civilians were killed or injured in Ukraine than throughout all of 2025. The high number of civilian casualties reporteed so far in September indicates that this extremely alarming trend is continuing, as missile and drone attacks increasingly hit populated areas, including cities located far from the front line,” DiCarlo said.

Another 53,693 civilians, including 3,247 children, have been injured,” she said, stressing that the actual figures are likely to be significantly higher.
DiCarlo emphasized: “Attacks directed against civilians and civilian infrastructure are prohibited. These attacks in Ukraine and the Russian Federation are unacceptable and must stop immediately.”
She also highlighted the danger posed by military activity at and around nuclear facilities. Any incident that threatens the safety of a nuclear facility could have catastrophic consequences, DiCarlo stressed.
“With another wartime winter approaching, the intensification of attacks targeting Ukraine’s already damaged energy infrastructure is of particular concern. The cumulative impact of these strikes could plunge millions of people into darkness and cold in the coming months. Everything possible must be done to prevent further deterioration of the humanitarian situation. We call for urgent measures to stop attacks on energy infrastructure and for an immediate moratorium on all attacks on populated areas,” the UN deputy chief emphasized.

EU plans sanctions on 77 candidates in Russian parliamentary elections held in Ukraine's occupied territories

Source: a European Pravda correspondent in Brussels citing EU diplomatic sources
Details: The European Union is preparing to add 77 candidates in Russia's State Duma elections to its sanctions lists.
"Today at Coreper, the European External Action Service presented a new draft list under the sanctions regime concerning Ukraine's territorial integrity, comprising 77 candidates who stood in Russian-occupied territories of Ukraine," a European Pravda source said.
Following the presentation, technical work will begin to prepare the list for approval. EU ambassadors in Brussels are expected to return to the issue in early October.
The new sanctions list is expected to be approved at a meeting of the Council of the EU in its Foreign Affairs configuration on 12 October.
Background:
- It was reported earlier that the Council of the EU adopted a final decision on 22 September to extend for a further 36 months sanctions against individuals and entities responsible for undermining or threatening Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. However, it has removed Russian oligarchs Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from the list.
- On 16 September, the European External Action Service presented a proposal for a new sanctions package targeting Russia's military-industrial complex. The package covers 1,576 individuals and entities.

Russian Insurgents Blow Up Tank Cars Carrying Over 10,000 Metric Tons of Oil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:19:12 UTC
02:19:12 KST

An insurgent movement in Russia carried out attacks on railroad tank cars, destroying over 10,000 metric tons of oil.
The rebels carried out Operation Barrel with the support of the Freedom of Russia Legion.
Following precision strikes on oil refineries and ports, the Kremlin attempted to hide the crude oil by shifting the responsibility for its storage and logistics to the Russian railway network.
The aim of the strategy was simple: by distributing reserves across the country in tank cars, ensure the oil’s preservation until it could be exported at the highest possible price per barrel.
The insurgents infiltrated the relevant agencies to obtain the necessary information.
They then conducted on-site reconnaissance, intercepted train schedules, and analyzed vulnerabilities and escape routes.
As a result of explosions and arson, over 10,000 metric tons of crude oil were destroyed.
Operations at a number of key rail junctions were also halted—a multi-day “traffic jam” on the tracks blocked supplies and paralyzed key logistics corridors.
Within the oil supply chain, rail logistics has traditionally been one of the most efficient and practical modes of transportation.
Railways crisscross the entire country for thousands of kilometers—this is one of the key advantages of this mode of transport.
“Over the past six months, we have destroyed dozens of locomotives and hundreds of other railway infrastructure facilities,” noted a member of the insurgent movement.
Without these locomotives and rail junctions, the regime has faced difficulties delivering fuel across the country.
“Destroying locomotives is just part of our systematic work,” added a member of the insurgent movement.
The enemy is forced to keep large quantities of petroleum products on the railroad tracks because it cannot ship them to refineries. This, in turn, creates an even greater logistical bottleneck along this route.
Faced with a shortage of locomotives and threats on the roads, the regime began using tank cars en masse as mobile storage units, periodically moving them between stations within the region.
“Operation Barrel has dealt a blow to Putin and the oligarchs that will have catastrophic consequences over time. As a result of the tanker explosions, the regime has lost over 10,000 metric tons of oil. Together with the cost of the tankers, that amounts to over $10 million,” said a member of the insurgent movement.
In addition to the direct damage to the war economy, the attack forced the Kremlin to spend additional resources on guarding such facilities.
In June, the insurgent movement in Russia helped Ukraine strike factories near Orenburg.

Netherlands to return to Eurovision after 2026 boycott
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
18:17:47 BST
02:17:47 KST

Netherlands to return to Eurovision after 2026 boycott
- Published
The Netherlands will return to the Eurovision Song Contest next year despite a boycott by the broadcaster that was previously in charge of the country's participation.
Dutch network Avrotros withdrew in 2026 and said it would also not take part in 2027 because the competition could "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over Israel's involvement and the Gaza war.
The NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, has now stepped in, saying coverage of the contest will be provided by broadcasting organisation NOS, while an independent panel will select the Dutch participant.
Jurre Bosman, NPO's director of media, said: "It is important that, as a public broadcaster, we remain part of this unifying European event at this moment in particular."
Israel's participation in the contest has become highly controversial, and five countries, including the Netherlands, boycotted this year's event.
Eurovision organiser the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) has subsequently announced a number of changes, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.
That means that, although Israel can still compete, the EBU would ask another country to host if it won.
The EBU has also proposed changes to to the voting, saying politically motivated voting has become "persistent" and is widely seen as "deeply worrying".
However, Avrotros said those changes did "not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored".
In a statement on Wednesday, the NPO said the EBU has "taken significant steps regarding the rules" of the contest, and that the Netherlands will return.
Acknowledging that the contest provokes "mixed feelings" in the Netherlands, the NPO said it had "explicitly asked the EBU to once again make the unifying character of the festival an important part of the event".
The NPO also said the Dutch entrant would be chosen by "an independent team of experts" who would "carefully guide the process surrounding the act".
Eurovision director Martin Green said in a statement: "We are delighted to welcome the Netherlands back to the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.
"We value the constructive conversations we have had with NPO and look forward to working together to reinforce the Contest as a place that truly reflects the spirit of 'United By Music'."
Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the 2026 contest in addition to the Netherlands.
The 2027 contest will take place on 14 May in Burgas, after Bulgarian singer Dara won this year's contest with Bangaranga.
Last month, it was announced that Canada will enter the contest for the first time.

Emine Erdogan calls for new systems to address environmental crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:17:21 UTC
02:17:21 KST

Türkiye's First Lady and chair of the UN Advisory Board of Eminent Persons on Zero Waste, Emine Erdogan, has highlighted the global environmental crisis in a video message at the opening of the Sustainable Development Impact Meetings, organised by the World Economic Forum in New York.
“Our planet resembles a ravaged mine, the oceans cannot breathe, and cities are struggling to cope with their waste. Therefore, a circular economy is not one of the options before us; it is a necessity for our future,” she said in the video on Wednesday.
The first lady expressed her regret at being unable to attend the gathering and said that current production and consumption systems are not capable of carrying humanity into the future.
'We see zero waste as a key'
Emine Erdogan noted that achieving a transition to a circular economy means strengthening sustainable development, expanding recycling, improving waste management and turning towards renewable energy sources.
“We see zero waste as a key to achieving all of this. Because zero waste is not merely a waste-management approach that individuals incorporate into their daily lives. Zero waste means redesigning our production and consumption models and redefining our relationship with nature,” she said, stressing the need for new economic models to transform the entire system from production to consumption.
“We must establish an order in which people who adopt zero waste in their lives are supported by the right systems, and in which the production of durable, repairable products whose materials can be reused is encouraged,” she added.
“Indeed, we still have a window of opportunity to combat the climate crisis and build a sustainable future. I believe that Zero Waste, which we launched in Türkiye in 2017 and which has now become a global movement, is a transformative force in making the most of this opportunity,” she said.
“With the right steps we take together, I hope we can make a new beginning — one in which we protect our resources rather than consume them, and create value instead of waste,” she added.
Thanking the World Economic Forum for organising the meeting, Emine Erdogan expressed her hope of meeting the participants at COP31, which will be held in Antalya.

Israel blocks 900 wheelchairs for Gaza's child amputees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:16:44 UTC
02:16:44 KST

Breadcrumb
'Calculated effort to destroy Palestinian life': Israel blocks 900 wheelchairs for amputee children in Gaza
More than 900 wheelchairs donated by two Australian charities for wounded and amputee children in Gaza have been blocked by Israel from entering the enclave, with the shipments stuck in storage in Jordan since 2025 and staff from the charities calling on Australian members of parliament to intervene in the matter.
The charity Kids on Wheels Alliance sent two shipments that arrived in Jordan in February 2025, while another shipment from Wheelchairs for Kids arrived in October that year.
The wheelchairs remain at a storage facility managed by the Jordan Hashemite Charity Organisation (JHCO), which said COGAT, the Israeli defence ministry body that oversees the entry of humanitarian aid into Gaza, had blocked their delivery.
Shaoquett Moselmane, the chair of the Kids on Wheels Alliance, told The New Arab that they have been raising funds for wheelchairs for over 15 years, with enormous efforts from local communities in covering the cost of the wheelchairs intended for Gaza. He added that the Palestine Australia New Zealand Medical Association (PANZMA) assisted with the shipping costs and delivery; however, Israel gave no reason, and "no security issues were raised," despite reports.
"In any event, there could be no legitimate reason to hold up wheelchairs for children with special needs. No reason of any nature given as they are just wheelchairs for the thousands of amputee children and the thousands more in need of support," he said.
"We have sought representations from Australian members of parliament at both house of reps and senate seeking their help to make high-level representations and doing what we can to alert people of this inhumane behaviour in the hope that Israeli authorities grant consent to deliver the wheelchairs," he continued.
Moselmane said a community meeting was held on Wednesday to discuss further follow-up action, with many suggesting to take the issue up with local federal members, the Australian government, and the Jordanian government, as well as other authorities in the hope that enough pressure is exerted to move those containers to Gaza.
According to Moselmane, Israel blocking the shipment will affect over 11,000 children in Gaza.
"The pain and suffering of the Palestinian people can not be ignored. Our humanity is at stake if people around the world don’t stand up and rally against the injustices perpetrated on the people of Palestine. They’ve suffered for over seven decades; this indignity of occupation and oppression must cease. For a peaceful future for all, humanity in Palestine must prevail".
Mohammad Helmy, a Melbourne-based pro-Palestine activist, told The New Arab that Israel's refusal to allow the wheelchairs into Gaza was intentional, accusing authorities of seeking to make life in the devastated enclave "impossible".
“Israel’s blockade of over 900 custom, all-terrain wheelchairs—hand-built by Australian volunteers to help amputee children navigate destroyed streets—exposes a calculated effort to destroy Palestinian life and render life in Gaza impossible,” Helmy said.
“By undertaking non-stop bombardment and then systematically denying the basic medical aid needed to survive it, Israel is actively executing an ongoing genocide. Trapping mobility gear in warehouses while children crawl through rubble is not a security measure—it is a deliberate policy of collective punishment and total destruction directed against the Palestinian people,” he continued.
The restrictions come as the UN has said Gaza has the largest group of child amputees in modern history as a result of Israel's attacks on the territory.
Greg Hebble, the CEO of Wheelchairs for Kids Australia, said their team is currently trying to figure out next steps, with the hopes that the wheelchairs reach people with difficult mobility challenges.
"We are currently working with our logistics, humanitarian and distribution partners to better understand the situation and explore all available avenues to facilitate the delivery of the wheelchairs. This includes seeking clarification regarding the reasons for the blockage and whether alternative pathways or approvals may be available," he said.
"Should the shipment ultimately be denied entry, it would be deeply disappointing, particularly for the individuals who have been identified as recipients. We will continue to explore any lawful and practical options available to ensure this assistance reaches those most in need," he continued.
Hebble said that aside from the shipment leaving thousands without independence, social participation and access to essential services, a great deal of financial and logistical resources were put into making the delivery.
"Significant financial resources have been invested, along with countless hours of planning, coordination, sourcing, transportation and compliance work to ensure the Wheelchairs could reach those in need. The cost to our organisation to supply this shipment of Wheelchairs is more than $100k AUS," he said.
"Our message is a simple humanitarian one, people living with disability should never be forgotten. Regardless of geography, politics, or conflict, vulnerable children and civilians deserve access to equipment that supports their mobility, wellbeing and dignity," he continued.
Status 'pending'
The JHCO said it filed an application in late February 2025 for the Kids on Wheels Alliance shipments to enter Gaza as part of an aid convoy, but COGAT rejected the request. According to reports, Israeli authorities said medical equipment and medicines had not been approved for inclusion in that convoy.
JHCO said its application has since remained "pending", with no further updates, leaving the organisation unable to submit a new application for the other shipments.
COGAT has not responded to media requests concerning the Australian donations. However, the Israeli agency has previously said that thousands of wheelchairs have been allowed into Gaza.
The wheelchairs donated by Wheelchairs for Kids are designed to withstand difficult terrain, including the rubble that now covers large parts of Gaza, and can be adjusted as children grow older and taller.
"The sooner they come out of there and get to the kids, the better, and the little kids can get a much better life," Brother Olly Pickett, co-founder of the charity, said in a statement.
"I think there's a lot of children waiting for them who have had amputations, and so they won't be able to walk around or get around. Once they get a wheelchair, they can get out and about, which would be wonderful,” he added.
Australian media reports, citing an informed source outside the region, said Israeli authorities had denied the wheelchairs entry because they considered them potentially "dual use", a classification applied to goods that authorities say could also have military applications.
Israeli rights group Gisha earlier this year published a report saying Israel had arbitrarily classified essential items, household goods and medical supplies as "dual use" since the start of the war on Gaza.
Items subjected to such restrictions have included flashlights, sleeping bags and portable toilets.
Rights groups have warned that restrictions on such goods have serious consequences for civilians, including tens of thousands of Palestinians attempting to recover from injuries and rebuild their lives amid the widespread destruction in Gaza.

Netanyahu’s New York visit reflects Israel’s growing tensions with Western countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-24
15:35:29 UTC
00:35:29 KST

Israel’s tensions with Western countries because it attacked the Gaza Strip and Lebanon, and actions in the occupied West Bank, have spilled into Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit Thursday to New York for the UN General Assembly.
Netanyahu’s scheduled meetings include no leaders from Western countries that have maintained longstanding relations with Israel, including the US.
Netanyahu was unable to arrange a meeting with US President Donald Trump, while a planned meeting with Elon Musk was canceled. His schedule does not include meetings with US political figures. 
International isolation
Israel’s international isolation has continued to grow after several countries, including France, the UK and Canada, recognized the State of Palestine at last year’s UN General Assembly amid Israeli genocide in Gaza.
Ahead of Oct. 27 elections, Israel moved to advance the illegal E1 settlement project in the occupied West Bank, where attacks by the Israeli army and Israeli settlers have intensified.
The project, which seeks to separate occupied East Jerusalem from the West Bank, and divide the territory’s north from its south, drew objections from Western countries, particularly the UK.
Some of 12 Western countries, including the UK, France and Canada, imposed sanctions on illegal Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank, while others signaled plans to do so.
In response to London’s sanctions, Tel Aviv decided to close the UK Consulate serving Palestinians in occupied East Jerusalem, expel British representatives from the city of Kiryat Gat and end British participation in training Palestinian Authority security forces.
It also barred 12 British nationals, most of them lawmakers, from entering Israel.
Netanyahu left Israel early Thursday for his New York visit, which is expected to last a few hours, amid tensions also reflected in Western leaders’ UN General Assembly speeches.
Israeli media reported ahead of the trip that efforts were underway to arrange meetings between Netanyahu and world leaders on the sidelines of the General Assembly, but said doing so was difficult.
The reports also noted that Netanyahu could face protests in New York, as he had in previous years.
Following the reports, the Israeli Prime Minister’s Office claimed that “many world leaders requested meetings,” but only some could be accommodated because of Netanyahu’s schedule.
His announced schedule includes the presidents of Argentina, Bolivia, Paraguay, Panama and Ethiopia, Colombia’s vice president, and the prime ministers of Greece, Slovenia and Papua New Guinea.
It includes no meetings with leaders from the US or other Western countries. 
‘Humiliating visit’
Alon Liel, a retired ambassador and former secretary at Israel’s Foreign Ministry, told Anadolu that Netanyahu’s trip was unprecedented.
“There has never been such a humiliating visit to the UN for an Israeli prime minister,” said Liel.
Liel said Israel’s international standing had deteriorated since October 2023, and argued that its future position would depend on whether the “right wing” remains in power.
“Compared with before Oct. 7, 2023, we are in a much weaker position internationally, including in the Middle East,” he said.
Liel said the recognition by Western countries of the State of Palestine last year dealt Netanyahu a greater blow than sanctions on illegal Jewish settlements in the occupied West Bank. 
‘Even in US, he no longer feels comfortable’
Liel argued that this year the biggest setback for Netanyahu came from Washington.
“Netanyahu can meet Argentine and Greek leaders, but he cannot meet any American politician or official,” he said. “This means not only Europeans but also Americans are avoiding him. I think this is the major blow because the only country Netanyahu can go to in the world is the US.”
Liel said Netanyahu had reached a point where “even in the US, he no longer feels comfortable,” adding that he could not land in New York or stay there overnight. Netanyahu’s plane is expected to land at a military airfield in New Jersey rather than John F. Kennedy International Airport in New York. Reports have cited security, logistical and protest concerns for the change.
With the US position added to the equation, Israel’s international standing had weakened further, said Liel.
“This is definitely not a normal visit. The political objections to him, the speeches against Israel at the UN and the security situation are not normal,” he said. “Even in the US, Netanyahu is acting like an unwanted person.”

Eli Ohana, a former soccer star and former president of Israeli club Beitar Jerusalem, said the situation in Israel is “not ideal,” adding that he avoids revealing his nationality while on foreign soil.
“The situation in Israel is not ideal, and we did not reveal our Israeli identity outside our country. When I was on vacation in Greece, I hid my identity,” Ohana told the same radio station.
“Today, we are going through an abnormal period,” he added.
Dan Shapiro, the former US ambassador to Tel Aviv, said Israel’s standing is facing an “unprecedented decline” in the US and that Netanyahu “is not part of the solution.”
Israeli radio station Reshet Bet quoted Shapiro, who served as ambassador from 2011 to 2017, as saying: “There is an unprecedented decline in Israel’s standing in the United States.”
He added that the decline is “unprecedented even among Republicans” – members of Trump’s party, who also tend to be pro-Israel – and that “it is difficult to see Netanyahu as part of the solution to this situation.”
“Trump may also reach the conclusion that it would be easier to deal with another government in Israel,” Shapiro added, with the Oct. 27 Israeli elections currently too close to call.
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022, a government described as the most right-wing in Israel’s history.  
Under a legal cloud
Netanyahu is scheduled to address the 81st session of the UN General Assembly at 2 pm New York time (1800GMT) Thursday.
Netanyahu’s current schedule in New York does not include a meeting with Trump, despite previous Israeli efforts to arrange a meeting between them, according to Israeli media reports.
The visit comes amid expectations of protests against Netanyahu in New York, in condemnation of Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip and attacks in the occupied West Bank.
Israel has been waging an extermination war in Gaza since Oct. 8, 2023, killing nearly 74,000 Palestinians and injuring over 175,000, most of them children and women.
In addition to the casualties, Israel has destroyed around 90% of Gaza’s civilian infrastructure, with the UN estimating the cost of reconstruction at about $70 billion.
Alongside its genocidal war in Gaza, attacks by the Israeli army and occupiers against Palestinians and their property in the occupied West Bank, including East Jerusalem, have intensified, drawing growing international condemnation.
Israel is scheduled to hold general elections on Oct. 27.
Netanyahu also faces charges of bribery, fraud, and breach of trust in three separate corruption cases. Critics in Israel and elsewhere say he has prolonged Israel’s military offensives to be able to continue delaying his court hearings.
Separately, in November 2024, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu, accusing him of war crimes and crimes against humanity.

ECHR holds hearing in case of 10 Ukrainian children from Crimea missing since 2014
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
20:13:15 EEST
02:13:15 KST

The European Court of Human Rights held oral hearings in the case "Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union on behalf of ten Ukrainian children v. Russia" concerning children from orphanages in Crimea whose whereabouts have been unknown since 2014.
According to a press release provided to Interfax-Ukraine, the children, who were born between 2009 and 2013 and were in the care of the Ukrainian state at the time of the occupation of Crimea, were incorporated into the Russian system of adoption and foster care after Russia established control over the peninsula.
"When Russia occupied Crimea, these children were between one and five years old. The Ukrainian state was their guardian, and since then it has been unable to get an answer to a simple question: where are they? Today, they are teenagers who may be living with a different citizenship and in foreign families. Justice for them is not just about punishing those responsible. It is the right of every child and their loved ones to know the truth: where they are, who they are with, and who decided that they are no longer Ukrainian. This is the fundamental importance of this case," Head of Bring Kids Back UA Maksym Maksymov said.
The Ukrainian Helsinki Human Rights Union filed the application with the ECHR in January 2023. The court examined the admissibility and merits of the case. According to the applicant, the Russian government did not submit any observations on the case and did not participate in the hearing.
Third parties in the case include, among others, the Ukrainian government and seven Ukrainian and international organizations. The International Bar Association's Human Rights Institute (IBAHRI) urged the Court to take into account the particular vulnerability of children and the context of the occupation.
The ECHR will issue its decision on the admissibility and merits of the case at a later date.

“The cascading effects of this war extend far beyond Ukraine, including through growing risks to global food security,” DiCarlo said, stressing that attacks on grain infrastructure, civilian vessels and ports, as well as serious disruptions to commercial shipping in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, have complicated agricultural exports.

Fifty-one countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement on Wednesday, urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations as large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine continue in the fifth year of war.
The statement was delivered during the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) in New York by Kaja Kallas, EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy, alongside Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha and French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot, according to Democrata.

Call for civilian returns
Russia was also urged to ensure the immediate, safe and unconditional return of Ukrainian civilians who have been illegally detained, forcibly transferred or deported.

Badrinath Dham sees record 17.79 lakh pilgrims so far this year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:09:14 UTC
02:09:14 KST

People visit the Badrinath Temple amid the ongoing 'Char Dham Yatra', in Chamoli district, Uttarakhand. (PTI Photo)
More than 17.79 lakh pilgrims have visited Badrinath Dham so far this year, surpassing the shrine's previous annual footfall record.A total of 1,779,805 devotees had visited the shrine as of September 22, 153 days after the Badrinath Yatra began on April 23. The shrine's portals are expected to remain open for another one-and-a-half to nearly two months before closing for the winter.The latest footfall has exceeded the previous record of 1,780,429 visitors recorded in 2023 when comparing the current figure with the year-to-date data provided by the government. The 2025 figure stood at 1,778,298.
According to the Tourism Department data, 695,332 pilgrims visited Badrinath in 2000, the year Uttarakhand was established.The number rose to 768,107 in 2007 and crossed the one-million mark in 2008 and 2010.The 2014 disaster led to a sharp decline in pilgrimage numbers, with footfall falling to 159,575.Visitor numbers subsequently recovered, with 1,048,051 pilgrims visiting Badrinath in 2018 and 1,244,993 in 2019. The Covid-19 pandemic again resulted in a steep decline, with 155,055 visitors recorded in 2020 and 199,409 in 2021.Footfall increased significantly from 2022 onwards. The shrine recorded 1,763,578 visitors in 2022, followed by 1,780,429 in 2023, 1,774,264 in 2024 and 1,778,298 in 2025.
On September 22, 6,685 devotees visited Badrinath, according to the data released by the state government.
Government focuses on pilgrim facilities
The government said arrangements for pilgrims had been strengthened in view of the increased footfall during the second phase of the Char Dham Yatra, including health and safety measures and facilities at the shrines and along the pilgrimage route.
“Keeping in view the increasing number of pilgrims during the second phase of the Char Dham Yatra, special focus has been placed on strengthening pilgrim facilities at the dhams and en-route halts. Health and safety arrangements have also been strengthened. Under the guidance of Hon’ble Prime Minister Narendra Modi ji, work is being carried out at a rapid pace to give Shri Badrinath Dham a grand, divine and well-organised form in keeping with its religious and mythological significance. This will provide better facilities and a more comfortable experience to devotees”, said Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami.

A new EU status for Canada? Israel has lived the model for decades - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

Ursula von der Leyen made a striking proposal in Strasbourg on September 16. With Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in attendance, the European Commission president opened the door to Canada becoming what she called the European Union’s first “associate member.”
There is only one problem. The European Union has no such status.
Associate membership does not appear in the EU treaties. There is no established package of rights and obligations attached to it, no predetermined place for an associate member in the Union’s institutions, and no agreement about how much access to the Single Market it would entail. Von der Leyen supplied a name before Europe had designed the institution.
But Brussels does not need to start with a blank sheet of paper.
It should look at Israel.
Canada may indeed become the first country formally granted whatever new status the EU eventually calls “associate membership.” But it would hardly be the first country to inhabit the space between membership and an ordinary third-country relationship. Israel has spent nearly seven decades constructing one version of such a relationship: integration without membership.
The story began almost as soon as the European project itself. In April 1958, only months after the Treaty of Rome entered into force, Israel became the third country, after Greece and the United States, to request the establishment of a diplomatic mission to the European Economic Community in Brussels. Full diplomatic relations followed in February 1959.
And Israel wanted more than trade.
From the beginning, Israeli policymakers sought association with the emerging Community. The Israeli ambition was substantially political as well as economic. Israel eventually accepted agreements that fell short of association, but the larger objective was to secure a recognized place alongside the developing European project.
What Israel was asking Europe in the late 1950s sounds surprisingly familiar in 2026: how close can a non-member country come to the European project without actually joining it?
The answer emerged gradually rather than through grand constitutional design.
Over the decades, Israel and Europe built their ties layer by layer. The 1995 EU-Israel Association Agreement, which entered into force in 2000, established the central institutional framework. The European Neighbourhood Policy later added an Action Plan intended to bring Israel closer to European policies and programs. Cooperation expanded into research and innovation, aviation, pharmaceuticals, education and regulatory cooperation.
Israel's largest trading partner
Today those ties reach remarkably far. The EU is Israel’s largest trading partner, accounting for 31.7% of Israel’s trade in goods in 2025, worth €43.3 billion. Israel participates in Horizon Europe. The EU-Israel aviation agreement connects the Israeli and European aviation markets, while another agreement facilitates trade in pharmaceuticals. Israel also participates in the Pan-Euro-Mediterranean system of rules of origin.
This is not EU membership. But neither is it a conventional relationship between two separate markets.
Nearly two decades ago, Joel Peters and I described the logic behind this arrangement as “integration without membership.” We proposed a Euro-Israeli Partnership that would sit deliberately below full membership while moving beyond the existing Association Agreement. It envisaged deeper political cooperation, Israeli participation in European agencies and programs, gradual convergence with relevant parts of the European acquis, and greater access to the Single Market.
The objective was not to prepare Israel for eventual accession. It was to recognize that European integration need not end at the Union’s formal borders.
Israel is not the only precedent. Switzerland offers the EU’s most developed example of sector-by-sector integration outside membership, with extensive agreements connecting it to large parts of the Single Market and numerous European programs. But Switzerland is geographically and economically embedded in Europe. Israel offers a different lesson: a country outside geographical Europe, with no realistic membership perspective, can nevertheless become deeply connected to selected parts of the European system.
That distinction suddenly matters far beyond Israel.
Carney has ruled out Canadian EU membership. What Ottawa is seeking instead is what he has called a “unique alliance,” extending across trade, defense, technology, energy, and critical minerals. Canada has already moved closer to European defense structures through its participation in the EU’s SAFE defense program.
Here the analogy with Israel has limits. Israel’s integration has developed overwhelmingly through economic, regulatory, scientific, and sectoral cooperation. It does not provide a blueprint for the defense and security dimension that Canada and the EU are now considering. If associate membership eventually encompasses defense procurement and strategic coordination, Brussels will be constructing something new.
But the Israeli experience does offer a model for how such a relationship can be constructed.
Closer ties do not have to be all or nothing. They can proceed sector by sector. Research systems can connect without political membership. Aviation markets can open. Regulations can converge in selected areas. European programs can admit non-member states. New areas of cooperation can be added as political circumstances and mutual interests change. None of that necessarily requires the full institutional rights of an EU member state.
The Israeli case also cautions against romanticizing such arrangements. EU-Israel relations are currently experiencing a period of severe political strain. EU institutions have debated Israel’s compliance with the human-rights provisions of the Association Agreement and possible restrictions on parts of the relationship over the war in Gaza.
That does not invalidate the model. It demonstrates something important about it. Deep institutional ties do not eliminate political disagreement. They create structures within which cooperation, conditionality, and conflict can coexist.
Canada has, therefore, exposed a gap in the EU’s institutional architecture. There are countries that may want much more than a trade agreement without seeking membership. Switzerland demonstrates how far that principle can extend within Europe. Israel demonstrates that it can extend beyond it. Canada may now add a strategic and defense dimension neither model fully provides.
Canada could still become the first country formally designated an EU associate member. But it would enter territory Europe has been exploring for decades.
The Canadian question is how a country can move much closer to the EU without becoming a member of it.
The name may be new. Much of the model is not.
The writer is a senior fellow at the Jewish People Policy Institute (JPPI) and a professor of European studies and international relations in the Department of Politics and Government at Ben-Gurion University of the Negev.

19:59:14 EEST

Participants in the sixth summit of the International Crimea Platform, held in New York City on Wednesday, September 23, adopted a joint statement in which, among other things, stated that ending Russia's armed aggression against Ukraine is absolutely essential for restoring Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty and is a decisive step toward restoring international peace and security; they also reaffirmed their support for international judicial and other mechanisms, including the International Criminal Court; called for unity and the strengthening of sanctions against Russia; and condemned any illegal elections in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
As stated in the text of the declaration published on the website of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA), the summit participants reaffirmed once again that the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, the city of Sevastopol, and other parts of Ukraine's territory temporarily occupied by the Russian Federation, were and remain integral parts of Ukraine's sovereign territory, and that their temporary occupation does not create any legal grounds for changing their status.
"We are convinced that the liberation of all temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine, including the Autonomous Republic of Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, as well as the restoration of Ukraine's territorial integrity and sovereignty within its internationally recognized borders, including its territorial sea, are crucial steps toward restoring international peace and security, strengthening the international legal order, and ensuring respect for the fundamental norms of international law," the summit participants said.
The statement also states that any illegal "elections" held by the aggressor state in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine cannot alter their status under international law, and that the liberation of Crimea is an integral part of restoring Ukraine's territorial integrity and a necessary prerequisite for restoring a comprehensive, just, and lasting peace and strengthening international security.
According to statement, restrictions on and infringements of freedom of navigation in the Black and Azov Seas, along with Russia's militarization of the Crimean Peninsula and its use as a military base for a full-scale military invasion of Ukraine, pose a threat to regional and global security and undermine international trade, energy, and food security.
Separately, the platform's participants emphasized the need to ensure full accountability for any war crimes and other serious international crimes committed in connection with Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine. "To this end, we support the work of international judicial and other relevant mechanisms, in particular the International Criminal Court, the European Court of Human Rights, and other institutions, to ensure accountability for international crimes and violations of international law, and we also encourage further sustained efforts within the Council of Europe aimed at facilitating the operational activities of the Special Tribunal on the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine and the International Commission for the Settlement of Claims for Ukraine," the document reads.
The summit participants called on the international community to take "decisive, coordinated, and consistent action," in particular, strengthening international sanctions against Russia and enhancing international coordination to prevent the circumvention of sanctions, intensifying efforts to secure the release of all civilians and political prisoners illegally detained and held by the Russian Federation, the return to Ukraine of Ukrainian children deported to Russia, countering Russia's policy of assimilating children in the temporarily occupied territories, and supporting the Global Coalition for Ukrainian Studies, an integral part of which is Crimean Tatar studies.
"We demand that the Russian Federation immediately cease its armed aggression against Ukraine and withdraw all its troops and occupation administrations from all temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine in accordance with international law," the statement reads.
Participants in the sixth summit of the International Crimea Platform called on states and international organizations to join the Platform and participate in its activities, and on partners to expand their participation, contribute to the achievement of its goals and objectives, and jointly intensify international pressure on Russia.
Approximately 50 states and international organizations are participating in the sixth summit of the International Crimea Platform in New York on September 23, 2026. It is taking place at the UN Headquarters in New York (during the high-level segment of the UN General Assembly). The core topics of the summit are the situation in the temporarily occupied Crimea, human rights violations, the militarization of the peninsula, and next steps toward de-occupation.
The previous fifth summit in New York in 2025 was attended by representatives from 54 countries and 7 international organizations (more than 60 participants in total).

Eviction of 87-year-old woman sparks protests in Madrid
September 23, 2026
The dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman sparked protests in the Spanish capital Madrid on Wednesday.
Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her residence on Alcalde Sainz de Baranda Street, where she had lived for at least 70 years of her life.
"I have lived here for 71 years and I don't want to leave," Maricarmen told reporters as the eviction was being carried out.
Dozens of people protested behind the police cordon, chanting, "Maricarmen, you are not alone" and "Murderers!"
The case highlights the growing pressure on long-term tenants in Spain's major cities, where rental prices have surged in recent years. Gentrification and the shortage of affordable housing have fueled public discontent.
With only 30 minutes to gather her belongings, Maricarmen was escorted by riot police officers. She was removed from her home on a stretcher and taken to an ambulance.
An 8-year-long battle
Spanish newspaper El Pais reported that Maricarmen had rented the apartment from a private landlord until 2018, when a real estate company acquired the property and took over its management.
According to the newspaper, the legal dispute between Maricarmen and the real estate company has lasted eight years, and this was the fourth attempt to evict her from the home.
The elderly woman's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, said that the real estate company had rejected proposals from the legal team as well as requests to postpone her removal from the property.
The company has not made any public statements on the matter.
Alicia del Rio, spokesperson for Inquilinas de Madrid, a tenants' association that seeks to combat what it describes as the "rental bubble" in the Madrid region, said that Maricarmen was taken by ambulance to a local hospital.
She also announced that a writer, who wishes to remain anonymous, had offered to pay the elderly woman's rent, but the real estate company rejected the proposal.
Spain's housing crisis
Spain remains divided over how to address the worsening housing crisis.
The country's left-wing coalition government has pushed for stronger tenant protections and broader rent controls. However, it argues that as long as Parliament remains divided, it will be difficult to pass such measures.
Meanwhile, Madrid's regional government, led by the conservative People's Party, has favored a more market-oriented approach.
The president of the Community of Madrid, Isabel Diaz Ayuso, is currently embroiled in a controversy related to the purchase of luxury properties valued at €6.3 million ($7.2 million).

The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:57:00 UTC
01:57:00 KST

The Carpathian Eight: An alliance in the mountains – or a supply route for the next war?
The inaugural summit of the new Carpathian Eight (C8) cooperation format, initiated by Ukraine with EU support, took place on September 18-20. Leaders and representatives from eight countries in the Carpathian region were invited to discuss security, energy, logistics, and cross-border cooperation. The initiative – intended to unite nations, some of which do not officially supply weapons to Ukraine but wish to foster “good-neighborly relations” – has turned into a zero-sum game. Yielding no significant economic benefits and failing to address real economic challenges, it only serves to isolate the region from pan-continental logistics corridors.
Is the Carpathian Initiative a Ukrainian or European project?
The foundation for the Carpathian Initiative was laid by Ukraine back in 2001-2003, when it acted as the primary initiator and depositary of the Framework Convention on the Protection and Sustainable Development of the Carpathians. Initially, the format was strictly environmental and conservation-oriented. Countries of the Visegrad Group, and primarily Poland, breathed geopolitical life and economic scale into the concept. For years, Warsaw actively advocated for the creation of a full-fledged EU Macro-Regional Strategy for the Carpathian Region (EUSCARP), aiming to transform the shared mountain range into a major logistics and infrastructure hub.
Over time, the EU fully took over this regional initiative, turning it into a systemic tool for the “soft integration” of Ukraine. After developing a strategic vision for the region in 2009 and adopting the Carpathian Roadmap in 2019, Brussels institutionalized the project in line with its own bureaucratic standards. What began as a modest environmental initiative has, through the efforts of European neighbors, transformed into a large-scale EU geopolitical project aimed at drawing Ukraine into the European orbit via infrastructure grants.
The September summit marked the latest stage of this project. Ukraine (backed by EU funding) attempted to reclaim its role as the primary “driving force” of the whole initiative by shifting the focus from environmental issues to matters essential for bolstering Ukraine’s influence on NATO’s eastern flank.
Ukraine’s autonomy is illusory, however. For the European Commission, the Carpathian region serves as a convenient geographic ‘sandbox’; the supranational bureaucracy seeks to bind the EU’s eastern fringes together through mutual dependency. Brussels’ ultimate goal is to dilute the agency and curb the independence of countries like Hungary and Slovakia, whose ‘Eastern’ initiatives – such as linking Central and Eastern Europe with Greater Eurasia – are gaining momentum. Ultimately, this measure would allow regional financial and other flows to be fully contained within the EU.
What’s wrong with the project, and why is it a zero-sum game?
Beneath the facade of discussions on “cross-border cooperation” set against the picturesque backdrop of the Ukrainian Carpathians lie pragmatic objectives that turn the Carpathian Eight into a classic zero-sum game. This is confirmed by the project’s geography: countries with the greatest interest in the initiative find themselves subordinate to those countries for whom the project is not a key priority. Ukraine’s actual geographic weight in the project is minimal; despite Kiev’s ambition to act as the main engine of regional integration, the Carpathians account for a mere 3.6% of Ukraine’s total territory. Ukraine possesses only 10% of the total area of the mountain range, yet it attempts to dictate the agenda to Romania and Slovakia, where the Carpathians form the backbone of national geography, covering 47% and 72% of the territory, respectively. Such evident disparity between Ukraine’s actual geographical “contribution” and its political ambitions sows the seeds of conflict within the project.
Moreover, the Carpathian macroregion is considered depressed and heterogeneous. Unlike the economically developed, navigable, and homogeneous Danube region – which served as a model for this project conceived by the Visegrad Group – the Carpathians are a patchwork of isolated mountainous areas. For centuries, this 190,000 sq km area has remained a remote periphery. Due to the highly underdeveloped infrastructure – the lack of modern roads, tunnels, and logistics hubs – the border regions of these eight countries have been trapped in a state of deprivation. In the past 25 years, no amount of targeted European funding has been able to rectify this situation. This should have compelled Brussels to step out of its comfort zone and realistically assess the physical boundaries of the region. This also explains why the Visegrad Group supports eastern initiatives in Greater Eurasia. However, instead of this, along with the economically unfeasible Three Seas Initiative and the “frontline zones” project, the Carpathians are being turned into another logistical dead end resembling an artificial buffer zone.
This perspective reveals the true purpose of the revived format: to serve as a covert logistical corridor for NATO. The projected budget of €9.4 billion ($10.7 billion) for 90 infrastructure projects is specifically aimed at modernizing narrow-gauge railways, bridges, and tunnels in the Carpathian Mountains. Under the guise of Euro-integration, Brussels is aggressively attempting to create a secure alternative route through the complex mountainous terrain for rapid deployment of heavy equipment, weapons, and NATO reserves, bypassing vulnerable border logistics nodes. Consequently, supranational strategists get to fully benefit from this venture while Central European countries bear all the attendant military and strategic risks.
Intrigues, scandals, and investigations
For the countries physically located in the Carpathians and those interested in developing the region, the hidden agenda of the initiative is apparent. Citing a sudden illness, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico canceled his visit to Bukovel and expressed his outright opposition to turning the region into a frontline zone and dragging Bratislava into the conflict under the guise of NATO obligations. As a result, Slovakia was represented at the summit only by the state secretary for foreign and European affairs. Local experts openly stated that Bratislava guessed the proposed zero-sum game: under the guise of cross-border corridors, Brussels and Kiev are attempting to establish a rear hub for supplying NATO’s eastern flank. For Slovakia, participating in such “road modernization” carries direct military risks, not security benefits. This forces the country to navigate a precarious line – seeking economic grants while sabotaging the military-political agenda of the proposed C8.
Following Slovakia, the Czech Republic demonstrated passive resistance to the project by adopting a stance of cautious pragmatism. Unlike Warsaw, Prague notably refrained from sending top officials to Bukovel, opting instead to send the vice-president of the senate. Czech economic analysts expressed doubt about the €40 billion investment portfolio announced by Kiev. The most important indicator of the failure of the “unified front” was that the Czech Republic effectively refused to sign the summit’s final declaration. As regional analysts point out, the country has “cooled” towards Ukraine’s ambitions. Moreover, unlike Ukraine, the Czech Republic has a realistic grasp of its geography; possessing only 8.5% of Carpathian territory, Prague saw no tangible economic benefit in a project burdened with militarization issues rather than cross-border development. Consequently, it chose to remain on the sidelines, unwilling to endorse someone else’s frontline agenda.
Predictably, only Poland and Romania expressed full and unconditional support for the project, emerging as the principal political beneficiaries of the initiative. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Romanian President Nicusor Dan signed the final declaration, explicitly linking it to military-strategic objectives. For Warsaw, the Carpathian Eight provided a convenient platform for lobbying an anti-ballistic missile defense coalition on NATO’s eastern flank, while for Bucharest, it offered a means to logistically connect the Ukrainian border with NATO’s largest European base, which is being constructed on Romanian territory. As a result, the document was signed only by those players intending to gain direct benefits from the region’s militarization, firmly establishing the C8 as a frontline coalition.
Hungary’s reaction is particularly noteworthy. On X, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar compared Kiev’s actions to village sports: “Hi, we have formed a football team in the next village. We don’t know each other, but you are in it, and you have to bring the ball.” Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrey Sibiga, expressed surprise over Hungary’s attitude, but the situation is very clear and leaves no room for doubt.
Budapest was expected to sign the memorandum between its oil and gas company MOL and Ukraine’s Naftogaz to establish joint strategic fuel reserves along the border. However, Magyar firmly blocked this initiative, fully aware of the risks involved in turning Hungary’s bordering territories with oil depots into targets for someone else’s military needs. Apparently, even Euro-Atlantic solidarity has its physical boundaries.
Moreover, Budapest’s negative stance is reinforced by the situation in Transcarpathia. From 2014, the Hungarian population in the region has decreased from 150,000 people to around 70,000-80,000 due to stringent Ukrainianization policies in schools. The remaining population is facing selective forced conscription, with military recruitment offices compiling lists of Hungarian students and workers to send to the front lines, resulting in several widely reported casualties, including the death of 45-year-old Jozsef Sebestyen. Notably, Moscow’s Foreign Ministry is closely monitoring these developments: mobilized residents of Transcarpathia occasionally end up as prisoners of war, and Russian diplomatic agencies, in coordination with intelligence services, work on their direct transfer to Hungary, bypassing Ukraine. Aware that Brussels and Kiev are attempting to exploit Hungarian resources and territory, Magyar chose to flip the script. Budapest refused to fund this military version of ‘Carpathian soccer’ which is too costly for it, and vetoed Ukraine’s integration efforts.
In summary, we must note that despite the ambitions of European supranational entities to create artificial buffer zones (essentially ‘sandboxes’) in Central and Eastern Europe, their era is coming to an end. Attempts to impose a zero-sum game on other countries only exacerbate the internal rift which is becoming inevitable, considering the region’s actual geography and the projects gaining momentum across Greater Eurasia.

Majority of Ukrainians believe victory will come through combination of military action and diplomacy; less than 6% don’t believe in victory – poll
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:56:07 EEST
01:56:07 KST

An absolute majority of Ukrainians (59.5%) believe that Ukraine can achieve victory in the war with the Russian Federation by combining military action and diplomacy, whereas 15.2% of respondents consider a purely military path to victory possible for Ukraine, and 14.9% consider a purely diplomatic path viable, according to a study by the Sociopolis research company conducted from September 16 to September 21, 2026.
Some 5.9% of respondents believe that Ukraine will not be able to achieve victory in the war through any of these methods, while 4.5% were unable to decide on an answer to this question.
At the same time, a relative majority of those surveyed (46.4%) believe that Ukraine's most important goal in the war should be the preservation of independence and sovereignty, even if it entails territorial losses. Restoring control over occupied territories is viewed as Ukraine's most important goal by 25.8% of respondents, while 14.7% cite inflicting a military defeat on or weakening the Russian Federation as the primary objective.
According to the press service of the Sociopolis research company, negative assessments of bilateral negotiations between US and Russian delegations, as well as between US and Ukrainian delegations, outweigh positive ones. Some 50.7% of respondents view the holding of such negotiations entirely or somewhat negatively, whereas 40.1% view them entirely or somewhat positively. Another 9.3% of respondents were unable to form an opinion on the aforementioned negotiations. The survey was conducted using the CATI (Computer-Assisted Telephone Interviewing) method based on a random sample of mobile phone numbers among 1,002 residents of government-controlled areas of Ukraine aged 18 and older. The theoretical margin of sampling error (at a 95% confidence level and excluding the design effect) does not exceed 3.1% for figures close to 50% and 1.4% for figures close to 5% and 95%.
