Trump's Board of Peace proposes $2.45B to rebuild Gaza
September 23, 2026
US President Donald Trump's Board of Peace has proposed a six-month plan for the reconstruction and governance of the Palestinian Gaza Strip, costing some $2.45 billion (roughly €2.15 billion).
The plan was unveiled during a meeting on Wednesday.
It involves a 66-project blueprint to kick things off, but acknowledges the enormous hurdles that must be overcome to rebuild the devastated enclave, where last October's ceasefire has only slowed Israeli attacks.
What do we know about the Board of Peace Gaza reconstruction plans?
Former UK prime minister Tony Blair, who serves on the organization's executive board, said that Palestinians in Gaza "don't need a slogan; they need a solution."
The reconstruction and governance projects include estimated spending for:
- Temporary housing
- Rubble removal
- Hospital repairs
- Economic recovery
- Deployment of a multinational security force
The initiatives are all designed to support Trump's 20-point plan to end the war.
"The need is immense," the board said, estimating that full reconstruction will cost roughly $35.2 billion over the medium term and another $71.4 billion in the next decade.
The proposal also calls for repairing border crossings, restoring electricity and water infrastructure, deploying 25,000 portable solar power kits and permanently filling tunnels beneath sites needed for priority reconstruction projects, as per an Axios report released ahead of the meeting.
Where do things stand in Gaza now?
Trump's Gaza peace plan, which ushered in the October 10 ceasefire last year, included:
- Additional Israeli military withdrawals from Gaza
- The disarmament of the Palestinian militant group Hamas
- The arrival of an international peacekeeping force
- A new apolitical Palestinian government to administer the territory's day-to-day business
However, almost a year on, completion of the plan has remained elusive..
Israel still occupies roughly 60% of the territory and regularly carries out deadly attacks it says target Hamas militants. Gaza health authorities say over 1,300 Palestinians, mostly civilians, have been killed since the ceasefire. The Israeli military says four of its soldiers have been killed.
Hamas, designated as a terrorist group by several countries, has thus far not given up its weapons, despite on some occasions expressing its readiness to do so. Israel has said it will not withdraw from areas it occupies until the group fully disarms and is removed from the enclave.
Meanwhile, most Palestinians continue to live in tent camps or ruins of their former homes, with no international military force or new government materializing.
The Board of Peace's high representative, Nikolay Mladenov, has said that progress relies heavily on Hamas disarming, but he has also called on Israel to scale back its military operations.

NEW DELHI, September 23. /TASS/. The law on new US sanctions, which provides for restrictions against main buyers of Russian energy resources (Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act), will not affect India’s oil purchases from Russia, Arvind Kumar, Professor at the School of International Relations at Nalanda University, told TASS.
"Basically, there is no impact on India. India is very confident to keep buying oil from Russia. So, this newly signed Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act by [US] President [Donald] Trump virtually will have no meaning for India," the expert said. "India is also going to be more confident in terms of its assertiveness in its foreign policy in working with the Russian Federation and keep continuing its ongoing cooperation," he added.
According to Kumar, Trump "is not understanding the larger issue that could perhaps impede the overall direct relations between India and the US." "The way they have signed the Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, which gives the US government the power to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that buy Russian oil and gas, is perhaps going to impact the US negatively. I think that is something which they have to consider because that will perhaps delay the whole process of the trade negotiation with India," he stressed.
"I think India’s reaction will be mute <…>. I think India will not do anything which is going to be in fact closed door. India will certainly negotiate with the US from a position of strength and that strength will obviously see that President Trump gives waiver to India," the expert said, adding that "the US will be very cautious in terms of dealing with India." "India will have the geopolitical space to work with both the US and Russia," he concluded.
On September 18, US President Donald Trump signed a bill designed to expand sanctions against Russia. It also provides for secondary sanctions against Russia’s trading partners, among other things. The document authorizes the US to impose 100% import tariffs on countries that are major buyers of Russian oil and gas. India is among them.

Alzheimer’s disease: which symptoms should raise concern and what may reduce the risk
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
19:28:21 EEST
01:28:21 KST

Alzheimer’s disease: which symptoms should raise concern and what may reduce the risk
Kyiv • UNN
Alzheimer’s manifests through progressive changes in memory, behavior, sleep, and gait. The doctor recommends physical activity, sleep, and health monitoring.
Alzheimer’s disease may manifest not only through memory problems. The first signs may also include changes in emotional state, difficulty performing familiar activities, sleep or gait disturbances. In an interview with UNN, neurologist of the highest category and Candidate of Medical Sciences Tetiana Maikova spoke in detail about what Alzheimer’s disease is, how to recognize it, and whether it can be cured.
Details
According to the doctor, Alzheimer’s disease is associated with degenerative changes in the brain, but it can begin differently in different people. However, ordinary age-related forgetfulness does not necessarily indicate an illness, which is why it is important to pay attention to whether the disturbances recur and gradually become more severe.
Some people may forget how to cook borscht, even though they have cooked it all their lives. Some may fail to recognize their loved ones. Some may forget how they ended up in a particular place. Others may develop difficulty walking. Emotional disturbances may also occur — depression, anxiety, increased irritability, or aggression. The key point is that these symptoms recur systematically and progress. If a person forgets where they put their glasses once but then remembers, that does not yet mean they have the disease
The disease most often develops in older age, and the risk increases over the years, the expert says. At the same time, early-onset forms of the disease also exist.
Usually, this disease develops later in life — statistically, most cases occur after the age of 60. However, early-onset forms of Alzheimer’s disease can also occur, even at age 40. As a rule, these are hereditary forms, when a specific gene associated with dementia is present in the family
According to the neurologist, it is impossible to detect the disease through a single examination alone. However, close relatives can play an important role, since they are usually the first to notice that a loved one’s behavior or habits have changed.
There is no special examination that can be administered to everyone and provide certainty that a person will develop Alzheimer’s disease. An MRI can show signs of neurodegeneration, but these signs alone do not confirm the diagnosis. We assess clinical manifestations more extensively and use tests. Most often, it is relatives, friends, or colleagues who notice that a person is becoming different
The doctor advises paying particular attention to lifestyle. Among the important factors, she names physical activity, social connections, having a purpose, and controlling metabolism. At the same time, she emphasizes the importance of adequate sleep.
The brain needs to know that it is needed — this is very important. A consistently active lifestyle, movement, engaging activities, work, and communication with people are necessary for a fulfilling life. It is important for a person to have a purpose. Adequate sleep is also necessary, because the immune system recovers at night and processes related to the restoration of the body take place
The doctor also emphasizes that prolonged stress can affect brain function. Therefore, it is worth listening to yourself and seeking medical attention in a timely manner.
Emotional stress triggers many negative processes in the body through the brain’s systems. If a person has difficulty coping with stress and cannot switch off, this is already a reason to seek help. After the age of 60, sleep disturbances, depression, anxiety, and panic attacks should be treated
Can Alzheimer’s disease be prevented?
The neurologist separately emphasizes the role of chronic pain and physical activity. She advises not to ignore pain that prevents a person from sleeping or moving normally, as this also indicates exhaustion of brain activity.
Chronic pain is a constant source of strain on the brain. If the pain is severe and interferes with sleep or movement, it must be treated
To reduce the risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease, Tetiana Maikova also emphasized the importance of diet. In particular, the doctor advises ensuring an adequate intake of protein and vegetables and generally following the principles of the Mediterranean diet. She also recommends limiting unhealthy drinks.
Protein should be part of the diet every day—it includes meat, fish, eggs, and fermented dairy products. Vegetables are also necessary. As for caffeinated drinks, they should be limited as much as possible: coffee, tea, cocoa, and cola, because caffeine makes the body expend more energy. And at night, this energy needs to be restored—which is why sleep is very important
Can Alzheimer's disease be cured?
For a long time, one of the main areas of Alzheimer's research was the so-called amyloid theory. According to the doctor, it determined the direction of much of the subsequent scientific research and the development of relevant drugs.
In 2006, the journal Nature published an article by scientists from the University of Minnesota. They showed that the main cause of Alzheimer's disease was amyloid plaques—proteins that disrupt communication between cells. There are also tau proteins, which impair their functioning. At that point, the entire world decided that if we fought amyloid plaques and tau proteins, we would be able to cure people with Alzheimer's disease
However, this theory turned out to be false, and the research had been falsified.
Last year, I believe, a relatively little-known independent researcher repeated the experiments once conducted at the University of Minnesota, on the basis of which the relevant conclusions had been drawn. His results could not be replicated, so he reviewed the photographs from the study and found signs of falsification. This shows that such things happen even in global science. At the same time, the journal Nature retracted its 2006 article on the amyloid theory
Unfortunately, this situation also affected the subsequent development of drugs against the disease, which failed to produce the expected results for patients.
For twenty years, the entire world followed the wrong path, and billions were spent on creating drugs against amyloid plaques. The plaques were removed, but Alzheimer's disease itself was not cured. It later became clear that plaques may be more of a protective mechanism in Alzheimer's disease rather than the cause of the condition. Therefore, approaches to studying the disease are now different
Thus, at present, treating Alzheimer's disease remains a complex issue, while approaches to its causes continue to be studied.
Alzheimer's disease is not a disease with a single cause. It is the result of many changes in the body that may ultimately lead to a loss of energy in the brain. Various approaches are now being studied, including their impact on neuronal function, metabolism, neuroinflammation, and deep brain stimulation. We still need to conduct a great deal of research to better understand how to influence these processes
For prevention, the doctor advises remaining physically and socially active, maintaining intellectual activity, and not giving up social interaction after retirement. She also recommends creating safe conditions for adequate sleep. In her view, caring for the brain should be part of a person's lifestyle at any age.

Red Cross says no access to prisoners of war in Russia since 2024
- The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has not had access to prisoners of war held in Russia since 2024, despite previously visiting thousands on both sides of the Ukraine conflict.
- ICRC emphasises that visiting prisoners is essential under the Geneva Conventions to check conditions, provide support, and communicate with families.
- The organisation is seeking to regain access to Russian detention facilities to ensure prisoners' welfare and provide families with information about their loved ones' fate.
AI generated
GENEVA - The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has been denied access to visit prisoners of war held in Russian detention since 2024, the organisation confirmed on Sept 23.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of neighbouring Ukraine in February 2022, the two countries have swopped thousands of prisoners of war and are both believed to be holding thousands more in captivity.
ICRC said on Sept 23 that it from the start and through August had visited more than 9,800 PoWs on both sides in the conflict, but “mainly in Ukraine”.
While it did conduct visits of prisoners held by Russia early on, an ICRC spokeswoman told AFP in an email that it currently “does not have full access to all PoWs”.
“We visit PoWs and detained civilians in Ukraine, (but) in Russia our last visit was in 2024,” she said, confirming a report by the BBC.
“We seek to regain access to facilities to visit those deprived of liberty (including PoWs) consistent with our mandate.”
Visiting prisoners of war is core to the ICRC’s mission enshrined in the Geneva Conventions, which define the laws of war.
Countries, it pointed out, were responsible for ensuring it had access to “see all prisoners of war and other persons deprived of their liberty... (and) to all places where they are held and be allowed to repeat visits as often as needed”.
The organisation insists that such visits are vital for checking detention conditions, offering support and sometimes books, hygiene items and other personal necessities, and also to relay information between the prisoners and their loved ones.
“Families have the right to know about the fate of their loved ones, whether they are alive, wounded or dead,” it said.
“Many have waited anxiously for many long months, and they need answers today,” it added.
“They are impatient, as are we.” AFP

Israel’s climate crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:22:21 UTC
01:22:21 KST

Israel’s climate crimes
TEHRAN - Israel’s environmental damage in Palestine has accompanied the destruction of Palestinian lives, homes and livelihoods. Farmlands and olive groves have been burned or destroyed, while homes, vehicles, cities and refugee camps have been repeatedly bombarded.
The thick clouds of soot produced by the bombardment of Gaza have also raised alarm among environmentalists over the war’s devastating impact on the environment.
In September 2025, the Palestinian Institute for Climate Strategy, together with Tipping Point North South, estimated that Israel and its allies owed Palestinians $148 billion in military- and conflict-related climate reparations dating back to the Nakba. The estimate is based on the calculated climate costs of traceable military-related emissions and assigns $103 billion to Israel and $40.8 billion to the United States, with smaller amounts attributed to several European allies. The researchers stressed that the figure represents only a measurable portion of the broader environmental and social damage.
Israel’s burning of agricultural land and forests in southern Lebanon and the destruction of homes in villages and cities, including Beirut, have further compounded the environmental damage caused by the conflict.
The war on Gaza has also generated enormous greenhouse-gas emissions. A study published in One Earth in March 2026 estimated that direct emissions from the conflict exceeded 1.3 million tons of CO? equivalent by January 2025. When emissions associated with pre-war military infrastructure and post-war reconstruction are included, the estimate rises to 33.2 million tons of CO? equivalent. Reconstruction alone accounts for an estimated 31.4 million tons.
The environmental consequences, however, extend far beyond carbon emissions. The war has created serious risks for both the Mediterranean marine environment and Gaza’s groundwater system. The two problems are closely linked: the destruction of water and sanitation infrastructure has allowed pollutants from the land and underground water system to reach the Mediterranean.
The most immediate impact has been the enormous discharge of untreated sewage into the sea. Gaza’s wastewater-treatment system has largely collapsed. UNEP estimated that in March 2024, around 60,000 cubic meters of wastewater and sewage were being discharged into the environment every day, primarily into the Mediterranean.
This wastewater can carry pathogens and disease-causing microorganisms, nitrogen and phosphorus that contribute to eutrophication and oxygen depletion, microplastics, organic pollutants, industrial chemicals and other hazardous substances. Damaged infrastructure and military activity may also introduce heavy metals and other contaminants.
UNEP’s September 2025 assessment found that Gaza’s marine and coastal ecosystems had been contaminated by sewage, solid waste and munitions. However, it said the precise scale and chemical composition of the contamination could not yet be determined because adequate environmental sampling has been severely constrained.
The war has also devastated marine life and fisheries. Pollution threatens Gaza’s coastal ecosystems, fish stocks and other marine organisms. UNEP has said the conflict has virtually eliminated Gaza’s fishing livelihoods, while the destruction of environmental-management systems has made contamination of the seafood chain more difficult to control.
There is also a longer-term concern. If enormous quantities of war debris are dumped into the sea or used for land reclamation without proper sorting and treatment, asbestos, heavy metals, hydrocarbons and other contaminants could enter marine ecosystems and potentially the food chain.
The war has also placed Gaza’s Coastal Aquifer, the enclave’s principal natural freshwater resource, under severe additional pressure. This could prove to be one of the conflict’s most serious long-term environmental consequences.
The destruction of sewage networks and wastewater-treatment plants, combined with widespread reliance on cesspits, allows contaminated water to infiltrate the porous ground and reach the aquifer. UNEP’s 2025 assessment says groundwater contamination is likely and warns that the destruction of piped systems and increased reliance on cesspits have increased the risk of aquifer contamination.
Potential contaminants include sewage and pathogens, nitrates and other nutrients, chemicals, heavy metals, hydrocarbons, and pollutants associated with munitions and destroyed infrastructure.
Soil contamination has further aggravated the groundwater problem. The crisis is not simply a matter of sewage. The destruction of buildings has generated tens of millions of tons of rubble, while military activity has contaminated soil with munitions, solid waste and untreated sewage.
UNEP’s September 2025 assessment estimated that the destruction of some 78 percent of Gaza’s buildings had generated approximately 61 million tons of debris. It warned that around 15 percent of the debris could pose relatively high contamination risks because of asbestos, industrial waste and heavy metals if waste streams are not properly segregated.
Rainwater moving through contaminated soil and rubble can carry pollutants downward toward groundwater. At the same time, the destruction and compaction of soil have reduced its capacity to absorb water, increasing runoff and reducing groundwater recharge.
Seawater intrusion could become an even greater problem. Gaza’s aquifer was already being over-pumped before the war. Excessive groundwater extraction lowers freshwater levels and can allow Mediterranean seawater to penetrate the aquifer.
The war has severely damaged pumping, storage, desalination and wastewater systems, making it much more difficult to manage both groundwater depletion and contamination. UNEP’s assessment found extensive damage to Gaza’s water infrastructure and warned that the environmental consequences could persist for decades.
The environmental damage is therefore not necessarily confined to Gaza’s shoreline.
The Mediterranean is a semi-enclosed sea, and pollutants discharged from Gaza can be transported by currents and coastal circulation. The precise regional extent of contamination remains uncertain because environmental monitoring has been severely restricted. Scientific modeling has nevertheless examined how wastewater pollutants can disperse from Gaza’s coastal waters into the Mediterranean.
UNEP’s latest assessment warns that repairing the damage to Gaza’s water resources, soils, freshwater ecosystems and marine environment could take decades.
Israel’s environmental impact on Palestinian land also predates the current war. Palestinian environmental advocates have for years documented the destruction of agricultural land and restrictions affecting water and other natural resources. Among the practices cited by Palestinian environmental groups is the spraying of herbicides on agricultural areas in Gaza and the destruction of farmland.
Palestinian environmental advocates have also accused Israel of policies that systematically restrict Palestinian access to water resources. Najla Abdellatif, founder of Zero Waste Palestine, told Middle East Eye that she had met Palestinian farmers whose groundwater sources were affected by measures involving Israel’s state-run water company.
Taken together, the destruction of agricultural land, water and sanitation infrastructure, soil, coastal ecosystems and natural resources has created an environmental crisis whose consequences are likely to extend well beyond the end of the fighting.

Explainer-Why new war in Ethiopia’s Tigray threatens to trigger wider conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:21:36 UTC
01:21:36 KST

Explainer-Why new war in Ethiopia’s Tigray threatens to trigger wider conflict
LONDON, Sept 23 - Regional forces in northern Ethiopia's Tigray on Wednesday seized control of three airports and clashed in multiple locations with federal troops, signalling the start of a major offensive after months of growing tensions.
The move shatters a peace deal that ended the 2020-2022 conflict between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and federal forces, and comes amid a backdrop of deteriorating ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea, Sudan's civil war, tensions over Red Sea access, and the Horn of Africa being dragged into Middle East conflicts.
WHY DOES NEW FIGHTING IN TIGRAY THREATEN A WIDER WAR IN ETHIOPIA?
The Pretoria Agreement, which formally ended a conflict that killed hundreds of thousands of people, has been under strain for months, each side accusing the other of violating the deal.
The peace process began to unravel after splits emerged within the TPLF, and a hardline faction of the party reasserted control over the region, kicking out an interim administration.
Most recently, the TPLF formed an alliance with six other armed groups from across Ethiopia, including former enemies from the war, aimed at overthrowing Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government.
It is not clear how many members of the alliance were involved in clashes on Wednesday but Ethiopia is home to many heavily armed regional groups.
Abiy's government has accused Eritrea of financially backing members of the alliance, allegations Asmara has denied.
WHAT ROLE WILL ERITREA PLAY?
As the situation unfolds, all eyes will be on Asmara, which has endured a turbulent relationship with Addis Ababa since independence in 1993.
Soon after coming to power, Abiy won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019 for ending two decades of hostility between Ethiopia and Eritrea.
When the civil war erupted the following year, Eritrean forces then supported Ethiopia's federal army. Relations have deteriorated since the Pretoria peace agreement, which Eritrea was not party to despite having fought in the war.
Access to the Red Sea is another flash point.
Landlocked Ethiopia had a coastline for decades until Eritrea broke away. Since then, Addis Ababa has repeatedly argued that restoring access to the sea - specifically the port of Assab - is vital for its long term security and economic development. Asmara has said it fears Addis Ababa will try to take Assab by force.
Earlier this month, the US government lifted sanctions on Eritrean Defense Forces and other entities.
It is not clear what impact removing sanctions would have on any conflict in Ethiopia, but the move is seen as a nod by the Trump administration to Eritrea’s strategic coastline opposite Saudi Arabia, and warning Ethiopia not to go to war with Asmara.
WHICH REGIONAL RISKS RAISE THE STAKES THIS TIME AROUND?
Diplomats warn that a renewed Tigray war would no longer be a largely isolated Ethiopian conflict.
Instead, it would unfold as the Horn of Africa faces its most volatile security environment in years, with war raging in Sudan, persistent instability in Somalia, tensions over the Nile and expanding war and geopolitics from the Middle East spilling into the region.
Ethiopia has been accused of backing the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) paramilitary group, which is fighting Sudan’s army in one of the world’s deadliest conflicts.
This support, which Ethiopia denies, is in line with its close relationship with the United Arab Emirates, the most active Gulf power in the region which UN experts say is also supporting the RSF. The UAE has denied the accusations.
For its part, Eritrea is closer to Sudan and has cultivated relatively close ties with Egypt, which is a long-time rival of Ethiopia. Egypt and Sudan both see Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, built on a tributary of the Nile, as a serious threat to their vital water supplies. REUTERS

Yemeni government in military and diplomatic push to reverse Houthi gains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:21:18 UTC

Yemeni government in military and diplomatic push to reverse Houthi gains
Government claims battlefield advances as diplomats attempt to put anti-Houthi fight at UN centre stage.
The Yemeni government suffered a significant blow earlier this month when it lost the country’s Red Sea coast to the Houthi rebels. It is now working on a two-pronged strategy, militarily and diplomatically, to restore the initiative and prevent the Houthis from consolidating their gains and pushing further into government-held territory.
Saudi-backed government forces claimed on Tuesday to have seized the strategic Mount Qarafan in southern Taiz’s al-Shamayatayn district. The military reported killing five Iranian-allied Houthi fighters and injuring 20 others during the operation.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3How much is UK supporting Saudi Arabia in its war with Iran-backed Houthis?
- list 2 of 3Despite flurry of New York diplomacy, US-Iran deal remains elusive
- list 3 of 3Yemen government forces claim control of Mount Qarfan in Taiz
Pro-government Homeland Shield Forces, also known as the Quwat Dira’ al-Watan in Arabic, also thwarted a Houthi infiltration attempt on the Kahboub front, which overlooks the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait. Government forces also reported the capture of Mount Zalat, near Kahboub, on Tuesday.
The battles in the mountainous regions of southwestern Yemen are critical because of the commanding positions the peaks being fought over provide. Qarafan overlooks valleys linking southern Taiz with western coastal areas, as the Houthis attempt to encircle government-held areas in the governorate. Kahboub, meanwhile, is significant because Houthi forces have been attempting to secure the high ground overlooking Bab al-Mandab to prevent a government counterattack and expand the territory under their control.
The Houthis, meanwhile, have claimed Saudi Arabia has conducted air strikes in Taiz, al-Jawf, and Marib. Riyadh has not confirmed the strikes.
The humanitarian toll is mounting, with recent hostilities displacing approximately 132,000 people, including 75,000 in Taiz alone, according to the International Organization for Migration.
UNGA diplomatic push
Meanwhile, at the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Yemeni government officials are attempting to rally support for their push against the Houthis.
Presidential Leadership Council member Abdullah al-Alimi is leading Yemen’s delegation and will address the General Assembly later this week, but has already met US politicians.
Foreign Minister Afrah al-Zouba is also attending the world gathering, and called for the disarmament of non-state armed groups at a meeting on the General Assembly’s sidelines.
Other world leaders have included references to events in Yemen in their own addresses to the General Assembly.
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani addressed the assembly, reaffirming support for UN efforts to reach a comprehensive political resolution. He emphasised that any settlement must be based on the outcomes of Yemen’s 2013-14 UN-facilitated national dialogue, in a manner that preserves Yemen’s unity, sovereignty, security, and stability.
Ireland also highlighted the crisis, expressing deep concern about the humanitarian situation and stressing that freedom of navigation must be protected in the Bab al-Mandab strait.
Tactical coastal battles
The Yemeni government is focusing its diplomatic efforts on impressing on other countries the dangers of Houthi control of the Bab al-Mandab strait, and the threat of more attacks against shipping in the region.
While the government has the support of Saudi Arabia, many other world powers are avoiding any involvement in the conflict, including the US. Washington is already entangled in a war with the Houthis’ primary ally, Iran.
The Yemeni government’s current military counterattacks against the Houthis therefore remain localised, rather than a larger campaign, analysts say.
Ibrahim Jalal, a Yemen-focused analyst, told Al Jazeera that the government’s recent attacks are an attempt to shift the momentum.
“Partially and tactically, the Yemeni Armed Forces stopped part of the Houthi rush seeking to secure and stabilise expansion on the coast, and moved to limited counter-attacks in the Taiz-Lahj [region] … while regaining dominant heights and positions,” Jalal told Al Jazeera. “The government is gradually regaining the initiative, but it has not yet launched a broad military campaign to reclaim the coast and other areas.”
Jalal noted the significance of the geography being fought over.
“Taiz is considered a key to protecting Bab al-Mandab from the east and communication routes with Lahj and Aden; therefore, regaining its dominant southern and western heights prevents the Houthis from stabilising and securing coastal gains and expanding south,” Jalal added.
Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow at Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme, told Al Jazeera that reasserting control remains a severe challenge for government forces.
“It is impossible for the government to regain momentum unless it manages to reclaim Bab al-Mandab,” Al-Muslimi said, adding that he believes it is unlikely, despite the flat and open nature of the geography of the region, which would make it easier for air power to target the Houthis.
Al-Muslimi said that, for the Houthis, the battles in Taiz may not be about seeking full control of the governorate, but instead be a way of keeping the main battle away from their newly gained territories.
“In Taiz, in my opinion, the Houthis do not need to control it as long as they besiege it, and in reality, they will not try to control it because it is a burden more than an opportunity,” Al-Muslimi noted.

However, the channel noted that the smoke could potentially be originating from a nearby thermal power plant (CHPP), leaving the exact impact site unconfirmed.
In response to the aerial threat, regional authorities declared a “drone danger” alert across Bashkortostan on the morning of September 23. Operations at Ufa International Airport were temporarily suspended, with strict restrictions placed on all arriving and departing flights during the attack, Astra reported.
The airport later resumed its normal flight schedule, and the regional drone alert was officially lifted. As of the afternoon of September 23, local Russian government officials had not yet released a formal statement acknowledging the attack or detailing any potential infrastructure damage.
It was recently reported that a major fire continued burning at Rosneft’s Kuibyshev Oil Refinery in Samara following Ukrainian drone strikes, while three major oil refineries in Ufa preemptively depressurized their systems during a drone attack as well.

Ethiopia: Where does the Tigray conflict go from here?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:13:00 UTC
01:13:00 KST

Ethiopia: Where does the Tigray conflict go from here?
September 23, 2026
The fighting reported in and around Ethiopia's northern Tigray region marks more than another episode of tension between the federal government in Addis Ababa and the region's leadership. It raises a fundamental question: What remains of the fragile peace established in 2022 — and where does the conflict go from here?
From 2020 to 2022, Ethiopia was devastated by a civil war between the federal government in Addis Ababa and Tigray's regional leadership. The conflict drew in neighboring regions and foreign troops from Eritrea, leading to a humanitarian crisis that displaced millions and left hundreds of thousands dead.
While a peace agreement halted the worst of the bloodshed in late 2022, it left many political and territorial disputes unresolved.
DW spoke to witnesses in the towns of Abala and Erebti on the border with Tigray who confirmed that new fighting had taken place there between Tigray forces and Ethiopian federal troops. Humanitarian sources also reported clashes in the area. Ethiopian Airlines has suspended flights to the cities of Mekelle, Shire and Axum, citing the "current situation in the Tigray region."
Reports that Tigray forces have taken control of airports in the region could not be independently verified by DW.
For Oslo-based peace researcher Kjetil Tronvoll, however, the latest developments represent a decisive escalation.
"I think the war has already begun," Tronvoll told DW.
German security analyst Gerrit Kurtz of the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP) in Berlin also sees the developments as a serious escalation.
"This is a step towards a war," he told DW.
Two competing narratives
The two sides are presenting fundamentally different accounts of what triggered the latest escalation.
In a statement issued on September 23, the National Regional Government of Tigray said its forces had been responding defensively to an attack by the federal government. It accused Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government of launching a new "genocidal invasion" and said Tigray forces had been ordered to defend the population.
The Tigray government also accused Addis Ababa of carrying out air and drone strikes and artillery attacks in recent months. It said it had previously refrained from responding to what it described as repeated provocations in an effort to de-escalate the situation.
The allegations could not independently be verified. The federal government, meanwhile, has portrayed the developments as part of a broader coordinated threat involving armed groups opposed to the prime minister.
The competing narratives illustrate one of the central problems facing any renewed peace effort: The parties do not even agree on the basic interpretation of the escalation.
A fragile peace under pressure
The current crisis cannot be separated from the shortcomings of the 2022 Pretoria peace agreement. The deal ended two years of devastating war between the federal government and the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), but it did not resolve some of the conflict's underlying political and territorial disputes.
Western Tigray remains particularly contentious. The return of hundreds of thousands of displaced people remains unresolved, while questions over Tigray's political representation and its relationship with the federal government continue to fuel tensions.
"The Pretoria agreement stopped the fighting, but it did not resolve the underlying political conflict," Tronvoll says.
At the heart of that conflict is a fundamental disagreement over Ethiopia's political order. The TPLF has traditionally defended a strong federal structure and substantial regional autonomy. Abiy Ahmed's government has pursued a more centralized political model.
The issue is therefore not simply whether individual provisions of the peace agreement are implemented. It is also about competing visions of how Ethiopia should be governed.
Former enemies join forces
The emergence of an alliance of seven armed groups opposing Abiy adds another layer of complexity.
The grouping includes the TPLF, Fano forces from the state of Amhara and the Oromo Liberation Army from another regional state within Ethiopia. Some of these organizations were bitter enemies during the Tigray war. Their decision to cooperate therefore represents a significant political development — but not necessarily a durable alliance.
Kurtz says the alliance has been developing for some time and that some of its leaders have apparently already met.
"It was a very important development," he says. "The alliance has been in the making for a long time."
At the same time, he points to the fundamental differences between its members.
"All the political differences that they have are certainly there to resolve once their overall joint aim is achieved, which is overthrowing the government of Abiy."
Tronvoll similarly describes the cooperation as primarily tactical. The question is whether the groups can turn their shared opposition to Abiy into a lasting political and military strategy.
There is another complicating factor: Eritrea.
The Ethiopian government has accused neighboring Eritrea of supporting the alliance. Eritrea has rejected such allegations. Kurtz says there have been reports of contacts between the armed groups and Eritrea, but stresses that the new alliance itself appears to be a domestic grouping.
The geography of the alliance is another obstacle. Its members operate in different parts of Ethiopia and pursue different political objectives. Coordinating military operations across such distances would be difficult.
Can the escalation still be contained?
The most urgent question is whether the current fighting can still be contained before it develops into another full-scale war.
Kurtz argues that the immediate priority is straightforward: The forces involved in the fighting need to stop.
"Both the Ethiopian armed forces as well as the Tigray security forces are involved in active hostilities right now. So they should stop this," he says.
But bringing the fighting to an end will require more than a ceasefire on the ground. Ethiopia's conflict has become increasingly fragmented. Armed groups are operating not only in Tigray, but also in Amhara and Oromia, two other regional states within Ethiopia. Regional actors such as Eritrea are potentially also playing a role.
Who can mediate?
International actors have repeatedly warned about the risk of renewed conflict. Yet sustained diplomatic engagement has so far failed to produce a new political process.
The United States remains an important actor, according to Kurtz, but he says Washington has not shown sufficient engagement. The African Union, the European Union and other international actors could also play a role.
The challenge is that there is no single actor with enough influence over all the parties.
"It will require a certain coalition of efforts," Kurtz says. He argues that preventing a wider war would require a broader diplomatic push, with international actors dividing responsibilities and coordinating their efforts.
The United Nations General Assembly in New York could provide an opportunity for international leaders to engage directly with the Ethiopian government, he says. But diplomacy would also have to address the armed groups involved in the new alliance.
Tronvoll is similarly critical of the international response so far. He argues that the warning signs had been visible for some time but that international efforts to bring the parties back to negotiations remained limited.
The political problem remains
For the people of Tigray, the stakes are particularly high. The region has yet to recover from the consequences of the 2020-2022 war. Many people remain displaced, infrastructure has been severely damaged and the economic recovery remains fragile.
A return to large-scale war would therefore not simply mean a resumption of an old conflict. It could open a new and potentially broader phase of Ethiopia's wider security crisis, particularly given the simultaneous conflicts in Amhara and Oromia.
The immediate priority is to prevent the latest fighting from developing into a wider war. But any sustainable settlement will have to address the political questions that the 2022 agreement left unresolved.
The key question is therefore not simply whether the war has returned.
It is whether Ethiopia and its international partners can still create enough diplomatic space to prevent the latest escalation from closing the door to a political solution.

Suspected Explosives Found Meters From Crashed Drone Near Germany’s Wunstorf Air Base

Suspected Explosives Found Meters From Crashed Drone Near Germany’s Wunstorf Air Base
German investigators are examining suspected explosives found meters from a crashed drone near Wunstorf Air Base in Lower Saxony, as authorities probe a possible link to the August sabotage attempt at Leipzig/Halle Airport.
The findings were reported by Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR in a joint investigation published September 22.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
A farmer discovered the drone, broken into several pieces, near the Wunstorf airfield about a week earlier, the outlets noted.
Officials later found suspicious material only a few meters from the site, which security circles believe be explosive, according to the investigation. Forensic analysis of the substance has not been completed, the outlets added.
The case now involves the federal prosecutor general's office and the Federal Criminal Police Office, the outlets wrote. Investigators are examining whether the Wunstorf drone connects to the Leipzig plot, though no link has been established.
The device was reportedly built similarly to the drones used in the Leipzig attack, with at least one component manufactured using a 3D printer, according to the outlets. Investigators also believe the drone may have been lying near the airfield for a longer period, possibly up to two years, the outlets indicated.
Wunstorf hosts the Bundeswehr's A400M transport fleet and is considered a central hub for supplying German forces worldwide with equipment and personnel, the outlets explained.
Germany has held Russia responsible for the Leipzig incident, in which attackers allegedly sought to destroy Ukrainian cargo aircraft.
Two suspects remain at the center of the case: Oleg L., a Latvian national holding a Russian passport, and Andrei K., a Belarusian-Russian dual citizen.
Officials believe Oleg L. flew into Germany via Berlin before the attack and drove a rental car toward Saxony. He reportedly left the country shortly before the attack occurred, acting as a logistical coordinator, the outlets confirmed.
The outlets reported that Oleg L. has maintained contacts with Russia's GRU military intelligence service for years, particularly with Colonel Denis Smolyaninov.
Western security agencies have linked Smolyaninov to sabotage operations against countries supporting Ukraine and have sanctioned him as a result.
Documents obtained by the London-based Dossier Center, funded by Kremlin critic Mikhail Khodorkovsky and shared with the three outlets, support that assessment, Süddeutsche Zeitung, NDR, and WDR indicated.
Andrei K., the second suspect, was previously flagged for minor offenses in the Baltic states and Finland, the outlets reported. He reportedly entered Germany on an Italian tourist visa, and his DNA was recovered at the Leipzig crime scene.
A spokeswoman for the federal prosecutor general's office pointed to the ongoing investigation and declined to comment further on the case, according to the investigation.
The Wunstorf discovery was also discussed Tuesday during the weekly intelligence briefing at the Chancellery, where the heads of Germany's security agencies meet, the outlets noted.
Smolyaninov and Oleg L. could not be reached for comment last week, the investigation added. Russia's Defense
The Ministry left questions about the allegations unanswered, and Moscow has denied involvement in the Leipzig sabotage attempt. No connection between the Wunstorf find and the Leipzig case has been confirmed, and both investigations remain ongoing.
This was not the first time a separate drone discovery prompted investigators to examine a possible link to the Leipzig case.
In mid-August, a drone forced repeated runway and airspace closures at Hanover-Langenhagen Airport, and police opened a parallel inquiry into a possible connection to the Leipzig plot. No direct link was confirmed, but investigators noted the device had evaded the airport's detection systems entirely, fueling concern about a broader pattern of interference with German aviation infrastructure.

Iran said Wednesday that it conveyed its conditions for reviving diplomacy with the US during a two-hour exchange of messages and clarifications mediated by Qatar on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei wrote on US social media platform X that the exchange took place Tuesday “as a continuation of the discussions” mediated by countries between Tehran and Washington.
“Another round of message exchange and clarification took place through Qatari mediation between Iran and America,” he added.
He said Iran used the process to communicate its positions and conditions for reviving diplomacy “in a manner that leaves no doubt or ambiguity and provides no excuses or pretexts for any party.”
Baqaei said Tehran’s conditions include an end to US “aggressive actions,” including the naval blockade and “economic terrorism,” as well as ending the war on all fronts and releasing Iranian assets that are frozen or restricted.

The comments came after US President Donald Trump said Tuesday that US officials had held talks in New York with representatives of the Iranian delegation for about three hours. He described the talks as having gone “very well.”
Iranian state television also reported that Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Trump’s special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and that the meeting took place “at the repeated request of US officials.”
After agreeing to a Pakistan-mediated ceasefire in April, the US and Iran signed the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding in June, which gave the two sides 60 days to discuss a long-term agreement.
But the two sides soon engaged in retaliatory attacks, and the US reimposed a military blockade of Iranian ports, while Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz.

£84 million to boost Plymouth's defence growth plans
Hundreds of new jobs will be created in Plymouth as Defence Minister Lord Vernon Coaker today confirmed the release of £50 million Government funding through the Defence Growth Deal, unlocking a potential further £34 million from industry and local partners.
- £84 million package, backed by £50 million from government and up to an additional £34 million from industry and local partners, will make Plymouth a national leader in defence maritime autonomy.
- Investment will create nearly 1,000 jobs and support 500 people into work, with a new National Centre for Marine Autonomy.
- Over 400 UK businesses will benefit, alongside new skills and training opportunities for thousands of young people in Plymouth.
Lord Coaker was in Market Hall in Plymouth today where he approved Team Plymouth’s strategic business case and announced the delivery of a major package of investment that will strengthen national security, support local businesses and help drive the city’s reindustrialisation.
The investment confirms delivery of Plymouth’s National Centre for Marine Autonomy, expected to create 120 jobs and attract more than 30 businesses, including start-ups and scale-ups developing advanced maritime technologies.
Alongside the investment in business and innovation, the newly confirmed £1.5 million ‘Get Plymouth Working’ scheme will help 500 people into jobs in defence, advanced manufacturing, engineering and construction, with a focus on veterans and young people aged 18 to 25. Around 750 people will gain new technical skills and qualifications, while more than 7,000 young people will benefit from STEM training.
More than 400 UK businesses are expected to benefit from the wider programme, including support for firms working in robotics, artificial intelligence and autonomous systems.
Defence Minister Lord Vernon Coaker said:
  The £84 million investment will establish Plymouth as a national leader in defence maritime autonomy, creating high-skilled jobs, backing businesses and providing new training opportunities for thousands of local people.
By bringing together Government, industry and local partners, we are creating nearly 1,000 jobs, developing the skills our Armed Forces and defence industry need, and establishing Plymouth as a leading centre for marine autonomy. This is investment that strengthens our national security while backing British jobs, businesses and communities.
Sir Chris Gardner, SRO, Team Plymouth:
  Today marks a major milestone for Team Plymouth and the partners who have worked together with a shared ambition to unlock this city and wider region’s potential.
The release of the Defence Growth Deal funding will help further establish Plymouth as the UK’s National Centre for Marine Autonomy, creating jobs, supporting businesses and investing in the skills needed for the future.
Neal Misell, Babcock CEO, Nuclear, said:
  The Plymouth Defence Growth Deal demonstrates what can be achieved when government, industry, education and local partners come together around a shared ambition. As one of the region’s largest employers and a founding member of Team Plymouth, Babcock is proud to be at the heart of this partnership. 
 
We are connecting people directly to the needs of industry, and that connection is critical to turning Plymouth’s defence strengths into lasting capability, skills, jobs and economic growth for the region.
Plymouth and the South West are already at the heart of UK defence. The MOD spent more than £6.6 billion in the South West in 2024/25, directly supporting 37,300 industry jobs with almost £400 million going to SMEs.
In addition, £7 billion is already being invested in HMNB Devonport as part of the largest naval infrastructure programme since the end of the Cold War.
This latest investment will also support regeneration of the Turnchapel waterfront and the development of new industrial and commercial space across the city, helping growing businesses expand and creating the conditions for long-term economic growth.
Lord Coaker visited HMNB Devonport, City College Plymouth and Babcock International during the visit, meeting local leaders, educators, businesses and students to see how defence investment is already supporting jobs, skills and growth across the city.

McDonald's CEO expects high inflation, flat traffic are not going away for restaurant industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:08:30 UTC
01:08:30 KST

McDonald's is predicting that flat traffic and higher inflation will continue to weigh on the restaurant industry, CEO Chris Kempczinski said Wednesday.
"One of the things I've talked to our team about is we need to stop talking about that being a difficult environment, and just say that is the environment," Kempczinski said on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street." "Because I think, as we look out forward, we're not expecting things to change."
For years, Kempczinski has been warning investors and analysts about the "challenging environment" faced by McDonald's and the broader industry. The burger chain reported U.S. same-store sales growth of just 0.8% in its most recent quarter as traffic to its domestic restaurants fell.
Diners have been eating out less frequently, pushing back against higher menu prices as they face increased costs on everything from gas to groceries. From August 2025 to July 2026, industry operators surveyed by the National Restaurant Association reported a net decline in customer traffic in every month but one.
To attract customers, McDonald's and its rivals have leaned into discounts. But diners aren't the only ones facing higher costs.
Restaurant operators — like McDonald's and its franchisees — have seen beef prices soar. Kempczinski said that beef costs have nearly doubled over the last five years in the company's biggest markets. Other expenses, like labor and construction, have also ticked higher, putting more pressure on margins.
"Across the board, we're seeing that inflation is sticky," Kempczinski said. "It's sticky, not just in the U.S., but around the world."
Faced with tougher operating conditions, McDonald's is focusing on stealing diners from its rivals.
"The biggest thing that you need to do in an environment like this is you have to be able to earn share," Kempczinski said. "You have to be able to actually grab growth from your competitors."
While he said McDonald's will likely have to consider price increases, he added the chain will have to be careful not to drive diners away. He reiterated that the company believes it erred by raising prices too quickly in the years after the Covid pandemic.
Kempczinski and other McDonald's executives will share more details about the company's plans to gain market share during its investor day on Wednesday.

Language Lab Turns 10 and Launches ‘Ukraine Connected,’ a Community for Internationals in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:07:00 UTC
01:07:00 KST

For a decade, Kyiv’s Language Lab has taught Ukrainian to foreigners, including online, and along the way become an informal support network for its students, helping with everything from everyday problems to calling an ambulance. Now, marking its tenth anniversary, the school is formalizing that role with Ukraine Connected, a curated community with coordinators, meetups and regular events that aims to become the biggest network for internationals in Ukraine.
For founder Ksenia Golubytska, reaching 10 years is about more than longevity.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“First and foremost, it’s about trust – the trust of my team, my clients, my close ones who supported me along the way, and myself,” she said.
She said the milestone also reflects a deeper shift in how people see the Ukrainian language: “More and more people are finding real importance and value in learning Ukrainian, and being part of that is something I cherish deeply.”
The road was not easy.
“We got through COVID, through the full-scale invasion and ongoing war, and everything that came with it – so reaching 10 years feels earned,” Golubytska said.
Finding its identity
Language Lab did not start out as a Ukrainian-language school. In its early years, Golubytska said, the team experimented with “different languages, different approaches, different formats.”
The school found its clear identity around the time of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, when it settled on Ukrainian and on a format that worked for its clients.
‘This Is My Personal Contribution to Ukraine's Victory’
“That gave us solid ground, a real foundation to build on,” she said.
Over the years, the school has had more than 1,500 clients and more than 200 organized events. Its client list includes major international humanitarian and aid organizations, as well as embassies and diplomatic staff, international and Ukrainian companies, and media outlets such as Kyiv Post, with which it has a partnership.
Golubytska said the school plans to widen its reach further. One goal is to serve Ukrainians in the diaspora who want to reconnect with the language, alongside new courses and formats for different kinds of learners.
More than a language school
Over the years, Language Lab’s role for many foreign students has gone well beyond grammar lessons.
“We’ve become something like an entry point for them into Ukraine,” Golubytska said. That has meant “supporting them, answering questions, helping with everyday problems, even things like calling an ambulance when needed.”
The school has also hosted cultural events and social meetups for its students. Ukraine Connected, Golubytska said, is designed to take that to the next level.
“It’s structured as a social initiative, and to us it feels like a natural, logical continuation of everything the school has been doing all along,” she said.
How Ukraine Connected will work
Members will be able to register and join organized chats around different topics. But Golubytska stressed that the chats are a means, not the goal.
“The main focus isn’t the chat itself – it’s real connection: people meeting in real life or online and doing things together,” she said.
Coordinators will curate who joins and help organize the community’s activities. Members will share recommendations, help each other with urgent questions, and suggest ideas for small meetups and activities. The whole community will gather for larger events at least once every six months.
The initiative is aimed at people who live or work in Ukraine, want to understand Ukrainian culture better, are looking for Ukrainian business partners, are interested in investment opportunities, or want to support and promote Ukraine abroad. Its stated mission is to help foreigners lead a comfortable and fulfilling life in the country.
The ambition is large.
“Our ambition is to build the biggest community for internationals in Ukraine,” Golubytska said.
A bet on Ukraine’s future
For Golubytska, the anniversary is ultimately about looking ahead.
“It’s about hope – hope that this will keep developing, that more people will visit, invest, and move to Ukraine, and that Ukraine will be in the spotlight in the way it deserves,” she said.
“More than anything,” she added, “we want Ukraine Connected to be an entry point – a place that helps people feel at home in Ukraine, genuinely welcomed and part of something, not just passing through.”

EU court strikes down sanctions extension against former Russian senator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:06:51 UTC
01:06:51 KST

EU court strikes down sanctions extension against former Russian senator
The EU has failed to provide sufficient evidence to keep a former Russian official on its sanctions blacklist, the bloc’s General Court ruled on Wednesday. The decision came a day after the EU removed two Russian businessmen from the list as part of a deal to extend restrictions on thousands of others.
The court annulled the September 2024 and September 2025 extensions of sanctions against former Russian Senator Oleg Tkach, who represented Kaliningrad Region in the Federation Council from 2004 to 2022. He was also involved in publishing, founding and chairing Olma Media Group.
The EU first sanctioned Tkach in March 2022 over his vote to ratify treaties with the Donetsk and Lugansk People’s Republics, which later became part of Russia following referendums rejected by Ukraine and most Western countries. The case centered on whether the EU Council had grounds to keep extending the restrictions after Tkach left office.
According to Wednesday’s ruling, the Council failed to demonstrate that Tkach retained close ties to Russian authorities. The court also found that his failure to publicly oppose Russia’s military operation in Ukraine did not, by itself, constitute continued support for the authorities.
Brussels had also cited Tkach’s publishing background, including his links to Olma Media Group and textbook publisher Prosveshcheniye. However, the court found the evidence insufficient to establish his current role or influence at the companies.
The ruling does not affect the EU’s most recent sanctions extension from March 2026, which Tkach is challenging separately. He argues that condemnation based on his former Senate position is outdated and that the Council’s evidence is unreliable and lacks a “sound factual basis.” He has also argued that the measures are disproportionate.
A day before Wednesday’s ruling, the EU agreed to remove Russian businessmen Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from its sanctions list. Both had previously mounted legal challenges related to EU restrictions, while Fridman has also filed a multibillion-dollar arbitration claim against Luxembourg.
Their removal came as part of a compromise to renew sanctions against around 3,000 other individuals and entities for three years, until September 2029, replacing the bloc’s usual six-month renewal cycle.

Race to evacuate war-damaged Gaza buildings after deadly apartment block collapse
GAZA/CAIRO, Sept 23 - Officials in Gaza say plans to evacuate people from war-damaged buildings after the deadly collapse of an apartment block last week face major challenges, including a lack of demolition equipment and limited land to relocate residents.
Nearly a year since a ceasefire ended major fighting between Israel and Hamas, officials say tens of thousands of people, with few options for shelter, are living in buildings damaged during Israel's military campaign, despite repeated warnings that they should leave.
In the early hours of September 16, the danger became clear when the Al-Saada building in Gaza City's Al-Rimal neighbourhood collapsed, killing 21 people. At least 45 survivors were rescued from the rubble.
Gaza officials say more than 2,000 buildings have been classified as being at risk. Other war-damaged buildings have previously collapsed, causing casualties, including amid winter storms.
"These buildings now represent ticking time bombs for residents and displaced people in many places," said Husni Muhanna, spokesperson for the Gaza City municipality, adding that this presented a "real danger" with the weather set to deteriorate into the winter.
On Sunday, Gaza authorities announced an emergency plan to evacuate people from 255 buildings most at risk of collapse and demolish them.
An Egyptian-led relief body had offered to provide transport to move those evacuated to designated shelters, said Ismail Al-Thawabta, head of the Hamas-run Gaza government's media office.
But he said the plan faced major obstacles, "including some families refusing to evacuate unsafe buildings despite the warnings, severe funding shortages, a lack of heavy equipment needed for safe demolition, and limited safe land available to relocate displaced people."
SHORTAGE OF EQUIPMENT
Large-scale reconstruction in Gaza has yet to begin, with US-brokered efforts to get Hamas to disarm and Israeli forces to withdraw largely stalled. A population of more than 2 million lives confined to about a third of the enclave, mainly housed in makeshift tents or overcrowded rooms in damaged buildings. Deadly Israeli airstrikes, which Israel says target militants, have continued.
Most of Gaza's buildings were destroyed by airstrikes or bulldozed by Israeli forces, and almost all others have suffered damage.
Palestinian and UN officials blame Israel's restrictions on Gaza for the lack of heavy machinery to clear rubble and materials and equipment to rebuild homes.
In response to a request for comment, Israel's military said it was committed to minimising harm to civilians and that any activities, including against "terrorist infrastructure", were carried out based on operational necessity.
COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, said entry of heavy equipment and reconstruction materials would not be authorised until Hamas disarmed. It said Hamas exploited humanitarian aid, something the Palestinian militant group denies.
Alessandro Mrakic, head of the United Nations Development Programme office in Gaza, said a shortage of equipment meant people had to dig through the rubble with their hands when the Al-Saada building collapsed, and that oil and spare parts were needed to keep the machinery already in Gaza in service.
He estimated the number of buildings at risk of collapse at 400. "We know that these buildings will collapse, especially now with the upcoming winter," he said. "We are running against time."
RESIDENTS SAY THEY HAVE NOWHERE ELSE TO GO
The Al-Saada building was in an area that was hit by Israeli bombardment two days after a Hamas-led attack on Israel on October 7, 2023, triggered Israel's offensive in Gaza. Israel launched heavy airstrikes followed by a ground campaign which it said were aimed at destroying Hamas and its underground network of tunnels.
Mohammad Arafa, head of the Gaza Engineers Association, said that based on assessments by fellow engineers who inspected the Al-Saada building over the past year, its collapse resulted from structural weakness after bombardment damaged several concrete pillars supporting its foundations.
But people had sheltered there because they had nowhere else to go, said Feryal Abu Ghanem, whose daughter-in-law was staying with her family when the building collapsed and was among those killed.
Bassam Naseer, a displaced man living in another damaged building nearby, said he feared the same thing would happen there. "No one is looking after us. The conditions are very difficult," he said.
After the Al-Saada's collapse, the Israel Defense Forces said in a social media post that it had not struck the building during the war. It did not respond to questions about residents saying it had struck the building, or about whether the building had been damaged by strikes on the surrounding area.
Eyad Azzam, who lost his pregnant wife and a 3-year-old son in the Al-Saada building's collapse, showed a video on his mobile phone of another son, Abdel-Rahman, trapped in the wreckage of the building before he was pulled to safety.
Abdel-Rahman, 7, had reached towards his mother, hoping to protect her from fallen rock, his father said. "He put out his hand and it wasn't a rock that had fallen, it was the entire ceiling."
People continued to live under damaged ceilings or columns for lack of other options, Azzam said.
"Today people say, 'This is a dangerous place to live in.' But where shall I go?" he said. "Even in the street there's no place." REUTERS

President De La Espriella orders militarization of Colombian resort city amid gang retaliation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-09-23
16:05:43 UTC
01:05:43 KST

Laura Gamba Fadul
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
Colombian President Abelardo De La Espriella ordered the immediate militarization of Santa Marta on Tuesday night, deploying troops and launching low-altitude air patrols to regain control of the Caribbean port city following a violent offensive by a powerful narco-paramilitary cartel.
The security crisis erupted after the military killed a senior leader of the Autodefensas Conquistadoras de la Sierra Nevada (ACSN) along with six associates during an operation in the region. In retaliation, the armed group declared an "armed strike," threatening merchants and drivers to enforce a commercial lockout and transport shutdown across Santa Marta and neighboring Cienaga, local media reported.
The intimidation campaign paralyzed the coastal city of almost 600,000 residents, a major domestic and international tourism hub renowned for its beaches and proximity to Tayrona National Natural Park. Local business representatives estimated that around 95% of commercial establishments remained closed Wednesday morning, while public transit services suspended operations and schools closed.
Throughout Tuesday and into Wednesday, armed men on motorcycles set fire to trucks and buses, engaged in sporadic shootouts with security forces, and forced shopkeepers to pull down their shutters.
President De La Espriella traveled to Santa Marta late Tuesday night, posting video footage on social media showing him walking through heavily guarded streets to reassure residents.
"Those who do not submit will be taken down, and I will not allow them to continue bringing our people to their knees through terror," De La Espriella declared, confirming that three suspects had been arrested in connection with the arson attacks and threats.
In office since August, De La Espriella has pursued a militarized strategy against illegal armed groups, backed by enhanced security cooperation with the US. He emphasized that organizations such as the ACSN, Los Pachenca, and the Gulf Clan would face the full force of state power.
"We are going after all those bandits without mercy," the president said.
The ACSN traces its origins to legacy far-right paramilitary groups that originally formed to fight leftist guerrilla forces in the 1990s and 2000s. Today, the heavily armed criminal network finances its operations through international cocaine trafficking, illegal mining, and systematic extortion.

'Too small for the future' defense establishment demands expansion of Israel Navy, as sixth submarine arrives from Germany
There is growing concerne from security officials because despite the arrival of the INS Drakon from Germany, Israel has only 6 submarines, while Turkey has 12 and Greece has 9
With the arrival of the INS Drakon submarine in Israel on Wednesday, the defense establishment is calling for the expansion of the Navy, as currently it is "too small for the challenges of the future."
Israel is currently monitoring the military buildup of various countries in the Middle East with developing naval fleets, such as Turkey and Egypt.
Turkey realized more than a decade ago the potential of the navy. The commander of the Turkish Navy coined the phrase "the Blue Homeland." A doctrine where they see the sea as a sovereign extension of Turkey, including the annexation of its economic waters.
According to an Israeli official, this represents significant potential to increase Turkey’s power projection and strength in the long term. Israeli assessments are that in the future Turkey will have 18 submarines (currently 12 and another 6 are planned), including an independent capability to produce submarines.
At the same time, the Syrian navy is beginning to re-arm with the help of the Turks, which places Israel at a crossroads. According to security sources, there is sufficient time to build up if the proper process is started in the near future. They recommend the acquisition of two additional submarines, semi-autonomous vessels, light Reshef-class corvettes and other means for naval warfare, preparation for combat on the open sea, and more.
The new submarine brings with it new capabilities and it is the largest ever to arrive in Israel. It took nearly 14 years to build the sophisticated vessel, and under the shadow of the war, its arrival in the country was even delayed by several months following Ireland and Norway's refusal to allow training in their maritime territory. It will take another two to three months for INS Drakon to become operational, after the installation of Israeli systems.
A senior official in the security establishment said that the blockage of Bab al-Mandeb should greatly worry Israel, among other reasons because it exposes the Mediterranean Sea to future risks and leads countries and organizations to impose a blockade on the State of Israel. In his definition, the closure of a strait is “asymmetric warfare” due to the circumstances. When the Houthis launch missiles from deep within Yemen toward a very narrow stronghold—it is almost impossible to effectively target them.

- Pentagon quietly extends troop deployments as Iran war drags toward 2027 - report | i24NEWS
- Military training in Tel Aviv and undisclosed agreements, what is happening between Israel and Somaliland? | i24NEWS, Henry Kirshner
- 'Effective immediately:' Secretary of US Navy Phelan abruptly departs position amid ongoing Iran blockade | i24NEWS
INS Drakon: From Germany to Israel
After a journey of about 4,000 nautical miles from Germany, the INS Drakon, arrived in Israel on Wednesday. Upon its arrival, the submarine joins the new generation of submarines built in Germany as part of the security cooperation between the two countries.
INS Drakon is equipped with an Air Independent Propulsion (AIP) system, which enables the submarine to generate energy and recharge its batteries even during prolonged stays underwater, without the need to surface or use external air. The system uses oxygen and hydrogen to produce energy, thereby allowing for an extended duration of covert underwater operations and maintaining operational capabilities over time. This is the third AIP submarine in the Israeli Navy.
The submarine is over 70 meters (230 feet) long and is about 30% larger than the Dolphin-class submarines. Despite its size, less than one-fifth of its volume is visible above the water.
Its arrival marks the completion of the second generation of Navy submarines built in Germany, and signifies another milestone in the longstanding security cooperation between Israel and Germany.
The voyage from Germany to Israel took about a month, along a route of approximately 4,000 nautical miles, which is about 8,000 kilometers. The journey included sailing in the Atlantic Ocean, passing through the Strait of Gibraltar, and continuing through the Mediterranean Sea to Israel.
The construction of the submarine lasted more than 12 years, and after its completion, months of tests and preparations were carried out ahead of its arrival in Israel.
Throughout the project, there was close cooperation between the Israeli Navy, the German Navy, the German Ministry of Defense, and the professional parties involved in the construction of the submarine.
Israeli involvement in the project has been ongoing for about 20 years, through an Israeli project management team operating in Germany, which oversees the planning, construction, and testing processes. The management team is staffed by officers and engineers from the Navy, who come to Germany together with their families for periods of several years. At a later stage, crews from the submarine flotilla also join the project, participating in sailings and evaluations prior to the delivery of the submarines and their integration into the Navy.
Alongside technology, the Submarine Flotilla emphasizes the importance of human capital: submarine crews are required to maintain high levels of professionalism, responsibility, composure, and operational sharpness. The submariners operate complex combat systems and work for extended periods deep at sea and in remote theaters, under conditions of secrecy and isolation from the outside world. Israeli involvement in Germany continues to this day, with an eye toward the next-generation project—the Dakar submarines, which are currently under construction and represent the next generation of the Navy's submarines.

Quran burning, mosque incident stir migration debate in Lithuania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Necva Taştan Sevinç
23 September 2026•Update: 23 September 2026
The burning of a Quran in Vilnius and an incident outside a historic Tatar mosque in Kaunas have intensified debate over immigration and religious tensions in Lithuania, public broadcaster LRT reported Wednesday.
A video showing a Quran being burned in central Vilnius circulated over the weekend, though police said the incident took place on Sept. 13. In Kaunas, bikers brought a pig’s head outside the mosque, shouted and sang during prayers, and allegedly threatened members of the Muslim community.
Mufti Aleksandras Beganskas said he had heard of threats to burn the mosque and harm him and his family.
The incidents have drawn differing political responses. Lawmaker Tomas Tomilinas accused unnamed figures of inciting discord, while opposition Homeland Union leader Laurynas Kasciunas called for a significant reduction in the annual quota for foreign workers.
Kasciunas proposed lowering the quota from nearly 25,000 this year to about 10,000, with exemptions for highly skilled workers. He also suggested recruiting from countries he considers culturally closer to Lithuania.
Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said the quota system was not working and that he was preparing a new migration policy model. Social Security Minister Inga Ruginiene, however, said the current system was strict and functioned effectively.
The quota for this year was exhausted in early September. Business representatives have warned that Lithuania needs a clearer long-term migration policy.
Lithuanian Tatars, also known as Lipka Tatars, have lived in the region since the late 14th century. The Kaunas Mosque, built by the Tatar community in the period between the two world wars, reflects that centuries-old Muslim presence.

MOSCOW, September 23. /TASS/. Russia’s exports of agricultural products to Malaysia climbed five-fold in volume terms and 5.5-fold in value terms to around 8,800 tons worth over $9 mln in January-August 2026, the Agroexport federal center reported.

In 2025, Russia exported 3,100 tons of products worth $3.1 mln to Malaysia, according to the report.
